category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
statement: Which of the following clinical features most strongly distinguishes the typical patient with Type 2 diabetes from one with Type 1 diabetes?
options: The association with obesity and a lack of islet autoantibodies
The occurrence of polydipsia and polyuria
A childhood or adolescent age of onset
The requirement for insulin to prevent ketoacidosis
The presence of chronic complications like retinopathy
correctOption: The association with obesity and a lack of islet autoantibodies
optionExplanations: Obesity is present in the vast majority of T2D patients and absent in T1D; similarly, T1D is defined by autoantibodies (anti-GAD, anti-insulin) which are absent in T2D.
Polydipsia and polyuria are the classic symptoms of hyperglycemia common to all forms of untreated diabetes.
While T1D usually starts in youth, T2D is increasingly diagnosed in adolescents; therefore, age of onset is becoming a less reliable differentiator than metabolic phenotype.
The absolute requirement for insulin to prevent life-threatening DKA is a hallmark of Type 1, whereas Type 2 patients are more prone to HHS.
Both types of diabetes lead to similar chronic microvascular and macrovascular complications over time.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1101 (Book Page): More than 80% of individuals with T2D are obese... unlike T1D, there is no evidence of an autoimmune basis.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: Which genetic alteration is found in more than half of cases of ACTH-secreting pituitary adenomas and involves the regulation of the epidermal growth factor receptor?
options: Loss-of-function mutations in the CDKN1B gene
Activating mutations in ubiquitin-specific protease 8 (USP8)
Inactivating mutations in the GNAS gene
Somatic activating mutations in the HRAS gene
Germline mutations in the MEN1 gene
correctOption: Activating mutations in ubiquitin-specific protease 8 (USP8)
optionExplanations: CDKN1B mutations are associated with an 'MEN-1-like' syndrome but are a very rare cause of corticotroph tumors overall.
USP8 mutations prevent the degradation of EGFR, enhancing signaling pathways that promote the growth and hormone production of corticotroph cells.
GNAS mutations are primarily associated with somatotroph adenomas (causing acromegaly) and are rare in corticotroph adenomas.
HRAS mutations are specifically associated with rare pituitary carcinomas, not the standard corticotroph adenomas that cause Cushing disease.
While MEN1 germline mutations can predispose to corticotroph adenomas, they are less common than somatic USP8 mutations in sporadic cases.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1066 (Book Page): Activating mutations of ubiquitin-specific protease 8 (USP8) also occur in 30% to 60% of corticotroph adenomas.

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
coreConcept: Morphological features of the preeclamptic placenta
statement: A 24-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks gestation presents with persistent headaches and upper abdominal pain. Vitals show a BP of 170/110 mmHg. Labs confirm proteinuria and elevated creatinine. Histological examination of the placenta would most likely reveal which of the following findings?
options: Complete absence of syncytiotrophoblasts and replacement by maternal decidual cells
Diffuse infiltration of the chorionic villi by malignant cytotrophoblasts and syncytiotrophoblasts
Placental infarcts that are more numerous and larger than those in normal term pregnancies
A unilocular cyst containing hair, sebaceous material, and tooth structures
Presence of huge, distended follicles filled with PAS-positive thyroglobulin
correctOption: Placental infarcts that are more numerous and larger than those in normal term pregnancies
optionExplanations: Syncytiotrophoblasts are essential for the maternal-fetal interface and are preserved, though they may show exaggerated ischemic changes like syncytial knots.
Malignant proliferation of cytotrophoblasts and syncytiotrophoblasts without villi is characteristic of choriocarcinoma, not preeclampsia.
In preeclampsia, placental malperfusion and ischemia lead to the formation of multiple and large infarcts, which compromise fetal nutrient exchange.
The description of a unilocular cyst with hair and teeth is indicative of a mature cystic teratoma, which is an ovarian germ cell tumor.
Large follicles filled with thyroglobulin are a feature of the thyroid gland, not the placenta, typically seen in goitrous conditions.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1030 (Book Page): These include (1) infarcts, which are larger and more numerous than those that may be seen in normal full-term placentas

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
statement: In the context of primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency, the metabolic effects of glucocorticoid deficiency most directly lead to which of the following?
options: Impaired gluconeogenesis and occasional hypoglycemia
Elevated cardiac contractility and increased caloric expenditure
Accumulation of glycosaminoglycans in the subcutaneous tissue
Persistent hypertension and left ventricular hypertrophy
Enhanced osteoclastic activity leading to osteoporosis
correctOption: Impaired gluconeogenesis and occasional hypoglycemia
optionExplanations: Cortisol is a counter-regulatory hormone that promotes gluconeogenesis; its absence can cause blood sugar to drop, especially during stress.
These features describe hyperthyroidism (thyrotoxicosis), whereas Addison disease involves fatigue and a 'feebleness' of the heart's action.
This refers to the non-pitting edema (myxedema) seen in hypothyroidism, not adrenal failure.
Hypertension is a feature of Cushing syndrome or hyperaldosteronism; Addison disease involves hypotension.
Excess glucocorticoids (Cushing) stimulate bone resorption; deficiency does not cause osteoporosis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1122 (Book Page): Hypoglycemia may occasionally occur as a result of glucocorticoid deficiency and impaired gluconeogenesis.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
coreConcept: Morphometric dimensions of parathyroid chief cells
statement: Histologically, the normal parathyroid chief cells are defined by a specific diameter range. What is the typical size of these polygonal cells?
options: 25 to 35 μm
40 to 50 μm
5 to 10 μm
12 to 20 μm
50 to 60 μm
correctOption: 12 to 20 μm
optionExplanations: 25 to 35 μm would be unusually large for chief cells, approaching the size of large oxyphil variants.
40 to 50 μm exceeds the dimensions of standard parathyroid parenchymal cells.
5 to 10 μm is smaller than the typical range for chief cells.
Chief cells are polygonal and measure 12 to 20 micrometers, containing uniform nuclei and pinkish cytoplasm.
60 μm is much larger than any normal cell type found within the parathyroid gland.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1091 (Book Page): [Chief cells... are polygonal, 12 to 20 μm in diameter, and have central, round, uniform nuclei and light to dark pink cytoplasm.]

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
statement: In postpubertal males, which viral infection is most frequently associated with the sudden onset of acute interstitial orchitis and a risk of subsequent sterility?
options: Adenovirus
Cytomegalovirus
Human Papillomavirus
Mumps
Epstein-Barr Virus
correctOption: Mumps
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Adenovirus can cause autoimmune-like prostatitis but is not the classic cause of post-pubertal viral orchitis.
Incorrect. CMV is not the primary cause of parotitis-associated orchitis described in the text.
Incorrect. HPV is associated with condyloma acuminatum and penile cancer, not with acute interstitial orchitis.
Correct. Mumps is a systemic viral disease; while parotitis is classic, it causes orchitis in 20-30% of postpubertal males, which can lead to testicular damage and sterility.
Incorrect. EBV is associated with certain lymphomas, including testicular lymphoma in rare cases, but not with classic post-parotitis orchitis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 968 (Book Page): In postpubertal males, however, orchitis occurs in 20% to 30% of cases. Most often, acute interstitial orchitis develops 1 week after the onset of swelling of the parotid glands.

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
statement: A pathologist examining a placenta from a pregnancy complicated by severe eclampsia identifies 'acute atherosis' in the decidual vessels. Which histological feature is most likely present in these vessels?
options: Extensive stromal infiltration by immature neuroepithelium
Malignant trophoblastic proliferation with absence of villi
Concentrically calcified psammoma bodies within the vascular lumen
Fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel wall and subendothelial macrophages
Hyperplastic nodules of vacuolated lipid-rich cells
correctOption: Fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel wall and subendothelial macrophages
optionExplanations: Immature neuroepithelium is the defining feature of an immature teratoma of the ovary, not a placental finding.
Malignant trophoblastic proliferation without villi describes choriocarcinoma, not the vascular changes of eclampsia.
Psammoma bodies are characteristic of papillary thyroid or serous ovarian carcinomas, but not the vascular pathology of preeclampsia.
Acute atherosis is a characteristic vascular lesion in the decidua of eclamptic patients, consisting of fibrinoid necrosis and lipid-laden macrophages.
Lipid-rich hyperplastic nodules are features of the adrenal gland in Cushing syndrome, not placental vessels.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1031 (Book Page): [Figure 22.51] Acute atherosis of uterine vessels in eclampsia. Note fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel wall and subendothelial macrophages.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
statement: A patient with meningococcemia experiences a rapid onset of hypotension, shock, and widespread purpura. Which pathological finding in the adrenal glands is most likely present?
options: Bilateral cortical atrophy with a normal zona glomerulosa.
Conversion of the adrenals to sacs of clotted blood.
Gradual replacement of cortex by small lymphocytes.
Large areas of caseous necrosis with multinucleate giant cells.
Yellow-brown nodular expansion of the zona fasciculata.
correctOption: Conversion of the adrenals to sacs of clotted blood.
optionExplanations: Cortical atrophy with a spared zona glomerulosa is the classic result of exogenous steroid administration causing secondary suppression.
The Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome involves massive, often bilateral, adrenal hemorrhage, typically triggered by Neisseria meningitidis septicemia.
Lymphocytic replacement is characteristic of autoimmune adrenalitis, which is a chronic process, not an acute hemorrhagic one.
Caseous necrosis with giant cells describes tuberculous adrenalitis, which presents as chronic, not acute, adrenal failure.
Nodular expansion describes adrenal hyperplasia or adenoma, associated with hyperfunction rather than acute hemorrhagic destruction.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1121 (Book Page): Whatever the basis, the adrenals are converted to sacs of clotted blood, which obscures virtually all of the underlying detail.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
statement: What is the primary pathological mechanism that accounts for the 'hemorrhagic' nature of the infarction typically observed in testicular torsion?
options: A primary inflammatory response mediated by neutrophils
The continued delivery of blood through patent arteries into an engorged gland
Fibrinoid necrosis of the spermatic cord vessels
The presence of a dual blood supply from the scrotal arteries
The sudden rupture of the tunica albuginea under high pressure
correctOption: The continued delivery of blood through patent arteries into an engorged gland
optionExplanations: Inflammation is a secondary response to tissue death; it does not cause the initial hemorrhagic state.

Because venous outflow is blocked but arterial inflow remains initially patent, the testis becomes massively engorged with blood. When infarction eventually occurs, the tissue is already saturated with extravasated blood.
Fibrinoid necrosis is characteristic of certain autoimmune or hypertensive states, not the mechanical twisting seen in torsion.
The testis does not have a functional dual blood supply that prevents infarction; the hemorrhagic nature is due to the sequence of venous-then-arterial compromise.
The tunica albuginea remains intact; the hemorrhagic appearance is due to vascular congestion within the parenchyma.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 968 (Book Page): The thick-walled arteries remain patent, producing intense vascular engorgement followed by hemorrhagic infarction.

category: Define thyroiditis
statement: Subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis is characterized as which of the following in relation to other thyroid disorders?
options: An IgG4-mediated fibrosing disorder of the neck
A result of dietary iodine deficiency in mountainous regions
A painful, viral-induced thyroiditis occurring in the summer
A malignant transformation of a follicular adenoma
A painless autoimmune thyroiditis that may occur postpartum
correctOption: A painless autoimmune thyroiditis that may occur postpartum
optionExplanations: This describes Riedel thyroiditis.
Iodine deficiency causes goiter and hypothyroidism but is not the underlying cause of the autoimmune subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis.
This describes granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis, not subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis.
Subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis is an inflammatory/autoimmune condition, not a neoplasm or a malignancy.
Subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis is defined by its painless nature and autoimmune association, often appearing in the postpartum period.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): Subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis, which is also referred to as painless thyroiditis, is a presumed autoimmune disease. ... A similar disease process can occur during the postpartum period in up to 5% of women (postpartum thyroiditis).

category: Define thyroiditis
statement: A 52-year-old female presents with a painless, symmetrical goiter and clinical apathy. Labs show elevated TSH and low T4. Fine-needle aspiration reveals a dense mononuclear infiltrate with germinal centers and follicular cells with abundant, granular, eosinophilic cytoplasm. What is the identifying feature of the specialized follicular cells observed?
options: They are neuroendocrine cells derived from the parafollicular C-cell line.
They represent malignant transformation into anaplastic carcinoma.
They are H%fcrthle cells, a metaplastic response to chronic injury.
They are clear cells indicative of a parathyroid adenoma.
They are signet-ring cells containing neutral mucopolysaccharides.
correctOption: They are H%fcrthle cells, a metaplastic response to chronic injury.
optionExplanations: C-cells give rise to medullary carcinoma and amyloid, not the lymphocytic goiter seen here.
These cells are benign metaplastic cells; anaplastic cells would show high pleomorphism and mitotic activity.
H%fcrthle (oxyphil) cells are classic findings in Hashimoto's, resulting from stress-induced metaplasia of the cuboidal epithelium.
Parathyroid clear cells are distinct from thyroid follicular cells and are not a feature of thyroiditis.
Signet ring cells are characteristic of certain lobular carcinomas or gastric cancers, not thyroiditis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1077 (Book Page): The thyroid follicles are atrophic and are lined in many areas by epithelial cells with abundant eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm, termed H%fcrthle cells, which represent a metaplastic response of the normally low cuboidal follicular epithelium to chronic injury.

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
statement: A 32-year-old woman is prescribed a broad-spectrum antibiotic for a respiratory infection. Two weeks later, she develops intense vulvovaginal pruritus and a thick vaginal discharge. Which pharmacological mechanism explains this development?
options: Direct cytotoxicity of the antibiotic on vaginal epithelium
Elevation of vaginal pH above 7.0 by the drug
Increase in glycogen vacuoles in squamous cells
Suppression of endogenous lactobacilli
Activation of Th17 T-cell inflammatory pathways
correctOption: Suppression of endogenous lactobacilli
optionExplanations: Antibiotics used for respiratory infections generally lack direct cytotoxic effects on the vaginal squamous epithelium.
While pH rises as lactobacilli disappear, the direct trigger for yeast overgrowth is the removal of microbial competition, and the pH rarely reaches 7.0 from antibiotics alone.
Glycogen vacuoles are increased by estrogen at menarche, providing a substrate for flora; their increase does not directly cause yeast overgrowth.
Antibiotics suppress the normal protective lactobacilli. This loss removes the inhibition of yeast, allowing Candida to proliferate and become symptomatic.
Compromise (not activation) of Th17 function is a risk factor for candidiasis. The antibiotic's primary effect is on the microbial ecosystem, not the T-cells.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 987 (Book Page): Diabetes mellitus, antibiotics, pregnancy, and conditions that compromise neutrophil or Th17 T-cell function increase the risk of symptomatic candidal infection

category: Describe salient morphological features of clinically significant subtypes of thyroiditis: i
coreConcept: Differential diagnosis of Subacute Thyroiditis subtypes
statement: A 40-year-old woman presents with a sudden onset of neck pain and a tender, unilaterally enlarged thyroid gland following a recent viral upper respiratory infection. Microscopy shows aggregates of activated macrophages and multinucleated giant cells associated with collapsed follicles. How does this condition typically differ from subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis?
options: It is associated with a painless, diffuse goiter
It results in permanent hypothyroidism in 90% of cases
It lacks the presence of multinucleated giant cells
It presents with significant thyroid tenderness and pain
It is characterized by extensive Hürthle cell metaplasia
correctOption: It presents with significant thyroid tenderness and pain
optionExplanations: A painless goiter is characteristic of subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis, not granulomatous thyroiditis.
Granulomatous thyroiditis is typically self-limiting and returns to euthyroid state, unlike Hashimoto which often leads to permanent failure.
Giant cells are the histological hallmark of granulomatous thyroiditis; lymphocytic thyroiditis lacks these and shows only lymphocytic infiltration.
The clinical presence of pain and tenderness is the primary clinical discriminator for granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis compared to 'painless' lymphocytic thyroiditis.
Hürthle cell metaplasia is prominent in Hashimoto thyroiditis but is not a feature of granulomatous thyroiditis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): [Granulomatous thyroiditis is the most common cause of thyroid pain. ... multinucleate giant cells enclose pools of colloid, hence the designation granulomatous thyroiditis.]

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: A 28-year-old male presents with weight loss, heat intolerance, and palpitations. His pulse is 115 bpm. Which set of laboratory findings is most characteristic of primary hyperthyroidism in this patient?
options: Low TSH, Low Free T4
Low TSH, High Free T4
Normal TSH, High Free T4
High TSH, Low Free T4
High TSH, High Free T4
correctOption: Low TSH, High Free T4
optionExplanations: Low TSH and low Free T4 are characteristic of secondary (central) hypothyroidism caused by pituitary or hypothalamic failure.
Primary hyperthyroidism is characterized by autonomous production of thyroid hormones by the thyroid gland, which then strongly suppresses TSH production by the pituitary via negative feedback.
A normal TSH with a high Free T4 is physiologically inconsistent in a primary hyperthyroid state due to the intact negative feedback loop.
High TSH with low Free T4 is the classic biochemical signature of primary hypothyroidism, as seen in Hashimoto thyroiditis.
High TSH and high Free T4 suggest secondary (central) hyperthyroidism, such as a TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma, which is very rare.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1074 (Book Page): Laboratory findings that support the diagnosis of hyperthyroidism include a low TSH value accompanied by an increase in free T4.

category: Describe salient morphological features of clinically significant subtypes of thyroiditis: i
statement: A 40-year-old woman presents with a sudden onset of severe neck pain, fever, and malaise following a viral upper respiratory infection. Biopsy during the early active phase would most likely show which inflammatory pattern?
options: Diffuse amyloid stroma staining with Congo red
Clear, 'ground-glass' nuclei with intranuclear pseudo-inclusions
Scattered follicles replaced by neutrophils forming microabscesses
Uniform tall columnar cells with scalloped colloid
Extensive dense fibrosis extending to skeletal muscle
correctOption: Scattered follicles replaced by neutrophils forming microabscesses
optionExplanations: Amyloid stroma is characteristic of medullary carcinoma, a malignancy of the parafollicular C cells, not an acute viral-triggered inflammation.
Orphan Annie eye nuclei and pseudo-inclusions are diagnostic for papillary thyroid carcinoma, not inflammatory thyroiditis.
Granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis begins with an acute phase involving neutrophils and microabscesses before progressing to the characteristic granulomatous inflammation.
Tall columnar cells and scalloped colloid are morphological features of Graves disease, associated with chronic hyperthyroidism rather than acute pain.
Dense fibrosis extending into adjacent structures is characteristic of Riedel thyroiditis, which is typically a chronic, painless condition.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): Early in the active inflammatory phase, scattered follicles may be disrupted and replaced by neutrophils forming microabscesses. Later, more characteristic features appear in the form of aggregates of lymphocytes, activated macrophages, and plasma cells associated with collapsed and damaged thyroid follicles.

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
statement: At what point in gestation does preeclampsia most commonly manifest in a typical pregnancy?
options: After 34 weeks
Only during active labor
Between 8 and 12 weeks
During the first trimester
Within 24 hours of conception
correctOption: After 34 weeks
optionExplanations: The vast majority of cases present in the third trimester, specifically after 34 weeks, although early-onset cases are possible in high-risk individuals.
While it can certainly worsen or first be recognized during labor, its most common clinical onset is during the late third trimester before labor begins.
Symptoms appearing this early would suggest a different diagnosis or possibly a hydatidiform mole, as preeclampsia is a late-gestation syndrome.
Preeclampsia is defined by symptoms occurring after 20 weeks of gestation; first-trimester hypertension is usually classified as chronic/preexisting.
The condition requires the presence of a maturing placenta and the physiological stress of late pregnancy to develop.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1030 (Book Page): Preeclampsia most commonly starts after 34 weeks of gestation but begins earlier in women with hydatidiform mole (discussed later) or preexisting kidney disease.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
statement: How is Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1) distinguished from other forms of chronic autoimmune adrenalitis?
options: It results solely from the production of autoantibodies against 17-hydroxylase in post-menopausal females.
It presents as a combination of adrenalitis and autoimmune thyroiditis without fungal associations.
It involves the destruction of the adrenal medulla alongside the cortex, leading to catecholamine deficiency.
It is characterized by a unique triad involving candidiasis, ectodermal dystrophy, and organ-specific autoimmunity.
It is caused by polymorphisms in the CTLA4 gene and presents primarily in middle-aged women.
correctOption: It is characterized by a unique triad involving candidiasis, ectodermal dystrophy, and organ-specific autoimmunity.
optionExplanations: While antibodies against steroidogenic enzymes are present, APS-1 is defined by a broader genetic defect in the AIRE gene rather than isolated antibody types.
The absence of fungal associations is characteristic of APS-2, not APS-1, which is defined by the presence of chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis.
In autoimmune adrenalitis, the medulla is typically preserved; the destruction is targeted specifically at the steroid-producing cells of the cortex.
APS-1 is a distinct clinical entity caused by AIRE mutations, leading to a failure of central tolerance and presenting with candidiasis, dental/nail abnormalities, and adrenal failure.
Polymorphisms in CTLA4 are associated with APS-2 and general autoimmune susceptibility, whereas APS-1 is specifically linked to AIRE gene mutations.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1121 (Book Page): APS-1, also known as autoimmune polyendocrinopathy, candidiasis, and ectodermal dystrophy, is characterized by chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis and abnormalities of skin, dental enamel, and nails (ectodermal dystrophy) in association with a combination of organ-specific autoimmune disorders.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: Pathological examination of the adrenal glands in a patient with ACTH-dependent Cushing disease typically reveals which of the following?
options: Bilateral cortical atrophy
Thinning of the zona glomerulosa with normal fasciculata
Bilateral diffuse thickening of the cortex
A solitary, yellow, 2-cm encapsulated mass
Massive hemorrhage replacing the glands
correctOption: Bilateral diffuse thickening of the cortex
optionExplanations: Bilateral atrophy is characteristic of exogenous steroid use, where ACTH is suppressed.
In Cushing, the zona fasciculata and reticularis are the expanded layers; the glomerulosa is usually unaffected as it is less dependent on ACTH.
In ACTH-dependent cases (pituitary or ectopic), the constant trophic stimulus leads to bilateral cortical expansion (hyperplasia).
A solitary encapsulated mass describes an adrenal adenoma, which causes ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome.
Massive hemorrhage is seen in Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome, not in stable Cushing syndrome.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1115 (Book Page): Diffuse hyperplasia is found in individuals with ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome... The adrenal cortex is diffusely thickened and variably nodular.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
statement: A 29-year-old female presents with a 3-year history of primary infertility and secondary amenorrhea. Physical examination reveals spontaneous milky nipple discharge. Laboratory testing shows a significantly elevated serum Prolactin level (165 ng/mL). Which sellar pathology is the most likely cause of her presentation?
options: Corticotroph cell hyperplasia
Somatotroph microadenoma
Gonadotroph adenoma
Lactotroph adenoma
Null cell macroadenoma
correctOption: Lactotroph adenoma
optionExplanations: Corticotroph hyperplasia leads to ACTH excess and Cushing syndrome, which has different clinical manifestations such as truncal obesity and moon facies.
Somatotroph adenomas secrete growth hormone, leading to acromegaly or gigantism rather than isolated galactorrhea and amenorrhea.
Gonadotroph adenomas are usually nonfunctioning or secrete small amounts of FSH/LH that do not typically produce a galactorrhea syndrome.
Lactotroph adenomas (prolactinomas) are the most common hyperfunctioning pituitary tumors and directly cause the triad of galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and infertility.
Null cell adenomas do not secrete hormones and typically present with mass effects and hypopituitarism rather than functional hormonal excess like prolactinemia.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1069 (Book Page): [Increased serum levels of prolactin, or prolactinemia, cause amenorrhea, galactorrhea, loss of libido, and infertility. Lactotroph adenoma is the cause of almost one-fourth of cases of amenorrhea.]

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
coreConcept: Pattern of Tuberculous Spread in Male Genitalia
statement: In the context of male genital tract infections, which anatomic site is almost invariably involved first in cases of tuberculosis, serving as the origin for subsequent testicular spread?
options: The epididymis
The seminal vesicles
The glans penis
The tunica vaginalis
The prostate gland
correctOption: The epididymis
optionExplanations: Tuberculosis in the male genital tract has a distinct preference for the epididymis as its starting point. From there, it induces caseating granulomatous inflammation and can subsequently involve the testis, causing secondary orchitis.
Seminal vesicles can be involved as the infection spreads, but they are not the initial site. Tuberculosis typically seeds the epididymis via the urinary tract or hematogenously and then progresses.
Glans penis involvement is extremely rare in tuberculosis and is usually associated with external inoculation rather than the standard systemic or ascending spread seen in genital TB.
The tunica vaginalis can be involved by extension, leading to a hydrocele or thickening, but it is not the primary site of the infectious process in genital tuberculosis.
The prostate can be involved in tuberculosis, often through hematogenous spread or infected urine, but it is not the classic primary site of origin for infection that then migrates to the testis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 969 (Book Page): When it involves the male genital tract, tuberculosis almost invariably begins in the epididymis, from where it may spread to the testis.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
statement: Which of the following metabolic events is primarily responsible for the 'fruity odor' detected on the breath of a patient in diabetic ketoacidosis?
options: Accumulation of sorbitol in the mucous membranes
Increased synthesis of glycogen in the liver
Lactic acid production from anaerobic glycolysis
Spontaneous decarboxylation of acetoacetate to acetone
Excessive excretion of sodium and potassium in the urine
correctOption: Spontaneous decarboxylation of acetoacetate to acetone
optionExplanations: Sorbitol accumulation is related to cataracts and neuropathy, not the breath odor of DKA.
Liver glycogen is depleted (glycogenolysis), not synthesized, during the catabolic state of DKA.
Lactic acidosis may occur but does not produce the characteristic fruity (acetone) odor.
The fruity odor is caused by acetone, which is produced from the ketone body acetoacetate during the severe insulin deficiency of DKA.
Electrolyte loss causes volume depletion and shock but does not affect the odor of the breath.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1104 (Book Page): The clinical manifestations of diabetic ketoacidosis include... a characteristic fruity odor... Oxidation of fatty acyl coenzyme A... produces ketone bodies (acetoacetic acid and β-hydroxybutyric acid).

category: Enumerate clinical manifestations along with hormone levels of anterior pituitary
statement: Which dynamic laboratory test is considered one of the most sensitive methods for confirming the diagnosis of acromegaly?
options: Dexamethasone suppression test
Random growth hormone level measurement
Oral glucose load suppression test
Water deprivation test
TSH stimulation test
correctOption: Oral glucose load suppression test
optionExplanations: The dexamethasone suppression test is used to evaluate the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis in cases of suspected Cushing syndrome (ACTH excess).
A single random GH measurement is unreliable because GH is secreted in a pulsatile manner and can be elevated by stress or exercise in normal individuals.
In a healthy person, a high load of glucose should suppress the release of growth hormone. Patients with a somatotroph adenoma fail to show this suppression, which confirms the diagnosis.
The water deprivation test is used to evaluate the posterior pituitary function, specifically to distinguish between different types of diabetes insipidus.
The TSH stimulation (or TRH) test is used to evaluate the thyroid axis and the pituitary's ability to produce thyrotropin, not growth hormone.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1069 (Book Page): In addition, failure to suppress GH production in response to an oral load of glucose is one of the most sensitive tests for acromegaly.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
statement: A 32-year-old woman presents with weight loss, heat intolerance, and bilateral exophthalmos. During a planned subtotal thyroidectomy for Graves disease, the patient develops sudden high fever (104°F) and extreme tachycardia. Which underlying physiological event most likely precipitated this acute clinical emergency?
options: Rapid decrease in the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3
Acute surge in catecholamine levels or sympathetic activity under stress
Sudden inhibition of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis
Iatrogenic damage to the parathyroid glands during surgery
Sudden massive release of thyroglobulin into the systemic circulation
correctOption: Acute surge in catecholamine levels or sympathetic activity under stress
optionExplanations: A rapid decrease in peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 would actually ameliorate thyrotoxic symptoms; thyroid storm involves a severe intensification of these symptoms.

Thyroid storm is a medical emergency often triggered by surgery or stress in hyperthyroid patients, where an acute elevation of catecholamines leads to life-threatening cardiac and metabolic acceleration.
Inhibition of the adrenal axis (adrenal crisis) would cause hypotension and shock, whereas thyroid storm is characterized by a hyperdynamic state and tachycardia.
Parathyroid damage would cause hypocalcemia and tetany, which present with neuromuscular irritability rather than high fever and extreme tachycardia.
While thyroid hormone levels are high, the 'storm' is generally considered to be triggered by the body's acute response to stress and catecholamines rather than simple thyroglobulin release.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1074 (Book Page)-1077: Thyroid storm refers to the abrupt onset of severe hyperthyroidism. This condition occurs most commonly in patients with Graves disease and probably results from an acute elevation in catecholamine levels, as might be encountered during infection, surgery, cessation of antithyroid medication, or any form of stress.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: Which of the following describes the characteristic histological appearance of metaplastic apocrine cells commonly found in breast cysts?
options: Spindle-shaped cells with elongated nuclei and inconspicuous nucleoli
Abundant granular, eosinophilic cytoplasm with round nuclei
Mucin-filled cells with peripherally displaced 'signet ring' nuclei
Flattened, atrophic cells with hyperchromatic, shrunken nuclei
Small cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios and scant cytoplasm
correctOption: Abundant granular, eosinophilic cytoplasm with round nuclei
optionExplanations: Spindle-shaped cells are more characteristic of stromal components or certain rare metaplastic carcinomas.
Metaplastic apocrine cells are easily recognized by their distinctively large, granular, pink cytoplasm and relatively large round nuclei.
Signet ring cells are a classic feature of invasive lobular carcinoma, not the benign apocrine metaplasia of breast cysts.
Cysts can be lined by flattened cells if the internal pressure is high, but 'metaplastic apocrine cells' specifically refer to the eosinophilic granular type.
This description fits malignant cells or primitive cells, not the benign apocrine metaplasia found in fibrocystic changes.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1040 (Book Page): The latter cells have abundant granular, eosinophilic cytoplasm and closely resemble the normal apocrine epithelium of sweat glands (Fig. 23.5C).

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
statement: In the fundamental pathogenesis of preeclampsia, the primary failure of physiological remodeling involves which of the following maternal vascular structures?
options: Umbilical arteries
Peripheral renal arterioles
Decidual spiral arteries
Chorionic plate vessels
Intervillous venous sinuses
correctOption: Decidual spiral arteries
optionExplanations: Umbilical arteries are fetal vessels and are not the site of the primary remodeling failure described in the maternal decidua.
Renal arterioles are affected by the systemic endothelial dysfunction secondary to placental factors, but are not the site of primary remodeling failure.
Failure of extravillous trophoblasts to remodel the high-resistance spiral arteries into low-resistance vessels is the initiating event in preeclampsia.
Chorionic plate vessels are fetal in origin; preeclampsia primarily involves the maternal decidual vessels.
The intervillous space is where exchange occurs, but the primary pathology is in the arterial supply to this space.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1030 (Book Page): This process converts the decidual spiral arteries from small-caliber resistance vessels to large-capacity uteroplacental vessels lacking a smooth muscle coat... In preeclampsia, this vascular remodeling fails to occur

category: Define thyroiditis
statement: Genetic susceptibility to Hashimoto thyroiditis is linked to polymorphisms in genes associated with immune regulation. Which gene polymorphism is most frequently shared between Hashimoto and type 1 diabetes?
options: Thyroglobulin promoter (TG)
Sodium-iodide symporter (NIS)
Cytotoxic T lymphocyte-associated antigen-4 (CTLA4)
TSH receptor (TSHR)
Paired box 8 (PAX8)
correctOption: Cytotoxic T lymphocyte-associated antigen-4 (CTLA4)
optionExplanations: Thyroglobulin gene variations are associated with thyroid-specific outcomes rather than the broader systemic failure of immune tolerance seen with CTLA4.
The sodium-iodide symporter is involved in iodide transport. Mutations in this gene can cause congenital hypothyroidism but are not linked to autoimmune pathogenesis.

CTLA4 is a key regulator of T-cell responses. Polymorphisms in this gene represent a shared genetic risk factor for several autoimmune conditions, including Hashimoto thyroiditis, Graves disease, and type 1 diabetes.
TSHR polymorphisms are linked to Graves disease, but they are specific to thyroid function rather than a general predisposition for various autoimmune diseases like type 1 diabetes.
PAX8 is a transcription factor essential for thyroid development. Mutations in PAX8 result in thyroid dysgenesis or hypoplasia, not the autoimmune destruction seen in thyroiditis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1076 (Book Page)-1079: Increased susceptibility is associated with polymorphisms in several immune regulation–associated genes, such as cytotoxic T lymphocyte–associated antigen-4 (CTLA4)... GWAS have found similar associations between CTLA4, PTPN22, and IL2RA polymorphisms and Graves disease... as well as with other systemic autoimmune diseases such as type 1 diabetes (T1D).

category: Hashimoto Thyroiditis ii
statement: A 42-year-old woman with chronic fatigue and a neck mass is evaluated. Lab tests show elevated TSH and low free T4. Fine-needle aspiration reveals Hürthle cells and a heterogeneous population of lymphocytes. If this patient also developed chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis and hypoparathyroidism, which genetic defect would be most likely?
options: Mutation in the CASR gene
Mutation in the CTLA4 gene
Mutation in the AIRE gene
A homozygous mutation in the PIT1 gene
Translocation involving chromosome 10q11
correctOption: Mutation in the AIRE gene
optionExplanations: CASR mutations cause issues with calcium sensing (like familial hypercalcemia) but not a systemic autoimmune syndrome.
CTLA4 polymorphisms are linked to isolated Hashimoto or Graves but do not classically cause the candidiasis-ectodermal dystrophy syndrome.

AIRE mutations lead to APS-1, which typically presents with a triad of mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and adrenal insufficiency. Hypothyroidism (often Hashimoto-like) can also be a component.
PIT1 mutations cause combined pituitary hormone deficiency (GH, PRL, TSH) resulting in central hypothyroidism, not the primary autoimmune gland destruction with candidiasis.
The RET/PTC translocation (10q11) is associated with papillary thyroid carcinoma, not autoimmune syndromes.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1121 (Book Page): APS-1, also known as autoimmune polyendocrinopathy, candidiasis, and ectodermal dystrophy... is caused by mutations in the autoimmune regulator (AIRE) gene... central T-cell tolerance to peripheral tissue antigens is compromised, promoting autoimmunity.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
statement: Which of the following clinical conditions is etiologically classified under 'Endocrinopathies' as a cause of secondary diabetes due to the secretion of hormones that oppose insulin action?
options: Down syndrome
Pheochromocytoma
Chronic pancreatitis
Cystic fibrosis
Congenital rubella
correctOption: Pheochromocytoma
optionExplanations: Down syndrome is listed under 'Genetic Syndromes Associated With Diabetes,' not as a specific endocrinopathy.
Pheochromocytoma is an endocrinopathy that causes hyperglycemia through the excess secretion of catecholamines which oppose insulin.
Chronic pancreatitis is an 'Exocrine Pancreatic Defect' (Type 3C) involving inflammatory destruction.
Cystic fibrosis is classified as an 'Exocrine Pancreatic Defect' because it leads to structural damage of the gland.
Congenital rubella is classified under 'Infections' that can damage the pancreas or trigger autoimmunity.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1097 (Book Page): [Table 24.6] Endocrinopathies: Acromegaly, Cushing syndrome, Hyperthyroidism, Pheochromocytoma, Glucagonoma

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: Which specific condition results from the failure of the embryo's Rathke pouch to correctly regress, potentially leading to both anterior and posterior pituitary dysfunction in children?
options: Craniopharyngioma.
Sheehan Syndrome.
Pituitary Adenoma.
Nelson Syndrome.
Empty Sella Syndrome.
correctOption: Craniopharyngioma.
optionExplanations: Craniopharyngiomas originate from Rathke pouch remnants and are a common cause of pediatric DI and hypopituitarism.
Sheehan Syndrome is postpartum ischemic necrosis, not a developmental vestige.
Pituitary adenomas are neoplasms of the anterior lobe cells, not Rathke pouch remnants.
Nelson Syndrome is the expansion of a corticotroph adenoma after adrenalectomy.
Empty sella refers to an enlarged sella with a flattened pituitary, often due to herniation of the arachnoid.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1072 (Book Page): Craniopharyngioma is thought to arise from vestigial remnants of Rathke pouch... these tumors may induce hypofunction or hyperfunction of the anterior pituitary, diabetes insipidus, or combinations.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
coreConcept: Bacterial agent morphological contrast in mastitis
statement: When contrasting the morphological manifestations of acute mastitis, which specific presentation is most classically associated with infections caused by Staphylococcus aureus?
options: Formation of localized single or multiple abscess cavities
Replacement of glandular tissue by dense, hyalinized collagen bundles
Ectatic dilation of the major lactiferous sinuses with nipple discharge
Small, numerous calcifications clustered within the terminal duct lobular units
A diffuse, spreading cellulitis involving the entire breast parenchyma
correctOption: Formation of localized single or multiple abscess cavities
optionExplanations: S. aureus characteristically causes focal suppurative necrosis leading to abscesses, which are localized collections of neutrophils and necrotic debris.
Fibrotic replacement is a chronic end-stage change of various inflammations but does not distinguish the acute localized presentation of S. aureus.
Ectatic dilation is the definition of duct ectasia, an inflammatory disorder of older women, whereas acute mastitis is generally associated with lactation and breastfeeding.
Clustered calcifications are features of epithelial lesions or fat necrosis, not the acute suppurative inflammation of bacterial mastitis.
Diffuse spreading cellulitis is the typical morphological pattern of Streptococcus infections, which lack the localized abscess formation characteristic of Staphylococci.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1038 (Book Page): Staphylococci infection often leads to single or multiple abscesses, whereas streptococci cause spreading infection in the form of cellulitis.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
statement: A 4-year-old child presents with a rapid onset of high fever, widespread purpuric skin rashes, and signs of cardiovascular collapse. Blood cultures are positive for Neisseria meningitidis. An autopsy reveals adrenal glands that are almost entirely converted to sacs of clotted blood. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Conn syndrome
Addison disease
Nelson syndrome
Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome
Cushing disease
correctOption: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome
optionExplanations: Conn syndrome is primary hyperaldosteronism, usually caused by an adenoma, not hemorrhage.
Addison disease is a chronic process of cortical destruction, not an acute hemorrhagic event associated with sepsis.
Nelson syndrome occurs after bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing disease, characterized by an enlarging pituitary tumor, not acute adrenal hemorrhage.
This is the classic presentation of WFS: meningococcemia, purpura, DIC, and catastrophic adrenal hemorrhage leading to acute insufficiency.
Cushing disease involves cortisol excess from a pituitary tumor, the opposite of the acute insufficiency seen here.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1120 (Book Page): Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome . . . Overwhelming bacterial infection, classically Neisseria meningitidis septicemia . . . Disseminated intravascular coagulation associated with widespread purpura, particularly of the skin . . . rapidly developing adrenocortical insufficiency associated with massive bilateral adrenal hemorrhage

category: Enumerate clinical manifestations along with hormone levels of anterior pituitary
statement: A 32-year-old female presents with persistent amenorrhea, spontaneous lactation (galactorrhea), and infertility. She also notes recent headaches and visual difficulties, specifically missing objects in her peripheral vision. Imaging confirms a 1.5 cm mass in the sella turcica. What is the most likely biochemical finding and its physiological consequence in this patient?
options: Hypersecretion of ACTH causing skin striae
Hypersecretion of TSH causing tachycardia
Hyposecretion of GH causing muscle weakness
Hyposecretion of FSH causing early menopause
Hypersecretion of Prolactin causing menstrual disruption
correctOption: Hypersecretion of Prolactin causing menstrual disruption
optionExplanations: ACTH hypersecretion leads to Cushing disease. While it could cause amenorrhea, it would not explain the milky nipple discharge (galactorrhea) observed in this case.

TSH-secreting tumors are very rare (1% of adenomas). Hyperthyroid symptoms like tachycardia would be present, but the primary symptoms of lactation and reproductive failure point to a lactotroph origin.
While GH deficiency can cause weakness, it does not typically present with galactorrhea or amenorrhea, and the primary issue here is the active secretion by a common adenoma type.
While hypopituitarism could involve low FSH, the presence of galactorrhea specifically points toward an active prolactin-secreting tumor rather than a simple loss of gonadotroph function.

The triad of galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and infertility is highly specific for prolactin excess. A mass larger than 1 cm (macroadenoma) can also cause pressure on the optic chiasm, leading to the reported peripheral vision defects (bitemporal hemianopsia).
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1069 (Book Page): Increased serum levels of prolactin, or prolactinemia, cause amenorrhea, galactorrhea, loss of libido, and infertility. The diagnosis of an adenoma is made more readily in women than in men... because hyperprolactinemia disrupts the menstrual cycle.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
statement: Which of the following describes the characteristic morphologic features of the testis in the advanced stages of untreated torsion?
options: A yellowish, fleshy mass with well-defined borders
Firm, white mass with central calcification
Small, shrunken, and fibrotic with thickened basement membranes
Soft, necrotic, hemorrhagic tissue
Multiple sessile red papillary excrescences
correctOption: Soft, necrotic, hemorrhagic tissue
optionExplanations: A yellowish fleshy mass is more characteristic of a seminoma (Page 972) than a hemorrhagic infarction.
This describes a hyalinized or old scarred lesion; acute torsion involves hemorrhagic necrosis.
This describes the morphology of cryptorchidism or old atrophy, not acute hemorrhagic infarction.
In advanced torsion, the organ undergoes total infarction, resulting in a soft, swollen, blood-filled necrotic organ.
Red papillary excrescences are characteristic of condyloma acuminatum (genital warts) as described on Page 966.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 968 (Book Page): In advanced stages, the swollen testis consists entirely of soft, necrotic, hemorrhagic tissue.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: A clinician evaluates a patient for a swollen, erythematous breast that mimics acute mastitis but fails to respond to antibiotics. The skin appears thickened with an 'orange peel' texture (peau d'orange). What is the underlying anatomical reason for this specific skin change?
options: Tethering of edematous skin to the breast by Cooper ligaments
Calcification of the superficial pectoral fascia
Rupture of an apocrine cyst into the dermis
Metaplastic change of the sebaceous glands of Montgomery
Infection of the skin by Corynebacterium
correctOption: Tethering of edematous skin to the breast by Cooper ligaments
optionExplanations: The skin becomes edematous due to tumor emboli plugging the lymphatics; because the skin is held down by the suspensory Cooper ligaments, the edema causes the skin to bulge between these tether points.
Calcifications in the breast are typically intraluminal or stromal and do not involve the pectoral fascia to create this skin texture.
Cyst rupture causes localized acute inflammation but does not produce the diffuse lymphatic obstruction seen in inflammatory carcinoma.
Montgomery glands are normal anatomical structures; their metaplasia is not the cause of thepeau d'orange sign.
While Corynebacterium can cause granulomatous mastitis, it does not typically cause the specific peau d'orange presentation seen in inflammatory carcinoma.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1056 (Book Page): The edematous skin is tethered to the breast by Cooper ligaments and mimics the surface of an orange peel, an appearance referred to as peau d’orange.

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
statement: In patients with severe preeclampsia, what is the characteristic laboratory finding associated with the renal glomerular lesions sometimes referred to as 'glomerular endotheliosis'?
options: Glucosuria due to a lowered renal threshold
Proteinuria and amorphous dense endothelial deposits
Elevated plasma renin activity
Profound hypokalemia from potassium wasting
Marked hypercalcemia and polyuria
correctOption: Proteinuria and amorphous dense endothelial deposits
optionExplanations: Glucosuria is the hallmark of diabetes mellitus; while diabetes increases preeclampsia risk, glucosuria is not the diagnostic feature of the preeclamptic renal lesion itself.
The renal lesion involves swelling of endothelial cells and dense subendothelial deposits, which leads to a decrease in the filtration barrier and clinical proteinuria.
Plasma renin activity is typically suppressed or low in preeclampsia because the hypertension is not primarily renin-dependent.
Hypokalemia is a feature of primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome), whereas preeclampsia typically involves sodium/water retention without primary potassium wasting.
Hypercalcemia is common in hyperparathyroidism or malignancy; it is not a feature of preeclampsia-induced renal damage.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1030 (Book Page): The glomeruli show marked swelling of endothelial cells, amorphous dense deposits on the endothelial side of the basement membrane... Immunofluorescent studies show abundant fibrin deposition in glomeruli.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: A 35-year-old female who is a heavy smoker presents with a painful subareolar mass and an inverted nipple. Histology reveals keratinizing squamous metaplasia extending deep into the nipple duct with evidence of ductal rupture. What histological finding is responsible for the acquired nipple inversion in this patient?
options: Traction produced by organized inflammation and scarring.
Accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages causing internal pressure.
Infiltration of the subareolar space by atypical neoplastic cells.
Atrophy of the underlying lobular acini.
Thinning of the ductal basement membrane and loss of elastin.
correctOption: Traction produced by organized inflammation and scarring.
optionExplanations: In Zuska disease, the chronic inflammatory response to extravasated keratin debris leads to significant fibrosis; this scar tissue contracts, pulling the nipple inward.
Lipid-laden macrophages are typical of duct ectasia, which rarely results in the intense scarring required for nipple inversion compared to Zuska disease.
While malignancy can cause nipple retraction, this patient's history of heavy smoking and keratinizing metaplasia points to an inflammatory etiology.
Lobular atrophy is characteristic of lymphocytic mastopathy, which typically presents as a firm mass but not necessarily with nipple inversion.
Thinning of the basement membrane is not a feature of this condition; rather, the ducts show squamous metaplasia and inflammatory thickening.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1038 (Book Page): In many affected women the nipple inverts due to traction produced by inflammation and scarring.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
statement: Which organism is identified as the most frequent cause of sexually transmitted cervicitis that can ascend to cause Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) and infertility in women under 35?
options: Candida albicans
Chlamydia trachomatis
Gardnerella vaginalis
Escherichia coli
Pseudomonas
correctOption: Chlamydia trachomatis
optionExplanations: Candida causes symptomatic vaginitis (yeast infection) but does not typically cause the tubal scarring associated with infertility.
Correct. Chlamydia trachomatis is a leading cause of 'silent' PID and subsequent tubal scarring/infertility in sexually active young women.
Gardnerella causes bacterial vaginosis but is not a typical cause of ascending salpingitis or PID leading to infertility.
E. coli is a common cause of epididymitis/orchitis in men older than 35 and UTI, but Chlamydia is the more frequent primary STIs in the younger cohort.
Pseudomonas is associated with infections in older men or catheterized patients, not standard sexually transmitted PID in young females.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 987 (Book Page): In sexually active men [and women] younger than age 35 years, the sexually transmitted pathogens C. trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae are most frequent. ... Chlamydia trachomatis infections mainly take the form of cervicitis. However, in some patients the infection may ascend to the uterus and fallopian tubes... thus Chlamydia is one of the causes of pelvic inflammatory disease.

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
statement: What is the physiological mechanism explaining why a non-functioning macroadenoma of the SF-1 lineage can cause mild elevations in serum prolactin?
options: The tumor cells undergo 'trans-differentiation' into lactotrophs due to lack of GATA-2.
Macroadenomas secrete a mutated form of TRH that selectively activates prolactin release.
Interruption of the portal venous system prevents hypothalamic dopamine from reaching normal lactotrophs.
SF-1 protein directly stimulates the transcription of the prolactin gene in adjacent cells.
Systemic stress from bitemporal hemianopsia induces a hypermetabolic state with increased PIF release.
correctOption: Interruption of the portal venous system prevents hypothalamic dopamine from reaching normal lactotrophs.
optionExplanations: Lineages are generally stable in adenomas. Trans-differentiation is not the mechanism for mild prolactinemia in gonadotroph tumors.
While TRH can stimulate prolactin, adenomas do not classically secrete mutated TRH; the mechanical compression of the stalk is the recognized mechanism.

The 'stalk effect' occurs when a mass compresses the infundibulum, blocking the flow of dopamine (Prolactin Inhibitory Factor). Without dopamine, normal lactotrophs in the residual pituitary over-secrete.
SF-1 is a nuclear factor for the gonadotroph lineage and does not act as a secretagogue for prolactin in other cells.
PIF (Prolactin Inhibitory Factor) is dopamine. Increased PIF would lower prolactin; the mass effect causes decreased PIF delivery to the pituitary.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1069 (Book Page): Any suprasellar mass (e.g., a pituitary adenoma) may disturb the inhibitory influence of the hypothalamus on prolactin secretion, resulting in hyperprolactinemia. Therefore, mild hyperprolactenemia in a person with a pituitary adenoma does not necessarily indicate a prolactin-secreting tumor.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
statement: Newer therapeutic agents for Type 2 Diabetes utilize the 'incretin effect' to maintain glucose homeostasis. What is the primary mechanism of action for dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors in these patients?
options: They act as monoclonal antibodies against the TSH receptor.
They inhibit the SGLT-2 transporter in the proximal convoluted tubule.
They prolong the half-life of GLP-1 and GIP by preventing their degradation.
They directly activate the GLUT-4 transporter in striated muscle.
They stimulate the de novo synthesis of mitochondrial DNA in adipocytes.
correctOption: They prolong the half-life of GLP-1 and GIP by preventing their degradation.
optionExplanations: Antibodies against the TSH receptor are the cause of Graves disease, not a mechanism used to treat Type 2 Diabetes.
Inhibiting SGLT-2 is the mechanism of a different class of drugs (gliflozins), which prevent glucose reabsorption in the kidney, rather than acting on the incretin loop.
DPP-4 is an enzyme that naturally breaks down GLP-1 and GIP. By inhibiting this enzyme, the levels of these hormones remain elevated, promoting glucose-dependent insulin secretion.
While increasing GLUT-4 translocation is a goal of exercise and insulin therapy, DPP-4 inhibitors work through the incretin system.
Mitochondrial biogenesis is not the mechanism for DPP-4 inhibition; their effect is targeted at regulating circulating intestinal hormones.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1098 (Book Page): DPP-4 inhibitors, which enhance levels of endogenous incretins by delaying their degradation.

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
coreConcept: Temporal and Spatial Variation in Thyroiditis
statement: A 48-year-old male is evaluated for a firm, painful neck mass that appeared three weeks ago. He notes his heart has been racing and he feels unusually warm. His radioactive iodine uptake is significantly low. If multiple biopsy sites are examined, why might the histological findings vary across the gland?
options: Varying degrees of TSH-receptor antibody density on follicular surfaces
Localized iodine sequestration within functional 'hot' pockets
Concurrent development of papillary and follicular neoplastic clones
Differential expression of IgG4 in various sectors of the parenchyma
Presence of different stages of destruction and repair occurring simultaneously
correctOption: Presence of different stages of destruction and repair occurring simultaneously
optionExplanations: TSH-receptor antibodies are the mechanism for Graves disease, which involves diffuse hyperplasia, not the destruction seen in granulomatous thyroiditis.
Low radioactive iodine uptake is a diffuse finding in this condition; there are no 'hot' pockets of iodine sequestration.
Granulomatous thyroiditis is an inflammatory condition, not a neoplastic one, and does not involve clones of malignant cells.
IgG4-related disease is specifically associated with Riedel thyroiditis, but granulomatous thyroiditis is not considered an IgG4-related disorder.
Histologic changes are patchy because the disease progresses in 'waves.' One area might show acute microabscesses while another shows multinucleate giant cells or reparative fibrosis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): Different histologic stages are sometimes found in the same gland, suggesting waves of destruction over a period of time.

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: Which of the following epidemiological criteria is used to define a geographic region as having endemic goiter?
options: Solitary thyroid nodules are present in >1% of adults
Goiters are present in more than 10% of the population
Congenital hypothyroidism affects 1 in 1000 live births
Hashimoto thyroiditis is the primary cause of neck swelling
Thyroid carcinoma incidence exceeds 5% annually
correctOption: Goiters are present in more than 10% of the population
optionExplanations: Solitary nodules are common even in non-endemic areas and do not define an endemic region.
An area is classified as endemic for goiter when the prevalence of thyroid enlargement in the community exceeds 10%.
Neonatal screening data is important but the 10% prevalence of goiter is the standard epidemiological threshold.
In endemic areas, iodine deficiency, not autoimmune thyroiditis, is the leading cause of goiter.
Thyroid carcinoma rates are not used to define endemic goiter regions, though iodine deficiency may shift the type of carcinoma seen.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1081 (Book Page): [The term endemic is used when goiters are present in more than 10% of the population in a given region.]

category: Hashimoto Thyroiditis ii
coreConcept: T-Cell Mediated Cytotoxicity in Autoimmune Thyroiditis
statement: The progressive destruction of thyroid parenchyma in Hashimoto thyroiditis is mediated by a breakdown in self-tolerance to thyroid autoantigens. Which of the following immunologic pathways is primarily responsible for the recruitment and activation of macrophages that damage the thyroid follicles?
options: Activation of Th2 cells producing IL-4 and IL-5
Secretion of IL-10 by regulatory T cells (Tregs)
Immediate Type I hypersensitivity mediated by IgE
CD4+ Th1 cell-mediated production of interferon-gamma
Formation of immune complexes in the vessel walls (Type III)
correctOption: CD4+ Th1 cell-mediated production of interferon-gamma
optionExplanations: Th2 responses are typically associated with allergic reactions and helminthic infections; Hashimoto is a Th1-driven autoimmune process.
IL-10 and Tregs normally suppress autoimmune responses. In Hashimoto thyroiditis, there is a hypothesized defect in these regulatory mechanisms, allowing destructive pathways to prevail.
Type I hypersensitivity involves mast cell degranulation and is not involved in the chronic, cell-mediated destruction of the thyroid gland.
The Th1 response is central to Hashimoto pathogenesis. Th1 cells release IFN-gamma, which is a potent activator of macrophages, leading to the parenchymal destruction observed in the gland.
While autoantibodies are present, the primary mechanism of tissue damage is T-cell mediated (Type IV) rather than Type III immune complex-mediated vasculitis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1077 (Book Page): Activation of CD4+ Th1 cells leads to the production of inflammatory cytokines such as interferon-γ in the thyroid gland, with resultant recruitment and activation of macrophages and damage to follicles.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
statement: A biopsy of a testis from a patient with a known history of chronic infection reveals extensive 'obliterative endarteritis' associated with perivascular cuffs of lymphocytes and plasma cells. This histologic hallmark is characteristic of inflammation caused by which organism?
options: Brucella abortus
Mumps virus
Treponema pallidum
Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Mycobacterium tuberculosis
correctOption: Treponema pallidum
optionExplanations: Brucellosis is a rare cause of orchitis that does not typically present with the specific vascular pattern described.
Mumps causes acute interstitial orchitis characterized by edema and lymphocytic infiltration, not the specific vascular changes of syphilis.
Obliterative endarteritis with plasma cell-rich perivascular cuffing is the classic microscopic finding in syphilis, whether in the primary chancre or late-stage testicular involvement.
Gonorrhea causes suppurative inflammation and abscesses rather than obliterative endarteritis.
Tuberculosis is characterized by caseating granulomatous inflammation, not primarily an endarteritis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 968 (Book Page): The morphologic pattern of the reaction takes two forms: (1) obliterative endarteritis associated with perivascular cuffs of lymphocytes and plasma cells, the histologic hallmark of syphilis, or (2) granulomatous inflammation, a lesion known as a gumma.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
statement: A 31-year-old female with primary infertility undergoes laparoscopy. The findings include 'chocolate cysts' on the ovaries and extensive fibrous adhesions obliterating the pouch of Douglas. Biopsies confirm the presence of ectopic endometrial glands and stroma with hemosiderin. Which additional finding in this clinical context most specifically contributes to her infertility?
options: Monomorphic small cells involving acini lacking E-cadherin expression.
Dense collagenous connective tissue in the subareolar male breast.
Intrapelvic bleeding leading to organizing hemorrhage and periuterine adhesions.
Phagocytosed gram-negative diplococci within neutrophils in the tubal lumen.
Squamous metaplasia of the lactiferous ducts with keratin plugs.
correctOption: Intrapelvic bleeding leading to organizing hemorrhage and periuterine adhesions.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. This describes the morphology of Lobular Carcinoma in Situ (LCIS) of the breast, which involves E-cadherin loss, not endometriosis.
Incorrect. This describes gynecomastia in males, which is irrelevant to female pelvic endometriosis.
Correct. In endometriosis, cyclic bleeding of ectopic tissue leads to organizing hemorrhage and severe pelvic adhesions that disrupt normal tubo-ovarian relationships and cause infertility.
Incorrect. This is the hallmark of acute gonococcal salpingitis (PID), whereas the patient's findings (chocolate cysts, glands/stroma) are diagnostic of endometriosis.
Incorrect. This describes Zuska disease (recurrent subareolar abscess) in the breast, which has no relationship to pelvic endometriosis or fertility.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1005 (Book Page): Endometriotic lesions bleed periodically in response to both extrinsic cyclic (ovarian) and intrinsic hormonal stimulation... When lesions are widespread, organizing hemorrhage causes extensive fibrous adhesions... and obliterates the pouch of Douglas.

category: Define thyroiditis
statement: Which of the following descriptions best encapsulates the broad clinical category of thyroiditis?
options: Dietary iodine deficiency leading to nodular compensatory growth.
The exclusive hypersecretion of calcitonin by parafollicular C cells.
A heterogeneous collection of conditions resulting in thyroid inflammation.
Congenital absence of thyroid tissue due to failed descent.
A group of neoplastic transformations of the follicular epithelium.
correctOption: A heterogeneous collection of conditions resulting in thyroid inflammation.
optionExplanations: This defines endemic goiter. While goiters can be present in thyroiditis (like Hashimoto), the fundamental cause of endemic goiter is iodine scarcity rather than a primary inflammatory process.

This describes the function of medullary carcinoma or normal C-cell activity. Thyroiditis involves the follicle-mediated inflammatory response and often the autoimmune system, not just C-cell secretion.

This is the foundational definition. The term 'thyroiditis' refers to various inflammatory states, ranging from autoimmune destruction like Hashimoto to infectious or viral-triggered states like granulomatous thyroiditis.
This describes thyroid agenesis or hypoplasia, which are developmental anomalies. While they cause hypothyroidism, they are not inflammatory 'itis' conditions.

Neoplastic transformations refer to tumors, not inflammatory processes. Thyroiditis is primarily inflammatory and can lead to gland destruction or transient leakage, distinct from clonal neoplastic growth.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1076 (Book Page): Thyroiditis encompasses a diverse group of disorders characterized by some form of thyroid inflammation.

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
statement: Corticotroph adenomas are subclassified based on their clinical activity and histological features. How are 'silent' corticotroph adenomas primarily distinguished from those causing Cushing disease?
options: They are derived from the PIT-1 lineage
They lack TPIT transcription factor expression
They produce mass effects without clinical hypercortisolism
They are exclusively microadenomas by definition
They fail to express pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)
correctOption: They produce mass effects without clinical hypercortisolism
optionExplanations: Corticotrophs belong to the TPIT lineage, not the PIT-1 lineage (which includes somatotrophs, lactotrophs, and thyrotrophs).
Silent corticotroph adenomas still express the TPIT transcription factor, as it defines their lineage.
Silent adenomas are immunoreactive for ACTH but do not cause hypercortisolism. Instead, they present clinically via mass effects like visual field defects or headaches.
Silent adenomas are actually more likely to be macroadenomas at the time of diagnosis because they lack early endocrine symptoms.
They still synthesize POMC and ACTH internally; the 'silence' refers to the lack of systemic clinical effects or hormone secretion.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1067 (Book Page): Note that nonfunctional (“silent”) adenomas in each category express the corresponding hormone(s) and transcription factor within the neoplastic cells... However, these adenomas do not produce the associated clinical syndrome and typically present with mass effects

category: Hashimoto Thyroiditis ii
statement: Gross examination of a thyroid gland removed from a patient with chronic Hashimoto thyroiditis typically reveals which appearance?
options: A beefy, deep red, soft parenchyma resembling muscle
Multiple large cysts filled with brown, gelatinous colloid
Massive hemorrhage and sacs of clotted blood
Radiodense calcifications within a thin fibrous capsule
A pale, yellow-tan, firm, and somewhat nodular cut surface
correctOption: A pale, yellow-tan, firm, and somewhat nodular cut surface
optionExplanations: A soft, beefy, deep red parenchyma is the classic gross description of the hyperplastic thyroid in Graves disease.
Large colloid-filled cysts are typical of multinodular goiter or colloid goiter, whereas HT follicles are usually atrophic.
Massive hemorrhage converting the gland into a sac of blood describes Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome of the adrenal glands, not thyroiditis.
HT is typically not radiodense; calcifications are more common in multinodular goiters or papillary carcinomas (psammoma bodies).
The gross appearance of HT reflects the extensive lymphocytic infiltration and fibrosis, which turns the normally reddish-brown thyroid tissue into a firm, pale, tan mass.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1076 (Book Page): The thyroid is usually diffusely enlarged. The capsule is intact... The cut surface is pale, yellow-tan, firm, and somewhat nodular.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
statement: A 40-year-old patient presents with symptoms of thyrotoxicosis. A radioactive iodine uptake scan reveals a low, patchy uptake throughout the gland. This finding most strongly differentiates this condition from Graves disease by suggesting which diagnosis?
options: Hyperfunctioning toxic multinodular goiter
Congenital biosynthetic defect
A TSH-secreting pituitary microadenoma
Functional thyroid adenoma (hot nodule)
Subacute thyroiditis
correctOption: Subacute thyroiditis
optionExplanations: Toxic multinodular goiter shows uneven, patchy, but generally high uptake in hyperfunctioning areas.
Biosynthetic defects usually result in goiter and hypothyroidism, not the thyrotoxic state mentioned in the stem.
A TSH-secreting tumor would cause increased stimulation and thus increased (not low) radioactive iodine uptake.
A hot nodule would show a localized area of very high uptake, unlike the low uptake seen here.
Thyroiditis involves the release of preformed hormone from damaged follicles; the damaged gland cannot trap iodine, resulting in low uptake.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1075 (Book Page): Once the diagnosis of thyrotoxicosis has been confirmed... measurement of radioactive iodine uptake by the thyroid gland can help determine the etiology. For example, there may be diffusely increased uptake in the gland (Graves disease)... or decreased uptake (thyroiditis).

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
coreConcept: Maternal-Fetal Thyroid Physiology in Brain Development
statement: A neonate is diagnosed with severe intellectual disability, a protruding tongue, and an umbilical hernia. Pathophysiological analysis suggests cretinism. The severity of the intellectual deficit is most closely linked to which factor?
options: Increased fetal T3 production after the 20th week
Iatrogenic maternal iodine supplementation
Maternal thyroid hormone deficiency during early pregnancy
Excessive maternal placental transfer of TSH
The development of a lingual thyroid during the second trimester
correctOption: Maternal thyroid hormone deficiency during early pregnancy
optionExplanations: The fetal thyroid becomes functional later in pregnancy, but this cannot compensate for the lack of early maternal hormones required for initial brain patterning.
Iodine supplementation prevents cretinism in endemic areas; it does not cause intellectual disability unless given in extreme toxic doses.
Maternal T3 and T4 are critical for fetal brain development before the fetal thyroid gland becomes functional; deficiency during this early window is catastrophic.
TSH does not cross the placenta in significant amounts and would not be the cause of intellectual disability in cretinism.
A lingual thyroid is an ectopic remnant of thyroid descent; while it may be insufficient, the timing of maternal deficiency is the primary driver of cretinism's severity.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1076 (Book Page): If there is maternal thyroid deficiency before the development of the fetal thyroid gland, intellectual disability is severe. In contrast, maternal thyroid hormone deficiency later in pregnancy... does not affect normal brain development.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
statement: The etiological classification include 'Infections' as a cause of secondary diabetes. Which set of pathogens is associated with this category in clinical practice?
options: Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes.
