One of the primary mechanisms of PTH is to signal the renal tubules to move filtered calcium back into the blood to maintain serum levels.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1091 (Book Page): Several metabolic functions of PTH regulate serum calcium levels: Increased renal tubular reabsorption of calcium, thereby conserving free calcium.

category: Define thyroiditis
coreConcept: Clinical and Pathological Correlation of de Quervain Thyroiditis
statement: A 42-year-old male presents with sudden onset of severe neck pain, fever, and a tender, firm, enlarged thyroid. He reports having a viral upper respiratory infection two weeks ago. Histological examination shows aggregates of lymphocytes and activated macrophages surrounding collapsed follicles, with prominent multinucleate giant cells. What is the diagnosis?
options: Granulomatous thyroiditis
Riedel thyroiditis
Hashimoto thyroiditis
Acute bacterial mastitis
Graves disease
correctOption: Granulomatous thyroiditis
optionExplanations: The history of a viral prodrome followed by painful thyroid enlargement and the presence of granulomatous inflammation with giant cells is pathognomonic for granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis.
Riedel thyroiditis presents as a rock-hard mass due to fibrosis and lacks the granulomatous giant cell reaction and viral trigger described.
Hashimoto thyroiditis is painless and characterized by Hürthle cells and germinal centers rather than multinucleate giant cells and acute pain.
Mastitis refers to inflammation of the breast, not the thyroid gland.
Graves disease presents with hyperthyroidism and diffuse hyperplasia but is not associated with fever, pain, or granulomatous histology.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): Granulomatous thyroiditis... is believed to be triggered by a viral infection. ... The gland may be unilaterally or bilaterally enlarged and firm... Multinucleate giant cells enclose pools of colloid, hence the designation granulomatous thyroiditis.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: A 28-year-old lactating female presents with a painful, erythematous area on her right breast and a high-grade fever. Physical examination reveals a localized fluctuant mass. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism for this specific presentation?
options: Corynebacterium species
Bacteroides fragilis
Staphylococcus aureus
Streptococcus pyogenes
Mycobacterium tuberculosis
correctOption: Staphylococcus aureus
optionExplanations: Corynebacterium species are more typically implicated in cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis rather than acute bacterial abscesses.
Anaerobes like Bacteroides may be seen in recurrent subareolar abscesses, but they are not the primary cause of acute lactational mastitis.
Staphylococcus aureus is the classic cause of localized abscess formation in the setting of acute lactational mastitis.
Streptococci are more commonly associated with diffuse spreading infections such as cellulitis rather than localized abscesses.
Mycobacterium causes granulomatous inflammation (tuberculous mastitis), not the acute, neutrophilic, fluctuant abscess described.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1038 (Book Page): Staphylococci infection often leads to single or multiple abscesses, whereas streptococci cause spreading infection in the form of cellulitis.

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: A researcher is studying the regulation of fluid balance. They observe that an increase in plasma osmotic pressure leads to the release of a specific peptide from the posterior pituitary. Where is this peptide primarily synthesized?
options: Anterior pituitary epithelial cells.
Chromophobe cells of the adenohypophysis.
Modified glial cells known as pituicytes.
The portal venous plexus.
Hypothalamic neurons.
correctOption: Hypothalamic neurons.
optionExplanations: The anterior pituitary synthesizes its own trophic hormones; the posterior pituitary only stores hypothalamic hormones.
Chromophobe cells are in the anterior pituitary and do not secrete ADH.
Pituicytes are supporting cells in the posterior pituitary; they do not synthesize ADH or Oxytocin.
The portal venous plexus carries releasing factors from the hypothalamus to the anterior lobe, not the hormones of the posterior lobe.
ADH (Arginine Vasopressin) is synthesized in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus and then transported to the posterior pituitary.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1071 (Book Page): These hormones are actually synthesized in the hypothalamus and are transported through axons to the posterior pituitary.

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
statement: A 24-year-old primigravida at 35 weeks gestation presents with a blood pressure of 165/110 mmHg, severe frontal headache, and epigastric pain. Laboratory evaluation reveals a platelet count of 85,000/μL, elevated serum aspartate aminotransferase (AST), and fragmented red blood cells (schistocytes) on a peripheral blood smear. What is the most likely diagnosis and its immediate clinical implication?
options: HELLP syndrome; necessitates immediate delivery regardless of gestational age
Chronic hypertension; suggests a preexisting renal artery stenosis
Gestational diabetes; requires immediate insulin therapy to prevent macrosomia
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura; requires urgent plasma exchange
Simple preeclampsia; manageable with bed rest and salt restriction
correctOption: HELLP syndrome; necessitates immediate delivery regardless of gestational age
optionExplanations: The combination of Hemolysis (schistocytes), Elevated Liver enzymes (AST), and Low Platelets in the context of preeclampsia defines HELLP syndrome, which is an absolute indication for delivery.
Chronic hypertension is diagnosed before 20 weeks; the late-gestation onset with multisystem involvement (liver, blood) points to a gestational syndrome.
While gestational diabetes is a pregnancy complication, it does not present with hypertension, hemolysis, and thrombocytopenia.
While schistocytes and low platelets occur in TTP, the context of third-trimester hypertension and liver enzyme elevation is highly specific for HELLP syndrome in pregnancy pathology.
This patient has severe preeclampsia signs and lab abnormalities. Bed rest is insufficient; end-organ dysfunction (liver, platelets) dictates delivery.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1029 (Book Page): Approximately 10% of women with preeclampsia develop microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets, referred to as the HELLP syndrome... eclampsia, severe preeclampsia with maternal end-organ dysfunction, fetal compromise, or the HELLP syndrome are indications for delivery regardless of gestational age.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: Molecular analysis of a sporadic parathyroid adenoma reveals a pericentromeric inversion on chromosome 11. Which gene is most likely overexpressed as a result of this specific rearrangement?
options: RET
Cyclin D1 (CCDN1)
MEN1
CDC73 (Parafibromin)
GNAS
correctOption: Cyclin D1 (CCDN1)
optionExplanations: RET mutations are associated with MEN-2 and thyroid medullary carcinoma, not primary sporadic parathyroid adenomas.
A pericentromeric inversion on chromosome 11 causes the CCDN1 gene to be overexpressed under the control of the PTH promoter in many sporadic adenomas.
MEN1 mutations involve loss-of-function/inactivation of a tumor suppressor, not typically a pericentromeric inversion leading to overexpression.
CDC73 mutations are associated with parathyroid carcinomas and hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumor syndrome, not chromosome 11 inversions involving CCDN1.
GNAS mutations are activating mutations in G-proteins seen in pituitary and some thyroid/adrenal lesions, not the characteristic chromosome 11 inversion.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): A pericentromeric inversion on chromosome 11 results in relocation of CCDN1 (normally on 11q), so that it is positioned adjacent to the 5′-flanking region of the PTH gene (on 11p). As a consequence of these changes, a 5′-regulatory element flanking the PTH gene directs overexpression of cyclin D1...

category: Describe salient morphological features of clinically significant subtypes of thyroiditis: i
statement: Which specific histological alteration is considered a hallmark morphological feature of Hashimoto thyroiditis, representing a metaplastic response of follicular epithelium to chronic injury?
options: Clear cell metaplasia
Hürthle cell change
Orphan Annie eye nuclei
Multinucleated giant cells
Psammoma body formation
correctOption: Hürthle cell change
optionExplanations: Clear cell metaplasia is not a standard feature of Hashimoto thyroiditis; the characteristic change is eosinophilic (oxyphilic) rather than clear.
Hürthle cells, or oxyphilic cells, are follicular epithelial cells that develop abundant, granular, eosinophilic cytoplasm in response to the chronic autoimmune stress of Hashimoto thyroiditis.
Orphan Annie eye nuclei (optically clear nuclei) are the diagnostic hallmark of papillary thyroid carcinoma.
Multinucleated giant cells are the defining feature of granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis, not Hashimoto.
Psammoma bodies are characteristic of papillary thyroid carcinoma, not thyroiditis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): [The thyroid follicles are atrophic and are lined in many areas by epithelial cells with abundant eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm, termed Hürthle cells, which represent a metaplastic response of the normally low cuboidal follicular epithelium to chronic injury.]

category: Define thyroiditis
statement: Which of the following is the suspected inciting event for the development of granulomatous thyroiditis?
options: Mutations in the autoimmune regulator (AIRE) gene
A viral infection producing host tissue damage
Exposure to high levels of dietary goitrogens like cassava
Systemic IgG4-related fibroinflammatory disease
A breakdown in self-tolerance to thyrotropin receptors
correctOption: A viral infection producing host tissue damage
optionExplanations: AIRE mutations are associated with Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome type 1, which causes autoimmune adrenalitis and hypoparathyroidism, not de Quervain's.
Granulomatous thyroiditis often follows a viral prodrome (like an upper respiratory infection) and is seasonal, suggesting a viral trigger.
Goitrogens like cassava interfere with thyroid hormone synthesis and lead to goiter, but they do not cause inflammatory granulomatous thyroiditis.
This is associated with Riedel thyroiditis, a rare fibroinflammatory disorder.
This is the mechanism for Graves disease, an autoimmune condition, not granulomatous thyroiditis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): Granulomatous thyroiditis is believed to be triggered by a viral infection. ... it results from virus-induced host tissue damage that stimulates a cytotoxic T-lymphocyte response.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
statement: Histopathological examination of the pancreas in a patient with a long-standing history of hyperglycemia and obesity is most likely to reveal which of the following features?
options: Accumulation of lipid droplets within alpha cells
Amyloid deposition replacing the islet parenchyma
Leukocytic infiltrates (insulitis) within the islets
Islet cell hyperplasia in response to glucotoxicity
Total absence of islet structures within the tail of the pancreas
correctOption: Amyloid deposition replacing the islet parenchyma
optionExplanations: Morphologic changes in Type 2 DM islets are centered on amyloidosis and mild beta-cell depletion, not intracellular lipid accumulation in alpha cells.
In Type 2 DM, islets characteristically show amyloid deposition (amylin), which can eventually obliterate the islet cells.
Insulitis (lymphocytic infiltration) is the classic morphologic feature of early Type 1 DM, reflecting an autoimmune process.
Islet hyperplasia is typically seen in the newborns of diabetic mothers, not in the adult progression of Type 2 DM.
Islets are generally preserved in number though dysfunctional or amyloidotic in Type 2 DM; total absence is not the typical finding.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1106 (Book Page): Amyloid deposition within islets in T2D begins in and around capillaries and between cells. At advanced stages, the islets may be virtually obliterated

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
statement: Which criteria form the primary basis for the current pathologic classification of pituitary adenomas?
options: Patient age at presentation and gender distribution
Radiographic appearance and proximity to the optic chiasm
Cytoplasmic staining density and reticulin network preservation
Specific hormones produced and lineage-specific transcription factors
Tumor size and degree of local invasiveness
correctOption: Specific hormones produced and lineage-specific transcription factors
optionExplanations: Clinical demographics are associated with certain adenoma types (e.g., lactotrophs in women) but are not used to classify the tumor pathologically.
Radiographic features assist in clinical staging but do not define the histologic or pathologic subtype of the adenoma.
Staining (acidophil/basophil/chromophobe) was used historically; modern classification requires hormone and transcription factor identification.
Modern pathology identifies the specific cell lineage via the hormones produced and the underlying transcription factors (like PIT-1, TPIT, or SF-1) that drove the differentiation.
While size (microadenoma vs. macroadenoma) is used for clinical designation, it is not the primary pathologic classification basis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1065 (Book Page): Pituitary adenomas are classified on the basis of the hormones and cell type–specific transcription factors that are expressed by the tumor cells (Table 24.1).

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
coreConcept: Stromal fat behavior in parathyroid pathologies
statement: What happens to the presence of stromal fat within the parathyroid gland parenchyma when either parathyroid adenoma or primary hyperplasia develops?
options: Adipose tissue remains constant at 30%
Adipose tissue undergoes metaplasia to oxyphil cells
Adipose tissue becomes inconspicuous
Adipose tissue forms a protective outer capsule
Adipose tissue becomes the dominant stromal component
correctOption: Adipose tissue becomes inconspicuous
optionExplanations: 30% fat is the normal adult baseline; pathologic cellular growth displaces this fat.
Adipose tissue does not transform into epithelial oxyphil cells.
A critical histological finding in parathyroid adenomas and hyperplastic glands is that the normal stromal fat disappears or becomes inconspicuous.
A capsule forms in adenoma from connective tissue, but stromal fat within the lesion is minimized.
Dominance of fat would be seen in atrophy, not in cellular adenoma or hyperplasia.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): [As in the case of adenomas, stromal fat is inconspicuous within hyperplastic glands.]

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
statement: In the evaluation of male infertility, a semen analysis reveals a failure of the seminal coagulum to liquefy. Which prostatic product is responsible for this physiological step?
options: Acid phosphatase
Inhibin
Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)
Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)
C-peptide
correctOption: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)
optionExplanations: Acid phosphatase is a prostatic enzyme but is not the primary protease responsible for seminal coagulum liquefaction.
Inhibin is a product of Sertoli or granulosa cells used to monitor sex cord-stromal tumors, not for semen liquefaction.
PSA is a serine protease that cleaves the seminal coagulum; deficiency in this enzymatic action prevents liquefaction, hindering sperm motility.
AFP is a biomarker for yolk sac tumors and is not involved in semen liquefaction.
C-peptide is a byproduct of insulin synthesis and is not present in prostatic secretions for semen processing.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 979 (Book Page): PSA is a product of prostatic epithelium and is normally secreted in the semen. It is an androgen-regulated serine protease whose function is to cleave and liquefy the seminal coagulum formed after ejaculation.

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
statement: A patient is evaluated for hyperthyroidism. Which laboratory finding specifically distinguishes Granulomatous thyroiditis from Graves disease during the initial phase of illness?
options: Suppression of serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels.
Elevation of serum free thyroxine (T4) levels.
Positive testing for antithyroid peroxidase antibodies.
A marked decrease in radioactive iodine uptake on thyroid scan.
A significant increase in radioactive iodine uptake on thyroid scan.
correctOption: A marked decrease in radioactive iodine uptake on thyroid scan.
optionExplanations: TSH suppression is common to all forms of hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis due to feedback inhibition.
Both conditions can present with elevated free T4 during their thyrotoxic phases, making this non-discriminatory.
Antithyroid peroxidase antibodies are hallmark features of Hashimoto thyroiditis and occasionally Graves, but are not the primary diagnostic differentiator for De Quervain.
In Granulomatous thyroiditis, the high T4 levels result from the leak of preformed hormone from damaged follicles, not new synthesis; thus, uptake of iodine is low.
Increased uptake is characteristic of Graves disease, where the gland is hyperfunctional and actively synthesizing new hormone.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): However, unlike in hyperthyroid states such as Graves disease, radioactive iodine uptake is diminished.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
statement: The histologic hallmark of syphilis in the testis, distinguishing it from other inflammatory conditions, is the presence of:
options: Fungal hyphae within the tubules
Neutrophilic microabscesses
Caseating granulomatous inflammation
Acute suppurative necrosis
Obliterative endarteritis with plasma cell cuffs
correctOption: Obliterative endarteritis with plasma cell cuffs
optionExplanations: Fungal hyphae would indicate a mycotic infection, which is a rare cause of orchitis.
Neutrophilic abscesses are seen in acute pyogenic epididymo-orchitis, not chronic syphilis.
Caseating granulomas point toward tuberculosis, not syphilis.
Suppurative necrosis is typical of acute bacterial infections like those caused by Neisseria.
Syphilis in the testis is characterized by obliterative endarteritis and a perivascular infiltrate rich in plasma cells and lymphocytes.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 968 (Book Page): (1) obliterative endarteritis associated with perivascular cuffs of lymphocytes and plasma cells, the histologic hallmark of syphilis.

category: Define thyroiditis
statement: Susceptibility to Hashimoto thyroiditis is genetically associated with polymorphisms in which of the following immune-regulation genes?
options: BRAF and PAX8
MEN1 and CDKN1B
TSHR and GNAS
RET and NTRK
CTLA4 and PTPN22
correctOption: CTLA4 and PTPN22
optionExplanations: BRAF point mutations and PAX8/PPARG fusions are associated with thyroid malignancies.
MEN1 and CDKN1B are associated with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndromes, not typically Hashimoto.
TSHR and GNAS mutations are found in toxic adenomas and multinodular goiters.
RET and NTRK rearrangements are associated with papillary thyroid carcinoma.
CTLA4 and PTPN22 are well-known susceptibility loci for several autoimmune diseases, including Hashimoto and Type 1 Diabetes.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1076 (Book Page): Increased susceptibility is associated with polymorphisms in several immune regulation–associated genes, such as cytotoxic T lymphocyte–associated antigen-4 (CTLA4), protein tyrosine phosphatase-22 (PTPN22)...

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
statement: A 30-year-old male is diagnosed with acute interstitial orchitis one week after the onset of parotid gland swelling. What is the risk associated with this condition in postpubertal males?
options: It is caused by the same organism as syphilis
It requires treatment with high-dose androgens
It occurs in nearly 100% of mumps cases
It always involves the epididymis first
It occurs in 20% to 30% of postpubertal cases and may lead to sterility
correctOption: It occurs in 20% to 30% of postpubertal cases and may lead to sterility
optionExplanations: Syphilis is caused by Treponema pallidum; mumps is a viral infection.
The source does not recommend androgen therapy; management is generally supportive as the Leydig cells are often spared.
Orchitis is relatively uncommon in children and occurs in only 20-30% of postpubertal mumps cases.
Mumps is a systemic viral disease that can affect the testis directly; it is not described as arising in the epididymis first like TB or gonorrhea.
Postpubertal mumps orchitis carries a significant risk of inflammation followed by scarring, which can result in sterility.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 966 (Book Page): In postpubertal males, however, orchitis occurs in 20% to 30% of cases. ... Inflammation of the epididymis and testis is often followed by fibrous scarring, which may produce sterility.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
statement: A 28-year-old male presents with sudden onset of unilateral scrotal pain, swelling, and a purulent urethral discharge. Physical examination confirms acute epididymitis. Which pair of pathogens is most likely responsible for this condition based on the patient's age?
options: Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas species
Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Treponema pallidum
Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes
Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Coxsackie B virus and Mumps virus
correctOption: Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
optionExplanations: E. coli and Pseudomonas are the most common causes of epididymitis in men older than 35, usually associated with UTIs.
Tuberculosis and syphilis are chronic infections; TB typically begins in the epididymis with caseation, while syphilis typically involves the testis first and lacks purulent urethral discharge.
These pyogenic bacteria can cause infection but are not the leading causes of sexually transmitted epididymitis in the <35 age group.
In sexually active males under 35, urethral infection with C. trachomatis or N. gonorrhoeae is the most frequent precursor to acute epididymitis.
Mumps causes orchitis, not primarily epididymitis with purulent discharge, and Coxsackie B is a rare cause of inflammation.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 967 (Book Page): In sexually active men younger than age 35 years, the sexually transmitted pathogens C. trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae are most frequent.

category: Hashimoto Thyroiditis ii
coreConcept: Feedback inhibition in Primary Thyroid Failure
statement: During the transition from the euthyroid state to the hypothyroid state in a patient with Hashimoto thyroiditis, which of the following compensatory physiological changes is most likely to be observed first?
options: Downregulation of the TRH receptor in the pituitary
Compensatory elevation of the serum TSH level
Increase in serum thyroid-binding globulin levels
Decreased production of somatostatin by the hypothalamus
Inhibition of peripheral T4 to T3 conversion
correctOption: Compensatory elevation of the serum TSH level
optionExplanations: In primary failure, TRH receptors would likely be upregulated or more active as the pituitary attempts to stimulate the failing gland.

The pituitary senses even minute drops in free T4/T3 and increases TSH production (loss of feedback inhibition). This often results in 'subclinical hypothyroidism' before T4 levels actually drop below the normal range.
Thyroid-binding globulin levels change with estrogen or liver disease; they are not a primary compensatory mechanism for gland failure.
Somatostatin inhibits TSH; decreased production would favor TSH release, but the primary driver of TSH elevation in Hashimoto is the loss of T3/T4 feedback, not hypothalamic somatostatin changes.
Inhibition of conversion would worsen the hypothyroid state; the body usually prioritizes T3 production in mild failure.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): As hypothyroidism supervenes, T4 and T3 levels fall, accompanied by a compensatory increase in TSH.

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
coreConcept: Preceding Viral Triggers in Subacute Thyroiditis
statement: An adult patient presents with a painful, enlarged thyroid gland that developed shortly after a viral cold. Which clinical history finding is most characteristic for this specific type of inflammatory thyroid disease?
options: A long-standing history of dietary iodine deficiency
Concurrent diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus
A preceding upper respiratory infection
A recent history of childbirth within the last month
Prior exposure to therapeutic ionizing radiation to the neck
correctOption: A preceding upper respiratory infection
optionExplanations: Iodine deficiency leads to compensatory hypertrophy (goiter) but not to an acute inflammatory granulomatous process.

While Hashimoto thyroiditis is associated with other autoimmune diseases like SLE, granulomatous thyroiditis is a virus-triggered, self-limited condition not primarily linked to systemic autoimmunity syndromes.
Granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis is believed to be triggered by a viral infection and is frequently preceded by an upper respiratory tract infection.
Postpartum thyroiditis is a variant of subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis, which is typically painless, unlike the granulomatous form which is the most common cause of thyroid pain.
Radiation exposure is a major risk factor for thyroid neoplasia (papillary carcinoma), not granulomatous inflammation.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): The majority of patients have a history of an upper respiratory infection just before the onset of thyroiditis.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: In the histopathological evaluation of a suspected parathyroid adenoma, which feature most effectively distinguishes it from primary parathyroid hyperplasia?
options: The presence of delicate fibrous strands enveloping cell nodules
An overall lesion weight that remains below 1.0 gram
A rim of compressed, non-neoplastic parathyroid tissue at the edge
The absence of stromal adipose tissue within the lesion
The presence of predominantly chief cells rather than oxyphil cells
correctOption: A rim of compressed, non-neoplastic parathyroid tissue at the edge
optionExplanations: Delicate fibrous strands can be seen in hyperplasia, particularly in the nodular pattern, and do not definitively identify an adenoma.
Adenomas typically weigh between 0.5 to 5 grams, whereas the combined weight of hyperplastic glands is often less than 1 gram.
Adenomas are typically solitary and compress the adjacent normal gland tissue into a visible rim, a feature usually absent in multiglandular hyperplasia.
The loss of stromal fat is a characteristic of both hyperplastic and adenomatous parathyroid tissue, making it a shared rather than distinguishing feature.
Chief cells predominate in both adenomas and hyperplasia, so their presence does not distinguish between the two entities.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): A rim of compressed, non-neoplastic parathyroid tissue, generally separated by a fibrous capsule, is often visible at the edge of the adenoma.

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
coreConcept: Risk Factors for Abnormal Implantation Sites
statement: A 30-year-old woman is found to have a twofold increased risk for ectopic pregnancy. Which factor in her medical history is most likely responsible for this specific statistical increase?
options: Prior history of gestational diabetes
Current status as a heavy cigarette smoker
Diagnosis of polycystic ovarian syndrome
Use of an intrauterine contraceptive device
Prolonged use of oral contraceptive pills
correctOption: Use of an intrauterine contraceptive device
optionExplanations: Gestational diabetes is a complication of late pregnancy and is not a established risk factor for abnormal implantation sites.
Smoking is a major risk factor for squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts but is not specifically cited as a 'twofold' risk factor for ectopic pregnancy in this text.
PCOS is associated with anovulation and infertility, not a specific twofold increase in ectopic placental implantation.
The use of an IUD increases the risk of ectopic pregnancy significantly if a pregnancy does occur, likely due to altered tubal motility or local inflammation.
Oral contraceptives generally reduce the risk of all pregnancies, including ectopics, by inhibiting ovulation.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1027 (Book Page): Another risk factor is use of an intrauterine contraceptive device, which is associated with a twofold increase in ectopic pregnancy.

category: Define thyroiditis
statement: A 60-year-old male presents with a hard, fixed anterior neck mass that clinically mimics an invasive thyroid carcinoma. Biopsy reveals dense fibrosis extending into adjacent muscles. This presentation of Riedel thyroiditis is now recognized as part of the spectrum of:
options: Mumps virus infection
Congenital biosynthetic defects
Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2
IgG4-related disease
Post-radiation necrosis
correctOption: IgG4-related disease
optionExplanations: Mumps is a viral trigger for de Quervain (granulomatous) thyroiditis, not the rare fibrosing Riedel thyroiditis.
Congenital biosynthetic defects (dyshormonogenetic goiter) lead to goitrous enlargement but not the infiltrative fibrosis seen in Riedel thyroiditis.
MEN-2 is associated with medullary thyroid carcinoma, which involves C-cell hyperplasia, not systemic fibrosing syndromes.
Riedel thyroiditis is considered a localized manifestation of IgG4-related disease, characterized by dense fibrosis and IgG4-secreting plasma cells.
Radiation can cause fibrosis and hypothyroidism, but Riedel thyroiditis is a specific idiopathic/autoimmune fibrotic syndrome, not usually caused by external radiation therapy.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): ...Riedel thyroiditis, a rare disorder characterized by extensive fibrosis involving the thyroid and contiguous neck structures. ... appears to be another manifestation of IgG4-related disease, which is associated with fibrosis and tissue infiltration by plasma cells producing IgG4.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
coreConcept: Diagnosis of Chronic Pelvic Pain Syndrome (CPPS)
statement: A 30-year-old male athlete presents with chronic perineal discomfort and suprapubic pain. He has no history of recurrent urinary tract infections. Expressed prostatic secretions demonstrate 15 leukocytes per high-power field, but repeated bacterial cultures are negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Chronic bacterial prostatitis
Granulomatous prostatitis
Chronic abacterial prostatitis
Acute bacterial prostatitis
IgG4-associated autoimmune prostatitis
correctOption: Chronic abacterial prostatitis
optionExplanations: Chronic bacterial prostatitis requires a history of recurrent UTIs and positive cultures from expressed prostatic secretions or urine.
Granulomatous prostatitis is often iatrogenic (BCG therapy) or fungal and would show distinct granulomas rather than simple non-specific leukocytosis.
Chronic abacterial prostatitis (CPPS) is the most common prostatic inflammation; it presents with leukocytosis in secretions (>10 WBC/HPF) but negative cultures and no history of recurrent UTI.
Acute bacterial prostatitis presents with fever, chills, and exquisitely tender, boggy prostate, along with positive urine cultures.
IgG4-associated prostatitis is a specific systemic autoimmune manifestation associated with plasma cell infiltrates and high serum IgG4, not typical for this clinical presentation.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 975 (Book Page): Chronic abacterial prostatitis, the most common form of prostatitis, is often referred to clinically as chronic pelvic pain syndrome. It is indistinguishable from chronic bacterial prostatitis in terms of signs and symptoms, but there is no history of recurrent urinary tract infection.

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: In the physiological regulation of the thyroid axis, which molecule is deiodinated in the periphery to produce the hormone with the highest affinity for target cell receptors?
options: Thyrotropin (TSH)
Thyroxine (T4)
Reverse T3
Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH)
Thyroglobulin
correctOption: Thyroxine (T4)
optionExplanations: TSH is a pituitary glycoprotein that acts on the thyroid follicular cell membrane receptor; it does not bind to nuclear receptors in target tissues like T3.
T4 is the primary secretory product of the thyroid but acts as a pro-hormone. Its deiodination in peripheral tissues produces T3, which is the active form with much higher receptor affinity.
Reverse T3 is a metabolically inactive byproduct of T4 deiodination and does not possess high affinity for receptors to initiate transcription.
TRH is a hypothalamic tripeptide that stimulates the pituitary; it is not a thyroid hormone and does not undergo deiodination for receptor affinity.
Thyroglobulin is a large storage protein within the thyroid follicle. It is proteolytically cleaved to release T4 and T3 into the blood but does not circulate as a hormone.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1073 (Book Page): In the periphery, the majority of free T4 is deiodinated to T3; the latter binds to thyroid hormone nuclear receptors in target cells with tenfold greater affinity than does T4.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
statement: How does preoperative administration of iodine solutions classically affect the morphology of the thyroid gland in a patient with Graves disease?
options: It increases epithelial hypertrophy and hyperplasia
It induces involution of the epithelium and colloid accumulation
It promotes the formation of new germinal centers
It stimulates the transformation of follicular cells into Hürthle cells
It triggers massive hemorrhagic necrosis of the follicles
correctOption: It induces involution of the epithelium and colloid accumulation
optionExplanations: Hyperplasia is increased by thionamides like propylthiouracil (due to rising TSH), not by iodine which has an inhibitory effect.

Iodine blocks the release of thyroid hormone and causes the hyperactive, tall columnar epithelium to become flatter and the follicles to fill with colloid, making the gland less vascular and firmer for surgery.
Iodine does not stimulate lymphoid proliferation; lymphoid infiltrates are a result of the primary autoimmune process.
Hürthle cell metaplasia is a feature of chronic injury classically seen in Hashimoto thyroiditis, not an effect of acute iodine administration.
Iodine is used to stabilize the gland; hemorrhagic necrosis is an acute destructive process unrelated to iodine therapy.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): Administration of iodine causes involution of the epithelium and the accumulation of colloid by blocking thyroglobulin secretion.

category: Hashimoto Thyroiditis ii
coreConcept: Endocrinologic Profiles of Autoimmune Thyroid Failure
statement: A patient with suspected Hashimoto thyroiditis undergoes a comprehensive evaluation. During the phase of overt thyroid failure, which combination of laboratory findings is most likely?
options: High TSH, low T3/T4, low radioactive iodine uptake
Normal TSH, normal T3/T4, presence of granulomas
High TSH, high T3/T4, low radioactive iodine uptake
Low TSH, high T3/T4, high radioactive iodine uptake
Low TSH, low T3/T4, high radioactive iodine uptake
correctOption: High TSH, low T3/T4, low radioactive iodine uptake
optionExplanations: In chronic Hashimoto, the gland cannot produce hormone (low T3/T4), and the pituitary responds by increasing TSH. Radioactive iodine uptake is low because the follicles are destroyed/atrophic.
Normal labs would suggest a euthyroid state or early subclinical disease, and granulomas are characteristic of De Quervain thyroiditis, not Hashimoto.
This is a physiologically discordant set of values; a high TSH should result in high T3/T4 only in rare TSH-secreting pituitary adenomas.
This profile describes Graves disease, where the gland is hyperfunctional and overproducing hormone.
Low TSH and low T3/T4 describe secondary (central) hypothyroidism due to pituitary or hypothalamic failure, not a primary thyroid disease like Hashimoto.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): As hypothyroidism supervenes, T 4 and T 3 levels fall, accompanied by a compensatory increase in TSH.

category: Hashimoto Thyroiditis ii
statement: A 52-year-old female presents with a painless, diffuse enlargement of the neck. Laboratory studies reveal an elevated serum TSH and the presence of anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient in an iodine-sufficient region?
options: Diffuse nontoxic goiter
Hashimoto thyroiditis
De Quervain thyroiditis
Riedel thyroiditis
Graves disease
correctOption: Hashimoto thyroiditis
optionExplanations: Diffuse nontoxic goiter involves enlargement due to iodine deficiency or goitrogens, but does not typically involve the specific autoimmune markers seen in Hashimoto.
Hashimoto thyroiditis is the primary cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-replete areas, characterized by autoimmune destruction and specific autoantibodies like anti-TPO.
De Quervain (granulomatous) thyroiditis usually presents with significant pain and is often preceded by a viral upper respiratory infection, rather than painless chronic failure.
Riedel thyroiditis is a rare manifestation of IgG4-related disease involving dense fibrosis that extends beyond the thyroid capsule, unlike the parenchymal destruction in Hashimoto.
Graves disease is an autoimmune condition but typically results in hyperthyroidism due to thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI), not primary hypothyroidism with elevated TSH.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1076 (Book Page): Hashimoto thyroiditis is an autoimmune disease that results in destruction of the thyroid gland and gradual and progressive thyroid failure. It is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in areas of the world where iodine levels are sufficient.

category: Describe salient morphological features of clinically significant subtypes of thyroiditis: i
statement: What is the characteristic color and consistency of the cut surface of a thyroid gland affected by Hashimoto thyroiditis?
options: Dark brown and necrotic with hemorrhagic sacs
Gelatinous and rich in sticky glycoproteins
Pale, yellow-tan, firm, and somewhat nodular
Brown, glassy, and translucent
Beefy deep red and soft
correctOption: Pale, yellow-tan, firm, and somewhat nodular
optionExplanations: Dark brown and necrotic with hemorrhage describes a gland in Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (adrenal) or perhaps a massive thyroid infarct, but not Hashimoto.
Gelatinous and rich in glycoproteins describes the appearance of mucinous tumors or perhaps large colloid-rich goiters.
The gross appearance of Hashimoto thyroiditis is pale and yellow-tan due to the dense lymphocytic infiltrate and the relative lack of red colloid-filled follicles.
Brown, glassy, and translucent is the description for a colloid goiter undergoing involution.
Beefy red and soft is characteristic of the thyroid in Graves disease due to hypervascularity.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1077 (Book Page): [The cut surface is pale, yellow-tan, firm, and somewhat nodular.]

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
statement: Preoperative treatment of a Grave’s patient with Propylthiouracil results in which morphological alteration of the thyroid gland?
options: Exaggeration of epithelial hypertrophy and hyperplasia
Involution of the follicular epithelium to a flattened state
Complete resolution of the lymphoid infiltrates
Increased accumulation of thick, darkly staining colloid
Reduction in the size and number of germinal centers
correctOption: Exaggeration of epithelial hypertrophy and hyperplasia
optionExplanations: Propylthiouracil blocks hormone synthesis, which reduces feedback inhibition and leads to a compensatory rise in TSH, worsening the hyperplasia.
Flattened epithelium is seen after iodine treatment, which causes involution, not after propylthiouracil.
Propylthiouracil does not target the autoimmune lymphocytic infiltrates responsible for the disease.
Colloid accumulation is a feature of iodine-induced involution, while propylthiouracil reduces hormone synthesis.
The lymphoid response remains largely unchanged by standard thionamide therapy which targets hormone synthesis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1081 (Book Page): [Treatment with the antithyroid drug propylthiouracil exaggerates the epithelial hypertrophy and hyperplasia by stimulating TSH secretion.]

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
coreConcept: Hypercalcemia of Malignancy vs Primary Hyperparathyroidism
statement: An 80-year-old male smoker with a history of weight loss and a cough is found to have a serum calcium of 14.2 mg/dL. His serum PTH level is undetectable (below 5 pg/mL). Which mechanism is most likely responsible for his hypercalcemia?
options: Formation of multiple brown tumors in medullary bone
Secretion of PTH-related protein (PTHrP) by a neoplasm
Mutational inactivation of the AIRE gene
Constitutive activation of the TSH receptor
Loss-of-function mutation in the Calcium-Sensing Receptor (CASR)
correctOption: Secretion of PTH-related protein (PTHrP) by a neoplasm
optionExplanations: Brown tumors are a consequence of severe hyperparathyroidism (which involves high PTH), not a primary cause of hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH.
Severe hypercalcemia in an elderly smoker with suppressed PTH strongly suggests hypercalcemia of malignancy, most often mediated by PTHrP from a squamous cell lung carcinoma.
AIRE gene mutations cause Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome Type 1, which typically presents with hypoparathyroidism (hypocalcemia), not hypercalcemia.
Activation of the TSH receptor causes hyperthyroidism, which can cause mild hypercalcemia through high bone turnover, but not severe hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH in this context.
Loss-of-function mutations in CASR lead to familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia, which is associated with inappropriately normal or high PTH, not suppressed PTH.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1094 (Book Page): [The most common mechanism (in ~80% of cases) through which osteolytic tumors induce hypercalcemia is by secretion of PTH-related peptide (PTHrP).]

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
statement: In the context of dysfunctional uterine bleeding, what is the primary pathophysiological consequence of an anovulatory cycle?
options: Acute neutrophilic infiltration of the stroma due to retained products of conception.
Premature dissolution of the corpus luteum leading to a drop in progesterone.
Inhibition of the estrogen receptor by stromal cell-derived growth factors.
Rapid growth of the basalis layer leading to failure of the functionalis to shed.
Excessive endometrial stimulation by estrogens that is unopposed by progesterone.
correctOption: Excessive endometrial stimulation by estrogens that is unopposed by progesterone.
optionExplanations: Neutrophilic infiltration is a feature of acute endometritis, which is a structural/infectious cause of bleeding, not a hormonal anovulatory mechanism.
In an anovulatory cycle, a corpus luteum is never formed, so it cannot undergo premature dissolution.
Growth factors from the stroma actually promote estrogen's effect on glandular proliferation rather than inhibiting the receptor.
The functionalis layer is the part that is shed during the cycle; the basalis provides the stem cells for regeneration but does not cause DUB by overgrowth.
Without ovulation, there is no progesterone to induce secretory differentiation, leaving the endometrium in a persistent, proliferative state driven solely by estrogen.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1001 (Book Page): Failure of ovulation results in excessive endometrial stimulation by estrogens that is unopposed by progesterone.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Diffuse and Multinodular goiter
statement: What is the primary role of goitrogens found in vegetables of the Brassicaceae family, such as cabbage and turnips, in the development of endemic goiter?
options: They stimulate the production of antibodies against thyroid peroxidase.
They contain thiocyanates that interfere with the transport of iodide into the gland.
They irreversibly bind to thyroglobulin, preventing hormone release.
They destroy thyroid follicular cells directly via toxic metabolites.
They act as molecular mimics of TSH, causing receptor downregulation.
correctOption: They contain thiocyanates that interfere with the transport of iodide into the gland.
optionExplanations: Dietary goitrogens do not induce autoimmunity; goiter formed through this mechanism is nutritional/toxic, not autoimmune.

Goitrogens like those found in cassava and the Brassicaceae family contain thiocyanates. These compounds competitively inhibit the iodide pump, preventing the gland from capturing the iodide needed for hormone synthesis.
While some goitrogens may interfere with organification, the specific role mentioned for the most potent goitrogens (like those in cassava) is the inhibition of iodide transport.
Dietary goitrogens do not cause direct follicular destruction; they act biochemically to impair hormone production pathways.
Goitrogens do not act as TSH mimics; they decrease thyroid hormone, which leads to a secondary rise in endogenous TSH.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1081 (Book Page): Cassava contains a thiocyanate that inhibits iodide transport within the thyroid, worsening any concurrent iodine deficiency.

category: Enumerate clinical manifestations along with hormone levels of anterior pituitary
statement: A patient with a lactotroph adenoma is prescribed bromocriptine to reduce the size of the lesion. This pharmacological intervention works by mimicking the effect of which hypothalamic factor?
options: Dopamine
Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH)
Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)
Growth hormone–releasing hormone (GHRH)
Somatostatin
correctOption: Dopamine
optionExplanations: Dopamine is the primary hypothalamic inhibitory factor for prolactin. Bromocriptine acts as an agonist at dopamine receptors, inhibiting prolactin release and shrinking the tumor.
TRH stimulates TSH and can also stimulate prolactin, but it is not the factor mimicked by bromocriptine to treat tumors.
GnRH stimulates the release of LH and FSH; its agonists are used for different indications, such as prostate cancer or endometriosis.
GHRH stimulates the somatotrophs to release growth hormone and is not involved in the inhibitory regulation of lactotrophs.
Somatostatin inhibits growth hormone and TSH release. Analogues like octreotide are used for somatotroph adenomas, not lactotroph adenomas.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1068 (Book Page): [Lactotroph adenomas are treated by surgery or, more commonly, with bromocriptine, a dopamine receptor agonist that causes the lesions to diminish in size.]

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
coreConcept: Infectious Causes and Morphology of Addison Disease
statement: A 50-year-old male with a history of recurrent pulmonary infections and night sweats presents with extreme lethargy and hypotension. An autopsy performed after his death from respiratory failure reveals adrenal glands that are significantly enlarged and contain numerous areas of caseous necrosis. Which is the most likely diagnosis for the adrenal pathology?
options: Primary amyloidosis
Metastatic adenocarcinoma
Hemorrhagic infarction
Tuberculous adrenalitis
Autoimmune adrenalitis
correctOption: Tuberculous adrenalitis
optionExplanations: Amyloidosis results in firm, waxy glands with extracellular protein deposition, not caseous necrosis or granulomas.
Metastatic disease can enlarge the glands, but it usually replaces them with tumor nests rather than classical caseous (cheeselike) necrosis.
Hemorrhagic infarction (Waterhouse-Friderichsen) presents as sacs of blood and is associated with acute sepsis, not a chronic history of pulmonary disease and night sweats.

Tuberculosis causes enlargement of the glands (initially) and classical caseating granulomatous inflammation. The patient's history of pulmonary infection and night sweats strongly supports this etiology.
Autoimmune adrenalitis results in shrunken, small glands, not the enlargement and caseous necrosis described here.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1121 (Book Page): Tuberculous adrenalitis... When present, tuberculous adrenalitis is usually associated with active infection in other sites, particularly in the lungs and genitourinary tract.

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: Which laboratory measurement is recognized as the most sensitive screening modality for the initial detection of hyperthyroidism in most clinical settings?
options: Thyroid-binding globulin (TBG)
Serum thyrotropin (TSH) concentration
Total triiodothyronine (T3)
Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI)
Free thyroxine (T4)
correctOption: Serum thyrotropin (TSH) concentration
optionExplanations: TBG is the carrier protein for thyroid hormones. Levels of TBG change in various physiological states (like pregnancy) but do not indicate the functional status of the thyroid gland or the presence of hyperthyroidism directly.

Due to the exquisite sensitivity of the pituitary-thyroid axis, even minute increases in circulating thyroid hormones lead to a profound suppression of TSH. Consequently, a low TSH is the most reliable indicator of thyroid hormone excess.

Total T3 levels can be elevated in hyperthyroidism, but they are often influenced by changes in binding proteins. T3 is less sensitive than TSH for early detection, although it is useful in cases of isolated 'T3 toxicosis'.

TSI is a specific marker for Graves disease. While highly diagnostic for that specific condition, it is not used as a general screening test for hyperthyroidism, which can have multiple other etiologies such as toxic multinodular goiters.

Free T4 is elevated in overt hyperthyroidism, but in subclinical cases, it may still be within the normal reference range. TSH changes occur much earlier and more dramatically due to the sensitivity of the pituitary feedback loop.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1075 (Book Page): The measurement of serum TSH concentration is the most useful single screening test for hyperthyroidism, because its levels are decreased even at the earliest stages

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
statement: A 28-year-old female presents with a 2-cm pituitary adenoma and a serum prolactin level of 45 ng/mL (Normal < 25). She has bitemporal hemianopsia. Following surgical resection, the tumor is found to express only FSH and LH. What explains the pre-operative hyperprolactinemia?
options: The patient has a co-existing somatotroph microadenoma
Primary hypothyroidism causing thyrotroph hyperplasia
Stalk effect due to mass compression of the hypothalamus
The tumor was a mammosomatotroph adenoma
Ectopic prolactin secretion by the gonadotroph cells
correctOption: Stalk effect due to mass compression of the hypothalamus
optionExplanations: While co-existing tumors are possible in MEN-1, the 'stalk effect' is a much more common cause of mild prolactin elevation with a large non-PRL mass.
Primary hypothyroidism can raise prolactin via TRH, but the presence of a 2-cm mass causing visual defects points to stalk effect.
The stalk effect occurs when a large mass (like a 2-cm gonadotroph adenoma) blocks the transport of dopamine (prolactin inhibitory factor) from the hypothalamus to the anterior pituitary.
Mammosomatotroph adenomas express GH and PRL, but the IHC in this case only showed gonadotropins (FSH/LH).
Gonadotroph cells do not typically secrete prolactin; ectopic secretion is not a feature of standard classification.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1069 (Book Page): Any suprasellar mass (e.g., a pituitary adenoma) may disturb the inhibitory influence of the hypothalamus on prolactin secretion, resulting in hyperprolactinemia. Therefore, mild hyperprolactenemia in a person with a pituitary adenoma does not necessarily indicate a prolactin-secreting tumor.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
statement: Which of the following systemic conditions causes diabetes mellitus by damaging the pancreas and is classified under 'Exocrine Pancreatic Defects' due to excessive iron accumulation?
options: Cystic fibrosis
Chronic autoimmune pancreatitis
Wilson disease
Hemochromatosis
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
correctOption: Hemochromatosis
optionExplanations: Cystic fibrosis does cause DM via exocrine damage, but it occurs due to mucous plugging and fibrosis, not iron accumulation.
Autoimmune pancreatitis is a form of inflammation, but it is not defined by iron accumulation like hemochromatosis.
Wilson disease involves the toxic accumulation of copper, mainly in the liver and brain, and is not a common cause of secondary diabetes.
Correct. Hemochromatosis involves excessive iron deposition ('bronze diabetes') which causes structural damage to the pancreas, placing it in the exocrine defect category.
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency primarily affects the lungs (emphysema) and liver (cirrhosis), not the pancreatic islets.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1097 (Book Page): Table 24.6: Exocrine Pancreatic Defects: ...Hemochromatosis

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: A 45-year-old male with sarcoidosis presents with symptomatic hypercalcemia. What is the mechanism for the elevated calcium levels in this patient?
options: Paraneoplastic secretion of PTH-related protein by activated macrophages
Ectopic secretion of native parathyroid hormone by pulmonary lesions
Hypensitivity of the calcium-sensing receptor to circulating vitamin D
Destruction of bone by direct infiltration of sarcoid non-caseating granulomas
PTH-independent conversion of vitamin D to its active form in granulomas
correctOption: PTH-independent conversion of vitamin D to its active form in granulomas
optionExplanations: Activated macrophages in sarcoidosis produce active vitamin D, not PTHrP; PTHrP is primarily a product of malignant epithelial cells.
Ectopic production of native PTH is extremely rare and is not a feature of sarcoidosis.
The calcium-sensing receptor is not hypersensitive to vitamin D; it is the increased levels of active vitamin D that drive the calcium elevation.
While sarcoid can involve bone, the hypercalcemia is typically a systemic metabolic effect of vitamin D overproduction rather than localized lytic bone destruction.

Macrophages within granulomatous lesions (like sarcoidosis) express alpha-1-hydroxylase, which converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, leading to increased intestinal calcium absorption.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1094 (Book Page): steatorrhea, and vitamin D deficiency, may also cause this disorder... [Context of Vitamin D pathway] Page 1073 (Book Page): conversion of vitamin D to its active dihydroxy form in the kidneys

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
statement: A patient undergoing evaluation for a suspected ectopic pregnancy has an endometrial biopsy. Which finding is most consistent with a gestation located at an extrauterine site?
options: Extensive Hürthle cell metaplasia of the endometrial glands
Decidua without the presence of chorionic villi
The presence of mature chorionic villi within the uterine cavity
Absence of any decidual changes in the uterine stroma
Squamous metaplasia of the endometrial lining
correctOption: Decidua without the presence of chorionic villi
optionExplanations: Hürthle cell metaplasia is a feature of thyroid pathology (Hashimoto thyroiditis) and is unrelated to gestational disorders.

In ectopic pregnancy, the uterus responds to pregnancy hormones by forming a decidua, but since the implantation site is extrauterine, the biopsy will show decidualized stroma without any chorionic villi.
The presence of chorionic villi in the uterus would indicate an intrauterine pregnancy (either viable or a miscarriage), not an ectopic one.
Decidual changes typically occur in the uterus during ectopic pregnancy due to the systemic effects of circulating progesterone.
Squamous metaplasia is not a characteristic finding of the gestational endometrium.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1029 (Book Page): endometrial biopsy (which shows decidua without chorionic villi or implantation site)

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
statement: A 1-year-old boy is diagnosed with cryptorchidism during a routine physical examination. Statistical data suggests that while the testis can arrest anywhere along its pathway of descent, a specific anatomical location is the most frequent site of arrest. Which of the following is the most common site for an undescended testis?
options: Obturator foramen
Superficial inguinal ring
Abdominal cavity
Femoral canal
Inguinal canal
correctOption: Inguinal canal
optionExplanations: The obturator foramen is located in the pelvis and is not involved in the standard embryological pathway of the testis into the scrotum.
While the testis passes through the superficial ring, the canal itself remains the most statistically common site of arrest.
Arrest within the abdomen is relatively uncommon, occurring in only approximately 5% to 10% of cryptorchidism cases.
The femoral canal is not a typical pathway for testicular descent and is associated with femoral hernias rather than undescended testes.
The inguinal canal represents the most frequent site of arrest for a testis failing to reach the scrotal sac during the second phase of descent.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 964 (Book Page): the most common site is in the inguinal canal, while arrest within the abdomen is uncommon, accounting for approximately 5% to 10% of cases.

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
statement: During a colposcopic examination of the cervix, a clinician notes a 'strawberry cervix' appearance. Which infectious agent is associated with this specific finding and its related discharge characteristics?
options: Trichomonas vaginalis with a yellow, frothy discharge
Ureaplasma urealyticum with a thin, watery discharge
Gardnerella vaginalis with a fishy, green-gray discharge
Candida albicans with a curdlike, white discharge
Chlamydia trachomatis with a purulent, endocervical discharge
correctOption: Trichomonas vaginalis with a yellow, frothy discharge
optionExplanations: Trichomonas vaginalis causes marked vessel dilation in the cervical mucosa, creating the 'strawberry' appearance, often accompanied by frothy yellow discharge.
Ureaplasma urealyticum is a cause of nongonococcal cervicitis but is not traditionally associated with the fiery-red punctate appearance of the cervix.
Gardnerella vaginalis is associated with bacterial vaginosis and a fishy odor, but does not typically cause the vascular dilation seen in a strawberry cervix.
Candida albicans causes erythema and pruritus with a thick, white discharge, but the classic punctate hemorrhages of the strawberry cervix are absent.
Chlamydia trachomatis causes cervicitis and salpingitis, but its presentation is usually less vascular and more focused on mucopurulent endocervical findings.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 987 (Book Page): The vaginal and cervical mucosa typically has a fiery-red appearance, with marked dilation of cervical mucosal vessels resulting in characteristic colposcopic appearance of “strawberry cervix.”

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
statement: The most common congenital cause of male infertility, which involves incomplete testicular descent, is identified in what percentage of 1-year-old boys?
options: Approximately 5%
Approximately 1%
Approximately 0.1%
Approximately 10%
Approximately 25%
correctOption: Approximately 1%
optionExplanations: 5% represents the estimated incidence at birth, but many cases resolve as the testes descend during the first year of life.
While the incidence is higher at birth (up to 5%), most testes descend spontaneously within the first year, leaving a prevalence of about 1% at age one.
0.1% is a significant underestimation of the clinical prevalence of cryptorchidism in infants.
10% is a figure often associated with premature male infants, but it does not represent the prevalence in the general 1-year-old population.
25% refers to the subset of cryptorchidism patients who have bilateral involvement, rather than the incidence in the general population.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 966 (Book Page): It is found in approximately 1% of 1-year-old boys.

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: What clinical sign is elicited by inflating a blood pressure cuff above systolic pressure for several minutes in a patient with suspected hypoparathyroidism?
options: Plummer syndrome
Superior vena cava syndrome
Chvostek sign
Trousseau sign
von Recklinghausen sign
correctOption: Trousseau sign
optionExplanations: Plummer syndrome refers to toxic multinodular goiter, which is a cause of hyperthyroidism.
Superior vena cava syndrome is caused by mass compression of the vessel, often by a large goiter or tumor, not hypocalcemia.
Chvostek sign is elicited by tapping the facial nerve, causing facial muscle contraction, not by a blood pressure cuff.
Trousseau sign is a carpal spasm resulting from neuromuscular irritability in hypocalcemic states (like hypoparathyroidism) during ischemia induced by a cuff.

While von Recklinghausen's name is associated with osteitis fibrosa cystica (bone disease in hyperparathyroidism), there is no specific 'sign' elicited by a blood pressure cuff with this name in this context.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1095 (Book Page): [Trousseau sign refers to carpal spasms produced by occlusion of the circulation to the distal arm with a blood pressure cuff for several minutes.]

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
coreConcept: Endometriosis as a Cause of Infertility
statement: How does the clinical presentation of infertility in patients with endometriosis contrast with that of patients with simple pelvic infections?
options: Endometriosis is exclusively associated with vaginal discharge
Simple infections are always caused by E-cadherin mutations
Endometriosis results in the thinning of the endometrial stroma
Simple infections typically cause chocolate cysts of the ovary
Infertility is the presenting complaint in 30% to 40% of endometriosis cases
correctOption: Infertility is the presenting complaint in 30% to 40% of endometriosis cases
optionExplanations: Vaginal discharge is a hallmark of infections like trichomoniasis or bacterial vaginosis, not a specific clinical feature of endometriosis.
E-cadherin (CDH1) mutations are associated with lobular carcinoma, while pelvic infections are microbial (e.g., Gonococcus, Chlamydia).
Endometriosis involves the presence of ectopic glands and stroma, whereas thinning of the native stroma is more typical of endometrial atrophy.
Chocolate cysts (endometriomas) are a classic morphologic feature of endometriosis resulting from internal bleeding, not simple infections.
The text explicitly states that 30% to 40% of women with endometriosis present primarily with infertility, often accompanied by severe dysmenorrhea and pelvic pain.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1005 (Book Page): Menstrual irregularities are common, and infertility is the presenting complaint in 30% to 40% of women.

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: A neonate is born with severe intellectual disability, short stature, and a protruding tongue. The severity of this condition is primarily determined by the timing of maternal thyroid hormone deficiency. At what point in gestation is maternal deficiency most critical?
options: When dietary iodine is supplemented too early
Only after the fetal thyroid becomes functional
During the third trimester only
Immediately following parturition
Before the development of the fetal thyroid gland
correctOption: Before the development of the fetal thyroid gland
optionExplanations: Early iodine supplementation is protective and does not cause these developmental defects.
Once the fetal thyroid is functional, it can provide its own hormone, making maternal deficiency less catastrophic for brain development.
The third trimester is less critical than the early phase of organogenesis and brain development when the fetal gland is not yet online.
Postnatal deficiency results in myxedema, but the severe intellectual disability of cretinism originates in utero.
During early pregnancy, the fetus relies entirely on maternal T3/T4 for brain development. Deficiency at this stage leads to irreversible cretinism.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1076 (Book Page): [If there is maternal thyroid deficiency before the development of the fetal thyroid gland, intellectual disability is severe.]

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
statement: Regarding the gender distribution of granulomatous thyroiditis, which of the following is true?
options: There is a significant male predominance of approximately 10:1
It affects females four times more frequently than males
It is found exclusively in males older than 65 years of age
The distribution between males and females is essentially equal
It occurs only in parous women during the third trimester
correctOption: It affects females four times more frequently than males
optionExplanations: This is incorrect; thyroid inflammatory diseases almost universally show a female predominance.
Correct. The female-to-male ratio is explicitly stated as 4:1.
The peak age is 40-50, and it is more common in women, not exclusively elderly males.
A 1:1 distribution is not typical for thyroid inflammatory conditions, which usually favor women.
This statement describes granulomatous lobular mastitis (a breast condition), not subacute thyroiditis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): The disorder is most common between 40 and 50 years of age and, like other forms of thyroiditis, affects women more often than men (4 : 1).

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
statement: Microscopic examination of a thyroid gland from an untreated Graves' patient reveals follicles lined by tall, crowded columnar cells and colloid with a 'scalloped' margin. What does this scalloping represent?
options: Dystrophic calcification within the follicle lumen
Active resorption of colloid by hyperplastic follicular cells
Passive atrophy of the epithelium due to pressure
Accumulation of thick, inspissated thyroglobulin
Formation of true papillae with fibrovascular cores
correctOption: Active resorption of colloid by hyperplastic follicular cells
optionExplanations: Psammoma bodies or dystrophic calcifications are features of papillary carcinoma and are not found in the colloid of Graves' follicles.
Scalloping at the interface between the follicular cells and the colloid is a classic sign of rapid hormone production and active resorption of thyroglobulin for conversion into T3 and T4.
The epithelium in Graves' is hypertrophic and tall, which is the opposite of the flattened, inactive epithelium seen in passive atrophy or colloid involution.
Colloid in Graves' is typically pale and depleted due to high turnover, not thick or inspissated.
While the crowded cells may form small papillae-like projections, Graves' is distinguished by the absence of true fibrovascular cores in these projections.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1080 (Book Page): The colloid within the follicle lumen is pale, with scalloped margins. ... The crowded, enlarged epithelial cells project into the lumens of the follicles. These cells actively resorb the colloid.

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
statement: A woman is diagnosed with an abdominal pregnancy. Which anatomical event is responsible for the implantation of the fetus in this unusual site?
options: Perforation of the uterine fundus during initial implantation
Development of the fetus within a Gartner duct cyst
Failure of the fertilized ovum to enter the tube or dropping out of the fimbriated end
Direct attachment of the ovum to the serosa of the sigmoid colon
Fertilization occurring within the posterior cul-de-sac
correctOption: Failure of the fertilized ovum to enter the tube or dropping out of the fimbriated end
optionExplanations: Uterine perforation is a possible complication of an invasive mole but is not the mechanism for abdominal ectopic pregnancy.
Gartner duct cysts are remnants of the mesonephric duct and are not sites of fetal implantation.
Abdominal pregnancy is identified as occurring when the fertilized ovum either fails to enter the fallopian tube initially or slips out of the distal (fimbriated) end before reaching the uterus.
While the ovum may attach to various abdominal serosal surfaces, the clinical definition hinges on its failure to enter or stay within the tubal system.
While the sac may implant in the cul-de-sac, fertilization typically occurs in the tube before the ovum exits the fimbria into the abdomen.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1027 (Book Page): Abdominal pregnancies occur when the fertilized ovum fails to enter or drops out of the fimbriated end of the tube.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: What is the defining microscopic feature of 'Crooke hyaline change' observed in the anterior pituitary cells of patients with Cushing syndrome?
options: Accumulation of lipid-laden vacuoles in the cytoplasm of somatotrophs.
Deposition of amyloid derived from calcitonin polypeptides.
Prominent ring-like structures of basophilic ribonucleoproteins.
Extensive necrosis of the pituitary parenchyma followed by fibrosis.
Replacement of granular cytoplasm with homogeneous intermediate keratin filaments.
correctOption: Replacement of granular cytoplasm with homogeneous intermediate keratin filaments.
optionExplanations: Lipid accumulation is a feature of adrenal cells in certain states, not the pituitary response to high cortisol.
Amyloid deposition is characteristic of medullary thyroid carcinoma or insulinomas, not the pituitary in Cushing syndrome.
Basophilic cytoplasm is normal for corticotrophs; Crooke change involves a loss of these granules in favor of hyaline keratin.
This describes Sheehan syndrome (ischemic necrosis), which causes hypopituitarism, not Cushing syndrome.
Correct. Crooke hyaline change is the hallmark of the pituitary's response to high glucocorticoid levels, characterized by pale, homogeneous keratin filament accumulation.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1114 (Book Page): The most common alteration, resulting from high levels of endogenous or exogenous glucocorticoids, is termed Crooke hyaline change. In this condition, the normal granular, basophilic cytoplasm of the ACTH-producing cells in the anterior pituitary becomes homogeneous and paler. This alteration is the result of the accumulation of intermediate keratin filaments in the cytoplasm.

category: Hashimoto Thyroiditis ii
statement: Which specific autoantibodies are detected in the vast majority of patients with Hashimoto thyroiditis, indicating a breakdown in self-tolerance?
options: Anti-centromere antibodies
Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI)
Antithyroglobulin and antithyroid peroxidase
Antiacetylcholine receptor antibodies
Anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies
correctOption: Antithyroglobulin and antithyroid peroxidase
optionExplanations: Anti-centromere antibodies are typically associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome) and are not involved in Hashimoto thyroiditis.
TSI are the hallmark of Graves disease (hyperthyroidism), where they mimic TSH to stimulate the gland, rather than causing its destruction.
Thyroglobulin and thyroid peroxidase (TPO) are the two primary targets of the autoimmune response in Hashimoto thyroiditis; testing for these antibodies is a standard part of the diagnostic workup.
Antiacetylcholine receptor antibodies are specific for Myasthenia Gravis; while patients with Hashimoto are at risk for other autoimmune diseases, these are not thyroid-specific.
Anti-dsDNA antibodies are specific for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), which can coexist with Hashimoto but is not the marker for the thyroid disease itself.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1076 (Book Page): Hashimoto thyroiditis is caused by a breakdown in self-tolerance to thyroid autoantigens. This is exemplified by the presence of circulating autoantibodies against thyroglobulin and thyroid peroxidase in the vast majority of patients.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
statement: When distinguishing causes of sterility, how does the outcome of chronic nonspecific epididymitis differ histologically from simple cryptorchidism?
options: Sterility is only seen when the inflammation spreads to the prostate
Inflammatory causes result in the total disappearance of Leydig cells
Nonspecific epididymitis is characterized by the presence of Reinke crystalloids
Sterility in epididymitis results from extensive fibrous scarring of the tubules
Epididymitis uniquely preserves the basement membrane of the tubules
correctOption: Sterility in epididymitis results from extensive fibrous scarring of the tubules
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Sterility can occur from isolated epididymal or testicular involvement regardless of whether the prostate is affected.
Incorrect. Leydig cells are usually not destroyed in inflammation, meaning androgen production often remains relatively unaffected.
Incorrect. Reinke crystalloids are characteristic of Hilus cell (Leydig) tumors, not inflammatory conditions.

Correct. Unlike cryptorchidism which involves primary maturation arrest and basement membrane thickening, inflammatory causes like nonspecific epididymitis lead to secondary fibrous scarring which physically obstructs or destroys the ducts and tubules.
Incorrect. Basement membrane thickening is a feature of cryptorchidism, but inflammation typically damages the entire architecture rather than preserving it.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 968 (Book Page): Inflammation of the epididymis and testis is often followed by fibrous scarring, which may produce sterility.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Diffuse and Multinodular goiter
statement: Which molecular observation supports the theory that multinodular goiter arises from intrinsic variations in follicular cell growth potential?
options: Constitutive inactivation of the GNAS gene in every cell
Diffuse BRAF V600E mutations in all hyperplastic follicles
The presence of monoclonal nodules within the same gland
A total lack of response to TSH stimulation in all nodules
The universal presence of RET/PTC translocations
correctOption: The presence of monoclonal nodules within the same gland
optionExplanations: Activating (not inactivating) mutations of GNAS or TSHR are associated with autonomous nodules.
BRAF mutations are specific to papillary carcinoma (especially tall cell variant).
The coexistence of monoclonal and polyclonal populations suggests that some nodules arise from specific genetic advantages while others are reactive.
Nodules in MNG remain responsive to TSH early on; only autonomous ('toxic') nodules function independently later.
RET/PTC translocations are specific to papillary thyroid carcinoma, not goiter.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1082 (Book Page): Consistent with this model, both polyclonal and monoclonal nodules coexist within the same multinodular goiter, the latter presumably having arisen because of the acquisition of a genetic abnormality favoring growth.

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
statement: Which morphological feature, often identified on a Papanicolaou (Pap) smear, is the diagnostic hallmark of a Gardnerella vaginalis infection in the lower female genital tract?
