optionExplanations: Histoplasmosis typically causes adrenal enlargement with granulomatous inflammation and necrosis, not shrunken glands.
Tuberculosis results in enlarged glands with caseous necrosis and granulomas, often obliterating the architecture.
Irregularly shrunken glands with lymphoid (mononuclear) infiltrates and cortical cell depletion are classic features of autoimmune destruction.
Metastatic disease results in enlarged adrenal glands with the normal architecture obscured by the infiltrating tumor cells.
This condition involves multiple pigmented nodules and is associated with hypercortisolism (Cushing), not the insufficiency (Addison) seen here.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1122 (Book Page): Primary autoimmune adrenalitis is characterized by irregularly shrunken glands, which may be difficult to identify within the suprarenal adipose tissue. Histologically, the cortex contains only scattered residual cortical cells in a collapsed network of connective tissue. A variable lymphoid infiltrate is present in the cortex

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
statement: Which set of findings constitutes the classic systemic syndrome of preeclampsia?
options: Fever, vaginal discharge, and adnexal tenderness
Hypotension, bradycardia, and skin pallor
Hyperglycemia, ketonuria, and polyuria
Jaundice, pruritus, and dark-colored urine
Hypertension, edema, and proteinuria
correctOption: Hypertension, edema, and proteinuria
optionExplanations: This describes Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID), which is unrelated to gestational hypertensive disorders.
Preeclampsia is characterized by hypertension (high BP) and tachycardia may occur, but not hypotension or bradycardia.
This triad describes diabetes mellitus, which is a risk factor for preeclampsia but not the definition of the syndrome itself.
These are features of cholestasis of pregnancy or liver involvement, but do not constitute the primary diagnostic syndrome of preeclampsia.
The definitive clinical criteria for diagnosing preeclampsia are high blood pressure, fluid retention (edema), and protein in the urine.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1029 (Book Page): Preeclampsia is a systemic syndrome... that presents during pregnancy with hypertension, edema, and proteinuria.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: In the evaluation of a patient with multiple hard palpable breast masses, histological examination shows atrophic ducts and lobules with thickened basement membranes surrounded by a prominent lymphocytic infiltrate. This patient should be primarily screened for which of the following underlying systemic conditions?
options: Secondary hyperparathyroidism due to renal failure
Type 1 diabetes mellitus
Metabolic syndrome with truncal obesity
Overwhelming bacterial sepsis with Neisseria meningitidis
Hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome)
correctOption: Type 1 diabetes mellitus
optionExplanations: Secondary hyperparathyroidism leads to metastatic calcification (calciphylaxis), but the specific inflammatory/atrophic pattern of lymphocytic mastopathy is not related.
Lymphocytic mastopathy, or sclerosing lymphocytic lobulitis, is highly associated with type 1 diabetes and autoimmune thyroiditis, suggesting an autoimmune pathogenesis.
While metabolic syndrome is associated with type 2 diabetes, lymphocytic mastopathy is specifically linked to the autoimmune-mediated type 1 diabetes.
Neisseria meningitidis is the classic cause of Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (adrenal hemorrhage), not a chronic inflammatory breast disorder.
Lynch syndrome increases the risk of colorectal and endometrial cancers but has no known association with lymphocytic mastopathy.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1039 (Book Page): Lymphocytic Mastopathy... atrophic ducts and lobules with thickened basement membranes that are surrounded by a prominent lymphocytic infiltrate. This condition is most common in women with type 1 (insulin-dependent) diabetes or autoimmune thyroid disease.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Diffuse and Multinodular goiter
statement: Which of the following describes the primary compensatory mechanism responsible for the development of diffuse nontoxic goiter?
options: Antibody-mediated activation of the TSH receptor
Inflammatory destruction of the thyroid capsule leading to glandular expansion
Reduced thyroid hormone production triggering a rise in serum TSH
Direct stimulation of follicular cells by dietary goitrogens
Autonomous hypersecretion of triiodothyronine (T3) by follicular cells
correctOption: Reduced thyroid hormone production triggering a rise in serum TSH
optionExplanations: This describes Graves disease (TSI-mediated), not the pathogenesis of diffuse nontoxic goiter.
Goiter is a hyperplastic process, not an inflammatory or mechanical destruction of the capsule.
This is the classic feedback loop where low hormone levels stimulate TSH, causing follicular hypertrophy and hyperplasia.
Goitrogens interfere with synthesis but do not directly stimulate cells; the enlargement is mediated through TSH.
Autonomous secretion describes toxic nodules or adenomas, not the initial pathogenesis of simple goiter.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1080 (Book Page): Enlargement of the thyroid, or goiter, is caused by impaired synthesis of thyroid hormone, which is most often the result of dietary iodine deficiency. Reduced thyroid hormone production leads to a compensatory rise in the serum TSH level, which, in turn, causes hypertrophy and hyperplasia of thyroid follicular cells and, ultimately, enlargement of the thyroid gland.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
statement: A 50-year-old female with severe rheumatoid arthritis has been on high-dose dexamethasone therapy for years. She undergoes an emergency cholecystectomy but fails to receive supplemental steroid doses during the perioperative period. She becomes profoundly hypotensive and enters a state of shock. What is the most likely underlying reason for her collapse?
options: Acute adrenal crisis due to suppression of the HPA axis
Myocardial infarction secondary to corticosteroid-induced hyperlipidemia
Sudden autoimmune destruction of the remaining adrenal tissue
Acute sepsis from a surgical site infection
Primary hyperaldosteronism induced by surgical stress
correctOption: Acute adrenal crisis due to suppression of the HPA axis
optionExplanations: Long-term exogenous steroids cause the pituitary and adrenal glands to become inactive and atrophic. When a major stress (like surgery) occurs, the body needs extra cortisol but the atrophic glands cannot provide it, leading to a life-threatening 'crisis'.
Although steroids increase cardiovascular risk, the acute shock following surgical stress without steroid supplementation is the classic presentation of an adrenal crisis.
Her failure is not autoimmune; it is iatrogenic/secondary due to the long-term suppression of her own glands by the medication she was taking.
While sepsis causes hypotension, the timing immediately following a stressor without dose adjustment in a steroid-dependent patient points specifically to adrenal crisis.
Hyperaldosteronism would cause high blood pressure, not the profound hypotension seen in this patient's collapse.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1120 (Book Page): In patients maintained on exogenous corticosteroids, in whom rapid withdrawal of steroids or failure to increase steroid doses in response to an acute stress may precipitate an adrenal crisis because of the inability of the atrophic adrenals to produce glucocorticoid hormones.

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
statement: How does the pathogenesis of an ovarian pregnancy typically differ from other forms of ectopic implantation?
options: It involves the migration of the zygote through the patent Gartner duct
It results from fertilization and trapping of the ovum within the follicle
It is always associated with the use of intrauterine contraceptive devices
It requires the fertilized ovum to drop out of the fimbriated end
It occurs only in the presence of endometriosis-related chocolate cysts
correctOption: It results from fertilization and trapping of the ovum within the follicle
optionExplanations: The Gartner duct is a mesonephric remnant in the vaginal walls and is not involved in the mechanism of ectopic implantation in the ovary.
Unlike tubal ectopics that occur during transport, ovarian pregnancy typically occurs when the ovum is fertilized and remains trapped within the graafian follicle at the moment of rupture.
While IUDs are a risk factor for ectopics, the specific mechanism of follicular trapping is an independent event related to the timing of fertilization and rupture.
Dropping out of the fimbriated end is the mechanism specifically associated with abdominal pregnancies, not the primary mechanism for ovarian implantation.
Endometriosis increases the general risk of ectopic pregnancy through scarring, but it is not a mandatory prerequisite for the specific mechanism of follicular trapping.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1027 (Book Page): Ovarian pregnancy results from the fertilization and trapping of the ovum within the follicle just at the time of its rupture.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
statement: How is diabetes classified in a patient where hyperglycemia arises as a direct complication of an underlying Pheochromocytoma?
options: Endocrinopathy-associated diabetes
Type A insulin resistance
Exocrine pancreatic defect
Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
Genetic defect in β-cell function
correctOption: Endocrinopathy-associated diabetes
optionExplanations: Excess catecholamines from a pheochromocytoma antagonize insulin and increase glucose levels; this is categorized as diabetes secondary to an endocrinopathy.
Type A insulin resistance refers specifically to mutations in the insulin receptor, not antagonism by adrenal hormones.
Pheochromocytomas affect systemic hormones, not the structural integrity of the exocrine pancreas (like pancreatitis).
Type 2 DM is a primary disorder of insulin resistance and beta-cell dysfunction; if the cause is a specific other disease like pheochromocytoma, it is classified separately.
The defect is hormonal antagonism, not a primary genetic mutation in the beta cell's internal machinery (like MODY).
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1097 (Book Page): Table 24.6: Endocrinopathies: Acromegaly, Cushing syndrome, Hyperthyroidism, Pheochromocytoma, Glucagonoma.

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: Which clinicopathologic feature is the only reliable criterion for a definitive diagnosis of parathyroid carcinoma?
options: Total tumor weight exceeding 5 grams
Invasion of surrounding tissues or metastasis
The presence of mitotic figures in chief cells
Presence of a dense fibrous capsule
Marked nuclear and cellular pleomorphism
correctOption: Invasion of surrounding tissues or metastasis
optionExplanations: While carcinomas are often large, weight is not a definitive criterion, as large adenomas can also reach significant sizes.
In the parathyroid, cytologic features are notoriously poor predictors of behavior; only biologic evidence of spread (invasion or metastasis) is diagnostic.
Mitotic figures can occasionally be seen in adenomas and are not exclusive to malignancy in the parathyroid.
Both adenomas and carcinomas can have capsules; a dense capsule might be suggestive but is not a definitive diagnostic criterion.
Cytologic pleomorphism (endocrine atypia) is common in many benign endocrine tumors and is not a reliable sign of cancer.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1093 (Book Page): [Diagnosis of carcinoma based on cytologic detail is unreliable, and invasion of surrounding tissues and metastasis are the only reliable criteria.]

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: A 35-year-old woman, three weeks postpartum, presents with a swollen, erythematous, and warm right breast. The skin exhibits a pitted, orange-peel texture. Despite being treated for presumed acute mastitis with broad-spectrum antibiotics for one week, the symptoms persist. What morphological finding would most likely be identified on skin biopsy?
options: Staphylococcal clusters within the lactiferous sinuses
Atrophic lobules surrounded by dense collagenous stroma
Necrotic adipocytes surrounded by foamy macrophages and calcium deposits
Extensive keratin plugs obstructing the major nipple ducts
Malignant tumor emboli plugging dermal lymphovascular spaces
correctOption: Malignant tumor emboli plugging dermal lymphovascular spaces
optionExplanations: This would represent acute bacterial mastitis, but the failure to respond to antibiotics and the presence of peau d'orange suggests a malignant mimic.
This describes lymphocytic mastopathy, which typically presents as a hard mass without the inflammatory features described.
This describes the healing phase of fat necrosis, which usually presents as a firm localized mass rather than diffuse erythema.
Keratin plugs are the cause of SMULD, which presents as a subareolar mass and fistula, not diffuse peau d'orange.
The clinical 'peau d'orange' and persistent 'inflammation' are hallmarks of inflammatory carcinoma, where tumor emboli in dermal lymphatics cause lymphedema.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1056 (Book Page): This form of carcinoma has a characteristic gross appearance caused by extensive plugging of the lymphovascular spaces of the dermis with carcinoma cells and carries a very poor prognosis... The edematous skin is tethered to the breast by Cooper ligaments and mimics the surface of an orange peel, an appearance referred to as peau d’orange.

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
statement: The systemic maternal manifestations of preeclampsia, such as hypertension and proteinuria, are primarily driven by an imbalance of factors released into the circulation. What is the mechanistic role of soluble FMS-like tyrosine kinase (sFlt1) in this pathway?
options: Antagonism of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)
Stimulation of prostaglandin I2 (PGI2) production
Inhibition of fibrin thrombi formation in portal capillaries
Potentiation of nitric oxide release from endothelium
Direct activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system
correctOption: Antagonism of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)
optionExplanations: sFlt1 acts as a decoy receptor that binds and antagonizes VEGF, preventing its normal pro-angiogenic and endothelial-protective signals.
Women with preeclampsia show decreased endothelial production of PGI2, likely due to sFlt1 antagonizing VEGF (which normally stimulates PGI2).
sFlt1 promotes a pro-coagulant state rather than inhibiting thrombi formation.
sFlt1 leads to endothelial dysfunction, which actually decreases the production of vasodilators like nitric oxide.
sFlt1 is an anti-angiogenic factor; while hypertension occurs, it is not via primary direct activation of RAAS by sFlt1.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1030 (Book Page): the blood levels of two placenta-derived antiangiogenic factors, soluble FMS-like tyrosine kinase (sFltl) and endoglin, which antagonize the effects of VEGF and TGFβ, respectively, are several orders of magnitude higher in women with preeclampsia

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: Which of the following physiological triggers is responsible for stimulating the release of preformed antidiuretic hormone (ADH) from the posterior pituitary?
options: Increase in blood pressure sensed by baroreceptors
Increase in plasma osmotic pressure detected by osmoreceptors
Decrease in plasma osmotic pressure
Increased atrial distention
Excessive volume expansion in the venous system
correctOption: Increase in plasma osmotic pressure detected by osmoreceptors
optionExplanations: An increase in blood pressure inhibits ADH release; it is a decrease in BP that stimulates it.
Osmoreceptors sense high salt/solute concentration and trigger ADH release to resorb water and normalize the concentration.
A decrease in osmotic pressure would inhibit ADH release, as the body does not need to conserve more water.
Atrial distention indicates hypervolemia, which inhibits ADH secretion to promote diuresis.
Volume expansion inhibits ADH secretion to allow the excess fluid to be excreted in the urine.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1065 (Book Page): An increase in plasma osmotic pressure detected by osmoreceptors also triggers ADH secretion.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
statement: The likelihood of sparing a testis from orchiectomy is significantly increased if manual or surgical untwisting occurs within which maximum timeframe from the onset of symptoms?
options: 24 hours
2 hours
6 hours
12 hours
48 hours
correctOption: 6 hours
optionExplanations: By 24 hours, the testis is usually completely necrotic and soft, consisting of hemorrhagic tissue.
While 2 hours is better, 6 hours is the clinically accepted standard window for viability cited in pathology literature.
The 6-hour window is critical; beyond this, the risk of irreversible hemorrhagic infarction and necrosis increases substantially.
At 12 hours, the likelihood of irreversible infarction is very high, often requiring orchiectomy.
48 hours is well beyond the window of viability for the specialized germinal epithelium and parenchymal tissue.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 968 (Book Page): If the testis is manually untwisted within approximately 6 hours of the onset of torsion, the affected testis may be spared an orchiectomy.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: A 40-year-old male with a history of end-stage renal disease presents with severe bone pain. Histological analysis of all four parathyroid glands removed during surgery shows a diffuse increase in chief cells with scattered nests of cells containing abundant glycogen. What is the correct term for this glycogen-rich cellular variant?
options: Oncocytic metaplasia
Medullary differentiation
Water-clear cell hyperplasia
Squamous metaplasia
Hürthle cell change
correctOption: Water-clear cell hyperplasia
optionExplanations: Oncocytic metaplasia (oxyphil cells in the parathyroid) is marked by mitochondria, giving the cytoplasm an eosinophilic rather than clear appearance.
Medullary differentiation refers to C-cell tumors of the thyroid, not parathyroid variants.
Water-clear cell hyperplasia is a morphologic variant where the cells are filled with glycogen, giving them a distinctively translucent appearance under the microscope.
Squamous metaplasia is the replacement of one epithelium by squamous cells, typically seen in the respiratory or cervical tracts, not the parathyroid.
Hürthle cell change refers to oncocytic change in thyroid follicular cells, characterized by mitochondria, not glycogen.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1094 (Book Page): the hyperplastic glands contain an increased number of chief cells, or water-clear cells in a diffuse or multinodular distribution.

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
statement: Which of the following best describes the pathophysiological sequence initiated by a viral trigger in Granulomatous thyroiditis?
options: Binding of thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins to the TSH receptor, mimicking its action.
Formation of IgG4-producing plasma cells leading to extensive extrathyroidal fibrosis.
Virus-induced host tissue damage stimulating a cytotoxic T-lymphocyte response to thyroid antigens.
Direct bacterial seeding of thyroid follicles leading to suppurative microabscesses.
Breakdown in self-tolerance to thyroglobulin resulting in germinal center formation.
correctOption: Virus-induced host tissue damage stimulating a cytotoxic T-lymphocyte response to thyroid antigens.
optionExplanations: This describes the mechanism of Graves disease, which involves autoantibodies, not a viral-induced T-cell response.
This describes Riedel thyroiditis or IgG4-related disease, which involves fibroinflammatory processes extending beyond the capsule.
The current model suggests that viral infection causes cellular damage, which exposes thyroid antigens and triggers a self-limited cytotoxic T-cell response.
Granulomatous thyroiditis is triggered by viruses, not direct bacterial seeding; bacterial infections cause acute suppurative thyroiditis.
This describes the pathogenesis of Hashimoto thyroiditis, which is characterized by a chronic autoimmune breakdown of tolerance.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): Although the pathogenesis of the disease is unclear, one model suggests that it results from virus-induced host tissue damage that stimulates a cytotoxic T-lymphocyte response to one or more thyroid antigens that damages thyroid follicle cells.

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
statement: In the pathologic classification of pituitary tumors, which markers are used to identify gonadotroph adenomas even when they do not produce a distinct clinical hypersecretion syndrome?
options: ACTH and TPIT
TSH and alpha-subunit
PRL and PIT-1
GH and PIT-1
SF-1 and GATA-2
correctOption: SF-1 and GATA-2
optionExplanations: ACTH and TPIT are used for corticotroph adenomas.
TSH is for thyrotrophs, which express PIT-1, not SF-1.
PRL and PIT-1 are associated with lactotroph adenomas.
GH and PIT-1 are characteristic of somatotroph adenomas.
Gonadotroph adenomas are identified by the transcription factors SF-1 and GATA-2, which define their lineage even when hormone secretion is low.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1070 (Book Page): [Gonadotroph adenomas... neoplastic cells express the common gonadotropin α-subunit and the specific β-FSH and β-LH subunits... also usually express steroidogenic factor-1 (SF-1), GATA-2, and ERα]

category: Describe salient morphological features of clinically significant subtypes of thyroiditis: i
statement: Which form of thyroiditis is clinically significant for presenting as a 'hard and fixed' thyroid mass that can clinically simulate a malignancy?
options: Granulomatous thyroiditis
Postpartum thyroiditis
Riedel thyroiditis
Hashimoto thyroiditis
Subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis
correctOption: Riedel thyroiditis
optionExplanations: Granulomatous thyroiditis is very tender and mobile, unlike the fixed mass of Riedel.
Postpartum thyroiditis is a variant of subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis and is not associated with hard fixed masses.
Riedel thyroiditis is unique for its extensive fibrosis that breaches the thyroid capsule and anchors the gland to neck tissues, mimicking cancer.
Hashimoto is firm and enlarged but usually not fixed to surrounding neck structures like muscle.
Subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis presents as a mild, mobile goiter, not a hard fixed mass.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1080 (Book Page): [Riedel thyroiditis, a rare disorder characterized by extensive fibrosis involving the thyroid and contiguous neck structures. The presence of a hard and fixed thyroid mass clinically simulates a thyroid carcinoma.]

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
statement: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department with a 3-day history of extreme thirst, frequent urination, and unintended weight loss. On examination, she is lethargic with deep, labored respirations and a fruity breath odor. Her random blood glucose is 480 mg/dL. Which of the following laboratory profiles is most likely to be present in this patient?
options: Elevated plasma renin activity and hypokalemia
Low serum C-peptide and metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap
Hyperglycemia without glycosuria due to high renal threshold
Arterial pH of 7.45 and high serum osmolality (>320 mOsm/kg)
Normal fasting insulin levels and absence of urinary ketones
correctOption: Low serum C-peptide and metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap
optionExplanations: Option D is unrelated to the primary pathology of DKA, though electrolyte shifts occur, the primary metabolic defect is insulin/glucagon imbalance.

Option B is correct. This patient presents with classic Type 1 Diabetes and DKA. Absolute insulin deficiency results in low C-peptide, while the production of ketone bodies (acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate) leads to high anion gap metabolic acidosis and Kussmaul breathing.
Option E is incorrect as the renal threshold for glucose (approx. 180 mg/dL) is far exceeded by a glucose of 480 mg/dL, leading to mandatory glycosuria and osmotic diuresis.
Option A describes a Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS), which is more typical of Type 2 Diabetes and lacks significant acidosis.
Option C is incorrect because Type 1 Diabetes is characterized by low/absent insulin and the presence of ketones in DKA.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1104 (Book Page): The insulin deficiency coupled with glucagon excess decreases peripheral utilization of glucose while increasing gluconeogenesis, severely exacerbating hyperglycemia... Oxidation of fatty acyl coenzyme A molecules within the hepatic mitochondria produces ketone bodies... resulting in a systemic metabolic ketoacidosis.

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
coreConcept: TSH receptor signaling pathway in thyroid autonomy.
statement: In the pathogenesis of toxic multinodular goiter and hyperfunctioning adenomas, which molecular pathway is primarily disrupted to facilitate hormone production independent of pituitary signals?
options: Loss-of-function mutations in the GNAS gene
Constitutive activation of the TSH receptor signaling pathway
Downregulation of the sodium-iodide symporter
Epigenetic silencing of the thyroglobulin gene
Inhibition of the TPO enzyme pathway
correctOption: Constitutive activation of the TSH receptor signaling pathway
optionExplanations: Gain-of-function (activating) mutations in GNAS are found in these conditions; loss-of-function mutations would inhibit signaling.
Activating mutations in the TSH receptor or G-protein alpha-subunit (GNAS) lead to constitutive activation of adenyl cyclase and increased cAMP, causing hormone secretion independent of TSH.
Upregulation, not downregulation, of the sodium-iodide symporter is typically seen to facilitate increased iodine uptake for hormone synthesis.
Silencing the thyroglobulin gene would impair hormone synthesis, whereas hyperfunctioning nodules overproduce hormone.
Inhibition of the thyroid peroxidase (TPO) enzyme would lead to hypothyroidism, not autonomous hyperthyroidism.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1083 (Book Page): Somatic mutations that lead to constitutive activation of the TSH receptor signaling pathway are found in toxic adenomas and toxic multinodular goiter.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
statement: Primary autoimmune adrenalitis is associated with which of the following characteristic histologic findings in the adrenal cortex?
options: Abundant eosinophilic, granular H#252rthle cells
Scattered residual cortical cells and variable lymphoid infiltrates
Extensive caseous necrosis with acid-fast bacilli
Cords of uniform polygonal cells lacking a reticulin network
Intense acute inflammatory reaction with neutrophils and microabscesses
correctOption: Scattered residual cortical cells and variable lymphoid infiltrates
optionExplanations: H#252rthle cells are found in Hashimoto thyroiditis, not in the adrenal gland.
The autoimmune process involves lymphocytic (lymphoid) destruction of the cortex, leaving only rare islands of surviving cortical cells.
Caseous necrosis is pathognomonic for tuberculous adrenalitis, not the autoimmune variant.
The loss of reticulin and monomorphism is characteristic of a pituitary adenoma, not autoimmune adrenalitis.
Acute neutrophilic inflammation is typical of bacterial infections or the early phase of de Quervain thyroiditis, not chronic autoimmune Addison disease.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1122 (Book Page): Histologically, the cortex contains only scattered residual cortical cells in a collapsed network of connective tissue. A variable lymphoid infiltrate is present in the cortex...

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
statement: Which of the following is considered a common primary site for metastatic neoplasms that result in secondary destruction of the adrenal cortex and resultant insufficiency?
options: Papillary thyroid carcinoma or medullary thyroid carcinoma.
Malignant tumors of the lung and the breast.
Primary glioblastoma multiforme or medulloblastoma.
Osteosarcoma and chondrosarcoma of the pelvic bones.
Primary hepatocellular carcinoma or gallbladder adenocarcinoma.
correctOption: Malignant tumors of the lung and the breast.
optionExplanations: Thyroid carcinomas rarely destroy enough of the bilateral adrenal cortex to induce the clinical symptoms of Addison disease.
The adrenal glands are highly vascular and represent a very common site for metastatic spread, especially from lung and breast primaries.
Primary brain tumors like glioblastoma almost never metastasize systemically to the adrenal glands; they are usually restricted to the CNS.
Bone sarcomas are not listed as the primary statistical sources for adrenal-destructive metastases leading to insufficiency.
While these can metastasize, they are not the most common primary sources for adrenal cortical destruction compared to lung and breast cancers.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1122 (Book Page): Carcinomas of the lung and breast are the source of a majority of metastases, although many other neoplasms... may also metastasize to the adrenals.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
statement: Which of the following is identified as one of the most common causative agents of balanoposthitis in uncircumcised males?
options: Candida albicans
Treponema pallidum
Mumps virus
Human Papillomavirus type 16
Chlamydia trachomatis
correctOption: Candida albicans
optionExplanations: Candida albicans is a frequent cause of balanoposthitis, especially when poor hygiene leads to the accumulation of smegma.
Treponema pallidum causes syphilis, which typically presents as a chancre rather than nonspecific inflammation of the glans and prepuce.
Mumps virus is associated with interstitial orchitis, not superficial inflammation of the penis like balanoposthitis.
HPV 16 is associated with undifferentiated penile intraepithelial neoplasia (PeIN) and carcinoma, not typically nonspecific balanoposthitis.
Chlamydia trachomatis is a common cause of epididymitis in sexually active men under 35, but not the primary agent for balanoposthitis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 964 (Book Page): common agents are C. albicans, anaerobic bacteria, Gardnerella, and pyogenic bacteria. Most cases occur as a consequence of poor local hygiene in uncircumcised males

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
statement: What is the characteristic appearance of endometrial glands during the periods of repeated anovulation that precede dysfunctional bleeding?
options: Pseudostratified glands with occasional mild cystic dilation
Complete regression of the glandular component with stromal fibrosis
Decidua-like transformation of the glandular epithelium
Extensive branching and back-to-back arrangement with atypia
Serrated 'sawtooth' architecture with secretory exhaustion
correctOption: Pseudostratified glands with occasional mild cystic dilation
optionExplanations: Anovulatory DUB is characterized by proliferative-type pseudostratified glands that may become cystically dilated due to unopposed estrogen.
Regression and fibrosis are more characteristic of postmenopausal atrophy, not the active growth seen in anovulation.
Decidua-like changes require progesterone stimulation, which is absent in anovulation.
Back-to-back glands with atypia describe atypical hyperplasia, not simple anovulatory DUB.
The sawtooth appearance is characteristic of the late secretory phase of a normal ovulatory cycle.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1001 (Book Page): Under these circumstances, the endometrial glands undergo mild architectural changes, including cystic dilation... the endometrium is composed of pseudostratified glands and contains scattered mitotic figures.

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: Which cells constitute the modified glial component of the neurohypophysis?
options: Somatotrophs
Pituicytes
Chromophobes
Corticotrophs
Acidophils
correctOption: Pituicytes
optionExplanations: Somatotrophs are epithelial cells of the anterior pituitary that produce growth hormone.
Pituicytes are the specific modified glial cells that provide structural support to the axons in the posterior pituitary.
Chromophobes are a staining-based classification of anterior pituitary cells that lack distinct eosinophilic or basophilic granules.
Corticotrophs are epithelial cells of the anterior pituitary that produce ACTH and POMC.
Acidophils are anterior pituitary cells (like somatotrophs and lactotrophs) that stain with acidic dyes.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1065 (Book Page): The posterior pituitary consists of modified glial cells (termed pituicytes) and axonal processes extending from the hypothalamus.

category: Describe salient morphological features of clinically significant subtypes of thyroiditis: i
coreConcept: Hürthle Cell Metaplasia in Hashimoto Thyroiditis
statement: In the histopathological evaluation of a thyroidectomy specimen, the presence of thyroid follicles lined by cells with abundant granular, intensely eosinophilic cytoplasm is a hallmark finding. This morphological feature is most characteristic of which condition?
options: Hashimoto thyroiditis
Diffuse nontoxic goiter
Subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis
Granulomatous thyroiditis
Graves disease
correctOption: Hashimoto thyroiditis
optionExplanations: Hashimoto thyroiditis is defined by a lymphocytic infiltrate with germinal centers and the characteristic metaplastic transformation of follicular cells into Hürthle cells (oxyphil cells) containing abundant mitochondria.

Diffuse nontoxic goiter typically shows enlarged follicles filled with colloid and flattened, inactive epithelium during the involution phase, without the specialized oxyphil change seen in autoimmune destruction.

Subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis (painless thyroiditis) features lymphocytic infiltration and germinal centers but is specifically noted for the absence of significant Hürthle cell metaplasia and fibrosis.
Granulomatous thyroiditis is characterized by multinucleate giant cells and granulomas surrounding colloid pools rather than widespread oxyphil metaplasia.

Graves disease is characterized by tall, crowded columnar epithelium forming small papillae without fibrovascular cores, but it lacks the characteristic eosinophilic granular Hürthle cells seen in chronic autoimmune injury.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1077 (Book Page): The thyroid follicles are atrophic and are lined in many areas by epithelial cells with abundant eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm, termed Hürthle cells, which represent a metaplastic response of the normally low cuboidal follicular epithelium to chronic injury.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
statement: A 24-year-old male presents with severe testicular pain and swelling that developed rapidly. One week prior, he experienced significant fever and bilateral swelling in the parotid region. Based on the likely diagnosis, what is the expected pathological finding in the testis?
options: Suppurative necrosis with abscess formation
Caseating granulomatous inflammation
Acute interstitial orchitis
Obliterative endarteritis with plasma cell cuffs
Gummatous necrosis
correctOption: Acute interstitial orchitis
optionExplanations: Suppurative necrosis is more characteristic of pyogenic bacterial infections like gonorrhea rather than viral mumps.
Caseating granulomas are the hallmark of tuberculosis, which typically starts in the epididymis, not following parotitis.
Mumps causes an acute interstitial orchitis in approximately 20-30% of postpubertal males, usually appearing a week after the salivary gland symptoms.
Obliterative endarteritis is the histologic hallmark of syphilis, which presents differently and is often chronic.
Gummas are localized areas of granulomatous inflammation seen in late-stage syphilis, not acute viral orchitis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 968 (Book Page): In postpubertal males, however, orchitis occurs in 20% to 30% of cases. Most often, acute interstitial orchitis develops 1 week after the onset of swelling of the parotid glands.

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
statement: A patient with De Quervain thyroiditis is currently in the fourth week of illness. Which physiological state is most expected at this specific timeline?
options: Persistent self-perpetuating autoimmune destruction of the entire gland
Transition toward recovery with return of normal thyroid function
Initial formation of microabscesses by infiltrating neutrophils
The height of the inflammatory phase with rising thyroid hormone release
Onset of massive permanent fibrosis and Riedel-like fixed mass
correctOption: Transition toward recovery with return of normal thyroid function
optionExplanations: The T-cell response in subacute thyroiditis is virus-initiated and limited, unlike the self-perpetuating autoimmune response seen in Hashimoto's disease.
Correct. Since the inflammatory phase typically lasts 2 to 6 weeks, a patient at week four is likely beginning to recover or transitioning toward euthyroidism.
Microabscesses and neutrophilic infiltration are the earliest histological features found at the very start of the inflammatory phase, not several weeks into the disease.
The peak of the hyperthyroid phase usually occurs earlier in the first few weeks; by week four, the transient hyperthyroidism is typically beginning to diminish.
Subacute thyroiditis does not lead to Riedel-like massive fibrosis; while some internal scarring occurs, the clinical course leads back to euthyroidism.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): Inflammation of the thyroid and hyperthyroidism are transient, usually diminishing in 2 to 6 weeks, even if the patient is not treated... After recovery, generally in 6 to 8 weeks, normal thyroid function returns.

category: Describe salient morphological features of clinically significant subtypes of thyroiditis: i
statement: In the pathogenesis of Hashimoto thyroiditis, which immunologic pathway is primarily responsible for the direct destruction of thyroid follicular cells?
options: Complement-mediated lysis via the alternative pathway
CD8+ cytotoxic T cell-mediated cell death
Eosinophil-mediated degranulation
Type I hypersensitivity mediated by IgE
TSI-mediated receptor activation
correctOption: CD8+ cytotoxic T cell-mediated cell death
optionExplanations: While antibodies are present, direct T-cell killing and cytokine release are the primary drivers of parenchymal depletion rather than isolated alternative complement activation.
The breakdown in self-tolerance leads to the activation of autoreactive CD8+ T cells that directly target and kill follicular cells, alongside cytokine-mediated injury.
Eosinophils are not major players in Hashimoto thyroiditis; the infiltrate is predominantly mononuclear (lymphocytes and plasma cells).
Type I hypersensitivity (allergic reaction) is not involved in the chronic autoimmune destruction of the thyroid.
Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) is the causative agent in Graves disease (hyperthyroidism), not the destructive mechanism in Hashimoto.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): [Multiple immunologic mechanisms may contribute to thyroid cell death, including... CD8+ cytotoxic T cell–mediated cell death: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells may destroy thyroid follicular cells.]

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
coreConcept: Gross Distinction Between Parathyroid Adenoma and Hyperplasia
statement: A pathologist examining a surgical specimen of a suspected parathyroid tumor notes a solitary, well-circumscribed, soft, tan to reddish-brown nodule. Which of the following gross features most strongly supports a diagnosis of parathyroid adenoma over primary hyperplasia?
options: An infiltrative border with the thyroid capsule
Involvement of only a single parathyroid gland
The presence of internal hemorrhage and cystic change
Diffuse enlargement of all four identified glands
A total specimen weight exceeding 10 grams
correctOption: Involvement of only a single parathyroid gland
optionExplanations: Adenomas are well-circumscribed and encapsulated; an infiltrative border would suggest malignancy (parathyroid carcinoma) rather than a benign adenoma.
Adenomas are characteristically solitary lesions involving only one gland, whereas primary hyperplasia typically involves multiple or all four glands.
Hemorrhage and cystic change can be seen in both larger adenomas and multinodular goiters, making them non-specific for the diagnosis of adenoma.
Multiglandular involvement is the hallmark of primary hyperplasia, not a solitary adenoma.
While adenomas vary in weight, the average is 0.5 to 5 grams; weight alone is not the primary diagnostic differentiator from hyperplasia.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): Parathyroid adenomas are almost always solitary and, like normal parathyroid glands, may be in close proximity to the thyroid or in an ectopic site (e.g., the mediastinum). The typical adenoma averages 0.5 to 5 g and consists of a well-circumscribed, soft, tan to reddish-brown nodule invested by a delicate capsule.

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
statement: A woman presents with persistent pelvic pain and infertility. Laparoscopy reveals the fallopian tubes are distended with clear fluid and show plicae that have fused to form glandlike spaces. What is the most likely initial infectious agent that triggered this sequence of scarring?
options: Treponema pallidum.
Molluscum contagiosum virus.
Haemophilus ducreyi.
Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
Human Papillomavirus type 16.
correctOption: Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
optionExplanations: Syphilis typically causes gummas or endarteritis; while it can involve the genital tract, it is not the classic cause of chronic hydrosalpinx.
Molluscum contagiosum is a localized cutaneous viral infection and does not cause pelvic inflammatory disease or internal scarring.
Haemophilus ducreyi causes chancroid (painful ulcers), not ascending pelvic inflammatory disease leading to tubal fusion.
Gonococcal infection often leads to acute suppurative salpingitis. The subsequent reparative scarring (chronic salpingitis) results in fused plicae, which is a major cause of infertility.
HPV is associated with neoplasia (warts/cancer), not with chronic suppurative salpingitis or tubal scarring.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 988 (Book Page): ...tubal plicae, denuded of epithelium, adhere to one another and slowly fuse in a reparative, scarring process that forms glandlike spaces and blind pouches, referred to as chronic salpingitis. [Page 987 (Book Page) mentions Gonococcal infection ensues acute suppurative salpingitis].

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
coreConcept: Mechanism of Progesterone in Endometrial Homeostasis
statement: During the therapeutic management of dysfunctional uterine bleeding, how does exogenous progesterone act to stabilize the endometrial lining histologically?
options: By down-regulating the expression of estrogen receptors in glands and stroma
By up-regulating the local synthesis of insulin-like growth factor-1
By inhibiting the formation of basal vacuoles in the glandular epithelium
By increasing the conversion of testosterone to estradiol in adipose tissue
By promoting the transition of tall columnar cells to squamous metaplasia
correctOption: By down-regulating the expression of estrogen receptors in glands and stroma
optionExplanations: Progesterone halts the estrogen-driven proliferative phase by reducing the receptors through which estrogen acts, thus limiting endometrial overgrowth.
Estrogen increases IGF-1; progesterone opposes this by suppressing the proliferative drive.
Progesterone actually promotes the formation of basal vacuoles as part of normal differentiation.
This describes the mechanism of aromatase in obesity, which increases estrogen and worsens DUB.
Squamous metaplasia is not a normal or stabilizing effect of progesterone in the endometrium; it is usually a sign of chronic irritation.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1001 (Book Page): Progesterone down-regulates the expression of estrogen receptor in both the glands and the stroma, and as a result endometrial proliferation is suppressed.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
statement: A 32-year-old male presents for an infertility evaluation. He has a history of severe testicular pain and swelling that occurred one week after an episode of parotitis during adolescence. Which pathophysiological mechanism most likely accounts for his current infertility?
options: Acute interstitial orchitis leading to subsequent fibrous scarring
Chronic pressure atrophy from a large spermatocele
Congenital failure of the müllerian-inhibiting substance
Testicular dysgenesis resulting in a ‘vanishing testis’
Obliterative endarteritis causing ischemic necrosis
correctOption: Acute interstitial orchitis leading to subsequent fibrous scarring
optionExplanations: Correct. Mumps in postpubertal males causes an acute interstitial inflammatory response. If severe, the resulting fibrous scarring disrupts the delicate architecture of the tubules, leading to permanent sterility.
Spermatoceles are small cystic accumulations in the efferent ducts; they rarely cause the widespread parenchymal destruction required for total sterility.
Müllerian-inhibiting substance controls the first phase of testicular descent; its failure leads to cryptorchidism, not post-viral orchitis.
Vanishing testis is an extreme form of atrophy resulting from various conditions like irradiation or ischemia, but mumps typically leaves a scarred remnant rather than complete regression.
Obliterative endarteritis is the histologic hallmark of syphilis involving the testis, not the viral inflammation seen in mumps.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 968 (Book Page): In postpubertal males, however, orchitis occurs in 20% to 30% of cases. Most often, acute interstitial orchitis develops 1 week after the onset of swelling of the parotid glands. ... Inflammation of the epididymis and testis is often followed by fibrous scarring, which may produce sterility.

category: Enumerate clinical manifestations along with hormone levels of anterior pituitary
statement: During a routine workup for headaches, an incidental pituitary lesion measuring 0.7 cm in maximum diameter is found on MRI. Histology confirms a monomorphic population of polygonal cells. How should this lesion be classified regarding its size?
options: Pituitary macroadenoma
Pituitary microadenoma
Pituitary carcinoma
Rathke cleft cyst
Pituitary blastoma
correctOption: Pituitary microadenoma
optionExplanations: A macroadenoma must be greater than or equal to 1.0 cm in diameter.
Any pituitary adenoma measuring less than 1.0 cm is defined as a microadenoma.
Pituitary carcinoma is defined by the presence of systemic or craniospinal metastases, not by the size of the primary lesion.
Rathke cleft cysts are cystic lesions lined by ciliated cuboidal epithelium, not solid monomorphic polygonal cell populations.
Pituitary blastoma is a rare childhood tumor associated with DICER1 mutations, typically presenting with primitive 'small round blue cells'.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1066 (Book Page): They are designated, somewhat arbitrarily, microadenomas if they are less than 1 cm in diameter and macroadenomas if they exceed 1 cm in diameter.

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: A 45-year-old female presents with palpitations, heat intolerance, and recent weight loss. Physical examination reveals a diffuse goiter and bitemporal hemianopsia on visual field testing. Laboratory results show markedly elevated free T4 and an inappropriately high-normal serum TSH level. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
options: Struma ovarii
Toxic multinodular goiter
TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma
Graves disease
Factitious thyrotoxicosis
correctOption: TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma
optionExplanations: Struma ovarii is ectopic thyroid tissue in an ovarian teratoma; like other primary sources of T4, it would cause suppressed TSH levels.
Toxic multinodular goiter involves autonomous thyroid nodules; high T4 would suppress TSH production via the normal feedback loop.
High T4 with high or normal TSH indicates secondary hyperthyroidism. The bitemporal hemianopsia suggests a pituitary macroadenoma compressing the optic chiasm.
Graves disease is a primary cause of hyperthyroidism; the high levels of T4 would provide negative feedback, causing the TSH to be suppressed (low).
Factitious thyrotoxicosis is the ingestion of exogenous T4, which would cause high T4 levels and suppress the pituitary, resulting in very low TSH.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1075 (Book Page): In rare cases of pituitary-associated (secondary) hyperthyroidism, TSH levels are either normal or raised.

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
statement: What is the key histologic feature that distinguishes pituitary adenomas from normal anterior pituitary tissue when viewed under low-power magnification?
options: Cellular monomorphism and loss of the reticulin network
Presence of numerous pituicytes and axonal processes
A mixture of acidophils, basophils, and chromophobes
Extensive infiltration by T lymphocytes and plasma cells
Prominent ciliated cuboidal epithelium
correctOption: Cellular monomorphism and loss of the reticulin network
optionExplanations: Correct. Pituitary adenomas consist of a single cell type (monomorphism) and lose the structured reticulin scaffolding found in normal gland tissue.
Incorrect. Pituicytes and axons are characteristic of the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis).
Incorrect. A colorful mixture of cells is the hallmark of the normal anterior pituitary, not a neoplastic adenoma.
Incorrect. While some inflammatory processes like lymphocytic hypophysitis show these cells, adenomas are characterized by monomorphic neoplastic epithelial cells.
Incorrect. Ciliated cuboidal epithelium is found in Rathke cleft cysts, not standard pituitary adenomas.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1068 (Book Page): This cellular monomorphism and the absence of a significant reticulin network distinguish pituitary adenomas from normal anterior pituitary parenchyma.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
statement: In the pathogenesis of male genital tract viral infections, which specific age-related factor determines the clinical prevalence of mumps-induced orchitis?
options: Orchitis is rare in children and occurs primarily in postpubertal males.
Incidence is highest in school-aged children due to lack of vaccination.
Elderly patients are most susceptible due to immunosenescence.
Neonatal infection causes irreversible testicular atrophy.
Orchitis occurs in 100% of postpubertal mumps cases.
correctOption: Orchitis is rare in children and occurs primarily in postpubertal males.
optionExplanations: Mumps orchitis is significantly more prevalent in postpubertal males, affecting 20-30% of cases, typically developing one week after parotid swelling.
While mumps as a systemic disease is common in children, testicular involvement is extremely rare in this demographic.
The disease is more common in children (systemically) and young postpubertal adults (orchitis), not the elderly.
The text does not identify neonatal mumps as a common cause of orchitis or atrophy; atrophy is an end-stage result of postpubertal inflammation.
Only 20% to 30% of postpubertal males with mumps develop orchitis, not all patients.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 968 (Book Page): Mumps is a systemic viral disease that most commonly affects school-aged children. Testicular involvement is extremely uncommon in this age group. In postpubertal males, however, orchitis occurs in 20% to 30% of cases.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: What is the most frequent overall cause of the clinical features associated with Cushing syndrome?
options: Paraneoplastic production of ACTH by lung cancer
Functional adrenocortical adenoma
Primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease
Pituitary microadenoma secreting ACTH
Administration of exogenous glucocorticoids
correctOption: Administration of exogenous glucocorticoids
optionExplanations: This paraneoplastic syndrome accounts for only about 5% to 10% of ACTH-dependent Cushing cases.
Primary adrenal neoplasms are a common cause of ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome (10%-20%), but are not the leading cause overall.
This is a rare cause of ACTH-independent bilateral micronodular hyperplasia, often associated with the Carney complex.
While the most common endogenous cause, it is significantly less frequent than exogenous steroid administration. It accounts for 60% to 70% of endogenous cases but not overall cases.
Glucocorticoid therapy for inflammatory or autoimmune conditions is the most prevalent reason for hypercortisolism in clinical practice.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1113 (Book Page): The vast majority of cases of Cushing syndrome are the result of the administration of exogenous glucocorticoids (iatrogenic Cushing syndrome).

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
statement: Which specific diagnostic criterion is used to identify the most common form of prostatitis in clinical practice?
options: A tender, boggy prostate associated with systemic chills and fever.
History of recurrent urinary tract infections caused by the same organism.
Presence of caseating granulomas in the peripheral zone.
Formation of a fistula tract between the urethra and the scrotal skin.
More than 10 leukocytes per high-power field in secretions with negative cultures.
correctOption: More than 10 leukocytes per high-power field in secretions with negative cultures.
optionExplanations: This describes acute bacterial prostatitis, which is a clinical emergency.
This describes chronic bacterial prostatitis, not the abacterial (most common) form.
This describes granulomatous prostatitis, which is a specific inflammatory pattern, not the most common form.
Fistula formation is associated with squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts or complex infections, not the standard diagnosis of abacterial prostatitis.
Chronic abacterial prostatitis (Chronic Pelvic Pain Syndrome) is characterized by inflammatory markers (WBCs) without an identifiable bacterial agent.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 975 (Book Page): Chronic abacterial prostatitis, the most common form of prostatitis... Expressed prostatic secretions contain more than 10 leukocytes per high-power field, but bacterial cultures are uniformly negative.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: If a patient develops Cushing syndrome due to the long-term use of high-dose dexamethasone for an autoimmune condition, what would be the expected appearance of their adrenal glands?
options: Marked bilateral enlargement with yellow nodules exceeding 3 cm
Bilateral cortical atrophy involving the fasciculata and reticularis
Diffuse thickening of the zona glomerulosa with sparing of other layers
Primary pigmented micronodular disease with lipofuscin accumulation
Unilateral yellow-brown tumor with a well-developed capsule
correctOption: Bilateral cortical atrophy involving the fasciculata and reticularis
optionExplanations: Bilateral macronodular enlargement is seen in endogenous ACTH-independent hyperplasia (BMAH), not in exogenous steroid use.
Exogenous steroids suppress pituitary ACTH, and since the inner layers of the cortex require ACTH for growth, they undergo profound atrophy.
The zona glomerulosa is spared because it is regulated by the renin-angiotensin system, but it does not thicken; the other layers atrophy.
Pigmented micronodular disease is a genetic condition (e.g., Carney complex) and is unrelated to iatrogenic steroid intake.
This describes a solitary adrenal adenoma, which is a cause of endogenous Cushing, not a consequence of exogenous steroids.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1114 (Book Page): In patients in whom the syndrome results from exogenous glucocorticoids, suppression of endogenous ACTH results in bilateral cortical atrophy, due to a lack of stimulation of the zonae fasciculata and reticularis by ACTH. The zona glomerulosa is of normal thickness in such cases, because this portion of the cortex functions independently of ACTH.

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
statement: A 31-year-old female at 36 weeks gestation is diagnosed with preeclampsia. Laboratory analysis reveals microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, elevated liver enzymes, and a platelet count of 85,000/µL. What is the specific clinical designation for this constellation of findings?
options: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
Sheehan syndrome
HELLP syndrome
Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome
Conn syndrome
correctOption: HELLP syndrome
optionExplanations: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome involves a gastrin-producing tumor leading to hypergastrinemia and severe peptic ulceration.
Sheehan syndrome is post-partum ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary usually following massive obstetric hemorrhage.
HELLP syndrome is a specific complication of preeclampsia consisting of Hemolysis (microangiopathic), Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets.
Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is characterized by massive bilateral adrenal hemorrhage secondary to overwhelming bacterial septicemia (like N. meningitidis).
Conn syndrome is primary hyperaldosteronism caused by a solitary aldosterone-secreting adrenocortical adenoma.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1029 (Book Page): Approximately 10% of women with preeclampsia develop microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets, referred to as the HELLP syndrome

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: What is the typical gross appearance of a parathyroid adenoma on cut section?
options: Multiloculated and cystic with thick 'machine oil' fluid
Soft, well-circumscribed, and tan to reddish-brown
Pale gray to tan, hard, and gritty with infiltrative margins
Bright yellow and lobulated with a distinct fibrous capsule
Deeply pigmented, brown to black, with atrophic intervening areas
correctOption: Soft, well-circumscribed, and tan to reddish-brown
optionExplanations: This describes an adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma, not a parathyroid adenoma.
Correct. Adenomas are characteristically soft, reddish-brown or tan nodules that are easily distinguished from the surrounding tissue by their circumscription and color.
This description (hard, gritty, infiltrative) is more typical of a scirrhous breast carcinoma or some thyroid cancers.
Bright yellow color is characteristic of aldosterone-producing adrenal adenomas or normal adipose tissue, not parathyroid adenomas.
Pigmented nodules with atrophy are characteristic of primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease, not parathyroid pathology.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): The typical adenoma... consists of a well-circumscribed, soft, tan to reddish-brown nodule invested by a delicate capsule.

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: In the physiological feedback loop regulating serum calcium, an increase in free ionized calcium levels inhibits parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion. Which secondary effect does this inhibition have on renal phosphate handling?
options: Inhibition of renal phosphate absorption in the proximal tubule
Increased urinary phosphate excretion
Stabilization of renal phosphate clearance
Decreased urinary phosphate excretion
Activation of renal alpha-1-hydroxylase
correctOption: Decreased urinary phosphate excretion
optionExplanations: Inhibition of absorption is what PTH *does*. Inhibition of PTH (the question's premise) would lead to *increased* absorption.
Increased phosphate excretion is an effect of PTH; when PTH is inhibited (due to high calcium), this effect is reversed.
Phosphate clearance is highly dynamic and sensitive to PTH levels; it does not remain stable when PTH secretion is suppressed.

PTH normally inhibits phosphate reabsorption in the kidney (causing phosphaturia). When PTH levels fall due to negative feedback from high calcium, renal phosphate excretion decreases (and reabsorption increases).
PTH *stimulates* renal alpha-1-hydroxylase. Suppression of PTH by high calcium would therefore lead to *decreased* activation of this enzyme.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1091 (Book Page): Increased urinary phosphate excretion, thereby lowering serum phosphate levels and further increasing calcium... The net result of these activities is to elevate the level of free calcium, which, in turn, inhibits further PTH secretion in a classic feedback loop.

category: Define thyroiditis
statement: What are the morphological diagnostic criteria for the granulomatous phase of de Quervain thyroiditis?
options: Extensive replacement of parenchyma by dense collagenous tissue.
Multinucleate giant cells enclosing pools of colloid.
Presence of Orphan Annie eye nuclei and psammoma bodies.
Diffuse hypertrophy and hyperplasia of tall columnar cells.
Islands of oxyphil cells surrounded by a thick fibrous capsule.
correctOption: Multinucleate giant cells enclosing pools of colloid.
optionExplanations: This describes Riedel thyroiditis or the end-stage fibrosis of various chronic conditions.
The presence of giant cells reacting to extravasated colloid is the defining histologic feature of this condition.
These are features of papillary thyroid carcinoma, not thyroiditis.
This describes the histological appearance of Graves disease (diffuse toxic goiter).
This describes a H%fcrthle cell adenoma, which is a discrete encapsulated neoplasm.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): Multinucleate giant cells enclose pools of colloid, hence the designation granulomatous thyroiditis.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: Which pathogen is the most frequent cause of localized abscess formation in acute mastitis during the early weeks of breastfeeding?
options: Streptococcus pyogenes
Staphylococcus aureus
Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Corynebacterium species
Bacteroides fragilis
correctOption: Staphylococcus aureus
optionExplanations: Streptococci are less commonly involved and typically result in a diffuse, spreading cellulitis rather than localized, walled-off abscesses.
Staphylococcus aureus is the primary causative organism for acute lactational mastitis and is specifically associated with the development of localized abscesses.
Mycobacteria cause rare chronic granulomatous infections, typically in immunocompromised hosts, and do not present as acute lactational abscesses.
Corynebacterium is associated with cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis rather than the acute bacterial mastitis seen in lactating women.
Bacteroides and other anaerobes are more frequently found in recurrent subareolar abscesses associated with squamous metaplasia, not primary acute mastitis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1038 (Book Page): Staphylococcus aureus or, less commonly, streptococci invade the breast tissue. ... Staphylococci infection often leads to single or multiple abscesses, whereas streptococci cause spreading infection in the form of cellulitis.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: Which molecular abnormality is identified in 10% to 20% of sporadic parathyroid adenomas and results in overactive cellular proliferation?
options: Inversion of the Cyclin D1 (CCDN1) gene.
Activating mutation of the USP8 gene.
Gain-of-function mutations in the GNAS gene.
Activating mutations in the RET proto-oncogene.
Loss of heterozygosity in the VHL tumor suppressor gene.
correctOption: Inversion of the Cyclin D1 (CCDN1) gene.
optionExplanations: The CCDN1 inversion places the cyclin D1 gene under the control of the PTH promoter, leading to pathological overexpression and cell cycle progression.
USP8 mutations are associated with pituitary corticotroph adenomas, not parathyroid lesions.
GNAS mutations are common in pituitary somatotroph adenomas but are not the primary driver in 10-20% of sporadic parathyroid adenomas.
RET mutations are characteristic of medullary thyroid carcinoma and MEN-2, not sporadic parathyroid adenomas.
VHL mutations are linked to von Hippel-Lindau syndrome and pheochromocytomas/renal cell carcinomas.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): A pericentromeric inversion on chromosome 11 results in relocation of CCDN1 (normally on 11q), so that it is positioned adjacent to the 5′-flanking region of the PTH gene (on 11p). ... Between 10% and 20% of sporadic parathyroid adenomas have this clonal rearrangement.

category: Describe salient morphological features of clinically significant subtypes of thyroiditis: i
coreConcept: Histological contrast between chronic and subacute thyroiditis
statement: When distinguishing the morphology of subacute lymphocytic (painless) thyroiditis from Hashimoto thyroiditis, which histological feature is notably absent or minimal in the former?
options: Germinal center formation
Mononuclear cell aggregates
Lymphocytic infiltration
Follicular disruption
Hürthle cell metaplasia
correctOption: Hürthle cell metaplasia
optionExplanations: Large germinal centers can be seen in both conditions, though they are more extensive and characteristic of the chronic Hashimoto variant.
Mononuclear aggregates are the common finding that groups these as 'lymphocytic' thyroiditis, though their clinical course differs significantly.
Lymphocytic infiltration is present in both Hashimoto and subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis, as both have an autoimmune component.
Follicular disruption occurs in both conditions as part of the inflammatory process, often leading to the release of preformed hormones.
Hürthle cell metaplasia is a hallmark of the chronic injury in Hashimoto thyroiditis but is specifically noted to be absent or minimal in subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): Microscopic examination reveals lymphocytic infiltration with large germinal centers within the thyroid parenchyma and patchy disruption and collapse of thyroid follicles. Unlike Hashimoto thyroiditis, however, fibrosis and Hürthle cell metaplasia are not prominent.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
statement: Examination of the pancreas in a patient with long-standing Type 2 Diabetes reveals characteristic extracellular deposits within the Islets of Langerhans. What is the composition of these deposits?
options: Psammoma bodies
Fibrinoid necrosis
Amyloid derived from amylin
T-lymphocytes and macrophages (insulitis)
Crystalloids of Reinke
correctOption: Amyloid derived from amylin
optionExplanations: Psammoma bodies are concentric calcifications often seen in papillary thyroid or ovarian cancers, but not in diabetic islets.
Fibrinoid necrosis is a vascular lesion seen in malignant hypertension or vasculitis, not a typical feature of the pancreatic islets in chronic diabetes.
Islet amyloid is a classic finding in Type 2 Diabetes. It is composed of amylin, which is co-secreted with insulin and accumulates over time, potentially contributing to beta-cell failure.
Insulitis, or lymphocytic infiltration of the islets, is the hallmark of the autoimmune destruction seen in Type 1 Diabetes.
Crystalloids of Reinke are characteristic of Leydig cell tumors of the testis, not the diabetic pancreas.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1108 (Book Page): Amyloid deposition within islets in T2D begins in and around capillaries and between cells. At advanced stages, the islets may be virtually obliterated

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
coreConcept: Stromal fat as a diagnostic marker in parathyroid pathology
statement: How does the adipose tissue content of a hyperplastic parathyroid gland compare to that of a normal adult parathyroid gland?
options: Adipose tissue content is unchanged from the normal 30% level.
Adipose tissue becomes highly vacuolated with prominent lipofuscin pigment.
Adipose tissue is replaced by dense, laminated spironolactone bodies.
Adipose tissue increases to approximately 75% of the total gland weight.
Adipose tissue is characteristically inconspicuous within the hyperplastic areas.
correctOption: Adipose tissue is characteristically inconspicuous within the hyperplastic areas.
optionExplanations: A normal adult gland has about 30% fat, but this is significantly reduced in hyperplastic or adenomatous glands.
Vacuolated cells with lipofuscin describe the 'pigmented' variant of adrenal hyperplasia, not parathyroid glands.
Spironolactone bodies are found in the adrenal cortex of patients treated with spironolactone, not in the parathyroid.
75% fat is seen in atrophy; hyperplasia involves a significant loss of stromal fat to make room for cellular proliferation.
The reduction or absence of stromal fat is a key histological feature used by pathologists to identify parathyroid hyperfunction.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): As in the case of adenomas, stromal fat is inconspicuous within hyperplastic glands.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
statement: A 6-year-old boy presents with acute epididymitis. Given his age, which of the following is the most likely clinical association according to the standardized causes of male genital tract inflammation?
options: Presence of a congenital genitourinary abnormality
Recent history of sexual abuse or activity
Disseminated tertiary syphilis
Secondary spread from a lung infection
Idiopathic autoimmune tubule destruction
correctOption: Presence of a congenital genitourinary abnormality
optionExplanations: Structural anomalies (like ureteral reflux) allow urinary tract bacteria to reach the epididymis more easily in children.
While possible, the text specifies that childhood epididymitis is statistically linked to congenital structural issues rather than STIs.
Syphilis in children is usually congenital and presents differently than acute bacterial epididymitis.
Hematogenous spread from lungs is more characteristic of TB, which is rare in this specific pediatric acute presentation.
Autoimmune orchitis is a middle-aged condition and does not involve the epididymis primarily.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 967 (Book Page): Though uncommon in children, epididymitis in childhood is usually associated with a congenital genitourinary abnormality and infection with gram-negative rods.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
coreConcept: Role of PSA in semen liquefaction
statement: A 32-year-old male undergoing a workup for primary infertility provides a semen sample that shows a failure of the seminal coagulum to liquefy within the standard clinical timeframe. This specific functional defect in the ejaculate is most likely related to a deficiency in which protein?
options: M¼llerian-inhibiting substance
Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)
Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)
Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)
Calcitonin gene–related peptide
correctOption: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)
optionExplanations: M¼llerian-inhibiting substance is critical for the transabdominal phase of testicular descent but does not regulate the physical properties of the ejaculate.
hCG is elevated in choriocarcinomas and some seminomas; while useful as a tumor marker, it has no physiological role in liquefying the seminal clot.
PSA is a serine protease produced by the prostate that cleaves the coagulum; a deficiency results in viscous semen that can trap sperm and impair fertility.
Alpha-fetoprotein is a biomarker for certain germ cell tumors like yolk sac tumors and does not play a role in normal seminal fluid rheology.
Calcitonin gene–related peptide is involved in the inguinoscrotal phase of testicular descent via the genitofemoral nerve, not semen liquefaction.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 981 (Book Page): PSA is a product of prostatic epithelium and is normally secreted in the semen. It is an androgen-regulated serine protease whose function is to cleave and liquefy the seminal coagulum formed after ejaculation.

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
statement: A patient with suspected de Quervain thyroiditis undergoes a radionuclide scan. Which finding would most likely distinguish this condition from Graves disease during the active inflammatory phase?
options: Presence of a solitary 'hot' autonomous nodule
Diffusely increased uptake of radioactive iodine
Uneven uptake with multiple 'cold' areas
Increased uptake restricted to the pyramidal lobe
Diminished uptake of radioactive iodine
correctOption: Diminished uptake of radioactive iodine
optionExplanations: A solitary hot nodule is characteristic of a toxic follicular adenoma, where one area of the gland is autonomous.
Graves disease shows diffusely increased uptake because the entire gland is hyperfunctioning under immunoglobulin stimulation.
Uneven uptake is the classic appearance of a multinodular goiter, reflecting different stages of hyperplasia and involution.
Uptake limited to anatomical variants like the pyramidal lobe is not a standard finding in any of these major inflammatory or hyperplastic disorders.
In granulomatous thyroiditis, follicular cells are damaged and cannot trap iodine effectively; furthermore, high levels of circulating hormone suppress TSH, further reducing uptake.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): however, unlike in hyperthyroid states such as Graves disease, radioactive iodine uptake is diminished.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
statement: The histologic hallmark of syphilitic inflammation in the male genital tract, characterized by perivascular cuffs of lymphocytes and plasma cells, is known as which of the following?
options: Koilocytic atypia
Suppurative inflammation
Caseating necrosis
Schiller-Duval body formation
Obliterative endarteritis
correctOption: Obliterative endarteritis
optionExplanations: Koilocytic atypia is the cytopathic effect seen in HPV infections, such as condyloma acuminatum.
Suppurative inflammation describes the neutrophil-rich response seen in acute bacterial infections like gonorrhea.
Caseating necrosis is the defining feature of mycobacterial (tuberculous) infections.
Schiller-Duval bodies are characteristic of yolk sac tumors, not inflammatory states.
Obliterative endarteritis with plasma cell-rich perivascular infiltrates is the classic histologic signature of syphilis in the testis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 968 (Book Page): The morphologic pattern of the reaction takes two forms: (1) obliterative endarteritis associated with perivascular cuffs of lymphocytes and plasma cells, the histologic hallmark of syphilis, or (2) granulomatous inflammation, a lesion known as a gumma.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
statement: Which clinical entity is identified as the most prevalent form of prostatitis encountered in medical practice?
options: IgG4-associated autoimmune prostatitis
Chronic bacterial prostatitis
Granulomatous prostatitis
Chronic abacterial prostatitis
Acute bacterial prostatitis
correctOption: Chronic abacterial prostatitis
optionExplanations: IgG4-associated autoimmune prostatitis is a recently described and highly specialized rare inflammatory condition that is not a major contributor to the overall prevalence of prostatitis.
Chronic bacterial prostatitis presents with recurrent UTIs from the same organism but is less common than the abacterial form in clinical surveys.
Granulomatous prostatitis is a specific reactive pattern, often following BCG therapy for bladder cancer, and is a relatively rare subtype compared to the general population.
Chronic abacterial prostatitis, or chronic pelvic pain syndrome, represents the majority of prostatitis cases; it is defined by inflammatory signs in secretions without bacterial growth.
Acute bacterial prostatitis is a serious infection typically caused by E. coli or staphylococci, but it occurs much less frequently than chronic abacterial variants.
