Thickened, nodular cortices are characteristic of Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH), which is an enzymatic defect, not an autoimmune destruction of the gland mass.
Granulomatous inflammation with caseous necrosis is the hallmark of adrenal tuberculosis, not autoimmune adrenalitis.
This describes the acute changes seen in Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1122 (Book Page): Primary autoimmune adrenalitis is characterized by irregularly shrunken glands, which may be difficult to identify within the suprarenal adipose tissue. Histologically, the cortex contains only scattered residual cortical cells in a collapsed network of connective tissue. A variable lymphoid infiltrate is present in the cortex and may extend into the adjacent medulla.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
statement: Which of the following measurements is the most reliable surrogate for endogenous beta-cell function, particularly in patients receiving exogenous insulin therapy?
options: Total glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
Random plasma glucose concentration
Serum C-peptide levels
Plasma free fatty acid levels
Urinary acetoacetic acid levels
correctOption: Serum C-peptide levels
optionExplanations: HbA1c measures long-term glycemic control but cannot distinguish between insulin produced by the patient and insulin administered via injection.
Glucose levels reflect the net effect of diet, physical activity, and medication, but do not directly quantify the secretory capacity of the pancreas.
C-peptide is a byproduct of proinsulin cleavage and is secreted in equimolar amounts with insulin, providing a direct measurement of the pancreas's own insulin production.
Free fatty acid levels are markers of adipose tissue lipolysis and insulin resistance rather than direct indicators of beta-cell secretory activity.
Ketone levels in the urine are markers of metabolic crisis or starvation but do not provide a quantitative measure of islet cell function.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1098 (Book Page): [C-peptide levels serve as a surrogate for ̢-cell function, decreasing with loss of ̢-cell mass in T1D and increasing with insulin resistance–associated hyperinsulinemia.]

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
statement: Which of the following is the most common fungal pathogen implicated in the etiology of balanoposthitis in uncircumcised males?
options: Aspergillus fumigatus
Histoplasma capsulatum
Blastomyces dermatitidis
Cryptococcus neoformans
Candida albicans
correctOption: Candida albicans
optionExplanations: Aspergillus species are typically associated with pulmonary or systemic infections in immunocompromised individuals rather than standard genital tract inflammation.
Histoplasma is a dimorphic fungus causing systemic mycosis, usually via inhalation, and does not typically target the male prepuce.
Blastomyces primarily causes pulmonary and skin lesions through systemic spread; it is not a documented common cause of balanoposthitis.
Cryptococcus is an encapsulated yeast usually causing meningitis or pneumonia; it is not a standard cause of local penile inflammation.
Candida albicans is a common commensal that becomes pathogenic in the setting of poor hygiene or diabetes, acting as a primary cause of balanoposthitis (inflammation of the glans and prepuce).
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 964 (Book Page): common agents are C. albicans, anaerobic bacteria, Gardnerella, and pyogenic bacteria. Most cases occur as a consequence of poor local hygiene in uncircumcised males, in whom the accumulation of desquamated epithelial cells, sweat, and debris, termed smegma, acts as a local irritant.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
statement: Prolonged anovulation can lead to specific histopathological changes that resemble menstrual endometrium but lack its hormonal prerequisites. Which feature is characteristic of such anovulatory tissue?
options: Extensive stromal pre-decidualization.
Absence of glandular mitotic activity.
Coordinated secretory transformation of all glands.
Formation of well-developed spiral arterioles.
Presence of eosinophilic epithelial metaplasia.
correctOption: Presence of eosinophilic epithelial metaplasia.
optionExplanations: Pre-decidualization is strictly progesterone-dependent and therefore absent in anovulatory cycles.
In anovulatory cycles, the glands are under estrogenic influence and typically demonstrate mitotic figures.
Secretory transformation requires progesterone from a corpus luteum, which is absent in anovulation.
Spiral arterioles require progesterone for maturation; their development is curtailed in anovulatory DUB.
Eosinophilic epithelial metaplasia is a finding in chronic anovulation that mimics some features of the menstrual phase.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1001 (Book Page): In this setting, biopsies reveal stromal condensation and eosinophilic epithelial metaplasia, features similar to those seen in menstrual endometrium.

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: Which of the following cell types constitutes the primary modified glial component of the neurohypophysis?
options: Thyrotrophs
Chromophobe cells
Somatotrophs
Corticotrophs
Pituicytes
correctOption: Pituicytes
optionExplanations: Thyrotrophs are the specific anterior pituitary cells that produce thyroid-stimulating hormone in response to hypothalamic thyrotropin-releasing hormone.
Chromophobe cells are poorly staining cells of the anterior pituitary that lack significant hormone storage granules.
Somatotrophs are acidophilic cells found in the anterior pituitary responsible for the production of growth hormone, not the posterior lobe.
Corticotrophs are basophilic cells of the adenohypophysis that synthesize pro-opiomelanocortin and adrenocorticotropic hormone.
Pituicytes are the specialized glial cells that provide structural and functional support to the axonal terminals of the neurosecretory neurons in the posterior pituitary.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1065 (Book Page): The posterior pituitary consists of modified glial cells (termed pituicytes) and axonal processes extending from the hypothalamus through the pituitary stalk to the posterior lobe (axon terminals).

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
statement: A 39-year-old male presents to the emergency department with sudden, severe unilateral scrotal pain, swelling, and fever of 101.5°F. Physical exam shows significant tenderness over the epididymis. Lab results show a leukocytosis of 15,000/mm³. Based on the patient's age, which infectious agents are most likely responsible for this condition?
options: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas species
Gram-negative rods associated with congenital malformations
Treponema pallidum
correctOption: Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas species
optionExplanations: Tuberculosis begins in the epididymis but usually presents as a chronic caseating granulomatous process rather than sudden acute emergency with high fever.
In sexually active men younger than 35, STI pathogens like Chlamydia and Gonorrhea are the most common causes of epididymitis.
In men over 35, the etiology shifts toward common urinary tract pathogens, often related to concurrent prostatitis or urinary obstruction.
Gram-negative rod infections in children are typically associated with underlying congenital genitourinary abnormalities.
Syphilis involves the testis first (orchitis) rather than the epididymis, and presents with distinctive obliterative endarteritis or gummas.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 967 (Book Page): In men older than age 35, common urinary tract pathogens, such as E. coli and Pseudomonas, are responsible for most infections [of the epididymis].

category: Describe salient morphological features of clinically significant subtypes of thyroiditis: i
statement: A 52-year-old female presents with a painless, diffuse enlargement of the thyroid gland. Histological examination reveals an extensive mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate with well-developed germinal centers. The thyroid follicles are atrophic and lined by cells with abundant granular, eosinophilic cytoplasm. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Hashimoto thyroiditis
Graves disease
Subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis
Riedel thyroiditis
Granulomatous thyroiditis
correctOption: Hashimoto thyroiditis
optionExplanations: Hashimoto thyroiditis is characterized by atrophic follicles, Hürthle cell metaplasia (eosinophilic granular cytoplasm), and a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with germinal centers.
Graves disease shows diffuse hypertrophy and hyperplasia of follicular epithelial cells with scalloped colloid, rather than atrophic follicles and Hürthle cell change.
While subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis shows lymphocytic infiltration, it lacks the prominent Hürthle cell metaplasia and extensive fibrosis often seen in Hashimoto.
Riedel thyroiditis is distinguished by extensive dense fibrosis that extends beyond the thyroid capsule into adjacent neck structures, which is not described here.
Granulomatous thyroiditis is characterized by multinucleate giant cells enclosing colloid and is typically painful, unlike the painless presentation of Hashimoto.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1077 (Book Page): The thyroid follicles are atrophic and are lined in many areas by epithelial cells with abundant eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm, termed Hürthle cells. In fine-needle aspiration biopsy samples, the presence of Hürthle cells in conjunction with a heterogeneous population of lymphocytes is characteristic of Hashimoto thyroiditis.

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
statement: A patient with subacute granulomatous thyroiditis is entering the second stage of the disease course, approximately 6 weeks after the onset of neck pain. Which of the following metabolic states is the patient most likely to experience at this specific juncture?
options: Permanent hypothyroidism due to total follicular exhaustion
Persistent, worsening thyrotoxicosis requiring radioiodine ablation
Development of toxic multinodular goiter and Plummer syndrome
Transient hypothyroidism before returning to a euthyroid state
Immediate and permanent recovery to euthyroidism without a hypothyroid phase
correctOption: Transient hypothyroidism before returning to a euthyroid state
optionExplanations: Permanent hypothyroidism is rare (less than 10-15%); the vast majority of patients regain normal thyroid function.
Thyrotoxicosis in de Quervain's is due to leakage, not hyperfunction, and is transient rather than worsening over time.
Toxic multinodular goiter is a chronic autonomous growth process and is not an outcome of subacute thyroiditis.
The disease follows a classic pattern: hyperthyroid (leakage) phase, followed by a hypothyroid phase (as hormone stores are depleted and follicles haven't recovered), and finally euthyroidism.
While some patients may bypass a symptomatic hypothyroid phase, the physiological standard involves a period of thyroid hormone dip during recovery from follicular damage.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): After recovery, generally in 6 to 8 weeks, normal thyroid function returns. Some patients transition from hyperthyroidism to hypothyroidism before recovery.

category: Describe salient morphological features of clinically significant subtypes of thyroiditis: i
statement: Which of the following immunologic mechanisms is primarily responsible for the progressive depletion of thyroid epithelial cells observed in the morphology of Hashimoto thyroiditis?
options: IgG4-related lymphoplasmacytic infiltration
Deposition of amyloid derived from calcitonin
CD8+ cytotoxic T cell-mediated cell death
Type I hypersensitivity with mast cell degranulation
Antibody-mediated blockade of TSH receptors
correctOption: CD8+ cytotoxic T cell-mediated cell death
optionExplanations: While Riedel thyroiditis is linked to IgG4-related disease, classic Hashimoto thyroiditis is defined by T-cell mediated destruction and germinal center formation.
Amyloid deposition derived from calcitonin is a feature of medullary thyroid carcinoma, not Hashimoto thyroiditis.
The destruction of thyrocytes in Hashimoto thyroiditis is mediated by CD8+ T cells and Th1-derived cytokines like interferon-gamma, leading to follicular atrophy.
Type I hypersensitivity involves IgE and is characteristic of allergic reactions, not the chronic autoimmune destruction seen in thyroiditis.
Blockade of TSH receptors is associated with atrophic thyroiditis or a subset of autoimmune hypothyroidism but is not the primary mechanism of cell death in the classic goitrous form.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1077 (Book Page): CD8+ cytotoxic T cell–mediated cell death: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells may destroy thyroid follicular cells. Cytokine-mediated cell death: Activation of CD4+ Th1 cells leads to the production of inflammatory cytokines such as interferon-gamma in the thyroid gland.

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: A 40-year-old male presents with symptoms of heat intolerance and palpitations. Examination reveals a diffuse goiter and lid lag. Laboratory studies show high serum free T4 and triiodothyronine. His serum TSH is also elevated. An administration of TRH results in a further rise in TSH. What is the most likely cause of his hyperthyroidism?
options: Ectopic thyroid tissue in an ovarian teratoma
Factitious intake of exogenous levothyroxine
Graves disease
Thyrotroph adenoma of the pituitary
Toxic multinodular goiter
correctOption: Thyrotroph adenoma of the pituitary
optionExplanations: Struma ovarii (ectopic thyroid) produces hormones that suppress the patient's endogenous TSH via feedback.
Exogenous intake of thyroid hormone (factitious) results in high T4/T3 which strongly suppresses TSH production.
In Graves disease (primary hyperthyroidism), the high T4/T3 levels would suppress TSH to undetectable levels.
High T4/T3 combined with high TSH indicates secondary hyperthyroidism, most commonly due to a TSH-secreting pituitary tumor.
Like Graves, toxic multinodular goiter is a primary thyroid disorder and would result in suppressed TSH levels.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1074 (Book Page): In rare cases of pituitary-associated (secondary) hyperthyroidism, TSH levels are either normal or raised. Page 1070 (Book Page): Thyrotroph (TSH-producing) adenomas are uncommon, accounting for approximately 1% of pituitary adenomas. They are a rare cause of hyperthyroidism.

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
statement: Which specific morphologic feature serves as the most reliable diagnostic characteristic to histologically distinguish a pituitary adenoma from the surrounding normal pituitary tissue?
options: Abundant cytoplasmic secretory granules in all cells
Cellular monomorphism and absence of a reticulin network
Presence of multiple cell types (acidophils and basophils)
Extensive stromal fibrosis and prominent vascularity
High mitotic rate and presence of psammoma bodies
correctOption: Cellular monomorphism and absence of a reticulin network
optionExplanations: While some adenomas are granulated, others are chromophobic (sparsely granulated). Granulation is not the distinguishing feature from the normal gland.
Pituitary adenomas are characterized by a single uniform cell population (monomorphism) and the complete breakdown of the normal reticulin fiber scaffold.
Normal pituitary tissue is heterogeneous (acidophils, basophils, chromophobes); adenomas are monomorphic (single cell type).
Adenomas are typically soft and gelatinous with sparse supporting tissue, rather than being characterized by extensive fibrosis.
Most adenomas have low mitotic rates. Psammoma bodies can be seen in lactotroph adenomas but are not the general distinguishing feature from normal tissue.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1068 (Book Page): This cellular monomorphism and the absence of a significant reticulin network distinguish pituitary adenomas from normal anterior pituitary parenchyma

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
coreConcept: Most common etiology of Cushing syndrome
statement: Which of the following represents the most frequent cause of clinical Cushing syndrome observed in medical practice overall?
options: Bilateral adrenocortical hyperplasia resulting from an ACTH-secreting pituitary microadenoma.
The administrative use of exogenous glucocorticoids for non-endocrine therapeutic purposes.
Bilateral macronodular adrenal hyperplasia associated with germline ARMC5 mutations.
Primary hypercortisolism caused by a functioning unilateral adrenocortical adenoma.
Ectopic secretion of adrenocorticotropic hormone by an underlying small-cell carcinoma of the lung.
correctOption: The administrative use of exogenous glucocorticoids for non-endocrine therapeutic purposes.
optionExplanations: While ACTH-secreting pituitary adenomas are the most common cause of endogenous Cushing syndrome (Cushing disease), they are not more common than iatrogenic causes overall.
Exogenous administration of steroids (iatrogenic) for conditions like autoimmune or inflammatory diseases remains the most prevalent cause of Cushingoid features in the general population.
Macronodular adrenal hyperplasia is a relatively rare subtype of ACTH-independent hypercortisolism and does not represent the majority of cases.
Primary adrenal neoplasms are ACTH-independent causes and are significantly less frequent than exogenous steroid use.
Ectopic ACTH is a rare paraneoplastic cause of Cushing syndrome, accounting for approximately 5% to 10% of endogenous cases, and is not the most common cause overall.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1113 (Book Page): The vast majority of cases of Cushing syndrome are the result of the administration of exogenous glucocorticoids (iatrogenic Cushing syndrome).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
coreConcept: Negative Feedback and Contralateral Adrenal Atrophy
statement: In a patient with an endogenous Cushing syndrome caused by a solitary cortical adenoma in the right adrenal gland, what is the expected morphologic state of the left adrenal gland?
options: Diffuse hypertrophy of the entire left cortex
Complete regression of the left adrenal medulla
Nodular hyperplasia of the zona reticularis
Metaplastic Hürthle cell change
Cortical atrophy of the left gland (except the zona glomerulosa)
correctOption: Cortical atrophy of the left gland (except the zona glomerulosa)
optionExplanations: Hypertrophy would only occur if ACTH levels were high.
The adrenal medulla is not regulated by ACTH and remains unaffected.
The reticularis would be atrophic, not hyperplastic, due to low ACTH.
Hürthle cell change is a feature of thyroid pathology (Hashimoto's), not adrenal cortical atrophy.

High cortisol from the right-sided tumor suppresses pituitary ACTH. Since the left zona fasciculata and reticularis depend on ACTH for maintenance, they atrophy. The zona glomerulosa survives because it is regulated by the renin-angiotensin system.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1114 (Book Page): With functioning tumors, both benign and malignant, the adjacent adrenal cortex and that of the contralateral adrenal gland are atrophic, as a result of suppression of endogenous ACTH by high cortisol levels... The zona glomerulosa is of normal thickness in such cases, because this portion of the cortex functions independently of ACTH.

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
statement: In the clinical management of a patient diagnosed with severe preeclampsia, which of the following is considered an absolute indication for immediate delivery regardless of the current gestational age?
options: The presence of trace proteinuria on a single random sample
Moderate headache relieved by mild analgesics
Gestational hypertension without associated proteinuria
Isolated lower extremity edema responding to rest
Identification of the HELLP syndrome
correctOption: Identification of the HELLP syndrome
optionExplanations: Trace proteinuria alone does not meet the diagnostic threshold for severe preeclampsia requiring immediate intervention.
Persistent, severe headaches are concerning, but if a headache is mild and transient, it does not constitute severe end-organ dysfunction on its own.
Gestational hypertension without proteinuria is a distinct, less severe condition that does not typically necessitate immediate preterm delivery.
Mild edema is common in pregnancy and is not an indication for preterm delivery in preeclampsia.
HELLP syndrome indicates severe multi-organ involvement and is a standard indication for prompt delivery to prevent further maternal morbidity.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1031 (Book Page): eclampsia, severe preeclampsia with maternal end-organ dysfunction, fetal compromise, or the HELLP syndrome are indications for delivery regardless of gestational age.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: Grossly, what is the typical color of a parathyroid adenoma on the cut surface, and how does its consistency compare to normal tissue?
options: Beefy deep red and meaty
Pale gray and translucent
Dark brown and gritty
Tan to reddish-brown and soft
Bright yellow and firm
correctOption: Tan to reddish-brown and soft
optionExplanations: Beefy deep red and meaty describes the hyperplastic thyroid in Graves disease.
Pale gray and translucent describe the appearance of colloid in the thyroid gland, not the parathyroid parenchyma.
A gritty consistency is more common in thyroid papillary carcinomas with psammoma bodies; adenomas are typically soft.
Parathyroid adenomas are characteristically soft, well-circumscribed nodules with a tan to reddish-brown appearance.
Bright yellow color is characteristic of the normal adrenal cortex or adrenal adenomas due to lipid content.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): The typical adenoma ... consists of a well-circumscribed, soft, tan to reddish-brown nodule invested by a delicate capsule.

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: During the pathogenesis of primary hyperparathyroidism, which physiological consequence is directly attributed to the effect of parathyroid hormone on renal tubular function?
options: Increased excretion of ionized calcium into the urine
Suppression of osteoclastic activity in the skeletal system
Enhanced reabsorption of phosphate in the proximal tubule
Increased urinary phosphate excretion and hypophosphatemia
Inhibition of vitamin D conversion to its active form
correctOption: Increased urinary phosphate excretion and hypophosphatemia
optionExplanations: PTH increases renal tubular reabsorption of calcium to conserve free calcium, rather than increasing its excretion, although hypercalciuria may eventually occur if the filtered load exceeds reabsorptive capacity.
PTH enhances, rather than suppresses, osteoclastic activity by promoting the differentiation of progenitor cells into mature bone-resorbing cells.
PTH inhibits the sodium-phosphate cotransporter in the proximal tubule, thereby decreasing phosphate reabsorption.
The reduction in proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption leads to phosphaturia (increased excretion), which classically results in the low serum phosphate levels seen in primary hyperparathyroidism.
PTH actually increases the conversion of vitamin D to its active 1,25-dihydroxy form by stimulating 1-alpha-hydroxylase in the kidney.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1091 (Book Page): Increased urinary phosphate excretion, thereby lowering serum phosphate levels and further increasing calcium (since phosphate binds to ionized calcium)

category: Define thyroiditis
coreConcept: Pain as a Differential Feature in Thyroiditis
statement: How does granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis typically differ from subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis in its clinical presentation?
options: Granulomatous thyroiditis exclusively occurs in the postpartum period
Granulomatous thyroiditis is associated with germinal center formation
Granulomatous thyroiditis typically presents with severe thyroid pain
Granulomatous thyroiditis is painless while lymphocytic is painful
Granulomatous thyroiditis is caused by autoantibodies while lymphocytic is viral
correctOption: Granulomatous thyroiditis typically presents with severe thyroid pain
optionExplanations: Lymphocytic thyroiditis has a specific postpartum variant; granulomatous thyroiditis is usually seasonal (summer) and unrelated to pregnancy.
Germinal centers are characteristic of Hashimoto and lymphocytic thyroiditis, while granulomatous thyroiditis is characterized by giant cells and colloid pools.
Severe neck pain and tenderness, often following a respiratory infection, is the classic presentation of de Quervain thyroiditis.
This is reversed; de Quervain is painful and subacute lymphocytic is known as 'painless' thyroiditis.
Subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis is presumed autoimmune, whereas granulomatous is believed to be triggered by viral infections.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): Granulomatous thyroiditis is the most common cause of thyroid pain. There is variable enlargement of the gland. Inflammation of the thyroid and hyperthyroidism are transient.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: A 24-year-old primiparous woman presents with a fever, breast pain, and localized erythema during her third week of breastfeeding. Physical examination reveals a palpable, fluctuant mass. Which pathogen is most frequently isolated from the purulent material in this specific clinical presentation?
options: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Bacteroides fragilis
Streptococcus pyogenes
Corynebacterium species
Staphylococcus aureus
correctOption: Staphylococcus aureus
optionExplanations: Mycobacterial infection of the breast is exceedingly rare and usually occurs in immunocompromised patients or as a manifestation of systemic disease, presenting with chronic granulomatous features.
Bacteroides are anaerobic organisms. While they can be involved in secondary infections of subareolar abscesses (Zuska disease), they are not the primary cause of acute lactational mastitis.
Streptococci are important causes of lactational mastitis, but they typically produce a diffuse, spreading infection known as cellulitis rather than focal, fluctuant abscesses.
Corynebacterium species are more commonly associated with cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis, a non-lactational inflammatory condition.

Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of acute mastitis during the first month of breastfeeding. It classically results in localized suppuration and abscess formation when bacteria enter through nipple fissures.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1038 (Book Page): Staphylococci infection often leads to single or multiple abscesses, whereas streptococci cause spreading infection in the form of cellulitis.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: What is the most frequent molecular alteration identified in approximately 10% to 20% of sporadic parathyroid adenomas, leading to clonal overexpression of a cell cycle regulator?
options: Inversion of the Cyclin D1 (CCDN1) gene
Amplification of the HER2/neu receptor
Point mutation in the BRAF V600E codon
Epigenetic silencing of the PTH promoter
Translocation of the RET proto-oncogene
correctOption: Inversion of the Cyclin D1 (CCDN1) gene
optionExplanations: The relocation of the CCDN1 gene next to the PTH promoter via inversion leads to its overexpression and drives cellular proliferation in sporadic adenomas.
HER2/neu amplification is a hallmark of certain breast and gastric cancers, not parathyroid lesions.
BRAF mutations are common in papillary thyroid cancer and melanomas, but not in parathyroid adenomas.
Overexpression of the regulator, not silencing of the hormone promoter, is the mechanism described for tumor growth.
RET translocations are typical of papillary thyroid carcinoma (RET/PTC), not parathyroid adenomas.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): Cyclin D1 (CCDN1) gene inversions leading to overexpression of cyclin D1 protein, a major regulator of the cell cycle. ... Between 10% and 20% of sporadic parathyroid adenomas have this clonal rearrangement.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
coreConcept: Morphology of Islets in Type 2 Diabetes
statement: Which of the following morphologic features is a characteristic histologic finding in the pancreatic islets of individuals with long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus?
options: Amyloid deposition within and between islet cells
Hyperplasia of beta cells to 15 times normal size
A dense T-lymphocytic infiltrate (insulitis)
The formation of multinucleated giant cells within the exocrine ducts
The presence of PAS-negative Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules
correctOption: Amyloid deposition within and between islet cells
optionExplanations: Amyloidosis of the islets is the classic histologic hallmark of long-standing T2D, likely resulting from islet amyloid polypeptide (IAPP) co-secretion.
While islet hyperplasia occurs in newborns of diabetic mothers, beta-cell mass in T2D is usually subtly reduced or obliterated by amyloid.
Insulitis (lymphocytic infiltration) is a characteristic morphologic feature of type 1 diabetes (early stage), not type 2 diabetes.
Giant cells are features of granulomatous inflammation (like thyroiditis); they are not a standard feature of the diabetic pancreas.
Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules are found in the kidney glomeruli of diabetics, not in the pancreatic islets, and they are PAS-positive.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1106 (Book Page): Amyloid deposition within islets in T2D begins in and around capillaries and between cells. At advanced stages, the islets may be virtually obliterated.

category: Describe salient morphological features of clinically significant subtypes of thyroiditis: i
coreConcept: Morphological differentiation between subacute lymphocytic (painless) thyroiditis and Hashimoto thyroiditis.
statement: When distinguishing subacute lymphocytic (painless) thyroiditis from Hashimoto thyroiditis under the microscope, which morphological combination would most strongly support a diagnosis of the subacute lymphocytic variant?
options: Infiltration of the interstitium by clusters of malignant signet-ring cells
Presence of well-developed germinal centers with extensive Hürthle cell metaplasia
Formation of dense collagenous bands extending beyond the thyroid capsule into neck muscles
Absence of prominent interstitial fibrosis and relative lack of Hürthle cell change
Focal areas of necrotizing vasculitis involving the small thyroidal arteries
correctOption: Absence of prominent interstitial fibrosis and relative lack of Hürthle cell change
optionExplanations: Option D refers to metastatic signet-ring cell carcinoma (usually from the GI tract), which is not a feature of any thyroiditis subtype.
Option A describes classic Hashimoto thyroiditis, where metaplastic Hürthle cells are a diagnostic requirement for the 'struma lymphomatosa' pattern.
Option E is characteristic of Riedel thyroiditis, a rare fibro-inflammatory disorder associated with IgG4-related disease, not painless thyroiditis.

Option B is correct. Subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis histologically mimics Hashimoto in its infiltrate but is distinguished by the relative absence of both follicular metaplasia (Hürthle cells) and significant scarring (fibrosis).
Option C describes a vasculitic process not seen in thyroiditis, though autoimmune components exist, the primary pathology is follicular and interstitial, not vascular.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): Microscopic examination reveals lymphocytic infiltration with large germinal centers within the thyroid parenchyma and patchy disruption and collapse of thyroid follicles. Unlike Hashimoto thyroiditis, however, fibrosis and Hürthle cell metaplasia are not prominent.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: Regarding stromal fat, how do both parathyroid adenomas and primary parathyroid hyperplasias typically differ from the normal adult parathyroid gland?
options: Stromal fat is present in adenomas but absent in hyperplasia
Stromal fat is only found in the water-clear cell variant
Stromal fat is replaced by amyloid in both conditions
The stromal fat is inconspicuous or absent in both lesions
The stromal fat is significantly increased in both lesions
correctOption: The stromal fat is inconspicuous or absent in both lesions
optionExplanations: The loss of stromal fat is a shared feature between both adenomas and primary hyperplasia, which helps distinguish them from normal parathyroid tissue.
Water-clear cell hyperplasia, like other forms of hyperplasia, is characterized by a decrease or absence of normal stromal fat.
Amyloid deposition is a feature of certain pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (insulinomas) or medullary thyroid carcinoma, not parathyroid hyperplasia or adenoma.
Normal adult parathyroid glands contain approximately 30% fat; in hyperplastic or neoplastic states, this adipose tissue becomes very sparse or disappears.
Increased stromal fat is not a feature of these proliferative lesions; in fact, the proliferation of epithelial cells displaces the normal fat stores.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): In contrast to the normal parathyroid parenchyma, adipose tissue is inconspicuous [in adenomas]... As in the case of adenomas, stromal fat is inconspicuous within hyperplastic glands.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
statement: In a 30-year-old sexually active male presenting with acute epididymitis, which pair of pathogens is statistically most frequent according to epidemiological patterns of the male genital tract?
options: Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas species
Treponema pallidum and Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes
Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Gardnerella vaginalis and anaerobic bacteria
correctOption: Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
optionExplanations: These are common urinary tract pathogens that typically cause epididymitis in men older than 35 years.
T. pallidum causes syphilis and M. tuberculosis causes TB; while both affect the genital tract, they are not the most frequent causes of acute epididymitis in this age group.
While pyogenic, these are not the primary statistically most frequent agents in the sexually active young adult demographic.
In males under 35, sexually transmitted infections (STIs) specifically caused by Chlamydia and Gonococcus are the predominant causes of epididymitis.
These agents are more commonly associated with balanoposthitis rather than ascending epididymitis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 967 (Book Page): The cause of epididymitis varies with the age of the patient. ... In sexually active men younger than age 35 years, the sexually transmitted pathogens C. trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae are most frequent.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
coreConcept: Physiological Function of PSA in Semen
statement: A laboratory technician notes that a semen sample has failed to liquefy after 60 minutes. A deficiency in which specific androgen-regulated enzyme, normally produced by the prostatic epithelium, is likely responsible?
options: Acid phosphatase
Aromatase
5-alpha reductase
Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)
Alkaline phosphatase
correctOption: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)
optionExplanations: Prostatic acid phosphatase was historically used as a marker for prostate cancer, but PSA is the specific enzyme required for liquefaction.
Aromatase converts androgens to estrogens; while relevant in certain endocrine pathways, it has no role in post-ejaculatory semen processing.
5-alpha reductase converts testosterone to DHT and is critical for prostatic growth, but it does not participate in the liquefaction of the seminal coagulum.

PSA is a serine protease that cleaves the proteins responsible for the viscosity of the seminal coagulum. A lack of PSA action results in a failure of semen to liquefy, which can trap sperm and cause infertility.
Alkaline phosphatase is a marker used in various medical contexts but is not the primary protease involved in seminal liquefaction.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 981 (Book Page): PSA is a product of prostatic epithelium and is normally secreted in the semen. It is an androgen-regulated serine protease whose function is to cleave and liquefy the seminal coagulum formed after ejaculation.

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
statement: Which diagnostic laboratory finding is most critical for distinguishing the early hyperthyroid phase of granulomatous thyroiditis from Graves disease?
options: Elevated serum levels of thyroglobulin
Markedly elevated serum Free T4 and T3 levels
Diminished radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU)
Presence of circulating antithyroid peroxidase antibodies
Increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
correctOption: Diminished radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU)
optionExplanations: Thyroglobulin can be elevated in various inflammatory and neoplastic thyroid conditions and is not a specific differentiator for de Quervain's.
Both Graves disease and early de Quervain thyroiditis present with elevated T3 and T4, so these levels do not help in the differential diagnosis.
In Graves disease, the gland is hyperfunctional and actively takes up iodine. In de Quervain's, the gland is damaged and ‘leaking’ preformed hormone, resulting in very low active iodine uptake.
Antithyroid peroxidase antibodies are found in Hashimoto's and some cases of painless thyroiditis, making them less specific for de Quervain's.
While ESR is typically very high in de Quervain's, it is a nonspecific marker of inflammation and doesn't directly measure thyroid function like an RAIU scan.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): However, unlike in hyperthyroid states such as Graves disease, radioactive iodine uptake is diminished.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
statement: Before the widespread use of effective antimycobacterial therapies, which condition was the leading cause of primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency?
options: Amyloidosis of the adrenal cortex
Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome
Secondary metastatic carcinoma
Tuberculous adrenalitis
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
correctOption: Tuberculous adrenalitis
optionExplanations: Amyloidosis is a rare cause of primary failure and has never been the dominant etiology in any historical period.
Autoimmune causes are now the most common, but they rose to prominence only after the decline of tuberculosis in high-income regions.
Metastatic disease is a cause, but it has never been the 'leading' cause in the way TB once was.
Historically, infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis was the primary reason for adrenal destruction. It remains a major cause in regions where the infection is still prevalent.
CAH is a congenital enzyme defect that causes hyperplasia, not the chronic destructive insufficiency described as Addison disease.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1121 (Book Page): Tuberculous adrenalitis, which once accounted for as much as 90% of cases of Addison disease, has become less common with the development of antimycobacterial drugs.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
statement: A 40-year-old male presents with chronic suprapubic discomfort and low back pain. Expressed prostatic secretions reveal 15 leukocytes per high-power field, but repeated bacterial cultures are negative. What is the most common clinical designation for this condition?
options: Chronic abacterial prostatitis (Chronic pelvic pain syndrome)
Chronic bacterial prostatitis
Acute bacterial prostatitis
Malakoplakia of the prostate
Granulomatous prostatitis secondary to BCG
correctOption: Chronic abacterial prostatitis (Chronic pelvic pain syndrome)
optionExplanations: Chronic abacterial prostatitis is characterized by typical symptoms and leukocytosis in secretions (>10/HPF) despite consistently negative cultures.
Chronic bacterial prostatitis presents with recurrent UTIs and positive cultures for the causative organism.
Acute bacterial prostatitis would present with systemic symptoms like fever and chills, and cultures would be positive for urinary pathogens.
Malakoplakia is a rare inflammatory condition; it is not the most common form of prostatitis and has specific histological features (Michaelis-Gutmann bodies).
Granulomatous prostatitis is a histological diagnosis; while common after BCG therapy, it does not match the clinical profile of 'abacterial' findings described.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 975 (Book Page): Chronic abacterial prostatitis, the most common form of prostatitis, is often referred to clinically as chronic pelvic pain syndrome... Expressed prostatic secretions contain more than 10 leukocytes per high-power field, but bacterial cultures are uniformly negative.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: Which histological feature is most useful in distinguishing a solitary parathyroid adenoma from primary hyperplasia when evaluating a single resected gland?
options: Identification of signet-ring cells
Formation of true papillae with fibrovascular cores
The presence of a rim of compressed, non-neoplastic tissue
The presence of large lakes of mucin
The absolute number of mitotic figures
correctOption: The presence of a rim of compressed, non-neoplastic tissue
optionExplanations: Signet-ring cells are associated with lobular breast carcinoma or gastric adenocarcinoma, but not parathyroid pathology.
True papillae with fibrovascular cores are the hallmark of papillary thyroid carcinoma, not parathyroid chief cell adenomas.
In an adenoma, a rim of normal, compressed parathyroid tissue is typically seen outside the tumor capsule, a feature usually absent in diffuse hyperplasia.
Lakes of mucin are characteristic of mucinous carcinomas (e.g., of the ovary or breast) and are not found in parathyroid lesions.
Mitotic figures are generally rare in both adenomas and hyperplasias; their presence alone is not a reliable differentiator for these benign entities.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): A rim of compressed, non-neoplastic parathyroid tissue, generally separated by a fibrous capsule, is often visible at the edge of the adenoma.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
coreConcept: Preoperative morphological changes in Graves disease
statement: During the surgical preparation of a patient with Graves disease, the administration of iodine solution is intended to induce which morphological change in the thyroid gland?
options: Direct destruction of follicles by inducing liquefactive necrosis
Stimulation of stromal fibrosis to increase gland firmness
Exaggeration of epithelial hypertrophy to facilitate easier resection
Induction of lymphocytic infiltration and germinal center formation
Epithelial involution and accumulation of colloid in the follicles
correctOption: Epithelial involution and accumulation of colloid in the follicles
optionExplanations: Iodine solutions do not cause liquefactive necrosis; they function by transiently inhibiting hormone release and altering follicular cell architecture.
While chronic injury can lead to fibrosis, the immediate effect of preoperative iodine is concentrated on the follicular epithelium and colloid content rather than stromal fibrous growth.
Epithelial hypertrophy is actually exaggerated by propylthiouracil due to rising TSH levels, making the gland more vascular and difficult to handle surgically.
Lymphocytic infiltration and germinal centers are intrinsic features of the autoimmune process in Graves and are not induced by preoperative iodine therapy.
Iodine treatment blocks the proteolysis of thyroglobulin, leading to the accumulation of colloid and flattening of the tall columnar epithelium, which decreases gland vascularity before surgery.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): Administration of iodine causes involution of the epithelium and the accumulation of colloid by blocking thyroglobulin secretion.

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: A 55-year-old male with a history of squamous cell carcinoma of the lung presents with a serum calcium level of 13.5 mg/dL. Imaging shows no evidence of skeletal metastases. What is the most likely pathophysiological mechanism for his hypercalcemia?
options: Secretion of parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP)
Direct osteolysis by tumor cells
Ectopic secretion of native parathyroid hormone (PTH)
Excessive intake of calcium-containing antacids
Increased renal 1-alpha hydroxylase activity
correctOption: Secretion of parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP)
optionExplanations: Humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy is most often caused by tumor secretion of PTHrP, which mimics PTH by activating the same receptors to increase bone resorption.
Direct osteolysis occurs in roughly 20% of malignancy-related hypercalcemia cases, typically in multiple myeloma or metastatic breast cancer, but imaging here shows no bone lesions.
Ectopic production of the native PTH molecule by non-parathyroid tumors is an extremely rare medical phenomenon and is not the standard mechanism.
Milk-alkali syndrome results from high calcium and alkali intake; while lung cancer patients can have poor nutrition, it does not explain the biochemical drive of hypercalcemia in this scenario.
Increased 1-alpha hydroxylase is characteristic of granulomatous diseases like sarcoidosis or certain lymphomas (Hodgkin), not usually squamous cell carcinomas.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1094 (Book Page): [The most common mechanism (in ~80% of cases) through which osteolytic tumors induce hypercalcemia is by secretion of PTH-related peptide (PTHrP)]

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
statement: A patient with Graves disease is treated with propylthiouracil in preparation for surgery. How does this specific pharmacological intervention affect the morphology of the thyroid follicular cells according to its physiological feedback loop?
options: Promotes the formation of Hürthle cell metaplasia
Exaggerates epithelial hypertrophy and hyperplasia
Induces involution of the tall columnar cells into flattened cuboidal cells
Increases the accumulation of dense, dark-staining colloid
Stimulates the development of multiple psammoma bodies
correctOption: Exaggerates epithelial hypertrophy and hyperplasia
optionExplanations: Hürthle cell metaplasia is a characteristic response to chronic injury found in Hashimoto thyroiditis, not a result of antithyroid medication in Graves.
By blocking T3/T4 synthesis, propylthiouracil causes a compensatory rise in TSH, which further stimulates the follicular cells, worsening the hyperplastic appearance histologically.
Involution and flattening of cells are effects of iodine administration, which blocks hormone release, rather than propylthiouracil.
Colloid accumulation occurs when the release of thyroglobulin is blocked (e.g., by iodine), whereas propylthiouracil-treated glands typically show scalloped, depleted colloid.
Psammoma bodies are characteristic of papillary thyroid carcinoma and are not produced in Graves disease, even after propylthiouracil treatment.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1080 (Book Page): Treatment with the antithyroid drug propylthiouracil exaggerates the epithelial hypertrophy and hyperplasia by stimulating TSH secretion.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
statement: A complete failure of the intra-abdominal testes to descend into the scrotal sac is present in approximately what percentage of 1-year-old boys?
optionExplanations: 0.1% is too low; cryptorchidism is more common than this in the general pediatric population.
25% refers to the percentage of cryptorchidism cases that are bilateral, not the overall prevalence.
10% is the frequency of cryptorchidism found in cases of testicular germ cell tumors, not its prevalence in 1-year-old infants.
Correct. According to epidemiologic data, roughly 1% of boys reach their first birthday with at least one undescended testis.
50% is the approximate percentage of enlarged inguinal nodes that actually contain cancer in penile squamous cell carcinoma, unrelated to infant descent.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 966 (Book Page): Cryptorchidism ... is found in approximately 1% of 1-year-old boys.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Diffuse and Multinodular goiter
statement: Certain dietary substances can exacerbate iodine deficiency by interfering with thyroid hormone synthesis. What is the specific mechanism by which cassava root contributes to goitrogenesis?
options: It contains antibodies that block the TSH receptor
It acts as a thiocyanate that inhibits iodide transport
It causes direct apoptosis of follicular C-cells
It stimulates the excessive proteolysis of thyroglobulin
It inhibits the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3
correctOption: It acts as a thiocyanate that inhibits iodide transport
optionExplanations: Cassava provides thiocyanate, a chemical inhibitor; it does not involve antibody-mediated receptor blockade.
Thiocyanates in cassava competitively inhibit the sodium-iodide symporter, preventing the thyroid from capturing necessary iodine.
Follicular C-cells produce calcitonin and are not the primary cells involved in the TSH-mediated goitrogenesis of the follicles.
Excessive proteolysis would release more hormone; goitrogens inhibit synthesis, leading to TSH-driven growth.
Propylthiouracil inhibits peripheral conversion; goitrogens like cassava typically act at the level of the gland's uptake or organification.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1081 (Book Page): Native populations subsisting on cassava root are particularly at risk. Cassava contains a thiocyanate that inhibits iodide transport within the thyroid, worsening any concurrent iodine deficiency.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
statement: What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism underlying anovulatory cycles in the context of dysfunctional uterine bleeding?
options: Excessive endometrial stimulation by estrogens unopposed by progesterone.
Infiltration of the functionalis layer by neutrophils and lymphocytes during menses.
Cessation of the proliferative phase due to excessive levels of serum androgens.
Decreased production of insulin-like growth factor-1 by the endometrial stroma.
Premature involution of the corpus luteum leading to progesterone withdrawal.
correctOption: Excessive endometrial stimulation by estrogens unopposed by progesterone.
optionExplanations: Anovulation prevents the formation of the corpus luteum, leaving the endometrium under constant estrogenic influence without the differentiating effects of progesterone.
The presence of these cells is a normal feature of late secretory changes and breakdown, not the driver of anovulation.
Androgens can contribute to anovulation in syndromes like PCOS, but the bleeding itself results from the estrogen-progesterone imbalance, not the cessation of proliferation.
Insulin-like growth factor-1 is actually produced by stroma in response to estrogen to drive proliferation; its absence is not the primary cause of anovulatory DUB.
This mechanism describes an inadequate luteal phase rather than the more common anovulatory cycle.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1001 (Book Page): Failure of ovulation results in excessive endometrial stimulation by estrogens that is unopposed by progesterone.

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
coreConcept: Distinguishing true lactotroph adenomas from 'stalk effect' hyperprolactinemia.
statement: A patient with a large nonfunctional pituitary tumor is found to have mild hyperprolactinemia (40 ng/mL). Histology shows a null cell adenoma. What is the most likely physiological explanation for the elevated prolactin in this case?
options: Loss of hypothalamic dopaminergic inhibition (stalk effect)
Co-secretion of GH and prolactin
Ectopic secretion of prolactin by the tumor cells
Mutations in the GNAS gene
Increased TRH stimulation on lactotrophs
correctOption: Loss of hypothalamic dopaminergic inhibition (stalk effect)
optionExplanations: The stalk effect occurs when a mass compresses the pituitary stalk, blocking the flow of dopamine (prolactin inhibitory factor) to lactotrophs.
Co-secretion would make it a plurihormonal or mammosomatotroph adenoma, not a null cell adenoma.
Null cell adenomas do not express or secrete hormones by definition.
GNAS mutations are associated with somatotroph adenomas, not null cell adenomas or hyperprolactinemia.
TRH can stimulate prolactin, but the 'stalk effect' from mass compression is the standard mechanism here.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1069 (Book Page): Any suprasellar mass (e.g., a pituitary adenoma) may disturb the inhibitory influence of the hypothalamus on prolactin secretion, resulting in hyperprolactinemia. Therefore, mild hyperprolactenemia in a person with a pituitary adenoma does not necessarily indicate a prolactin-secreting tumor.

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
statement: A 45-year-old female presents with a painfully enlarged thyroid gland. Her history reveals a recent upper respiratory tract infection. Which of the following is the most likely demographic and incidence profile for her suspected condition?
options: Predominantly seen in elderly males with a history of autoimmune disorders.
Almost exclusively found in postmenopausal women over age 65.
More common in women than men, typically occurring between 40 and 50 years of age.
Equally common in men and women between the ages of 20 and 30.
Most common in children following a streptococcal pharyngeal infection.
correctOption: More common in women than men, typically occurring between 40 and 50 years of age.
optionExplanations: This profile does not match De Quervain thyroiditis; autoimmune disorders are more characteristic of Hashimoto thyroiditis, which is typically painless.
The peak incidence is in the fifth decade (40-50 years), not exclusively in the elderly population over 65.
According to the text, the disorder is most prevalent in the 40-50 age bracket and follows a 4:1 female-to-male ratio, often following a viral trigger.
Granulomatous thyroiditis is not equally distributed among genders; it shows a strong female predilection (4:1) and usually occurs later than the third decade.
While it follows a respiratory infection, the trigger is viral rather than streptococcal, and it is an adult disease rather than a pediatric one.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): Granulomatous thyroiditis (also called de Quervain thyroiditis) occurs much less frequently than does Hashimoto thyroiditis. The disorder is most common between 40 and 50 years of age and, like other forms of thyroiditis, affects women more often than men (4 : 1).

category: Enumerate clinical manifestations along with hormone levels of anterior pituitary
statement: A 28-year-old female with amenorrhea and galactorrhea is found to have a 0.6 cm pituitary lesion. Medical therapy is initiated to decrease the size of the lesion and normalize hormone levels. The drug used acts primarily as an agonist for which of the following receptors?
options: Dopamine receptors
Thyrotropin-releasing hormone receptors
ACTH receptors
Somatostatin receptors
Growth hormone receptors
correctOption: Dopamine receptors
optionExplanations: Bromocriptine and other dopamine agonists mimic the natural inhibitory effect of hypothalamic dopamine on lactotrophs, effectively reducing both prolactin secretion and tumor volume.
TRH can stimulate prolactin release; an agonist would worsen the condition.
There is no clinical role for ACTH receptor agonists in the treatment of prolactinomas.
Somatostatin analogues are typically used for somatotroph adenomas, not primary lactotroph adenomas.
Growth hormone receptor antagonists block the effects of GH in the periphery but do not treat the underlying lactotroph adenoma.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1068 (Book Page): Lactotroph adenomas are treated by surgery or, more commonly, with bromocriptine, a dopamine receptor agonist that causes the lesions to diminish in size.

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: In the metabolic regulation of calcium, parathyroid hormone (PTH) directly enhances which of the following renal processes?
options: Inhibition of calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule
Reduction of cAMP levels in follicular cells
Conversion of vitamin D to its active dihydroxy form
Urinary calcium excretion
Reabsorption of phosphate in the proximal tubule
correctOption: Conversion of vitamin D to its active dihydroxy form
optionExplanations: PTH actually promotes calcium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule of the nephron.
PTH signaling in its target cells involves the stimulation of adenyl cyclase and subsequent increase in cAMP, not its reduction.
PTH stimulates the 1-alpha-hydroxylase enzyme in the kidney, which converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D into the active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.
PTH acts to increase renal reabsorption of calcium, thereby decreasing its urinary excretion.
PTH increases urinary phosphate excretion by inhibiting its reabsorption, which helps increase the ionized fraction of calcium in blood.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1091 (Book Page): [Increased conversion of vitamin D to its active dihydroxy form in the kidneys, which, in turn, augments gastrointestinal calcium absorption]

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
statement: Which of the following scenarios specifically leads to the development of an abdominal ectopic pregnancy?
options: The fertilized ovum drops out of the fimbriated end of the tube
Primary invasion of the placenta into the uterine serosa
Fertilization occurring within the endometrial cavity
Implantation in the intrauterine portion of the fallopian tube
Failure of the decidual layer to develop in the uterus
correctOption: The fertilized ovum drops out of the fimbriated end of the tube
optionExplanations: Abdominal pregnancy occurs when the embryo either never enters the tube or exits the distal opening (fimbriae), subsequently attaching to peritoneal or visceral surfaces.
Placental invasion through the entire wall of the uterus into the serosa is known as placenta percreta, not an abdominal ectopic pregnancy.
Fertilization in the cavity followed by normal implantation is the definition of a healthy intrauterine pregnancy.
Implantation in the intrauterine tube segment is called a cornual pregnancy, not an abdominal one.
Lack of decidua in the uterus results in placenta accreta, an intrauterine abnormality.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1027 (Book Page): Abdominal pregnancies occur when the fertilized ovum fails to enter or drops out of the fimbriated end of the tube.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
coreConcept: Crooke Hyaline Change in the Pituitary
statement: In a patient with a functional cortisol-secreting adrenal adenoma, the non-neoplastic ACTH-producing cells of the anterior pituitary undergo a characteristic change. What is the pathophysiological mechanism of this 'Crooke hyaline change'?
options: Depletion of secretory granules due to chronic TSH stimulation
Hyperplasia of pituicytes in response to low ACTH
Atrophy and loss of pro-opiomelanocortin synthesis
Liquefactive necrosis due to lack of blood supply
Accumulation of intermediate keratin filaments in the cytoplasm
correctOption: Accumulation of intermediate keratin filaments in the cytoplasm
optionExplanations: This change is related to ACTH-producing cells and high glucocorticoids, not TSH stimulation.
Pituicytes are glial cells of the posterior pituitary and are not involved in this anterior pituitary corticotroph response.
While ACTH synthesis is suppressed, the specific 'hyaline' morphology is due to filament accumulation rather than simple atrophy.
This is a reactive cellular change, not an ischemic necrotic process.
Crooke hyaline change represents the accumulation of intermediate keratin filaments, making the cytoplasm look homogeneous and pale under the microscope in response to high cortisol.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1114 (Book Page): The most common alteration, resulting from high levels of endogenous or exogenous glucocorticoids, is termed Crooke hyaline change. In this condition, the normal granular, basophilic cytoplasm of the ACTH-producing cells in the anterior pituitary becomes homogeneous and paler. This alteration is the result of the accumulation of intermediate keratin filaments in the cytoplasm.

category: Hashimoto Thyroiditis ii
statement: Which of the following autoantigens are the primary targets of the circulating autoantibodies found in the vast majority of Hashimoto thyroiditis patients?
options: Transthyretin and Albumin
TSH receptor and Iodine pump
Calcitonin and Retinoic acid receptor
Pendrin and Monoamine oxidase
Thyroglobulin and Thyroid peroxidase
correctOption: Thyroglobulin and Thyroid peroxidase
optionExplanations: Transthyretin and Albumin are plasma proteins that bind and transport thyroid hormones in the blood. They are not thyroid-specific antigens. Autoantibodies in Hashimoto's target the components of the thyroid gland itself (intrinsic proteins) rather than the external transport proteins that circulate in the general systemic blood flow.

The TSH receptor is the target of antibodies in Graves disease (stimulating) or occasionally in rare cases of atrophic hypothyroidism (blocking). While Hashimoto's involves a broad immune breakdown, the specific, high-frequency diagnostic markers are those directed against thyroglobulin and the peroxidase enzyme.

Calcitonin is produced by C cells and is a marker for medullary thyroid carcinoma, not autoimmune thyroiditis. The retinoic acid receptor is involved in gene transcription but is not a recognized primary target of autoantibodies in the chronic inflammatory destruction of the thyroid gland seen in Hashimoto's.

Pendrin is a protein involved in iodide transport (defective in Pendred syndrome), and Monoamine oxidase is an enzyme involved in neurotransmitter metabolism. Neither of these proteins are the classic autoantigens tested in the clinical workup for Hashimoto thyroiditis, which remains focused on TPO and thyroglobulin.

Thyroglobulin and thyroid peroxidase (TPO) are the two major autoantigens in Hashimoto thyroiditis. Antibodies against these proteins are found in over 90% of patients. Thyroglobulin is the precursor to thyroid hormones, and TPO is the enzyme responsible for the organification of iodine; both are essential for normal hormone synthesis and are targeted by the immune system.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1076 (Book Page): Hashimoto thyroiditis is caused by a breakdown in self-tolerance to thyroid autoantigens. This is exemplified by the presence of circulating autoantibodies against thyroglobulin and thyroid peroxidase in the vast majority of patients.

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
statement: Which of the following clinical conditions is uniquely associated with a site of abnormal placental implantation in the lower uterine segment or cervix, often necessitating a cesarean delivery?
options: Abruptio placentae
Placenta accreta
Cornual pregnancy
Hematosalpinx
Placenta previa
correctOption: Placenta previa
optionExplanations: Abruptio placentae is the premature separation of a normally implanted placenta, not a site-specific abnormal implantation.
Placenta accreta involves the absence of decidua leading to direct myometrial adherence but is not defined strictly by the 'lower segment' location, though it can coexist with previa.
Cornual pregnancy is a form of ectopic pregnancy in the tubal-uterine junction, not a lower segment implantation.
Hematosalpinx is a blood-filled fallopian tube, a classic morphologic consequence of a ruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy, not a site of implantation itself.
Placenta previa specifically involves implantation at or near the internal os in the lower uterus, posing a risk of hemorrhage and requiring surgical delivery.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1029 (Book Page): Placenta previa is a condition in which the placenta implants in the lower uterine segment or cervix, often leading to serious third-trimester bleeding. A complete placenta previa covers the internal cervical os and thus requires cesarean delivery.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
statement: Which of the following is the most common cause of granulomatous prostatitis in clinical practice in the United States?
options: Reflux of sterile urine with high uric acid content
Chronic infection by Proteus mirabilis
Instillation of Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) for bladder cancer
Disseminated Histoplasma capsulatum in HIV patients
Systemic sarcoidosis
correctOption: Instillation of Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) for bladder cancer
optionExplanations: Reaction to prostatic secretions is 'nonspecific' granulomatous prostatitis, not the leading cause compared to BCG.
Proteus causes acute or chronic bacterial prostatitis, which is suppurative rather than granulomatous.
BCG, an attenuated mycobacterium used intravesically, triggers a local granulomatous inflammatory response that can involve the prostate; this is the leading cause of this finding.
Fungal causes are typically restricted to immunocompromised hosts and are not the overall most common cause.
Sarcoidosis is a systemic cause of granulomas but is less common in the prostate than iatrogenic BCG-induced reactions.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 975 (Book Page): Granulomatous prostatitis may be caused by a specific infectious agent or may refer to a pattern of tissue reaction to noninfectious stimuli. In the United States, the most common cause is instillation of BCG for treatment of bladder cancer.

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: A molecular analysis of a sporadic parathyroid adenoma reveals an inversion of chromosome 11. This rearrangement most likely leads to the overexpression of which cell cycle regulator?
options: RB protein
Parafibromin
Cyclin D1
Menin
p53 tumor suppressor
correctOption: Cyclin D1
optionExplanations: The retinoblastoma (RB) protein is a cell cycle inhibitor; its loss is found in some aggressive tumors but is not the target of the chromosome 11 inversion.
Parafibromin is the product of the CDC73 gene, which is primarily mutated in parathyroid carcinomas rather than sporadic adenomas via this inversion.
The inversion places the Cyclin D1 gene under the control of the potent parathyroid hormone promoter, driving unchecked cell proliferation.
Menin is the protein product of the MEN1 gene; while MEN1 mutations occur in parathyroid tumors, they do not involve this specific inversion mechanism.
p53 is a tumor suppressor involved in many cancers, but the specific chromosome 11 inversion in parathyroid adenomas targets Cyclin D1.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): A pericentromeric inversion on chromosome 11 results in relocation of CCDN1 (normally on 11q), so that it is positioned adjacent to the 5′-flanking region of the PTH gene (on 11p). As a consequence of these changes, a 5′-regulatory element flanking the PTH gene directs overexpression of cyclin D1.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
coreConcept: Molecular precursor of pigmentation in Addison disease
statement: Which pituitary-derived precursor molecule is elevated in Addison disease and responsible for the 'bronzing' of the skin?
options: Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)
Melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH)
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)
Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)
Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)
correctOption: Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)
optionExplanations: FSH is a gonadotropin and has no role in the pathology or clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency.
MSH is the active hormone that acts on the skin, but it is a cleavage product of the larger POMC precursor molecule mentioned in the text.
TSH is part of the thyroid axis and is not involved in adrenal feedback or skin pigmentation.
POMC is the large precursor protein synthesized by the pituitary. Because it contains the amino acid sequences of both ACTH and MSH, its elevation leads to the classic pigmentation.
ACTH is elevated, but the specific precursor molecule that contains the MSH sequence is POMC.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1122 (Book Page): This is caused by elevated levels of pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC), which is derived from the anterior pituitary and is a precursor of both ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH).

category: Hashimoto Thyroiditis ii
statement: A patient diagnosed with Hashimoto thyroiditis initially presents with symptoms of hyperthyroidism, including palpitations and weight loss, despite a low radioactive iodine uptake scan. What is the specific term for this clinical phenomenon?
options: Cretinism
De Quervain syndrome
Hashitoxicosis
Myxedema coma
Plummer syndrome
correctOption: Hashitoxicosis
optionExplanations: Cretinism refers to severe hypothyroidism during infancy or early childhood.
De Quervain syndrome is granulomatous thyroiditis, which causes pain and is often viral in origin.
Hashitoxicosis is a transient hyperthyroid state occurring early in Hashimoto thyroiditis when inflammation destroys follicles, spilling preformed hormone into the blood.
Myxedema refers to the severe, chronic hypothyroid state in adults, the opposite of thyrotoxicosis.
Plummer syndrome is toxic multinodular goiter, caused by autonomous nodules, not autoimmune follicle destruction.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): In some patients, however, it may be preceded by transient thyrotoxicosis caused by disruption of thyroid follicles and release of thyroid hormones (hashitoxicosis).

category: Enumerate clinical manifestations along with hormone levels of anterior pituitary
statement: A somatic mutation in the GNAS gene, leading to the loss of GTPase activity in the Gsα protein, is most characteristically associated with which clinical manifestation?
options: Bitemporal hemianopsia without hormonal excess
Hypothyroidism and cold intolerance
Gigantism or acromegaly
Cushingoid features and hyperpigmentation
Galactorrhea and amenorrhea
correctOption: Gigantism or acromegaly
optionExplanations: Bitemporal hemianopsia is a mass effect of large adenomas but is not a direct biochemical consequence of GNAS-mediated hormone hypersecretion.
Hypothyroidism results from TSH deficiency (hypopituitarism) rather than G-protein mediated hypersecretion.
GNAS mutations lead to constitutive cAMP signaling, which in somatotrophs causes Growth Hormone (GH) hypersecretion, resulting in gigantism (children) or acromegaly (adults).
Cushingoid features result from ACTH excess (Corticotroph adenomas), which are more commonly linked to USP8 mutations rather than GNAS.
Galactorrhea and amenorrhea are features of Prolactinomas, which typically do not involve GNAS mutations.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1066 (Book Page): Approximately 40% of somatotroph cell adenomas bear somatic GNAS mutations that abrogate the GTPase activity of Gsα, leading to constitutive activation of Gsα, persistent generation of cAMP, and unchecked cellular proliferation.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: In the presence of a functional parathyroid adenoma, what is the typical morphologic state of the remaining three non-neoplastic parathyroid glands?
options: Fibrotic replacement with prominent lymphocytic infiltration
Increased stromal fat deposition with oxyphil cell metaplasia
Diffuse chief cell hyperplasia due to compensatory hormonal drive
Multinodular transformation with water-clear cell accumulation
Normal size or shrunken appearance due to feedback inhibition
correctOption: Normal size or shrunken appearance due to feedback inhibition
optionExplanations: Fibrosis and inflammation are not typical responses to the suppression of PTH production by hypercalcemia.
While stromal fat is present in normal glands, an increase is not the characteristic response to a functional adenoma in a neighboring gland.
Diffuse hyperplasia would occur in primary or secondary hyperplasia, not as a response to a functional adenoma in the other glands.
Multinodular transformation is a feature of primary hyperplasia (multiglandular disease), not the secondary atrophy seen in adenoma cases.

Correct. A functional adenoma produces excess PTH, leading to hypercalcemia. This high calcium level provides negative feedback to the normal parathyroid tissue, causing the other glands to involute or shrink.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): [In contrast to primary hyperplasia, the glands outside the adenoma are usually normal in size or shrunken because of feedback inhibition by elevated levels of serum calcium.]

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
coreConcept: Pathways of infection spread in Pelvic Inflammatory Disease
statement: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) can be caused by various bacteria depending on the inciting event. How does the anatomical spread of non-gonococcal bacterial infections, such as those following a surgical procedure or abortion, typically differ from gonococcal infections?
options: They utilize the squamous metaplasia of the transformation zone.
They are exclusively transmitted through retrograde menstruation.
They are restricted to the endocervical glands.
They spread through the lymphatics or venous channels.
They spread via the mucosal surfaces of the fallopian tubes.
correctOption: They spread through the lymphatics or venous channels.
optionExplanations: While the transformation zone is highly susceptible to HPV, it is not the primary route of ascending spread for acute bacterial non-gonococcal PID.
Retrograde menstruation is a theory for the pathogenesis of endometriosis, not the primary mechanism of bacterial invasion in post-surgical PID.
Neither gonococcal nor non-gonococcal PID is restricted to the endocervical glands; they are characterized by their ability to ascend and involve the upper genital tract.

Non-gonococcal PID (puerperal infections) usually results from bacteria like staphylococci or streptococci that invade the deeper tissue layers and spread systemically or locally via venous channels and lymphatics.
Gonococcal infections primarily spread along the mucosal surfaces, such as the endocervix and then upward to the fallopian tube mucosa.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 986 (Book Page): The non-gonococcal bacterial infections that follow induced abortion, dilation and curettage of the uterus, and other surgical procedures are thought to spread upward from the uterus through the lymphatics or venous channels rather than on the mucosal surfaces.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
coreConcept: Diagnostic Contrast of Specific Genital Tract Infections
statement: During a clinicopathologic conference, the primary site of infection for two chronic granulomatous diseases of the male genital tract is compared. Which of the following statements correctly identifies the anatomical sequence of involvement for Tuberculosis and Syphilis?
options: Tuberculosis involves the vas deferens first, whereas Syphilis involves the prostate first.
Both Tuberculosis and Syphilis involve the testis first.
Tuberculosis involves the testis first, whereas Syphilis involves the epididymis first.
Tuberculosis involves the epididymis first, whereas Syphilis involves the testis first.
Both Tuberculosis and Syphilis involve the epididymis first.
correctOption: Tuberculosis involves the epididymis first, whereas Syphilis involves the testis first.
optionExplanations: Neither Tuberculosis nor Syphilis typically originates in the vas deferens or prostate as their primary sentinel site of inflammation within the male genital system according to this reference context.
This statement is incorrect because Tuberculosis typically originates in the epididymis and only affects the testis through secondary extension.
This statement reverses the characteristic pathological patterns for both diseases as described in standard urogenital pathology.

Tuberculosis of the male genital tract almost invariably begins in the epididymis, often spreading from the urinary tract. In contrast, both acquired and congenital syphilis preferentially involve the testis first.
