The posterior lobe is neural tissue composed of the terminals of hypothalamic axons supported by specialized glia called pituicytes.
Somatotrophs and lactotrophs are specific hormone-producing epithelial cells of the anterior pituitary.
Basophils and acidophils are the histologic classifications of cells in the anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis).
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1071 (Book Page): The posterior pituitary consists of modified glial cells (termed pituicytes) and axonal processes extending from the hypothalamus.

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
statement: A 24-year-old male presents with acute scrotal pain and swelling. Clinical evaluation confirms acute epididymitis. Considering the patient's age, which of the following pairs of infectious agents are the most likely cause of this condition?
options: Staphylococci and Streptococci
Candida albicans and Gardnerella
Treponema pallidum and Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas species
correctOption: Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
optionExplanations: While these cause pyogenic infections, they are typically associated with puerperal PID in females or childhood epididymitis.
These agents are more commonly associated with balanoposthitis in uncircumcised males due to poor hygiene.
Syphilis typically involves the testis first (orchitis), and Tuberculosis begins in the epididymis but is less common in this age group than STIs.
In sexually active men under 35, STI-related organisms like Chlamydia and Gonorrhea are the predominant causes of epididymitis.
These gram-negative rods are the primary cause of epididymitis in men older than 35 years.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 967 (Book Page): In sexually active men younger than age 35 years, the sexually transmitted pathogens C. trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae are most frequent.

category: Describe salient morphological features of clinically significant subtypes of thyroiditis: i
coreConcept: Identifying Hürthle cells as the diagnostic metaplastic feature of Hashimoto thyroiditis.
statement: Which histological finding is considered the hallmark of the metaplastic response to chronic follicular injury in Hashimoto thyroiditis?
options: Small, uniform follicles containing pale, peripheral scalloped colloid
Epithelial cells with abundant eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm
Dense neutrophilic infiltrates forming numerous microabscesses
Diffuse squamous metaplasia extending into the perithyroidal tissue
Multinucleated giant cells surrounding extracellular pools of colloid
correctOption: Epithelial cells with abundant eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm
optionExplanations: Option D describes the hyperfunctional follicles typically seen in Graves disease, where active resorption leads to the scalloped appearance of colloid margins.

Option A is correct because Hürthle cells (also known as oxyphil cells) are follicular cells that undergo metaplasia in response to chronic autoimmune injury, accumulating numerous mitochondria that provide the granular eosinophilic appearance.
Option C describes an acute inflammatory response often seen in the early phase of granulomatous thyroiditis or acute infectious thyroiditis; Hashimoto is a chronic mononuclear process.

Option E is incorrect as squamous metaplasia is not a characteristic feature of Hashimoto thyroiditis; it is more associated with certain variants of papillary carcinoma or specific inflammatory conditions of the breast and ducts explored in other chapters of the text. Hashimoto fibrosis is restricted to the capsule and does not involve diffuse squamous changes in the parenchyma or surrounding tissue like Riedel thyroiditis might involve the muscle via fibrosis (not squamous metaplasia).
Option B describes the granulomatous response seen in subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis, not the autoimmune destruction typical of Hashimoto disease.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1077 (Book Page): The thyroid follicles are atrophic and are lined in many areas by epithelial cells with abundant eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm, termed Hürthle cells, which represent a metaplastic response of the normally low cuboidal follicular epithelium to chronic injury.

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
statement: Which of the following best describes the typical clinical course of the hypermetabolic state in granulomatous thyroiditis?
options: It results in progressive fibrosis extending to the carotid sheath
It is transient and usually lasts for 2 to 6 weeks
It typically bypasses the hyperthyroid phase and goes directly to myxedema
It is characterized by alternating phases of hypermetabolism every 6 months
It is permanent and requires lifelong thionamide therapy
correctOption: It is transient and usually lasts for 2 to 6 weeks
optionExplanations: Extensive fibrosis beyond the capsule is the hallmark of Riedel thyroiditis, not granulomatous thyroiditis.
The hyperthyroid phase is caused by leakage of hormone from damaged follicles and subsides as the hormone is metabolized and the follicles begin to heal, typically within 2-6 weeks.
The hyperthyroid phase is the most common clinical presentation due to the acute inflammatory release of hormones stored in the colloid.
There is no evidence of a cyclical alternating pattern; the disease usually follows a single sequence of hyperthyroid, transient hypothyroid, then euthyroid.
The condition is self-limiting and does not involve increased synthesis, so thionamides (which block synthesis) are not the standard long-term treatment.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): The inflammatory response is transient, usually diminishing in 2 to 6 weeks, even if the patient is not treated.

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
coreConcept: Histological subclassification and architectural features of pituitary adenomas.
statement: Histological examination of a pituitary mass reveals a uniform population of polygonal cells arranged in sheets, with a notably sparse reticulin network. Which feature most reliably distinguishes this lesion from normal anterior pituitary parenchyma?
options: Presence of multiple cell types (acidophils and basophils)
Active spermatogenesis
Cellular monomorphism
Presence of neuroglial stroma
Extensive keratinization
correctOption: Cellular monomorphism
optionExplanations: A mixture of cell types (acidophils, basophils, chromophobes) is characteristic of the normal pituitary, not an adenoma.
Spermatogenesis occurs in the testes, not the pituitary gland.
Cellular monomorphism (one uniform cell type) is the classic hallmark of a pituitary adenoma.
Neuroglial stroma is characteristic of the pineal gland or posterior pituitary, not an adenohypophyseal adenoma.
Keratinization is a feature of craniopharyngiomas (wet keratin), not adenomas.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1068 (Book Page): This cellular monomorphism and the absence of a significant reticulin network distinguish pituitary adenomas from normal anterior pituitary parenchyma (Fig. 24.5).

category: Describe salient morphological features of clinically significant subtypes of thyroiditis: i
statement: A 48-year-old female presents with gradual thyroid failure. Histology shows a dense mononuclear infiltrate and germinal centers. Which of the following immunologic mechanisms is primarily responsible for the thyrocyte injury observed in this condition?
options: Hyperplasia induced by iodine deficiency
Activation of the TSH receptor signaling pathway by GNAS mutations
TSH receptor stimulation by autoantibodies
CD8+ cytotoxic T cell-mediated cell death
Direct viral lysis of follicular epithelial cells
correctOption: CD8+ cytotoxic T cell-mediated cell death
optionExplanations: Iodine deficiency leads to compensatory hypertrophy and hyperplasia (goiter) to overcome hormone deficiency, not the autoimmune destruction of follicles.
GNAS mutations are associated with autonomous hormone secretion in functional (toxic) adenomas, not the autoimmune failure seen in Hashimoto thyroiditis.
This mechanism describes Graves disease, where thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) mimics TSH to cause hyperfunction rather than thyroid cell destruction.
The destruction of thyroid parenchyma in Hashimoto thyroiditis is mediated by cytotoxic T cells, cytokine-mediated injury from Th1 cells, and antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity.

Direct viral lysis is not a confirmed mechanism for autoimmune thyroiditis; although granulomatous thyroiditis has a viral trigger, the resulting damage is inflammatory rather than directly cytopathic.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1077 (Book Page): Multiple immunologic mechanisms may contribute to thyroid cell death, including... CD8+ cytotoxic T cell-mediated cell death: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells may destroy thyroid follicular cells.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: Which of the following represents the most frequent cause of clinical Cushing syndrome in medical practice?
options: ACTH-secreting pituitary microadenomas
Primary adrenocortical hyperplasia
Administration of exogenous glucocorticoids
Functioning adrenocortical adenomas
Ectopic secretion of corticotropin by small-cell lung cancer
correctOption: Administration of exogenous glucocorticoids
optionExplanations: While this is the most common endogenous cause (Cushing disease), it is not the most common cause overall across all clinical presentations.
Primary hyperplasia is an endogenous cause but is significantly rarer than iatrogenic causes.
Iatrogenic or exogenous administration of steroids for inflammatory or autoimmune conditions is the most common cause of the clinical constellation of hypercortisolism.
Adrenal neoplasms account for only a minority (approximately 15-25%) of endogenous cases.
Ectopic ACTH is a paraneoplastic syndrome that is less common than both iatrogenic and pituitary causes.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1113 (Book Page): The vast majority of cases of Cushing syndrome are the result of the administration of exogenous glucocorticoids (iatrogenic Cushing syndrome).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: In the setting of ectopic ACTH syndrome, particularly from a small-cell lung carcinoma, what is the characteristic morphologic change occurring within the adrenal glands?
options: Diffuse medullary hypertrophy
Unilateral cortical atrophy
Bilateral cortical hyperplasia
Bilateral cortical atrophy
Solitary yellow-tan adenoma
correctOption: Bilateral cortical hyperplasia
optionExplanations: The adrenal medulla is developmentally and functionally distinct from the cortex; its size is not increased by ACTH, which specifically targets the cortical zones for steroidogenesis.
Unilateral atrophy occurs when a primary tumor in the opposite adrenal gland suppresses ACTH, which is not the case in ectopic ACTH production where hormone levels are high.

High levels of circulating ACTH, whether from a pituitary source or an ectopic tumor, provide continuous trophic stimulation to both adrenal glands, resulting in bilateral thickening and expansion of the cortex.
Bilateral atrophy is the hallmark of exogenous glucocorticoid use, where high levels of synthetic steroids suppress the pituitary-adrenal axis, leading to a lack of trophic ACTH.
A solitary adenoma is a primary neoplastic cause of Cushing syndrome rather than a reactive change to high ACTH levels produced by a distant malignancy.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1113 (Book Page): As in the pituitary variant, the adrenal glands undergo bilateral cortical hyperplasia, but the rapid downhill course of patients with these cancers often limits the extent of the adrenal enlargement.

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
coreConcept: Secondary vs. Primary Hyperthyroidism Lab Patterns
statement: A 45-year-old female presents with palpitations and weight loss. Laboratory studies reveal elevated serum levels of free thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3). Unlike most cases of thyrotoxicosis, her thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level is inappropriately normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
options: Graves disease
Factitious thyrotoxicosis
TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma
Toxic multinodular goiter
Struma ovarii
correctOption: TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma
optionExplanations: Graves disease is primary hyperthyroidism caused by stimulating antibodies; the high T3/T4 levels would normally result in a severely depressed TSH level.
Factitious thyrotoxicosis is caused by exogenous intake of thyroid hormone; this would suppress the pituitary, resulting in a low TSH level.
In secondary (central) hyperthyroidism, the pituitary itself overproduces TSH, leading to elevated thyroid hormones in the presence of inappropriately normal or high TSH.
Toxic multinodular goiter involves autonomous hormone production by the thyroid gland, which would suppress TSH to low or undetectable levels via negative feedback.
Struma ovarii involves ectopic thyroid tissue production of hormones, which would similarly suppress the pituitary TSH through the normal feedback loop.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1075 (Book Page): In rare cases of pituitary-associated (secondary) hyperthyroidism, TSH levels are either normal or raised.

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
statement: A preeclamptic patient's laboratory panel reveals microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, elevated liver enzymes, and a platelet count of 85,000/μL. What is the most appropriate clinical designation for this constellation of findings?
options: Nelson Syndrome
Waterhouse-Friderichsen Syndrome
Plummer Syndrome
HELLP Syndrome
Kimmelstiel-Wilson Disease
correctOption: HELLP Syndrome
optionExplanations: Nelson syndrome involves the development of a pituitary adenoma after bilateral adrenalectomy, resulting in hyperpigmentation and mass effects.
Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is characterized by massive bilateral adrenal hemorrhage and acute adrenal insufficiency secondary to overwhelming sepsis (e.g., N. meningitidis).
Plummer syndrome, or toxic multinodular goiter, is a condition where a hyperfunctional nodule develops within a long-standing goiter, causing hyperthyroidism.
HELLP syndrome is the acronym for Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets, a severe manifestation found in a subset of preeclamptic patients.
Kimmelstiel-Wilson disease refers to nodular glomerulosclerosis, a characteristic renal lesion of long-standing diabetes mellitus.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1029 (Book Page): Approximately 10% of women with preeclampsia develop microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets, referred to as the HELLP syndrome

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: What is the direct effect of Parathyroid Hormone (PTH) on renal handling of minerals?
options: Inhibition of vitamin D activation
Suppression of osteoclastic activity
Reduction of gastrointestinal calcium absorption
Increased urinary phosphate excretion
Decreased renal tubular reabsorption of calcium
correctOption: Increased urinary phosphate excretion
optionExplanations: PTH increases the conversion of vitamin D to its active dihydroxy form by stimulating the enzyme alpha-1-hydroxylase in the kidneys.
PTH enhances osteoclastic activity to release calcium from the skeletal system into the circulation.
PTH indirectly increases gastrointestinal calcium absorption by upregulating active vitamin D production.
PTH inhibits phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubules, leading to phosphaturia (increased phosphate excretion).
PTH actually increases the renal tubular reabsorption of calcium to conserve free ionized calcium in the blood.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1091 (Book Page): Increased urinary phosphate excretion, thereby lowering serum phosphate levels and further increasing calcium (since phosphate binds to ionized calcium).

category: Define thyroiditis
statement: Histological examination of a thyroid gland reveals disruption of follicles and the presence of multinucleate giant cells enclosing pools of colloid. This morphology is characteristic of which condition?
options: Graves disease
Granulomatous thyroiditis
Subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis
Hashimoto thyroiditis
Riedel thyroiditis
correctOption: Granulomatous thyroiditis
optionExplanations: Graves disease morphology includes crowded follicular cells and scalloped colloid without inflammation or giant cells.
Granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis shows a characteristic granulomatous reaction with giant cells in response to extravasated colloid.
Subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis shows germinal centers and follicle collapse but lacks the giant cell reaction and granulomatous features.
Hashimoto thyroiditis is characterized by lymphocytes, plasma cells, germinal centers, and Hürthle cells, not granulomas or giant cells enclosing colloid.
Riedel thyroiditis presents with extensive, hard fibrosis, not granulomatous inflammation.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): Multinucleate giant cells enclose pools of colloid, hence the designation granulomatous thyroiditis.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: Acute mastitis, most commonly occurring during the first month of breastfeeding, is primarily caused by which causative organism?
options: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Candida albicans
Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Staphylococcus aureus
Corynebacterium lipophilum
correctOption: Staphylococcus aureus
optionExplanations: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a cause of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), not acute mastitis.
Candida albicans is a common cause of vulvovaginitis but not primary acute mastitis.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis causes chronic granulomatous inflammation and is a very rare cause of mastitis, typically non-lactational.
Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of acute lactational mastitis and breast abscesses; streptococci are the second most common.
Corynebacterium is associated with cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis, a rarer entity.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1038 (Book Page): From this portal of entry, Staphylococcus aureus or, less commonly, streptococci invade the breast tissue.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: Which description best matches the typical gross appearance of a parathyroid adenoma?
options: Beefy deep red gland with diffuse symmetric enlargement
Soft, tan to reddish-brown, well-circumscribed nodule
Multiloculated cystic structure filled with watery fluid
Hard, gray-white irregular mass weighing over 20 grams
Opaque gray-white plaque resembling parchment
correctOption: Soft, tan to reddish-brown, well-circumscribed nodule
optionExplanations: This describes the thyroid in Graves disease, not a parathyroid adenoma.
Correct. This is the classic gross appearance of a parathyroid adenoma.
Cystic change can occur in adenomas but is not the typical defining gross description.
This describes parathyroid carcinoma or a very large invasive tumor.
This describes lichen sclerosus of the vulva, not a parathyroid lesion.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): The typical adenoma averages 0.5 to 5 g and consists of a well-circumscribed, soft, tan to reddish-brown nodule invested by a delicate capsule.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: Which molecular alteration is found in approximately 10% to 20% of sporadic parathyroid adenomas, leading to cell cycle dysregulation?
options: BRAF V600E point mutation
RET proto-oncogene point mutation
GNAS gene inactivating mutation
CASR gene inactivating mutation
Cyclin D1 (CCDN1) gene inversion
correctOption: Cyclin D1 (CCDN1) gene inversion
optionExplanations: BRAF V600E is a driver in papillary thyroid carcinoma, not parathyroid adenomas.
RET mutations are associated with MEN-2 and medullary thyroid carcinoma, not sporadic parathyroid adenomas.
Activating GNAS mutations are seen in some somatotroph adenomas; inactivating mutations do not drive parathyroid adenoma proliferation.
Inactivating CASR mutations lead to familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia, not the clonal CCDN1 inversions seen in adenomas.
Relocation of the Cyclin D1 gene next to the PTH promoter via chromosome 11 inversion is a recognized driver in about 10-20% of sporadic cases.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): A pericentromeric inversion on chromosome 11 results in relocation of CCDN1... Between 10% and 20% of sporadic parathyroid adenomas have this clonal rearrangement.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
statement: A pathology resident is examining pancreatic tissue sections from a patient with a 20-year history of diabetes. Which histopathological finding would most strongly suggest the patient had Type 2 Diabetes rather than Type 1?
options: A marked increase in the number of beta cells with prominent mitotic figures.
The presence of necrotizing granulomas with multinucleated giant cells.
The deposition of amyloid within the islets of Langerhans.
A total absence of islet structures throughout the entire gland.
A dense lymphocytic infiltrate within the islets (insulitis).
correctOption: The deposition of amyloid within the islets of Langerhans.
optionExplanations: Option E is incorrect; beta cells are depleted in Type 1 and generally dysfunctional/reduced in late Type 2; they do not show marked mitotic increases.
Option D is incorrect; granulomas suggest diseases like sarcoidosis or tuberculosis, not diabetes.
Option C is correct because islet amyloid is present in over 90% of Type 2 diabetic patients and is not a feature of Type 1.
Option B is incorrect; while islets are reduced in Type 1, a total absence is rare, and islets are generally present in Type 2.
Option A is incorrect; insulitis (T-cell infiltrate) is a classic feature of Type 1 diabetes, not Type 2.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1107 (Book Page): Amyloid deposition within islets in T2D begins in and around capillaries and between cells.

category: Describe salient morphological features of clinically significant subtypes of thyroiditis: i
coreConcept: Differential Morphology of Autoimmune Thyroiditis Subtypes
statement: In contrasting the morphologies of subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis and Hashimoto thyroiditis, which finding is typically absent in the subacute lymphocytic variant?
options: Lymphocytic infiltration within the thyroid parenchyma
Patchy disruption and collapse of thyroid follicles
The presence of well-developed germinal centers
Circulating antithyroid peroxidase antibodies
Prominent Hürthle cell metaplasia and extensive fibrosis
correctOption: Prominent Hürthle cell metaplasia and extensive fibrosis
optionExplanations: Lymphocytic infiltration is a common feature of both conditions, reflecting the autoimmune nature of both Hashimoto and subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis.
Follicular disruption can occur in both, leading to a transient thyrotoxic phase early in the disease course as preformed hormone is released.
Germinal centers are frequently seen in both disorders, though they are often more robust and numerous in Hashimoto thyroiditis.
Most patients with subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis actually do have circulating antithyroid peroxidase antibodies, similar to Hashimoto's, making serology alone insufficient for distinction.

The absence of prominent Hürthle cells and significant fibrosis is the key histologic differentiator that separates subacute lymphocytic (painless) thyroiditis from the classic Hashimoto's morphology.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): [Unlike Hashimoto thyroiditis, however, fibrosis and Hürthle cell metaplasia are not prominent.]

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
statement: Epididymitis in childhood is relatively uncommon compared to adults. When it does occur, what is the most frequent underlying clinical association and type of pathogen involved?
options: Congenital genitourinary abnormality and Gram-negative rods
Idiopathic autoimmune reaction
Sexually transmitted C. trachomatis
Tuberculosis of the urinary tract
Viral infection with Mumps virus
correctOption: Congenital genitourinary abnormality and Gram-negative rods
optionExplanations: Childhood epididymitis is statistically linked to anatomical anomalies of the urinary tract which facilitate infection by common intestinal Gram-negative bacilli.
While granulomatous orchitis may have an autoimmune basis, it is a disease of middle-aged men and not a standard etiology for childhood epididymitis.
Chlamydia is a major cause in sexually active adults, but is not the primary cause of epididymitis in children who are not sexually active.
Tuberculosis typically presents in adults and begins in the epididymis, but it is a very rare cause of acute pediatric scrotal inflammation.
Mumps virus primarily causes orchitis in postpubertal males; testicular involvement is extremely rare in school-aged children.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 967 (Book Page): though uncommon in children, epididymitis in childhood is usually associated with a congenital genitourinary abnormality and infection with gram-negative rods.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: What happens to the amount of stromal fat in parathyroid tissue that has undergone adenomatous or hyperplastic transformation?
options: It increases significantly to occupy 60% of the gland weight
It remains constant at approximately 30% of the total gland
It converts into hemosiderin-laden brown tumors
It undergoes liquefactive necrosis and forms 'machine oil' cysts
It becomes inconspicuous or decreased within the involved area
correctOption: It becomes inconspicuous or decreased within the involved area
optionExplanations: Stromal fat increases with age in normal glands, but decreases in hyperactive/pathological states.
30% is the maximum amount of fat in a normal adult parathyroid gland, not in adenoma or hyperplasia.
Brown tumors are skeletal manifestations of hyperparathyroidism, not changes in parathyroid stromal fat.
Liquefactive necrosis and 'machine oil' fluid are descriptions associated with craniopharyngiomas, not parathyroid fat.
A hallmark of parathyroid hyperactivity (both adenoma and hyperplasia) is that the parenchymal cells replace the normal stromal fat.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): As in the case of adenomas, stromal fat is inconspicuous within hyperplastic glands.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
statement: During semen analysis, the liquefaction of the seminal coagulum is found to be delayed. Which androgen-regulated serine protease, essential for this process, is likely deficient or dysfunctional?
options: Lactate dehydrogenase
Alpha-fetoprotein
Human chorionic gonadotropin
Acid phosphatase
Prostate-specific antigen
correctOption: Prostate-specific antigen
optionExplanations: Lactate dehydrogenase is a marker of tumor burden in germ cell malignancies, not a functional component of seminal liquefaction.
Alpha-fetoprotein is a marker for yolk sac tumors and does not play a role in seminal liquefaction.
hCG is a hormone produced by trophoblastic tissue or certain germ cell tumors, not a protease in semen.
Prostatic acid phosphatase is present in the prostate but is not the primary enzyme responsible for liquefying the seminal clot.
PSA (Prostate-specific antigen) is the enzyme responsible for cleaving the proteins that form the seminal coagulum, allowing sperm to move freely.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 981 (Book Page): PSA is a product of prostatic epithelium and is normally secreted in the semen. It is an androgen-regulated serine protease whose function is to cleave and liquefy the seminal coagulum formed after ejaculation.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
coreConcept: Differential of Chronic Pelvic Pain Syndrome
statement: A 40-year-old male complains of chronic pelvic pain and suprapubic discomfort. Expressed prostatic secretions reveal more than 15 leukocytes per high-power field, but repeated bacterial cultures are negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Chronic abacterial prostatitis
Chronic bacterial prostatitis
Acute bacterial prostatitis
Malakoplakia of the prostate
Granulomatous prostatitis
correctOption: Chronic abacterial prostatitis
optionExplanations: Chronic abacterial prostatitis is clinically identical to the bacterial form but is distinguished by the absence of recurrent UTIs and consistently negative cultures despite leukocytosis in secretions.
Chronic bacterial prostatitis is characterized by recurrent UTIs caused by the same organism and yields positive cultures from expressed prostatic secretions.
Acute bacterial prostatitis presents with systemic symptoms like fever, chills, and an exquisitely tender, boggy prostate, and is culture-positive.
Malakoplakia is a rare inflammatory condition often associated with E. coli but has specific morphologic features (Michaelis-Gutmann bodies) and is not the most common form of abacterial prostatitis.

Granulomatous prostatitis is a specific histologic pattern often resulting from BCG instillation, fungal infection, or as a reaction to ruptured ducts, rather than a generic chronic pain syndrome with leukocytosis and negative cultures.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 975 (Book Page): Chronic abacterial prostatitis, the most common form of prostatitis... Expressed prostatic secretions contain more than 10 leukocytes per high-power field, but bacterial cultures are uniformly negative.

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
coreConcept: Differential Diagnosis by Radioactive Iodine Uptake
statement: In the initial phase of thyroid hyperfunction seen in granulomatous thyroiditis, which diagnostic finding distinguishes it from Graves disease?
options: Presence of a palpable neck mass
History of preceding weight loss
Suppression of serum TSH levels
Elevated serum levels of free T3 and T4
Decreased radioactive iodine uptake
correctOption: Decreased radioactive iodine uptake
optionExplanations: Palpable enlargement can be seen in both diffuse goiter (Graves) and inflammatory enlargement (de Quervain).
Weight loss is a general metabolic consequence of excess thyroid hormone and occurs in both conditions.
Low TSH is a shared feature of any primary thyrotoxicosis due to negative feedback on the pituitary gland.
Both conditions show elevated free hormones during the hyperthyroid phase, so this does not distinguish them.

In granulomatous thyroiditis, the hyperthyroidism is caused by the release of preformed hormone from damaged follicles, not increased synthesis; thus, uptake of new iodine is low. In Graves, synthesis is increased, leading to high uptake.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): However, unlike in hyperthyroid states such as Graves disease, radioactive iodine uptake is diminished.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
statement: Preoperative administration of high-dose iodine to a Grave’s Disease patient is intended to achieve which histological effect?
options: Involution of the epithelium and accumulation of colloid
Induction of follicular cell necrosis to reduce gland volume
Activation of the TSH receptor to stimulate hormone storage
Upregulation of T-cell apoptosis within germinal centers
Expansion of the fibrous septae to facilitate easier surgical handling
correctOption: Involution of the epithelium and accumulation of colloid
optionExplanations: Iodine suppresses the hyperplastic cells, causing them to shrink (involution) and thyroglobulin to accumulate, making the gland less vascular for surgery.
Iodine causes cellular involution (atrophy/shrinkage), not frank tissue necrosis.
Iodine inhibits the release of thyroid hormone and the activity of the gland; it does not activate the receptor.
The primary effect of iodine is on the follicular epithelium and its secretions, not on the lymphocytic infiltrates.
While the gland becomes firmer, this is due to colloid accumulation and involution, not primary expansion of the fibrous septae.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1081 (Book Page): [Administration of iodine causes involution of the epithelium and the accumulation of colloid by blocking thyroglobulin secretion.]

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism by which most solid tumors without bone metastases induce hypercalcemia?
options: Direct secretion of native parathyroid hormone (PTH)
Ectopic production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
Secretion of parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP)
Production of calcitonin-blocking antibodies
Release of IL-1 and TNF from tumor cells
correctOption: Secretion of parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP)
optionExplanations: Native PTH secretion by non-parathyroid tumors is extremely rare; malignancy-associated hypercalcemia is typically associated with low or suppressed native PTH levels.
Ectopic vitamin D production is generally restricted to granulomatous diseases like sarcoidosis or certain lymphomas, rather than most solid tumors.
PTHrP acts on the same receptors as PTH to stimulate bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption, and is the dominant cause of hypercalcemia in non-metastatic solid tumors.
Calcitonin-blocking antibodies are not a recognized clinical mechanism for malignancy-induced hypercalcemia; calcitonin levels are usually secondary to calcium levels.
The release of cytokines like IL-1 and TNF is the mechanism in the remaining 20% of cases, primarily associated with direct bone metastases rather than purely humoral mechanisms.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1094 (Book Page): The most common mechanism (in ~80% of cases) through which osteolytic tumors induce hypercalcemia is by secretion of PTH-related peptide (PTHrP), which (like PTH) induces osteoclastic bone resorption and hypercalcemia.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
coreConcept: Distinction between parathyroid adenoma and hyperplasia
statement: Which of the following histological findings is most reliable for distinguishing a parathyroid adenoma from primary parathyroid hyperplasia?
options: The presence of mitotic figures within the chief cell population
Diffuse involvement of all four parathyroid glands
The total weight of the excised parathyroid glandular tissue
A rim of compressed non-neoplastic tissue at the lesion's edge
An increase in the number of oxyphil cells within the lesion
correctOption: A rim of compressed non-neoplastic tissue at the lesion's edge
optionExplanations: Mitotic figures are generally rare in both adenomas and hyperplasias and are not a reliable differentiating feature.
While diffuse involvement points toward hyperplasia, the microscopic presence of a compressed rim is the diagnostic indicator for adenoma within the specimen itself.
While hyperplastic glands collectively often weigh less than 1g, weight is less definitive than the architectural presence of a compressed rim.
The presence of a compressed rim of normal parathyroid parenchyma is a classic histological clue identifying a solitary adenoma, as opposed to hyperplasia.
Oxyphil cells can be found in both adenomas and hyperplastic glands and do not aid in the differential diagnosis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): A rim of compressed, non-neoplastic parathyroid tissue, generally separated by a fibrous capsule, is often visible at the edge of the adenoma.

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
statement: Granulomatous thyroiditis is most likely to be encountered in which of the following patient demographics?
options: Women between 40 and 50 years of age
Postmenopausal women over age 70
Adolescent girls during puberty
Male infants with congenital goiter
Elderly men with history of radiation exposure
correctOption: Women between 40 and 50 years of age
optionExplanations: The peak incidence is in middle-aged women, which is consistent with many inflammatory and autoimmune thyroid disorders.
While Hashimoto and multinodular goiter are seen in elderly women, the classic acute de Quervain presentation is more frequent in the 40-50 age bracket.
Sporadic diffuse goiter (simple goiter) often peaks at puberty, but granulomatous thyroiditis is more common in the fifth decade.
Congenital goiter and hypothyroidism (cretinism) in infants are typically due to iodine deficiency or dyshormonogenetic goiter, not de Quervain.
Radiation exposure is a high-risk factor for thyroid carcinoma, particularly papillary type, but not specifically for granulomatous thyroiditis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): The disorder is most common between 40 and 50 years of age and, like other forms of thyroiditis, affects women more often than men (4 : 1).

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
statement: Propylthiouracil is often administered to patients with Grave’s Disease to manage hypermetabolic symptoms. What is the expected secondary morphological change in the thyroid gland following this pharmacological intervention?
options: Resolution of lymphocytic infiltrates and disappearance of germinal centers.
Involution of the follicular epithelium and massive accumulation of thick colloid.
Dystrophic calcification of the follicular basement membranes producing 'pituitary stone' mimics.
Exaggeration of epithelial hypertrophy and hyperplasia due to elevated TSH.
Development of extensive stromal fibrosis that extends beyond the capsule.
correctOption: Exaggeration of epithelial hypertrophy and hyperplasia due to elevated TSH.
optionExplanations: While the hyperthyroid state is managed, the underlying autoimmune nature of Graves (lymphocytic infiltrates) typically persists despite antithyroid drug therapy.
Iodine administration, not PTU, causes the gland to involute and accumulate colloid by blocking thyroglobulin secretion pre-operatively.
Dystrophic calcification is mentioned in the context of lactotroph adenomas (pituitary stones), but is not a standard response to PTU in Graves disease.
PTU blocks thyroid hormone synthesis; the resulting low T4 levels trigger the pituitary to release more TSH, which ironically increases the physical size and cellularity of the thyroid.
Fibrosis beyond the capsule is characteristic of Riedel thyroiditis, a form of IgG4-related disease, rather than a drug effect in Graves.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1080 (Book Page): [Treatment with the antithyroid drug propylthiouracil exaggerates the epithelial hypertrophy and hyperplasia by stimulating TSH secretion.]

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Diffuse and Multinodular goiter
statement: Dietary consumption of cassava root can worsen goiter in iodine-deficient populations. What is the specific pathophysiological mechanism by which this occurs?
options: Inhibition of thyroglobulin proteolysis
Suppression of TSH receptor expression
Interference with iodide transport within the thyroid
Direct destruction of follicular epithelial cells
Acceleration of peripheral T4 to T3 conversion
correctOption: Interference with iodide transport within the thyroid
optionExplanations: Inhibition of thyroglobulin proteolysis is a mechanism associated with high doses of exogenous iodide, not thiocyanates found in dietary goitrogens like cassava.
Thiocyanates do not suppress TSH receptor expression; they act on the active transport of the substrate needed for hormone synthesis (iodide).
Cassava contains cyanogenic glycosides that are converted to thiocyanates, which competitively inhibit the sodium-iodide symporter, thus blocking the first step in thyroid hormone synthesis.
Direct destruction of follicular cells is characteristic of autoimmune processes like Hashimoto thyroiditis or physical injury, not the metabolic inhibition caused by goitrogens.
Goitrogens typically decrease the synthesis of thyroid hormone rather than accelerating peripheral conversion; the latter would potentially ameliorate rather than worsen goiter symptoms.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1081 (Book Page): Cassava contains a thiocyanate that inhibits iodide transport within the thyroid, worsening any concurrent iodine deficiency.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
statement: In the pathogenesis of the most common form of dysfunctional uterine bleeding, which hormonal imbalance is primarily responsible for the resulting endometrial morphology?
options: Elevated human chorionic gonadotropin from a molar pregnancy
Excessive progesterone production by a persistent corpus luteum
Excessive endometrial stimulation by estrogens unopposed by progesterone
Decreased levels of follicle-stimulating hormone leading to atrophy
Inadequate luteal phase due to premature regression of the corpus luteum
correctOption: Excessive endometrial stimulation by estrogens unopposed by progesterone
optionExplanations: Molar pregnancy is a structural gestational disorder, not a functional hormonal disturbance classified as DUB.
Persistent progesterone would lead to a prolonged secretory phase, which is not the standard mechanism for DUB; DUB usually involves progesterone deficiency.
Anovulation prevents corpus luteum formation; without progesterone to counteract estrogen, the endometrium undergoes excessive proliferative changes and eventual breakdown.
Endometrial atrophy usually causes postmenopausal bleeding rather than the classic DUB seen in reproductive years associated with anovulation.
While inadequate luteal phase is a cause of bleeding, it is less frequent than the total failure of ovulation (anovulation).
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1001 (Book Page): Failure of ovulation results in excessive endometrial stimulation by estrogens that is unopposed by progesterone.

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
statement: Besides the fallopian tube, which of the following is explicitly listed in the reference as a site where an ectopic pregnancy can occur?
options: The pineal gland
The tunica vaginalis
The transition zone of the prostate
The abdominal cavity
The inner surface of the prepuce
correctOption: The abdominal cavity
optionExplanations: The pineal gland is a site for germinomas (pinealomas), not ectopic pregnancy.
The tunica vaginalis is an anatomic structure of the male scrotum.
The transition zone of the prostate is the primary site for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).
The text lists the fallopian tube, ovary, abdominal cavity, and cornua as the valid sites for ectopic gestation.
The prepuce is a site for squamous cell carcinoma of the penis, not pregnancy.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1027 (Book Page): Ectopic pregnancy refers to implantation of the fetus in a site other than the normal intrauterine location; ... Other sites include the ovary, the abdominal cavity

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
statement: A patient with a non-secreting suprasellar mass is found to have a serum prolactin level of 80 ng/mL (Normal < 20). Which mechanism best explains this classification of 'stalk effect'?
options: Loss of hypothalamic dopaminergic inhibition on normal lactotrophs
The tumor is an acidophilic stem cell adenoma secreting low levels of prolactin
Malignant transformation into a prolactin-secreting pituitary carcinoma
Co-secretion of Prolactin and TSH from a thyrotroph adenoma
The mass is a lactotroph microadenoma with inefficient hormone release
correctOption: Loss of hypothalamic dopaminergic inhibition on normal lactotrophs
optionExplanations: Dopamine (Prolactin Inhibitory Factor) normally travels down the stalk; any mass blocking this allows normal lactotrophs to hypersecrete, causing 'mild' elevations.
Acidophilic stem cell adenomas are functional tumors; stalk effect refers to non-secreting tumors causing elevated prolactin.
Pituitary carcinomas are defined by systemic metastases and are extremely rare, not by mild prolactin elevation from a local mass.
Co-secretion is a feature of plurihormonal tumors, but 'stalk effect' specifically refers to the mechanical disruption of hypothalamic control.
If the tumor were a lactotroph adenoma, the prolactin level would usually be much higher and proportional to tumor size.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1069 (Book Page): Any suprasellar mass (e.g., a pituitary adenoma) may disturb the inhibitory influence of the hypothalamus on prolactin secretion, resulting in hyperprolactinemia. Therefore, mild hyperprolactenemia in a person with a pituitary adenoma does not necessarily indicate a prolactin-secreting tumor.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: What is the characteristic histological change observed in the non-adenomatous anterior pituitary of a patient with prolonged hypercortisolism?
options: Crooke hyaline change in corticotrophs
Diffuse hyperplasia of thyrotroph cells
Psammoma body deposition
Formation of a fibrous reticulin network
Ischemic necrosis (Sheehan syndrome)
correctOption: Crooke hyaline change in corticotrophs
optionExplanations: High cortisol levels cause the accumulation of intermediate keratin filaments in pituitary corticotrophs, resulting in the pale, homogeneous 'Crooke hyaline change'.
Thyrotrophs are unrelated to the ACTH/Cortisol axis and do not undergo hyperplasia in response to cortisol.
Psammoma bodies are calcifications typical of thyroid papillary cancer or meningiomas, not the pituitary in Cushing syndrome.
The absence of a reticulin network is a feature of the pituitary adenoma itself, not the reactive change in the normal gland.
Sheehan syndrome is postpartum necrosis due to hypotension, not a result of cortisol feedback.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1114 (Book Page): The most common alteration, resulting from high levels of endogenous or exogenous glucocorticoids, is termed Crooke hyaline change. In this condition, the normal granular, basophilic cytoplasm of the ACTH-producing cells in the anterior pituitary becomes homogeneous and paler.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
statement: Which clinical intervention is recognized as the most common cause of granulomatous prostatitis in the United States?
options: Manual untwisting of a testicular torsion
Instillation of BCG for the treatment of bladder cancer
Prolonged use of antiandrogens for prostate cancer
Frequent catheterization in elderly patients
Injection of collagenase into penile plaques
correctOption: Instillation of BCG for the treatment of bladder cancer
optionExplanations: Testicular torsion management is unrelated to the development of prostatic granulomas.
BCG (Bacillus Calmette-Guérin) therapy for bladder cancer often results in a granulomatous inflammatory reaction within the prostate.
Antiandrogens are linked to testicular atrophy, not granulomatous prostatitis.
Catheterization is a risk factor for acute bacterial prostatitis, not typically the granulomatous form.
Collagenase injections are used for Peyronie disease and do not involve the prostate gland.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 975 (Book Page): In the United States, the most common cause is instillation of BCG for treatment of bladder cancer.

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
statement: Which clinical condition is defined by placental implantation in the lower uterine segment or cervix, often necessitating a cesarean delivery to prevent maternal hemorrhage?
options: Placenta accreta
Chorioamnionitis
Placenta previa
Cornual gestation
Velamentous insertion
correctOption: Placenta previa
optionExplanations: Placenta accreta is a defect in the depth of implantation (to the myometrium) rather than the location relative to the cervical os, though the two can coexist.
Chorioamnionitis is an infection of the placental membranes, not an abnormality in the physical site of placental implantation.
Placenta previa describes the low-lying position of the placenta. If it covers the internal os, it blocks the birth canal and is prone to life-threatening bleeding during labor.
Cornual gestation is an ectopic pregnancy in the junction of the tube and uterus; while it can cause bleeding, it is not a term used for low uterine segment placental implantation.
Velamentous insertion refers to the umbilical cord inserting into the membranes rather than the placenta itself; it is not a primary implantation site abnormality of the placenta itself.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1029 (Book Page): Placenta previa is a condition in which the placenta implants in the lower uterine segment or cervix... requires cesarean delivery to avert placental rupture and fatal maternal hemorrhage during vaginal delivery.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
statement: In a patient with primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency, the skin hyperpigmentation is most directly linked to which of the following molecular events?
options: Excessive secretion of aldosterone by the zona glomerulosa
Reduced synthesis of hepatic transport proteins
Peripheral conversion of androstenedione to melanin
Feedback stimulation of hypothalamic TRH neurons
Elevated levels of pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) from the anterior pituitary
correctOption: Elevated levels of pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) from the anterior pituitary
optionExplanations: Aldosterone has no stimulatory effect on melanocytes; its absence leads to electrolyte derangements, not pigment changes.
Hepatic proteins are not involved in the pathogenesis of Addisonian hyperpigmentation.
Melanin is synthesized by melanocytes in response to MSH, not by the peripheral metabolism of adrenal sex steroids.
TRH and thyroid hormones are regulated by a different axis; while autoimmune thyroiditis may coexist, the pigment is specific to the ACTH/MSH axis.
Due to low cortisol, ACTH levels rise. ACTH is synthesized from POMC, which also contains MSH sequences. High POMC/ACTH levels stimulate cutaneous melanocytes.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1122 (Book Page): This is caused by elevated levels of pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC), which is derived from the anterior pituitary and is a precursor of both ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH).

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: A patient is diagnosed with primary hyperparathyroidism. Genetic analysis reveals a pericentromeric inversion on chromosome 11 that relocates the PTH gene promoter next to which cell-cycle regulator?
options: TP53
RET
BRAF
Cyclin D1 (CCND1)
MEN1
correctOption: Cyclin D1 (CCND1)
optionExplanations: TP53 mutations are generally late events in tumor progression and are not the primary driver in parathyroid adenomas via chromosome 11 inversion.
RET is a proto-oncogene associated with MEN-2 and medullary thyroid carcinoma, not parathyroid chromosome 11 inversions.
BRAF is an oncogene common in papillary thyroid carcinoma, not parathyroid adenoma pathogenesis.
In about 10-20% of parathyroid adenomas, the PTH promoter drives overexpression of Cyclin D1, leading to excessive cellular proliferation.
MEN1 is a tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 11q13 often mutated in parathyroid tumors, but it is not the gene relocated in this specific inversion.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): [A pericentromeric inversion on chromosome 11 results in relocation of CCDN1 (normally on 11q), so that it is positioned adjacent to the 5′-flanking region of the PTH gene (on 11p).]

category: Define thyroiditis
statement: Which condition is characterized by a thyroid that is usually symmetrically and diffusely enlarged, showing widespread lymphocytic infiltration with germinal centers and atrophic follicles?
options: Follicular adenoma.
Toxic multinodular goiter.
Hashimoto thyroiditis.
Cretinism.
Papillary thyroid carcinoma.
correctOption: Hashimoto thyroiditis.
optionExplanations: Adenomas are solitary, encapsulated, and lack a diffuse lymphocytic background.
Multinodular goiter is characterized by irregular nodules of variable colloid and hyperplasia, not diffuse inflammatory infiltration.
This is the classic description of Hashimoto's, focusing on the lymphocytic response and the symmetric goiter.
Cretinism is a clinical state of congenital hypothyroidism, which can be due to many causes, but the definition here is a histological one.
Carcinoma usually presents as a discrete nodule, not diffuse inflammatory enlargement.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): The thyroid is usually diffusely enlarged... There is extensive infiltration of the parenchyma by a mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate containing small lymphocytes, plasma cells, and well-developed germinal centers.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: In the context of primary hyperparathyroidism, what is the typical status of the non-involved parathyroid glands in a patient with a solitary parathyroid adenoma?
options: They are enlarged and reddish-brown in color
They contain numerous cystic spaces with machine oil fluid
They show extensive infiltration by lymphoid follicles
They demonstrate diffuse chief cell hyperplasia
They are normal in size or shrunken due to feedback
correctOption: They are normal in size or shrunken due to feedback
optionExplanations: Enlargement would indicate that the patient likely has hyperplasia or multiple adenomas rather than a solitary adenoma.
Cystic machine-oil changes are characteristic of certain brain tumors, not the parathyroid response to feedback.
Lymphoid follicles with germinal centers are characteristic of Hashimoto thyroiditis, not parathyroid atrophy.
Diffuse hyperplasia would suggest primary hyperplasia rather than a solitary adenoma with uninvolved glands.
Elevated serum calcium from a functional adenoma causes feedback inhibition of PTH, leading to atrophy or normal size in the remaining glands.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): In contrast to primary hyperplasia, the glands outside the adenoma are usually normal in size or shrunken because of feedback inhibition by elevated levels of serum calcium.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
statement: A 14-year-old male presents with sudden, exquisite scrotal pain that began 8 hours ago. Physical examination reveals a swollen, tender, and elevated right testis. Upon surgical exploration, the pathologist notes that the testis is soft, necrotic, and dark red. What is the most likely morphological diagnosis?
options: Suppurative orchitis with abscess formation
Testicular atrophy following mumps infection
Germ cell neoplasia with extensive necrosis
Hemorrhagic infarction secondary to torsion
Granulomatous inflammation of the spermatic tubules
correctOption: Hemorrhagic infarction secondary to torsion
optionExplanations: Suppurative orchitis typically follows epididymitis and presents with fever and pyuria; the dark discoloration here is characteristic of hemorrhage, not pus.
Atrophy presents as a small, firm testis; this case describes a swollen, hemorrhagic gland.
While tumors can undergo necrosis, the acute presentation and the uniform dark discoloration point toward a vascular emergency.
The clinical history of 8 hours (beyond the 6-hour salvage window) and the gross appearance of soft, dark, necrotic tissue are classic for hemorrhagic infarction following torsion.
Granulomatous orchitis is an idiopathic, often painless or moderately tender mass in middle-aged men, not an acute surgical emergency in a teen.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 968 (Book Page): In advanced stages, the swollen testis consists entirely of soft, necrotic, hemorrhagic tissue... Depending on the duration of torsion, the morphologic changes range from intense congestion to widespread hemorrhage and testicular infarction.

category: Enumerate clinical manifestations along with hormone levels of anterior pituitary
statement: A 40-year-old male is diagnosed with a somatotroph adenoma. Molecular analysis reveals a mutation in the GNAS gene that abrogates the GTPase activity of the alpha subunit of the stimulatory G-protein (Gs-alpha). What is the direct intracellular consequence of this mutation leading to hormone excess?
options: Constitutive activation of adenylyl cyclase and persistent cAMP generation
Immediate degradation of growth hormone within secretory granules
Hyper-secretion of dopamine into the portal venous system
Inactivation of the PIT-1 transcription factor
Reduced transcription of insulin-like growth factor receptors
correctOption: Constitutive activation of adenylyl cyclase and persistent cAMP generation
optionExplanations: Gs-alpha normally activates adenylyl cyclase. When GTPase activity is lost, the G-protein remains in its active GTP-bound state, continuously stimulating cAMP production, which drives somatotroph proliferation and GH release.
The GNAS mutation enhances hormone synthesis and secretion rather than promoting intracellular hormone degradation.
Dopamine is an inhibitory factor for lactotrophs, and its levels are not directly regulated by the somatotroph's internal GNAS mutation status.
PIT-1 is the transcription factor required for somatotroph lineage development; the GNAS mutation acts downstream of lineage commitment to drive oncogenesis.
GH excess typically increases peripheral production of IGF-1 rather than reducing the expression of its receptors.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1066 (Book Page): Approximately 40% of somatotroph cell adenomas bear somatic GNAS mutations that abrogate the GTPase activity of Gs-alpha, leading to constitutive activation of Gs-alpha, persistent generation of cAMP, and unchecked cellular proliferation.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
coreConcept: Mechanism of Lipotoxicity in Insulin Resistance
statement: The metabolic defects in Type 2 Diabetes are characterized by peripheral insulin resistance and inadequate beta-cell compensation. Which of the following describes the impact of excess free fatty acids (FFAs) on intracellular signaling in this disorder?
options: Inhibition of the inflammasome within islet macrophages
Attenuation of insulin receptor signaling via toxic lipid metabolites like diacylglycerol (DAG)
Downregulation of the gluconeogenic enzyme phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase
Reduction in pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion from adipose tissue
Increased translocation of GLUT-4 to the plasma membrane
correctOption: Attenuation of insulin receptor signaling via toxic lipid metabolites like diacylglycerol (DAG)
optionExplanations: Excess FFAs actually activate the inflammasome, leading to the secretion of IL-1beta and increasing tissue inflammation.
Excess FFAs lead to the accumulation of diacylglycerol and ceramides, which interfere with the insulin receptor signaling pathway, causing resistance.
Attenuated insulin signaling actually allows gluconeogenic enzymes like phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase to ‘ramp up’, increasing glucose production.
Obesity and FFA excess increase, rather than decrease, the secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines (adipokines) that promote insulin resistance.
Insulin resistance is characterized by a failure or reduction in the translocation of GLUT-4 to the cell membrane, which impairs glucose uptake.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1102 (Book Page): [These ‘toxic’ lipid metabolites can attenuate signaling through the insulin receptor and activate inflammatory pathways in the islets]

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
statement: When comparing the pathogenesis of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), how does the spread of non-gonococcal puerperal infections typically differ from the spread of Neisseria gonorrhoeae?
options: Puerperal infections spread upward through the lymphatics or venous channels into deeper tissue layers.
Gonococcal infections primarily bypass the endocervix to seed the pelvic peritoneum via blood.
Puerperal infections typically involve the tubal lumen directly, causing early pyosalpinx.
Puerperal infections spread primarily along the mucosal surfaces of the fallopian tubes.
Gonococcal infections utilize retrograde menstruation to seed the myometrium exclusively.
correctOption: Puerperal infections spread upward through the lymphatics or venous channels into deeper tissue layers.
optionExplanations: Puerperal infections, often caused by staphylococci or streptococci following trauma or surgery, travel via deeper lymphatic and venous routes. This often leads to more severe systemic bacteremia and inflammation of the serosa rather than localized mucosal suppuration.

Gonococcal infection typically begins in the endocervical mucosa or vestibular glands and ascends along the mucosal linings. It does not normally bypass these areas to seed the peritoneum hematogenously in the initial stages.

While puerperal infections can cause tubal issues, they tend to show less involvement of the tube lumen and mucosal surfaces compared to N. gonorrhoeae. They are more likely to cause inflammation within the deeper tissue layers of the broad ligaments.

This is incorrect because spreading along mucosal surfaces is the hallmark of gonococcal infections, which cause superficial inflammation and epithelial injury in the tubal plicae. Puerperal agents avoid these surfaces.

Retrograde menstruation is a theory for the spread of endometriosis, not gonococcal infection. Gonococcal agents follow the mucosal continuity from the vagina and cervix up into the fallopian tubes, usually sparing the endometrium itself.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 988 (Book Page): the non-gonococcal bacterial infections that follow induced abortion, dilation and curettage of the uterus, and other surgical procedures are thought to spread upward from the uterus through the lymphatics or venous channels rather than on the mucosal surfaces.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
statement: When comparing the patterns of infection in the male genital tract, how does the initial site of involvement typically differ between tuberculosis and syphilis?
options: Both tuberculosis and syphilis invariably begin in the seminal vesicles.
Tuberculosis starts in the epididymis, while syphilis involves the testis first.
Tuberculosis involves the prostate first, while syphilis starts in the vas deferens.
Tuberculosis involves the testis first, while syphilis starts in the epididymis.
Both infections are restricted to the interstitial connective tissue of the scrotum.
correctOption: Tuberculosis starts in the epididymis, while syphilis involves the testis first.
optionExplanations: Neither infection is noted for starting in the seminal vesicles; they typically arise in the epididymis or testis.
Tuberculosis almost always begins in the epididymis before spreading to the testis, whereas syphilis characteristically targets the testis as the primary site in the scrotum.
Tuberculosis can reach the prostate, but its primary site of involvement in the scrotal contents is the epididymis.
This is the reverse of the actual clinical pattern; syphilis is known for primary testicular involvement.
These infections are not restricted to the scrotum and frequently involve the tubules (TB) or cause endarteritis (syphilis).
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 968 (Book Page): Several, including tuberculosis and gonorrhea, arise first in the epididymis and only involve the testis secondarily, while others, such as syphilis, involve the testis first.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
statement: Which of the following human leukocyte antigen (HLA) associations is observed in over 90% of Caucasians with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus?
options: HLA-DR2
HLA-DQ6
HLA-DR3 or HLA-DR4
HLA-B51
HLA-B27
correctOption: HLA-DR3 or HLA-DR4
optionExplanations: HLA-DR2 is actually associated with a protective effect against Type 1 Diabetes in certain populations; it is also linked to multiple sclerosis.
HLA-DQ6 is generally considered protective against the development of Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus.
The MHC class II locus, specifically DR3 and DR4, provides the strongest genetic link to Type 1 DM, contributing up to 50% of the heritable risk.
HLA-B51 is a classic marker for Beh'et disease and is not related to the pathogenesis of autoimmune diabetes.
HLA-B27 is strongly associated with seronegative spondyloarthropathies such as ankylosing spondylitis, not Type 1 diabetes.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1099 (Book Page): Ninety percent to 95% of Caucasians with this disease have either an HLA-DR3 or HLA-DR4 haplotype, in contrast to about 40% of normal subjects

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
statement: What is the primary cause of the hypercoagulable state that contributes to the formation of thrombi in the liver and kidneys of patients with preeclampsia?
options: Mutations in the GNAS gene causing constitutive cAMP generation
Reduced endothelial production of prostacyclin (PGI2)
Overproduction of insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) by the liver
Accumulation of sorbitol via the polyol pathway in the endothelium
Inhibition of the TSH receptor by stimulatory immunoglobulins
correctOption: Reduced endothelial production of prostacyclin (PGI2)
optionExplanations: GNAS mutations are found in somatotroph pituitary adenomas and cause hyperpituitarism, not the hypercoagulability of pregnancy.

In preeclampsia, high sFlt1 levels neutralize VEGF. Since VEGF normally stimulates the production of prostacyclin (PGI2)—a major antithrombotic agent—its reduction favors the formation of thrombi and a hypercoagulable state.
Excessive IGF-1 is the mediator of tissue growth in acromegaly and gigantism, which is unrelated to the thrombotic complications of eclampsia.
Sorbitol accumulation via the polyol pathway is a mechanism of tissue damage in chronic diabetes mellitus, leading to cataracts and neuropathy.
Stimulatory immunoglobulins (TSI) binding to TSH receptors is the mechanism of Graves disease, not coagulation in preeclampsia.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1030 (Book Page): Hypercoagulability is likely related to the reduced endothelial production of PGI2, a potent antithrombotic factor, and increased release of procoagulant factors. Production of PGI2 is stimulated by VEGF, and women with preeclampsia have decreased endothelial production of PGI2, presumably due to antagonism of VEGF by sFlt1.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
statement: Chronic hyperglycemia leads to the formation of Advanced Glycation End Products (AGEs). Which pathogenic effect of AGEs directly contributes to the development of diabetic microangiopathy?
options: Nonenzymatic cross-linking of type IV collagen in basement membranes
Suppression of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) in the retina
Increased synthesis of protective high-density lipoproteins
Inhibition of inflammatory cytokine release from activated macrophages
Enhancement of antioxidant mechanisms by regenerating reduced glutathione
correctOption: Nonenzymatic cross-linking of type IV collagen in basement membranes
optionExplanations: The nonenzymatic glycation and subsequent cross-linking of basement membrane proteins like type IV collagen leads to increased permeability and the structural thickening characteristic of diabetic small vessel disease.
AGEs and protein kinase C activation actually increase the levels of VEGF, which is a major driver of proliferative diabetic retinopathy.
Hyperglycemia and insulin resistance generally worsen lipid profiles by increasing LDL and decreasing HDL levels.
AGEs bind to the RAGE receptor, which triggers, rather than inhibits, the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines like IL-1 and TNF from macrophages.
The polyol pathway associated with hyperglycemia actually depletes NADPH, which prevents the regeneration of reduced glutathione and increases oxidative stress.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1106 (Book Page): [AGE-induced cross-linking of type IV collagen in basement membrane decreases endothelial cell adhesion and increases extravasation of fluid... accounting in part for the basement membrane thickening that is characteristic of diabetic microangiopathy.]

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
statement: A 62-year-old male with a 20-year history of Type 2 Diabetes presents with persistent proteinuria. A renal biopsy reveals ovoid, laminated, PAS-positive nodules within the glomerular mesangium. What is the correct designation for this pathognomonic lesion?
options: Kimmelstiel-Wilson disease
Amyloid plaque deposition
Hyaline arteriolosclerosis
Necrotizing papillitis
Diffuse mesangial sclerosis
correctOption: Kimmelstiel-Wilson disease
optionExplanations: Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules are the pathognomonic nodular glomerulosclerosis lesions associated with renal failure in long-term diabetes.
While amyloid deposits in islets in Type 2 DM, it is not the term for the glomerular nodules of diabetic nephropathy.
Hyaline arteriolosclerosis affects the afferent and efferent arterioles, not the glomerular mesangium.
Necrotizing papillitis is an acute inflammatory complication (papillary necrosis) of pyelonephritis, not a glomerular nodular disease.
Diffuse mesangial sclerosis involves a generalized increase in matrix but lacks the specific, rounded nodular appearance.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1109 (Book Page): Nodular Glomerulosclerosis. This is also known as intercapillary glomerulosclerosis or Kimmelstiel-Wilson disease. The glomerular lesions take the form of ovoid or spherical, often laminated, PAS-positive nodules.

category: Hashimoto Thyroiditis ii
statement: During a fine-needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy of a patient with a firm, nodular goiter, the pathologist identifies numerous cells with abundant, intensely eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm. These cells represent which of the following processes?
options: A metaplastic response of follicular epithelium to chronic injury
Hyperplasia in response to excess iodine ingestion
Malignant transformation into anaplastic carcinoma
Viral-induced syncytial giant cell formation
Accumulation of calcified debris known as psammoma bodies
correctOption: A metaplastic response of follicular epithelium to chronic injury
optionExplanations: Hürthle cells (oncocytes) are a hallmark of HT. They are metaplastic follicular cells that develop granular, eosinophilic cytoplasm rich in mitochondria as a reaction to chronic inflammation.
Excess iodine can cause goiter (Wolff-Chaikoff effect) but does not specifically induce the Hürthle cell metaplasia characteristic of HT.
Anaplastic carcinoma cells are highly pleomorphic and spindle-shaped, quite different from the uniform, granular Hürthle cells found in HT.
Giant cells are found in granulomatous (De Quervain) thyroiditis, not HT. HT is characterized by a mononuclear (lymphoplasmacytic) infiltrate.
Psammoma bodies are concentric calcifications found in papillary carcinoma, not intracellular eosinophilic granules.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1077 (Book Page): The thyroid follicles are atrophic and are lined in many areas by epithelial cells with abundant eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm, termed Hürthle cells, which represent a metaplastic response of the normally low cuboidal follicular epithelium to chronic injury.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
statement: Testicular atrophy may sometimes be classified as 'exhaustion atrophy.' Which physiological state is specifically associated with this histological regression?
options: Low levels of luteinizing hormone (LH)
Persistent stimulation by high levels of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)
Excessive production of calcitonin gene-related peptide
Blockade of the androgen receptor by estrogen analogs
Reduced secretion of müllerian-inhibiting substance
correctOption: Persistent stimulation by high levels of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)
optionExplanations: Low LH typically leads to decreased androgen production but is not the defined trigger for 'exhaustion atrophy' in this context.
High FSH levels, often due to a lack of negative feedback from damaged germ cells, can paradoxically lead to a state where the remaining epithelium is exhausted and atrophies further.
Calcitonin gene-related peptide is involved in the inguinoscrotal phase of descent, not chronic atrophy of the mature gland.
Estrogen analogs cause atrophy through the feedback axis (imbalance) rather than the direct 'exhaustion' mechanism described for FSH hyperstimulation.
Müllerian-inhibiting substance controls the transabdominal phase of descent in infants and is not a factor in adult exhaustion atrophy.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 967 (Book Page): Testicular atrophy may be caused by one of several conditions... (10) exhaustion atrophy, which may follow persistent stimulation by high levels of follicle-stimulating pituitary hormone.

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
statement: Which specific pathophysiological failure occurs during the initial stages of placentation in women who later develop preeclampsia?
options: Formation of arteriovenous shunts in a monochorionic placenta
Inability of fetal trophoblasts to remodel maternal spiral arteries
Excessive production of nitric oxide by the decidual endothelial cells
Premature rupture of the chorioamnionic membranes by bacterial toxins
Acute atherosis within the fetal umbilical arteries
correctOption: Inability of fetal trophoblasts to remodel maternal spiral arteries
optionExplanations: Vascular anastomoses and shunts are complications specifically related to twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome in monochorionic pregnancies, not the general pathogenesis of preeclampsia.

The core defect in preeclampsia is the failure of extravillous trophoblasts to invade decidual vessels and replace maternal endothelium. This prevents the conversion of spiral arteries from high-resistance to high-capacity vessels.
In preeclampsia, there is a decrease in nitric oxide production due to the inhibition of TGF-beta by endoglin, leading to vasoconstriction rather than excessive production.
Bacterial infection causing membrane rupture describes ascending placental infection (chorioamnionitis), which is a cause of preterm labor but not the underlying mechanism of preeclampsia.
Acute atherosis occurs in the maternal decidual vessels, not the fetal umbilical arteries. It is characterized by fibrinoid necrosis and intimal lipid deposition.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1030 (Book Page): In preeclampsia, this vascular remodeling fails to occur, leaving the placenta ill equipped to meet the increased circulatory demands of late gestation and setting the stage for the development of placental ischemia.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
statement: A 28-year-old woman presents with a three-month history of anxiety, excessive sweating, and a feeling of 'grittiness' in her eyes. Physical examination reveals a symmetrically enlarged, non-tender thyroid with a palpable thrill and audible bruit. Vitals: HR 118 bpm, Temp 99.2°F. Labs confirm a TSH level of <0.01 mU/L. If a biopsy were performed, which feature would most likely be identified alongside tall, columnar follicular epithelium?
options: Sharply demarcated nests of cells resembling urinary tract epithelium.
Large, pleomorphic giant cells with a sarcomatous spindle-cell background.
Amyloid deposits staining positive for calcitonin within the stroma.
Small papillae without fibrovascular cores projecting into the follicle lumen.
Numerous psammoma bodies scattered within the fibrovascular papillary cores.
correctOption: Small papillae without fibrovascular cores projecting into the follicle lumen.
optionExplanations: This describes a Brenner tumor, which is a transitional cell tumor of the ovary, not a thyroid pathology.
This describes anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, a highly aggressive malignancy in older patients, rather than the benign hyperplasia of Graves.
Stromatoid amyloid and calcitonin production are the hallmarks of medullary thyroid carcinoma, which arises from parafollicular C cells.
In Graves, the epithelial crowding leads to the formation of small papillae, but they are distinguished from malignancy by their lack of supportive fibrovascular stalks.
Psammoma bodies and fibrovascular cores are classic indicators of papillary thyroid carcinoma, not the hyperplastic papillae of Graves disease.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1080 (Book Page): [This crowding often results in the formation of small papillae that project into the follicle lumen and encroach on the colloid... Such papillae lack fibrovascular cores, in contrast to those of papillary carcinoma.]
