Homonymous hemianopsia results from lesions in the optic tract or radiation posterior to the chiasm, indicating a post-chiasmatic pathology.
Bitemporal hemianopsia is the classic presentation because the pituitary gland lies directly beneath the optic chiasm, where the nasal retinal fibers (carrying temporal field information) decussate.
Total unilateral blindness occurs with complete transection of the optic nerve anterior to the chiasm, not typically from a midline pituitary expansion.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1065 (Book Page): expanding pituitary lesions often compress decussating fibers in the optic chiasm. This gives rise to visual field abnormalities, classically in the form of defects in both lateral (temporal) visual fields, so-called bitemporal hemianopsia.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: When distinguishing a parathyroid carcinoma from a large parathyroid adenoma, which of the following is considered the only reliable histological criterion for malignancy?
options: Follicular patterns containing colloid
Invasion of surrounding tissues or metastasis
The presence of a thin fibrous capsule
Weights exceeding 2 grams
The presence of oxyphil cells
correctOption: Invasion of surrounding tissues or metastasis
optionExplanations: Parathyroid cells rarely form follicles, and they do not contain thyroid colloid.
Cytologic atypia is deceptive in the parathyroid; hence, only gross invasion into adjacent structures or documented metastasis confirms carcinoma.
Adenomas are typically invested by a thin, delicate capsule; it is the destructive invasion through the capsule into other tissues that marks carcinoma.
Large adenomas can weigh several grams; therefore, weight alone is insufficient for a diagnosis of carcinoma.
Oxyphil cells can be found in normal glands, adenomas, and hyperplasia; they are not an indicator of malignancy.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1093 (Book Page): Diagnosis of carcinoma based on cytologic detail is unreliable, and invasion of surrounding tissues and metastasis are the only reliable criteria.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
coreConcept: Anatomy and Clinical Significance of Varicocele
statement: Which of the following conditions is characterized by a dilated vein within the spermatic cord and is recognized as a surgically correctable contributing factor to male infertility?
options: Hydrocele
Varicocele
Spermatocele
Hematocele
Chylocele
correctOption: Varicocele
optionExplanations: A hydrocele is an accumulation of serous fluid in the tunica vaginalis, causing scrotal enlargement but not typically primary infertility via venous dilation.
Correct. A varicocele involves the dilation of the pampiniform plexus veins. It is a common clinical finding in infertility workups and can be repaired surgically.
A spermatocele is a cystic accumulation of semen in the efferent ducts or rete testis, presenting as a small cyst rather than a dilated vein.
A hematocele is a collection of blood in the tunica vaginalis, usually following trauma or torsion.
A chylocele is an accumulation of lymph, typically seen in elephantiasis/filariasis, caused by lymphatic obstruction.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 974 (Book Page): Varicocele is a dilated vein in the spermatic cord. Varicoceles may be asymptomatic but have also been implicated in some men as a contributing factor to infertility.

category: Hashimoto Thyroiditis ii
coreConcept: Malignant complications of Chronic Autoimmune Thyroiditis
statement: A 55-year-old female with a long-standing history of a firm, symmetrically enlarged, painless goiter and gradual weight gain presents with a new, rapidly enlarging mass within the same thyroid gland. Laboratory studies confirm a chronic hypothyroid state. Given her underlying condition, which of the following neoplasms is she at significantly increased risk of developing?
options: Follicular thyroid adenoma
Extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma
Medullary thyroid carcinoma
Anaplastic (undifferentiated) carcinoma
Parathyroid adenoma
correctOption: Extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma
optionExplanations: Follicular adenomas are benign neoplasms that do not have a specific causal link with the autoimmune destruction seen in Hashimoto.

Hashimoto thyroiditis is characterized by chronic lymphocytic stimulation. This persistent inflammatory milieu increases the risk of developing a primary thyroid B-cell lymphoma, specifically the marginal zone type.
Medullary carcinoma arises from C-cells and is associated with RET mutations or MEN-2 syndromes, not autoimmune thyroiditis.
While anaplastic carcinoma is aggressive, its primary precursor is usually a pre-existing well-differentiated follicular or papillary carcinoma, not Hashimoto thyroiditis.
Parathyroid adenomas are related to calcium metabolism and are often seen in MEN-1 or MEN-2A syndromes, but they have no established association with Hashimoto thyroiditis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): They are also at increased risk for development of extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma within the thyroid gland (Chapter 13).

category: Describe salient morphological features of clinically significant subtypes of thyroiditis: i
statement: A patient with Hashimoto thyroiditis initially experiences a period of transient hyperthyroidism before progressing to permanent hypothyroidism. This initial phase, termed 'hashitoxicosis', is morphologically associated with:
options: Hyperplasia of parafollicular C cells
Activating mutations in the TSH receptor gene
Disruption of thyroid follicles and release of preformed hormone
Malignant transformation into B-cell lymphoma
TSI-mediated stimulation of follicle growth
correctOption: Disruption of thyroid follicles and release of preformed hormone
optionExplanations: C-cell hyperplasia is a precursor to medullary carcinoma, particularly in familial syndromes, and is unrelated to hashitoxicosis.
Mutations in the TSH receptor are found in toxic adenomas or toxic multinodular goiters, not in autoimmune thyroiditis.
The hyperthyroid phase in Hashimoto (hashitoxicosis) results from the physical breakdown of follicles by the inflammatory infiltrate, spilling stored hormone into the blood.
While Hashimoto increases the risk for marginal zone B-cell lymphoma, the lymphoma itself presents as a growing mass rather than transient thyrotoxicosis.
Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) are the cause of hyperthyroidism in Graves disease, not the transient phase of Hashimoto.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): In some patients, however, it may be preceded by transient thyrotoxicosis caused by disruption of thyroid follicles and release of thyroid hormones (hashitoxicosis). During this phase, free T4 and T3 levels are elevated, TSH is diminished, and radioactive iodine uptake is decreased.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
statement: A 19-year-old female presents with persistent hyperglycemia and dark, velvety skin patches on her neck and axillae. Molecular testing reveals a mutation in the insulin receptor gene. This presentation is the diagnostic hallmark of which classification?
options: Metabolic syndrome associated with Type 2 Diabetes
Idiopathic Type 1 Diabetes
Type A insulin resistance
Maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY)
Rabson-Mendenhall syndrome
correctOption: Type A insulin resistance
optionExplanations: While Type 2 also features resistance and acanthosis, the specific presence of a genetic receptor mutation defines Type A.
Idiopathic Type 1 involves insulin deficiency without markers of autoimmunity, but lacks receptor mutations.
Type A insulin resistance is classified by specific receptor mutations that lead to severe resistance and compensatory hyperinsulinemia, causing acanthosis nigricans.
MODY involves primary defects in insulin secretion (beta-cell function), not receptor-mediated action.
Rabson-Mendenhall is a much more severe form of receptor mutation seen in children with distinct dysmorphic features.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1103 (Book Page): Rare insulin receptor mutations... can cause severe insulin resistance... (type A insulin resistance). Such patients often show a velvety hyperpigmentation of the skin known as acanthosis nigricans.

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
statement: Which histological finding in the decidual vessels of the placenta is characteristic of preeclampsia/eclampsia and features fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel wall with subendothelial macrophages?
options: Dissecting osteitis
Chorioamnionitis
Syncytial knots
Acute atherosis
Villus capillary dilatation
correctOption: Acute atherosis
optionExplanations: Dissecting osteitis is a skeletal manifestation of hyperparathyroidism, where osteoclasts tunnel through medullary bone; it is unrelated to placental pathology.
Chorioamnionitis is an ascending bacterial infection of the placental membranes, usually characterized by a neutrophil infiltrate rather than fibrinoid necrosis of decidual vessels.
Syncytial knots are exaggerated ischemic changes seen in the chorionic villi and trophoblast in preeclampsia, but they are not the necrotizing vascular lesion described.
Acute atherosis refers to the specific vascular damage in preeclampsia characterized by fibrinoid necrosis and the presence of lipid-laden subendothelial macrophages.
Preeclampsia is associated with placental malperfusion and ischemia, which typically results in constricted vessels or thrombi rather than capillary dilatation.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1030 (Book Page): (4) abnormal decidual vessels, which may show thrombi, lack of normal physiologic conversion (described earlier), fibrinoid necrosis, or intimal lipid deposition (acute atherosis) (Fig. 22.51).

category: Define thyroiditis
statement: Which immunologic pathway is primarily responsible for the depletion of thyroid epithelial cells in Hashimoto thyroiditis?
options: CD8+ cytotoxic T cell–mediated destruction of follicular cells.
Secondary pressure atrophy from massive deposition of amyloid protein.
Excessive accumulation of iodine leading to direct chemical thyrocyte toxicity.
Neutrophilic liquefactive necrosis triggered by pyogenic bacterial invasion.
Antagonistic binding of TSH-receptor antibodies mimicking pituitary hormones.
correctOption: CD8+ cytotoxic T cell–mediated destruction of follicular cells.
optionExplanations: Correct. The disease involves a breakdown in self-tolerance where cytotoxic T cells recognize thyroid antigens, leading to progressive follicular cell loss.
Amyloid deposition is characteristic of medullary thyroid carcinoma or systemic amyloidosis, not the lymphocytic and fibrotic changes of Hashimoto.
Iodine is an essential substrate; while iodine status influences thyroid disease, it is not the primary mechanism of cell death in autoimmune thyroiditis.
Bacterial invasion and neutrophilic response characterize acute suppurative thyroiditis, not the chronic autoimmune process of Hashimoto.
Binding that mimics TSH action is the hallmark of Graves disease (TSI), whereas Hashimoto involves destructive pathways including cytokines and T-cell attack.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1077 (Book Page): Multiple immunologic mechanisms may contribute to thyroid cell death, including... CD8+ cytotoxic T cell–mediated cell death

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
statement: What is the primary mechanism for the transient hyperthyroidism observed in the early stages of granulomatous thyroiditis?
options: Excessive release of preformed thyroid hormone due to follicle disruption
Loss of feedback inhibition at the pituitary level due to fever
Increased synthesis of T3 and T4 due to viral enzymes
Ectopic production of TSH by inflammatory macrophages
Constitutive activation of G-proteins in follicular cells
correctOption: Excessive release of preformed thyroid hormone due to follicle disruption
optionExplanations: The inflammatory process causes physical breakdown of thyroid follicles, allowing the stored colloid (thyroglobulin and hormones) to leak into the bloodstream.
Fever is a systemic response to cytokines; it does not cause a primary loss of feedback inhibition in the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis.
Viruses trigger inflammation and cell damage; they do not possess metabolic machinery to synthesize human thyroid hormones.
Macrophages involved in granulomas release cytokines (like IL-1), but they do not produce pituitary hormones like TSH.
Activating G-protein mutations are seen in toxic adenomas (GNAS mutations), not in inflammatory thyroiditis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1075 (Book Page): In certain conditions the oversupply is related to either excessive release of preformed thyroid hormone (e.g., in thyroiditis) or to an extrathyroidal source, rather than hyperfunction of the gland.

category: Describe salient morphological features of clinically significant subtypes of thyroiditis: i
statement: A 42-year-old woman presents with severe neck pain, fever, and a firm, enlarged thyroid following a recent upper respiratory tract infection. Fine-needle aspiration reveals granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells. What is the most likely pathological stage of this lesion?
options: Late reparative phase characterized by extensive follicular hypertrophy
Intermediate phase involving giant cells enclosing pools of colloid
Active inflammatory phase with neutrophilic microabscesses
Neoplastic phase with invasion of the thyroid capsule by spindle cells
Chronic phase with diffuse lymphocytic infiltration and germinal centers
correctOption: Intermediate phase involving giant cells enclosing pools of colloid
optionExplanations: Follicular hypertrophy is typical of Graves disease or the hyperplastic phase of goiter, not the destructive process of granulomatous thyroiditis.

The diagnosis of granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis is based on the intermediate histologic finding of multinucleated giant cells surrounding extravasated colloid 'pools' due to follicular rupture.
The very early phase of de Quervain thyroiditis involves neutrophils and microabscesses, but the classic 'granulomatous' appearance with giant cells occurs slightly later.
Spindle cell invasion of the capsule suggests anaplastic carcinoma or Riedel thyroiditis, not the self-limited granulomatous process typically triggered by viral infections.
Diffuse lymphocytic infiltration with germinal centers describes Hashimoto thyroiditis. While granulomatous thyroiditis has lymphocytes, it is the granulomatous response that is diagnostic.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): [Later, more characteristic features appear in the form of aggregates of lymphocytes, activated macrophages, and plasma cells associated with collapsed and damaged thyroid follicles. Multinucleate giant cells enclose pools of colloid, hence the designation granulomatous thyroiditis.]

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
statement: Testicular Dysgenesis Syndrome (TDS) is a clinical spectrum proposed to result from in utero environmental exposures. Which of the following is a component of this syndrome?
options: Prostatitis
Condyloma acuminatum
Nutcracker syndrome
Poor sperm quality
Peyronie disease
correctOption: Poor sperm quality
optionExplanations: Prostatitis is an inflammatory condition and is not a component of the congenital TDS spectrum.
Condyloma acuminatum is a benign wart caused by HPV, not a congenital dysgenesis component.
Nutcracker syndrome is a vascular compression involving the renal vein, not part of the TDS definition.
TDS includes cryptorchidism, hypospadias, and impaired spermatogenesis (poor sperm quality).
Peyronie disease involves reactive fibrosis of the penile shaft, not developmental dysgenesis of the testis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 970 (Book Page): Components of this syndrome include cryptorchidism, hypospadias, and poor sperm quality.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: Which specific change in the physiological secretion of cortisol is a mandatory component for the laboratory diagnosis of Cushing syndrome?
options: Suppression of serum cortisol to less than 1.8 µg/dL after low-dose dexamethasone.
Loss of the normal diurnal variation in plasma cortisol levels.
A significant reduction in the insulin-to-glucose ratio.
The presence of high-titer autoantibodies against 21-hydroxylase.
Elevated plasma renin activity associated with secondary hypertension.
correctOption: Loss of the normal diurnal variation in plasma cortisol levels.
optionExplanations: The failure to suppress cortisol after low-dose dexamethasone is diagnostic; if suppression occurs, the diagnosis is excluded.
Correct. Normal cortisol levels peak in the morning and dip at night. This rhythm is obliterated in Cushing syndrome, where levels remain inappropriately high throughout the 24-hour period.
A high insulin-to-glucose ratio is characteristic of insulinomas; Cushing syndrome causes glucose intolerance but not this specific ratio.
Autoantibodies against 21-hydroxylase are characteristic of autoimmune adrenalitis (Addison's), not Cushing syndrome.
Hypercortisolism suppresses renin; high renin is seen in secondary hyperaldosteronism, not Cushing syndrome.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1116 (Book Page): The laboratory diagnosis of Cushing syndrome is based on the following: (1) the 24-hour urine free-cortisol concentration, which is increased; and (2) loss of normal diurnal pattern of cortisol secretion.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
statement: The primary immune effector mechanism responsible for the destruction of beta cells in Type 1 diabetes is believe to be mediated by which of the following?
options: Mast cell degranulation in response to islet antigens
Natural Killer (NK) cell-mediated antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity
Direct destruction by CD8+ cytotoxic T cells and cytokine release from Th1 cells
Excessive activation of the classical pathway of the complement system by immune complexes
Autoantibodies inducing complement-mediated lysis
correctOption: Direct destruction by CD8+ cytotoxic T cells and cytokine release from Th1 cells
optionExplanations: Mast cells are involved in Type I hypersensitivity (allergies); they do not play a significant role in the selective autoimmune destruction of islets.
While NK cells can be involved in various immune responses, the dominant and specific destruction in the islets is driven by T-lymphocytes.
Type 1 diabetes is primarily a T-cell-mediated autoimmune disease where autoreactive CTLs and Th1-derived cytokines (IFN-gamma, TNF) destroy the insulin-producing cells.
Immune complex deposition and complement activation are typical of Type III hypersensitivity reactions (like SLE), not the cellular autoimmunity of T1D.
Islet autoantibodies are common markers for diagnosis, but they are generally thought to be secondary to islet damage rather than the primary cause of destruction.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1100 (Book Page): Multiple T-cell populations have been implicated in this damage, including Th1 cells... and CD8+ CTLs (which kill β cells directly).

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
statement: A 38-year-old male with coarsened facial features, broadening of the lower face, and enlarged hands is found to have a fasting blood glucose of 138 mg/dL. He is eventually diagnosed with a somatotroph adenoma of the pituitary. Which category of the etiological classification of diabetes explains his hyperglycemia?
options: Type 2 diabetes
Genetic defects of beta-cell function
Infections
Endocrinopathies
Drug-induced diabetes
correctOption: Endocrinopathies
optionExplanations: While the patient has hyperglycemia and insulin resistance, the 'etiological' classification identifies the somatotroph adenoma (acromegaly) as the specific cause under endocrinopathies.
Genetic defects of beta-cell function involve monogenic mutations like MODY, not secondary effects of pituitary tumors.
Infections like CMV or Coxsackie can cause diabetes but do not present with the physical features of acromegaly.
Acromegaly (excess growth hormone from a somatotroph adenoma) causes diabetes by inducing insulin resistance and promoting gluconeogenesis, classified as an endocrinopathy.
Drug-induced diabetes results from medications like glucocorticoids or protease inhibitors, not endogenous hormone excess.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1097 (Book Page): [Table 24.6] Endocrinopathies... Acromegaly

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: A 45-year-old woman with a 20-year history of Type 1 diabetes mellitus presents with multiple hard, palpable masses in both breasts. Biopsy reveals atrophic lobules with thickened basement membranes and a prominent lymphocytic infiltrate. Which of the following is the most likely underlying pathophysiology?
options: Dystrophic calcification of necrotic adipose tissue
Bacterial infection following traumatic nipple cracks
Keratin plugging resulting from vitamin A deficiency
Autoimmune-mediated lymphocytic mastopathy
Persistent irritation from inspissated lipid secretions
correctOption: Autoimmune-mediated lymphocytic mastopathy
optionExplanations: Dystrophic calcification of necrotic fat is the end-stage of fat necrosis, which does not show the specific lobular lymphocytic pattern of lymphocytic mastopathy.
Traumatic cracks lead to acute mastitis, characterized by acute inflammation rather than chronic lymphocytic lobulitis and atrophic ducts.
Vitamin A deficiency is hypothesized to play a role in squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts, not lymphocytic mastopathy.
Lymphocytic mastopathy is strongly associated with Type 1 diabetes and autoimmune thyroid disease, suggesting an autoimmune origin for the lymphocytic infiltration and fibrosis.
Inspissated secretions are the driver for duct ectasia, not the sclerosing lymphocytic changes seen in diabetic patients.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1039 (Book Page): Within the stroma are atrophic ducts and lobules with thickened basement membranes that are surrounded by a prominent lymphocytic infiltrate. This condition is most common in women with type 1 (insulin-dependent) diabetes or autoimmune thyroid disease and is hypothesized to have an autoimmune basis.

category: Hashimoto Thyroiditis ii
statement: Hashimoto thyroiditis is most prevalent in which demographic group?
options: Postpartum women within the first 6 weeks of delivery
Men older than 70 years with multinodular goiter
Adolescent males during puberty
Women between 45 and 65 years of age
Neonates with congenital iodine deficiency
correctOption: Women between 45 and 65 years of age
optionExplanations: While a 'postpartum thyroiditis' exists and is mentioned as a variant of subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis, it is a specific, usually self-limited clinical entity. Classic Hashimoto thyroiditis is a chronic, progressive disease with a different demographic peak (45-65 years) and is the broader, more common category of autoimmune thyroid failure.

Multinodular goiter is more common in the elderly, but it is a distinct pathological entity resulting from long-standing simple goiter and cycles of hyperplasia and involution. While Hashimoto's can present with nodularity, the autoimmune destruction is most prevalent in the 45-65 age bracket rather than being a disease primarily of very old men.

Hashimoto thyroiditis is significantly more common in females than in males (up to 20:1 ratio). While it is a major cause of goiter in children, it is not primarily a disease of adolescent males. The peak incidence across the population is much later in life, during the middle-age years.

The classic patient for Hashimoto thyroiditis is a middle-aged woman. The peak prevalence occurs between ages 45 and 65. The high female-to-male ratio (up to 20:1) and the specific age range are important diagnostic clues when evaluating a patient presenting with a new painless goiter or symptoms of metabolic slowing.

Neonates with iodine deficiency develop endemic cretinism, which is a nutritional and developmental form of hypothyroidism. Hashimoto thyroiditis is an autoimmune condition that is actually the most common cause of hypothyroidism in 'iodine-sufficient' areas. It is not the primary cause of neonatal thyroid failure.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1076 (Book Page): It is most prevalent between 45 and 65 years of age and is more common in women than in men, with a female predominance of 10 : 1 to 20 : 1.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
statement: In the etiological classification of diabetes, which endocrine disorder is most likely to cause secondary hyperglycemia by inducing excess growth hormone secretion?
options: Hyperthyroidism
Acromegaly
Cushing syndrome
Glucagonoma
Pheochromocytoma
correctOption: Acromegaly
optionExplanations: Hyperthyroidism increases glucose turnover and can worsen glycemic control but is not characterized by growth hormone excess.
Acromegaly involves a GH-secreting pituitary adenoma; excess GH antagonizes insulin action and stimulates hepatic glucose production, causing secondary DM.
Cushing syndrome causes diabetes via excess cortisol, which promotes gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance, but it is distinct from GH-mediated effects.
Glucagonomas cause diabetes by secreting excess glucagon, which directly increases hepatic glucose output via glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
Pheochromocytoma leads to hyperglycemia via catecholamine-induced inhibition of insulin release and stimulation of glycogenolysis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1097 (Book Page): Table 24.6 Classification of Diabetes ... Endocrinopathies: Acromegaly, Cushing syndrome, Hyperthyroidism, Pheochromocytoma, Glucagonoma

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: A 39-year-old woman presents with a red, swollen, and edematous breast. The skin has a pitted appearance resembling an orange peel. What is the fundamental morphological feature of the malignant condition that mimics this inflammatory presentation?
options: Infiltration of the dermis by eosinophilic Hürthle cells
Dilation of lactiferous sinuses by inspissated lipid debris
Extensive plugging of dermal lymphovascular spaces by tumor cells
Necrotizing granulomas within the terminal duct units
Proliferation of myofibroblasts in a collagenized stroma
correctOption: Extensive plugging of dermal lymphovascular spaces by tumor cells
optionExplanations: Hürthle cells are associated with thyroid and sometimes breast cysts, but do not drive the 'peau d'orange' effect.
Dilation by lipid debris is seen in duct ectasia, which is a benign inflammatory mimic.
The edema and 'peau d'orange' seen in inflammatory carcinoma are caused by lymphatic obstruction due to tumor emboli in the dermis.
Granulomas are seen in granulomatous mastitis, which can mimic carcinoma, but the malignancy itself does not form them.
Myofibroblast proliferation is characteristic of fibromatosis or myofibroblastoma, not inflammatory carcinoma.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1056 (Book Page): This form of carcinoma has a characteristic gross appearance caused by extensive plugging of the lymphovascular spaces of the dermis with carcinoma cells... The name 'inflammatory' is a misnomer, as typically no inflammation is present.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
coreConcept: Prevalence of Autoimmune Adrenalitis in Addison Disease
statement: In high-income countries, what is the most common underlying cause of primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency?
options: Metastatic carcinoma of the lungs
Disseminated tuberculosis
Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome
Autoimmune adrenalitis
Amyloidosis of the adrenal cortex
correctOption: Autoimmune adrenalitis
optionExplanations: Metastatic carcinoma can cause adrenal insufficiency, but it is not the most common cause in high-income nations; the adrenal glands are frequent sites for metastases, but function is usually preserved unless destruction is massive.
Tuberculosis was once the leading cause of Addison disease, and remains significant in lower-income countries, but it has been surpassed by autoimmune causes in high-income regions.
AIDS can cause adrenal insufficiency via opportunistic infections like cytomegalovirus or Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare, but it is less frequent than primary autoimmune destruction.

Autoimmune adrenalitis is the leading cause of Addison disease in developed countries, characterized by autoimmune destruction of steroidogenic cells and detectable autoantibodies against enzymes like 21-hydroxylase.
Amyloidosis is a rare cause of primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency and does not represent the majority of cases in any demographic.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1121 (Book Page): Autoimmune adrenalitis accounts for 80% to 90% of cases of primary adrenal insufficiency in high-income countries.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Diffuse and Multinodular goiter
coreConcept: The TSH-driven compensatory mechanism of goitrogenesis
statement: Which of the following describes the sequence of events leading to the pathogenesis of simple goiter?
options: Primary pituitary failure results in low TSH and subsequent glandular atrophy.
Activating mutations in G-proteins lead to autonomous follicular proliferation without TSH influence.
Impaired hormone synthesis leads to a compensatory rise in serum TSH, causing follicular hyperplasia.
Excessive iodine intake causes toxic follicular destruction and fibrosis.
TSH receptor antibodies stimulate follicular growth despite normal T3 levels.
correctOption: Impaired hormone synthesis leads to a compensatory rise in serum TSH, causing follicular hyperplasia.
optionExplanations: Pituitary failure results in secondary hypothyroidism and gland atrophy, the exact opposite of goitrous enlargement.

This describes the pathogenesis of a toxic adenoma or toxic multinodular goiter (Plummer syndrome), where nodules become autonomous. Simple diffuse goiter remains TSH-dependent during its early phases.

The primary defect is a lack of iodine or a biosynthetic error that prevents adequate thyroid hormone synthesis. The hypothalamus and pituitary sense this deficiency and increase TSH, which forces the thyroid to expand its functional mass via hyperplasia to maintain a euglycemic state.
Excessive iodine can actually lead to the Wolff-Chaikoff effect or iodine-induced hyperthyroidism (Jod-Basedow), but simple goiter is typically caused by deficiency, not excess.
This mechanism describes Graves disease, not simple goiter. In simple goiter, growth is driven by elevated TSH, not autoantibodies.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1080 (Book Page): Reduced thyroid hormone production leads to a compensatory rise in the serum TSH level, which, in turn, causes hypertrophy and hyperplasia of thyroid follicular cells and, ultimately, enlargement of the thyroid gland.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: Which histological variant of parathyroid hyperplasia is characterized by cells containing abundant cytoplasmic glycogen?
options: Water-clear cell hyperplasia
Oxyphil cell hyperplasia
Chief cell hyperplasia
Medullary hyperplasia
Oncocytic hyperplasia
correctOption: Water-clear cell hyperplasia
optionExplanations: Correct. Water-clear cell hyperplasia is a less common pattern where the cells are filled with glycogen, making the cytoplasm look transparent or 'clear' in standard H&E sections.
Oxyphil cell hyperplasia consists of cells packed with mitochondria, giving the cytoplasm an eosinophilic, granular appearance, not a clear one.
Chief cell hyperplasia is the most common form and consists of polygonal cells with pink-staining cytoplasm, not the clear appearance of glycogen accumulation.
Medullary is not a term used to describe variants of parathyroid hyperplasia; it is commonly associated with thyroid carcinoma (C-cells).
Oncocytic refers to cells with high mitochondrial content (like oxyphils), which appear granular and eosinophilic.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): [Less commonly, the constituent cells contain abundant glycogen, giving them a clear appearance in histologic sections (“water-clear cell hyperplasia”).]

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: Which physiological stimulus is the most potent trigger for the secretion of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) under normal homeostatic conditions?
options: An increase in plasma osmotic pressure
Distention of the cardiac atria due to hypervolemia
Suppression of hypothalamic osmoreceptors
A decrease in the concentration of serum potassium
Elevation of systemic arterial blood pressure
correctOption: An increase in plasma osmotic pressure
optionExplanations: The primary regulator of ADH is plasma osmolality. When it rises, osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus trigger the release of ADH to conserve water.
Atrial distention (hypervolemia) signals the body to get rid of fluid, which inhibits ADH secretion.
Suppression of osmoreceptors would happen in hypoosmolar states and would lead to decreased ADH, not a trigger for its secretion.
Potassium levels are not the primary regulator of ADH; sodium and water balance are the main drivers.
Elevated blood pressure actually inhibits ADH release to encourage diuresis and reduce volume.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1065 (Book Page): An increase in plasma osmotic pressure detected by osmoreceptors also triggers ADH secretion.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
statement: A patient is diagnosed with Addison disease resulting from malignant infiltration. Which primary cancer sites are the most frequent sources for these adrenal metastases?
options: Stomach and Liver
Brain and Skin
Prostate and Colon
Lung and Breast
Thyroid and Bone
correctOption: Lung and Breast
optionExplanations: Stomach and liver cancers can spread to the adrenals, but statistical records indicate that thoracic and mammary malignancies remain the dominant sources for these metastatic deposits.

Primary brain tumors rarely metastasize outside the central nervous system. Melanoma (skin) is a frequent source of adrenal metastases, but it is grouped after lung and breast in terms of total volume of cases.

While colon and prostate cancers can metastasize to the adrenals, they are not the primary culprits associated with the destruction of the adrenal cortex at frequencies seen with other epithelial cancers.

Lung and breast carcinomas are highly aggressive and frequently seed the adrenal glands. They account for the majority of metastatic adrenal involvement, which can occasionally lead to functional insufficiency.
Thyroid and primary bone tumors are less common sources of massive, bilateral adrenal replacement than lung and breast cancers.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1122 (Book Page): Carcinomas of the lung and breast are the source of a majority of metastases, although many other neoplasms... may also metastasize to the adrenals.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
statement: What is the critical management step that must occur within a specific time window to maximize the chances of sparing the affected testis from orchiectomy?
options: Elevation of the scrotum for 48 hours to promote venous return
Manual untwisting within approximately 6 hours of onset
Immediate administration of high-dose intravenous anticoagulants
Surgical aspiration of the hemorrhagic fluid within 12 hours
Application of cold compresses to reduce engorgement for 24 hours
correctOption: Manual untwisting within approximately 6 hours of onset
optionExplanations: Scrotal elevation (Prehn's sign) may help in epididymitis but is ineffective and dangerous as a primary treatment for the mechanical blockage of torsion.

Torsion is an emergency because it leads to infarction. If the cord is untwisted (manually or surgically) within about 6 hours, blood flow can be restored before permanent necrotic death occurs, potentially saving the organ.
Anticoagulants are not used; the issue is mechanical twisting, which requires mechanical correction.
Aspiration does not restore the blood supply obstructed at the spermatic cord level.
Delaying treatment for 24 hours would almost certainly result in complete infarction and loss of the testis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 968 (Book Page): If the testis is manually untwisted within approximately 6 hours of the onset of torsion, the affected testis may be spared an orchiectomy.

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
statement: What is the suspected primary pathophysiological trigger for the development of granulomatous thyroiditis?
options: Congenital biosynthetic defects in the organization of iodine molecules
Chronic exposure to goitrogens found in Brassicaceae family vegetables
Breakdown in self-tolerance to thyroglobulin and TSH receptors
Viral-induced tissue injury promoting a limited T-cell response to thyroid antigens
Persistent deficiency of iodine in the diet leading to follicle collapse
correctOption: Viral-induced tissue injury promoting a limited T-cell response to thyroid antigens
optionExplanations: Congenital biosynthetic defects lead to dyshormonogenetic goiter and cretinism, rather than the painful inflammatory destruction characteristic of the subacute form.
Goitrogens interfere with hormone synthesis and cause thyroid enlargement but do not trigger a granulomatous inflammatory response.
The breakdown of self-tolerance to specific thyroid proteins is the primary driver of autoimmune conditions like Hashimoto thyroiditis and Graves disease, not subacute granulomatous thyroiditis.
Correct. The disease is believed to be a self-limited process triggered by viral infections (like mumps or adenovirus) causing a cytotoxic T-cell response.
Iodine deficiency causes compensatory hyperplasia and goiter, but it does not cause the acute inflammatory and granulomatous reaction seen in subacute thyroiditis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): Although the pathogenesis of the disease is unclear, one model suggests that it results from virus-induced host tissue damage that stimulates a cytotoxic T-lymphocyte response to one or more thyroid antigens that damages thyroid follicle cells.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
statement: A patient is diagnosed with ovulatory dysfunctional uterine bleeding specifically due to an inadequate luteal phase. What is the expected physiological finding in this condition?
options: Complete absence of progesterone throughout the cycle.
Inadequate progesterone production by the corpus luteum.
Prolonged estrogenic stimulation due to a pituitary somatotroph adenoma.
Malignant transformation of the endometrial stromal cells.
Failure of the endometrial functionalis to shed during menses.
correctOption: Inadequate progesterone production by the corpus luteum.
optionExplanations: Absence of progesterone characterizes anovulation; in an inadequate luteal phase, ovulation occurs but the corpus luteum is dysfunctional.
This results in a lag in endometrial secretory maturation, which can lead to abnormal bleeding despite ovulation.
Somatotroph adenomas cause GH excess, not direct primary DUB through estrogen pathways.
This describes stromal sarcoma, a malignancy unrelated to functional DUB.
DUB is characterized by abnormal or untimely shedding, not a total failure to shed.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1001 (Book Page): Table 22.3... Ovulatory dysfunctional bleeding (e.g., inadequate luteal phase). [Context: Differentiation of functional disorders].

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
statement: Poor local hygiene in uncircumcised males leads to the accumulation of a specific substance that acts as a local irritant, predisposing the individual to inflammatory scarring and phimosis. What is the name of this substance?
options: Caseum
Gumma
Plaque
Verruca
Smegma
correctOption: Smegma
optionExplanations: Caseum is the cheese-like necrotic material found in tuberculosis granulomas and is not a product of local skin hygiene.
A gumma is a necrotic granulomatous lesion characteristic of tertiary syphilis, not a hygiene-related irritant.
In the context of the penis, 'plaque' typically refers to the collagenous deposits in Peyronie disease, not the debris related to poor hygiene.
Verruca refers to a wart caused by HPV; while common on the genitals, it is a viral proliferation rather than an irritant debris substance.
Smegma is the accumulation of desquamated epithelial cells, sweat, and debris beneath the foreskin; it serves as a chemical and mechanical irritant that facilitates infection and subsequent scarring.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 964 (Book Page): uncircumcised males, in whom the accumulation of desquamated epithelial cells, sweat, and debris, termed smegma, acts as a local irritant.

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
coreConcept: Common Etiology of Pelvic Inflammatory Disease
statement: Which of the following microorganisms is identified as a common primary cause of Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) and remains a leading infectious agent associated with serious sequelae such as infertility?
options: Molluscum contagiosum virus
Candida albicans
Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Gardnerella vaginalis
Group B Streptococcus
correctOption: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
optionExplanations: Molluscum contagiosum is a poxvirus causing cutaneous or mucosal papules with a dimpled center; it is a localized viral infection and not an agent that causes the inflammatory upper tract syndrome of PID.

Candida albicans is a fungal agent that causes significant symptomatic discomfort, such as pruritus and curdlike discharge, but typically does not result in serious upper tract sequelae or infertility.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a major sexually transmitted pathogen that commonly ascends from the endocervix to the fallopian tubes, causing suppurative salpingitis and potentially leading to permanent infertility.

Gardnerella vaginalis is the main agent associated with bacterial vaginosis, causing malodorous discharge, but it is generally considered a lower genital tract infection without the severe upper tract sequelae typical of PID.
Group B Streptococcus is primarily implicated in neonatal infections, stillbirths, and preterm deliveries rather than being a primary or most common driver of classic Pelvic Inflammatory Disease.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 986 (Book Page): Neisseria gonorrhoeae continues to be a common cause of PID, the most serious complication of gonorrhea in women.

category: Describe salient morphological features of clinically significant subtypes of thyroiditis: i
statement: During a pathology lab, a student observes a thyroid gland that is diffusely enlarged, with a pale, yellow-tan, firm, and somewhat nodular cut surface. This gross appearance is most likely associated with which underlying pathology?
options: Thyroglossal duct cyst
Graves disease
Follicular adenoma
Toxic multinodular goiter
Hashimoto thyroiditis
correctOption: Hashimoto thyroiditis
optionExplanations: Thyroglossal duct cysts present as midline fluid-filled swellings, often with mucinous secretions, rather than diffuse firm nodular enlargement of the entire gland.
Graves disease glands typically have a 'beefy' deep red, soft appearance resembling muscle due to increased vascularity and hypercellularity.
Follicular adenoma is a solitary, well-circumscribed, encapsulated nodule that compresses the adjacent thyroid, rather than causing diffuse nodular enlargement of the whole gland.
Toxic multinodular goiter would show multiple irregular nodules filled with brown, gelatinous colloid, often with areas of hemorrhage and calcification.
The pale yellow-tan and firm cut surface is characteristic of the lymphocytic infiltration and follicular atrophy found in Hashimoto thyroiditis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1077 (Book Page): The thyroid is usually diffusely enlarged... The cut surface is pale, yellow-tan, firm, and somewhat nodular.

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
coreConcept: Natural History of De Quervain Thyroiditis
statement: Which of the following describes the typical natural history and clinical resolution of granulomatous (De Quervain) thyroiditis in an untreated patient?
options: Rapid development of airway obstruction requiring emergency thyroidectomy
Transformation into a high-grade extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma
Development of a hard, fixed mass that mimics an invasive undifferentiated carcinoma
Progression to permanent, life-long hypothyroidism in over 90% of cases
Spontaneous return to normal thyroid function within approximately 6 to 8 weeks
correctOption: Spontaneous return to normal thyroid function within approximately 6 to 8 weeks
optionExplanations: Airway obstruction is rare in granulomatous thyroiditis; this symptom is more concerning in cases of anaplastic carcinoma or massive goiters.
Extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma is a recognized complication of the chronic lymphocytic inflammation found in Hashimoto thyroiditis, not granulomatous thyroiditis.
A hard, fixed mass is more suggestive of Riedel thyroiditis or anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, whereas De Quervain's typically presents with a firm but mobile and tender gland.
De Quervain's is usually self-limited and returns to euthyroidism, unlike Hashimoto thyroiditis which typically leads to permanent hypothyroidism.
The disease course is characteristically self-limited, with inflammation subsiding and thyroid stores replenishing over a couple of months without surgical intervention.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): After recovery, generally in 6 to 8 weeks, normal thyroid function returns.

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: The neurohypophysis consists of which two primary cellular and structural components?
options: Acidophils and basophils
Pituicytes and Rathke pouch epithelium
Chromophobe cells and somatotrophs
Pituicytes and hypothalamic axonal processes
Corticotrophs and thyrotrophs
correctOption: Pituicytes and hypothalamic axonal processes
optionExplanations: Acidophils and basophils are types of hormone-secreting epithelial cells located in the anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis).
Rathke pouch epithelium gives rise to the anterior pituitary, while the posterior pituitary develops as an extension of the brain's floor.
Chromophobes and somatotrophs are components of the anterior lobe; the posterior lobe is neural in origin and lacks these epithelial cell types.
The posterior pituitary is a neuro-hemal organ consisting of supporting glia (pituicytes) and the terminals of axons that originate in the hypothalamus.
Corticotrophs and thyrotrophs are anterior pituitary cells that synthesize ACTH and TSH respectively.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1065 (Book Page): The posterior pituitary consists of modified glial cells (termed pituicytes) and axonal processes extending from the hypothalamus...

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
statement: A histological section of a surgically removed anterior pituitary mass shows a monotonous population of polygonal cells arranged in sheets. There is a notable absence of a specific stromal component that usually partitions the normal gland into small nests. Which feature is most characteristic of this neoplastic growth?
options: Absence of reticulin network
Presence of numerous mitotic figures
Extensive focal necrosis
Dense neutrophilic infiltrate
Prominent pleomorphic giant cells
correctOption: Absence of reticulin network
optionExplanations: Normal pituitary tissue is organized into small nests of cells separated by a delicate reticulin framework. Adenomas show cellular monomorphism and loss of this reticulin network.
Mitotic figures are typically sparse in common pituitary adenomas; a high mitotic index is used to categorize more aggressive variants or carcinomas.
While macroadenomas can have foci of necrosis, it is not the defining histological distinction between normal pituitary and adenoma.
Inflammatory infiltrates are not a feature of pituitary adenomas; pituitary inflammation is characteristic of lymphocytic hypophysitis or granulomatous disease.
Adenomas are typically characterized by cellular monomorphism. Bizarre pleomorphic cells are rare and are more indicative of carcinoma or anaplastic change.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1068 (Book Page): This cellular monomorphism and the absence of a significant reticulin network distinguish pituitary adenomas from normal anterior pituitary parenchyma (Fig. 24.5).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: What is the most frequent clinical cause of Cushing syndrome encountered in medical practice overall?
options: Bilateral macronodular hyperplasia due to ARMC5 mutations
Small-cell carcinoma of the lung producing ectopic hormones
Exogenous administration of therapeutic glucocorticoids
Primary adrenocortical adenoma with autonomous secretion
Pituitary microadenoma secreting adrenocorticotropic hormone
correctOption: Exogenous administration of therapeutic glucocorticoids
optionExplanations: Bilateral macronodular hyperplasia is a rare form of ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome compared to steroid use.
Ectopic ACTH from lung cancer is a rare paraneoplastic cause, representing only 5-10% of endogenous cases.
Iatrogenic Cushing syndrome from therapeutic steroid use is the single most common cause overall in clinical practice.
Primary adrenal adenomas are less common than exogenous causes of hypercortisolism.
While pituitary microadenomas (Cushing disease) are a major endogenous cause, they are significantly less common than iatrogenic causes.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1113 (Book Page): The vast majority of cases of Cushing syndrome are the result of the administration of exogenous glucocorticoids (iatrogenic Cushing syndrome).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: In patients with ACTH-independent bilateral macronodular adrenal hyperplasia (BMAH), what is the most frequently identified genetic aberration implicated in the familial forms of the disease?
options: Loss-of-function mutations in the AIRE gene.
Biallelic inactivating mutations in the USP8 deubiquitinase.
Point mutations in the RET proto-oncogene.
Inactivating germline mutations in the ARMC5 gene.
Activating somatic mutations in the TSH receptor gene.
correctOption: Inactivating germline mutations in the ARMC5 gene.
optionExplanations: AIRE mutations cause Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome type 1 (APS-1), which results in adrenal insufficiency, not Cushing syndrome.
USP8 mutations are frequently found in corticotroph adenomas of the pituitary (Cushing disease), not in the adrenal hyperplasia forms.
RET mutations are associated with Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma and MEN-2 syndromes, which include pheochromocytoma, but not Cushingoid hyperplasia.
ARMC5 is a tumor suppressor gene recently linked to the majority of familial and many sporadic cases of BMAH.
TSH receptor mutations are associated with toxic thyroid adenomas, not macronodular adrenal hyperplasia.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1114 (Book Page): Familial forms associated with germline mutations in the armadillo repeat containing 5 (ARMC5) gene, a putative tumor suppressor gene, have been reported; of note, up to 50% of apparently sporadic BMAH cases harbor germline ARMC5 mutations.

category: Describe salient morphological features of clinically significant subtypes of thyroiditis: i
statement: What is the primary immunological mechanism responsible for the progressive depletion of follicular epithelial cells and resulting thyroid failure in Hashimoto thyroiditis?
options: CD8+ cytotoxic T cell-mediated cell death
Type III hypersensitivity resulting in immune complex deposition
Complement-mediated lysis triggered by TSI autoantibodies
Vascular endothelial injury leading to ischemic necrosis
Bacterial seeding of follicles inducing suppurative necrosis
correctOption: CD8+ cytotoxic T cell-mediated cell death
optionExplanations: Progressive depletion of thyrocytes in Hashimoto is primarily driven by CD8+ T-cell killing and cytokine-mediated injury from CD4+ Th1 cells.
While antibodies are present, Hashimoto is primarily a T-cell mediated (Type IV) autoimmune disorder rather than a Type III complex-mediated disease.
TSI autoantibodies are the cause of Graves disease, not Hashimoto; in Hashimoto, antithyroglobulin and antithyroid peroxidase antibodies are present but their role in primary cell death is secondary.
Ischemic necrosis is not a feature of Hashimoto; the process is a slow autoimmune destruction involving lymphocytic infiltration.
Hashimoto is a non-infectious autoimmune condition; bacterial seeding causes acute infectious thyroiditis, which is rare.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1077 (Book Page): CD8+ cytotoxic T cell–mediated cell death: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells may destroy thyroid follicular cells.

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
statement: A laboratory evaluation of a pregnant patient with severe hypertension reveals schistocytes on peripheral smear, a platelet count of 60,000/μL, and an AST level of 250 U/L. This clinical picture is most specifically referred to as:
options: HELLP syndrome
Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
Sheehan syndrome
Kimmelstiel-Wilson disease
Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome
correctOption: HELLP syndrome
optionExplanations: HELLP syndrome (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets) is a specific severe variant of preeclampsia/eclampsia.
Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is characterized by gastrin-secreting tumors leading to peptic ulcers.
Sheehan syndrome is postpartum pituitary necrosis due to hypovolemic shock.
Kimmelstiel-Wilson disease refers to nodular glomerulosclerosis in diabetic nephropathy.
Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome involves bilateral adrenal hemorrhage usually due to meningococcemia.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1029 (Book Page): Approximately 10% of women with preeclampsia develop microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets, referred to as the HELLP syndrome

category: Define thyroiditis
statement: On histologic examination of a thyroid involved in subacute granulomatous thyroiditis, which finding is most characteristic of the later inflammatory phase?
options: Small, uniform follicles mimicking normal parenchyma.
Extensive 'wet keratin' and calcified lamellar structures.
Orphan Annie eye nuclei with psammoma bodies.
Cords of small cells with salt-and-pepper chromatin.
Multinucleate giant cells enclosing pools of colloid.
correctOption: Multinucleate giant cells enclosing pools of colloid.
optionExplanations: This describes a normal thyroid or potentially a follicular adenoma, whereas thyroiditis involves significant disruption and inflammation.
This describes adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma, a CNS tumor, not thyroiditis.
These are the diagnostic hallmarks of papillary thyroid carcinoma, a malignancy, not an inflammatory thyroiditis.
This describes the neuroendocrine features seen in medullary carcinoma or pheochromocytoma, not the granulomatous response in thyroiditis.
The pathognomonic feature of de Quervain (granulomatous) thyroiditis is the formation of granulomas where multinucleate giant cells surround leaked thyroid colloid.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): Later, more characteristic features appear in the form of aggregates of lymphocytes, activated macrophages, and plasma cells associated with collapsed and damaged thyroid follicles. Multinucleate giant cells enclose pools of colloid, hence the designation granulomatous thyroiditis.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: Which pathogen is most frequently isolated from localized abscesses in the setting of acute bacterial mastitis occurring during the first month of breastfeeding?
options: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Corynebacterium species
Bacteroides fragilis
Streptococcus pyogenes
Staphylococcus aureus
correctOption: Staphylococcus aureus
optionExplanations: Mycobacterium tuberculosis causes chronic granulomatous inflammation of the breast, which is rare and presents as a cold abscess, not an acute lactational infection.
Corynebacterium is associated with cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis, an idiopathic condition unrelated to acute lactational infections.
Bacteroides and other anaerobes may cause secondary infections in chronic conditions like SMULD but are not the primary cause of acute lactational mastitis.
Streptococci (like S. pyogenes) are less common and typically cause a diffuse, spreading cellulitis rather than the localized abscesses mentioned in the stem.
Staphylococcus aureus is the primary cause of acute mastitis during lactation, specifically known for inducing localized suppurative necrosis and abscess formation.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1038 (Book Page): From this portal of entry, Staphylococcus aureus or, less commonly, streptococci invade the breast tissue. The breast is erythematous and painful, and fever is often present. At the outset only one duct system or sector of the breast is involved. If not treated, the infection may spread to the entire breast. Staphylococci infection often leads to single or multiple abscesses, whereas streptococci cause spreading infection in the form of cellulitis.

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: Regarding the regulation of mineral homeostasis, what is the specific mechanistic effect of parathyroid hormone (PTH) on renal tubular function?
options: Stimulation of calcitonin release from C cells
Inhibition of osteoclast progenitor differentiation
Decreased conversion of vitamin D to its active dihydroxy form
Increased urinary phosphate excretion
Decreased renal tubular reabsorption of calcium
correctOption: Increased urinary phosphate excretion
optionExplanations: Calcitonin is released by thyroid C cells in response to hypercalcemia to lower calcium levels. PTH does not stimulate calcitonin; they are counter-regulatory hormones with opposing effects on calcium homeostasis.

PTH promotes rather than inhibits osteoclast activity. It stimulates the differentiation of osteoclast progenitors into mature osteoclasts, which resorb bone matrix and release calcium and phosphate into the systemic circulation.

This is the opposite of the true effect; PTH stimulates the enzyme alpha-1-hydroxylase in the kidney, which increases the conversion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to its active form, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, facilitating gut absorption of calcium.

PTH reduces the reabsorption of phosphate in the proximal tubule, leading to phosphaturia. By lowering serum phosphate, it reduces the amount of calcium bound to phosphate, thereby increasing the concentration of free ionized calcium in the blood.

This is incorrect because PTH actually increases the renal tubular reabsorption of calcium, particularly in the distal convoluted tubule, which serves to conserve free calcium and elevate serum levels during hypocalcemic states.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1091 (Book Page): Increased urinary phosphate excretion, thereby lowering serum phosphate levels and further increasing calcium

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
coreConcept: CCDN1/PTH inversion in parathyroid adenoma pathogenesis
statement: A 52-year-old female is diagnosed with a solitary parathyroid adenoma. Molecular analysis of the tumor reveals a pericentromeric inversion on chromosome 11. Which pathophysiological mechanism is directly driven by this specific genetic rearrangement?
options: Loss-of-function mutation in the CDC73 gene leading to the absence of the protein parafibromin.
Germline inactivation of the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 11q13.
Relocation of the CCDN1 gene adjacent to the PTH gene 5'-flanking region, causing Cyclin D1 overexpression.
Constitutive activation of the G-protein alpha subunit (GNAS) leading to persistent cAMP generation.
Point mutation in the CASR gene resulting in decreased sensitivity to extracellular calcium.
correctOption: Relocation of the CCDN1 gene adjacent to the PTH gene 5'-flanking region, causing Cyclin D1 overexpression.
optionExplanations: CDC73 mutations and loss of parafibromin are characteristically associated with parathyroid carcinoma and hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumor syndrome, not this specific adenoma inversion.
While MEN1 is located on chromosome 11 and its mutation is associated with parathyroid tumors, the specific mechanism of 'pericentromeric inversion' refers to the CCDN1/PTH rearrangement.

The pericentromeric inversion on chromosome 11 places the Cyclin D1 gene (CCDN1) under the control of the highly active parathyroid hormone (PTH) promoter, leading to clonal overexpression of Cyclin D1 and subsequent cell cycle progression.
GNAS mutations are a major cause of pituitary somatotroph adenomas and are not the result of the chromosome 11 inversion described.
CASR mutations are associated with familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia and are not driven by the chromosomal inversion mentioned.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): A pericentromeric inversion on chromosome 11 results in relocation of CCDN1 (normally on 11q), so that it is positioned adjacent to the 5′-flanking region of the PTH gene (on 11p). As a consequence of these changes, a 5′-regulatory element flanking the PTH gene directs overexpression of cyclin D1, causing the cells to proliferate.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
coreConcept: Morphologic Differentiation of T1D and T2D
statement: Examination of the pancreatic islets in an individual with long-standing Type 2 Diabetes reveals characteristic extracellular deposits. What is the primary constituent of these deposits?
options: H&E-positive glycogen granules
Neutral fats within vacuolated cells
Psammoma bodies
Lymphocytic infiltrates (insulitis)
Amyloid (amylin)
correctOption: Amyloid (amylin)
optionExplanations: Glycogen granules are not the characteristic extracellular deposit in T2D islets; the primary finding is proteinaceous amyloid.
While systemic obesity involves neutral fats in adipocytes, the characteristic finding within the islets themselves is amyloid, not intracellular fat.
Psammoma bodies are laminated calcifications common in papillary thyroid carcinoma or meningiomas; they are not features of diabetic islet pathology.
Insulitis (lymphocytic infiltration) is the characteristic morphologic feature of Type 1 Diabetes, representing the autoimmune attack; it is absent in T2D.
Amyloid deposits, composed of islet amyloid polypeptide (amylin), are present in the majority of Type 2 Diabetes cases and can obliterate islets in late stages.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1107 (Book Page): [Amyloid deposition within islets in T2D begins in and around capillaries and between cells. At advanced stages, the islets may be virtually obliterated]

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: Which of the following macroscopic features is most typical of a parathyroid adenoma?
options: A solitary, soft, tan to reddish-brown, encapsulated nodule
Multiple small, darkly pigmented brown to black micronodules
Bilateral wedge-shaped hyperplasia extending from the periphery
Multiglandular enlargement with a total weight under 1 gram
A large, irregular, gray-white mass exceeding 10 grams
correctOption: A solitary, soft, tan to reddish-brown, encapsulated nodule
optionExplanations: Adenomas are typically solitary, encapsulated, and have a tan to reddish-brown appearance.
Darkly pigmented micronodules are a feature of primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease, not parathyroid adenomas.
Wedge-shaped hyperplasia is more characteristic of bilateral idiopathic hyperaldosteronism in the adrenal gland.
Primary hyperplasia is characterized by multiglandular involvement and often a total weight less than 1 gram.
This description is more typical of a parathyroid carcinoma, which is often large and gray-white.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): The typical adenoma averages 0.5 to 5 g and consists of a well-circumscribed, soft, tan to reddish-brown nodule invested by a delicate capsule.

category: Describe salient morphological features of clinically significant subtypes of thyroiditis: i
statement: A pathologist is comparing surgical specimens of Hashimoto thyroiditis and subacute lymphocytic (painless) thyroiditis. Which morphological feature would most reliably distinguish Hashimoto thyroiditis from the subacute lymphocytic variant?
options: Presence of a mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate
Diffuse symmetric enlargement of the thyroid gland
Prominent H'u00fcrthle cell metaplasia and interstitial fibrosis
Disruption and collapse of thyroid follicles
Formation of well-developed germinal centers
correctOption: Prominent H'u00fcrthle cell metaplasia and interstitial fibrosis
optionExplanations: Both Hashimoto and subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis share mononuclear (lymphocytic) infiltrates.
Diffuse symmetric enlargement can occur in both, though it may be more modest in the subacute lymphocytic variant.
While lymphocytic thyroiditis resembles Hashimoto, it lacks the extensive oxyphilic (H'u00fcrthle cell) metaplasia and the significant fibrosis found in classic Hashimoto.
Follicular disruption is a common finding across most inflammatory thyroid conditions during active destruction.
Germinal centers are seen in both Hashimoto and subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis specimens.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): Microscopic examination reveals lymphocytic infiltration with large germinal centers within the thyroid parenchyma and patchy disruption and collapse of thyroid follicles. Unlike Hashimoto thyroiditis, however, fibrosis and H'u00fcrthle cell metaplasia are not prominent.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
statement: Nonspecific bacterial epididymitis in a 10-year-old child should prompt an immediate investigation for which underlying condition?
options: Reflux of contaminated urine from the posterior urethra
Sexually transmitted pathogens
Congenital genitourinary abnormality
Systemic viral parotitis
Ischemic infarction from torsion
correctOption: Congenital genitourinary abnormality
optionExplanations: While reflux of urine is a mechanism in adults, the primary driver in children is often a structural anomaly.
Sexually transmitted infections are causes in sexually active adults, typically those under the age of 35.
In children, epididymitis is rare and generally signals the presence of a congenital abnormality that facilitates infection by gram-negative rods.
Mumps (viral parotitis) causes orchitis in postpubertal males, but is extremely uncommon in children.
Torsion is a vascular disorder and an emergency, but it is not the same as bacterial epididymitis, though it is part of the differential diagnosis for scrotal pain.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 967 (Book Page): Though uncommon in children, epididymitis in childhood is usually associated with a congenital genitourinary abnormality and infection with gram-negative rods.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: How does the distribution of stromal fat typically change in a parathyroid gland affected by either hyperplasia or adenoma?
options: Fat increases to over 50% of the total gland volume
Stromal fat becomes inconspicuous or disappears
Adipocytes undergo metaplasia into oxyphil cells
Fat becomes the predominant component of the secretory nodules
Fat accumulates specifically at the tumor center
correctOption: Stromal fat becomes inconspicuous or disappears
optionExplanations: Normal parathyroid glands contain about 30% fat by adulthood; an increase is not seen in neoplastic or hyperplastic processes.
Correct. One of the key histological markers of hyperactive parathyroid tissue (adenoma or hyperplasia) is the loss or marked reduction of the normal stromal fat.
Adipocytes do not transform into oxyphil cells; oxyphils are derived from the epithelial lineage of the gland.
If fat was the predominant component, it would be a lipoma or a normal involuted gland, not a functional adenoma or hyperplasia.
Fat is typically lost throughout the involved area, rather than accumulating at any specific point within the lesion.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): [In contrast to the normal parathyroid parenchyma, adipose tissue is inconspicuous.] [As in the case of adenomas, stromal fat is inconspicuous within hyperplastic glands.]

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
statement: What is the expected gender predilection for the development of granulomatous thyroiditis?
options: Exclusively occurs in pregnant females
Affects males twice as often as females
Primarily affects prepubertal children
Affects females four times more often than males
Equal incidence in males and females
correctOption: Affects females four times more often than males
optionExplanations: Postpartum thyroiditis is a variant of subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis; while granulomatous can occur in women of reproductive age, it is not restricted to pregnancy.
Males are affected significantly less frequently than females.
It is most prevalent in the 4th and 5th decades of life (middle-aged adults).
The female-to-male ratio is specifically cited as 4:1.
The condition shows a clear female predominance, common to many thyroid disorders.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): The disorder is most common between 40 and 50 years of age and... affects women more often than men (4:1).

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
statement: A 42-year-old patient is evaluated for chronic pelvic pain and suprapubic discomfort. Expressed prostatic secretions reveal 25 leukocytes per high-power field, but repeated bacterial cultures of both urine and secretions are negative. What is the most common form of inflammation affecting the prostate in this clinical setting?
options: Chronic abacterial prostatitis
Acute bacterial prostatitis
Chronic bacterial prostatitis
IgG4-associated autoimmune prostatitis
Granulomatous prostatitis due to BCG
correctOption: Chronic abacterial prostatitis
optionExplanations: Chronic abacterial prostatitis (Chronic Pelvic Pain Syndrome) is the most frequent type of prostatitis; it presents with clinical symptoms and leukocytosis in prostatic secretions without identifiable bacterial growth.
Acute bacterial prostatitis is associated with fever, chills, and positive bacterial cultures (most commonly E. coli), which are absent in this patient.
Chronic bacterial prostatitis is characterized by recurrent urinary tract infections caused by the same organism, which is not present here given the negative cultures.
IgG4-associated prostatitis is a rare autoimmune form characterized by systemic involvement and specific plasma cell infiltrates, rather than being the 'most common' form of prostatitis.
Granulomatous prostatitis due to BCG typically follows intravesical therapy for bladder cancer and is characterized by a specific histologic pattern of granulomas, not just non-specific leukocytosis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 975 (Book Page): Chronic abacterial prostatitis, the most common form of prostatitis... Expressed prostatic secretions contain more than 10 leukocytes per high-power field, but bacterial cultures are uniformly negative.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
statement: A patient scheduled for thyroidectomy for Graves disease is administered an iodine solution preoperatively. What is the expected histological effect of this treatment on the thyroid gland?
options: Extensive fibrosis extending through the thyroid capsule
Increased lymphocytic infiltration and germinal center formation
Exaggeration of epithelial hypertrophy and tall columnar shape
Involution of the epithelium and accumulation of colloid
Transformation of follicular cells into oncocytes (Hürthle cells)
correctOption: Involution of the epithelium and accumulation of colloid
optionExplanations: Extensive extracapsular fibrosis is a feature of Riedel thyroiditis, not a pharmacological response in Graves.
Iodine is used to decrease the vascularity and hyperplastic activity, not to increase the immunological/lymphoid response.
This effect is seen with propylthiouracil, which increases TSH via feedback and worsens the hyperplasia histologically.
High doses of iodine block the release of thyroid hormone and cause the hyperplastic, crowded cells to involute, making the gland easier to manage surgically.
Hürthle cell change is a metaplastic response to chronic injury or autoimmune destruction, not a response to iodine therapy.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1080 (Book Page): Administration of iodine causes involution of the epithelium and the accumulation of colloid by blocking thyroglobulin secretion.

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
statement: Which of the following immunohistochemical or laboratory findings is the most reliable feature to distinguish the hyperthyroid phase of granulomatous thyroiditis from Graves disease?
options: Elevated serum levels of thyroglobulin
Decreased radioactive iodine uptake on scintigraphy
Low to undetectable serum TSH levels
Presence of anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies
Significantly elevated serum free T4 and T3 levels
correctOption: Decreased radioactive iodine uptake on scintigraphy
optionExplanations: Thyroglobulin can be elevated in various inflammatory and neoplastic thyroid conditions and is not a specific differentiator between these two hyperthyroid states.
In granulomatous thyroiditis, the hyperthyroidism is due to the release of preformed hormone from damaged follicles (low uptake), whereas in Graves, it is due to active new synthesis (high uptake).
TSH is suppressed in both conditions due to feedback inhibition from high T3/T4 levels, making it useless for differentiating the underlying cause.
Anti-TPO antibodies are more specific for Hashimoto thyroiditis; they may be present in many thyroid conditions and do not differentiate the cause of thyrotoxicosis in this context.
Both conditions present with elevated T3 and T4 during the thyrotoxic phase, so this value does not differentiate the two etiologies.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): However, unlike in hyperthyroid states such as Graves disease, radioactive iodine uptake is diminished.

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
statement: Which site of abnormal implantation is specifically associated with the fertilized ovum failing to enter or dropping out of the distal end of the fallopian tube?
options: Cornual segment
Abdominal cavity
Endocervical canal
Intramural portion of the uterus
Ovary
correctOption: Abdominal cavity
optionExplanations: The cornual segment is the most proximal part of the tube, opposite to the fimbriated distal end.
If the ovum is fertilized but fails to be swept into the fimbria, it can implant on peritoneal surfaces in the abdominal cavity.
The endocervical canal is accessed through the internal os of the uterus, not by dropping out of the fallopian tube's distal end.
The intramural portion refers to the segment of the tube within the uterine wall, which is not reached if the ovum drops out distally.
Ovarian pregnancy involves fertilization within the follicle, not dropping out of the distal tube.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1027 (Book Page): Abdominal pregnancies occur when the fertilized ovum fails to enter or drops out of the fimbriated end of the tube.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: Which of the following architectural findings is most useful for a pathologist to definitively identify a parathyroid lesion as an adenoma rather than primary hyperplasia?
options: Observation of all four glands being involved by diffuse chief cell proliferation
Detection of high mitotic activity and necrotic foci within the chief cells
The presence of amyloid deposits derived from calcitonin polypeptides
Laminated cytoplasmic inclusions known as spironolactone bodies
Identification of a rim of compressed, non-neoplastic parathyroid tissue at the edge
correctOption: Identification of a rim of compressed, non-neoplastic parathyroid tissue at the edge
optionExplanations: Multiglandular involvement is the definition of hyperplasia, which contrasts with the typically solitary nature of an adenoma.
Mitotic activity and necrosis are rare in adenomas. If prominent, they raise concern for carcinoma, although they are not definitive markers of malignancy.
