Parafibromin is encoded by CDC73; mutations are largely associated with parathyroid carcinomas rather than the classic Cyclin D1 inversion in adenomas.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): [Cyclin D1 (CCDN1) gene inversions leading to overexpression of cyclin D1 protein, a major regulator of the cell cycle. ... Between 10% and 20% of sporadic parathyroid adenomas have this clonal rearrangement.]

category: Describe salient morphological features of clinically significant subtypes of thyroiditis: i
coreConcept: Morphological distinctions between painless and Hashimoto thyroiditis
statement: A comparison between subacute lymphocytic (painless) thyroiditis and Hashimoto thyroiditis reveals that the former lacks which significant morphological characteristic?
options: Infiltration of the thyroid by small lymphocytes
Patchy disruption and collapse of thyroid follicles
Symmetric enlargement of the thyroid gland
Prominent Hürthle cell metaplasia and interstitial fibrosis
The presence of well-developed germinal centers
correctOption: Prominent Hürthle cell metaplasia and interstitial fibrosis
optionExplanations: Both painless thyroiditis and Hashimoto thyroiditis demonstrate lymphocytic infiltration, so this does not distinguish them.
Follicle disruption occurs in both, though it is usually more progressive and destructive in Hashimoto.
Both conditions can present with symmetric enlargement (goiter), although the thyroid may appear grossly normal in some cases of painless thyroiditis.
While both share autoimmune features, the absence of metaplastic Hürthle cells and significant fibrosis helps distinguish subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis from Hashimoto.
Germinal centers are common in both types of autoimmune-related thyroiditis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): Unlike Hashimoto thyroiditis, however, fibrosis and Hürthle cell metaplasia are not prominent [in subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis].

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
statement: Which microorganism is the most common cause of acute epididymitis in men over the age of 35?
options: Escherichia coli
Chlamydia trachomatis
Gardnerella vaginalis
Treponema pallidum
Neisseria gonorrhoeae
correctOption: Escherichia coli
optionExplanations: In men over 35, epididymitis is usually secondary to a UTI or prostatitis, most commonly caused by enteric gram-negative rods like E. coli.
C. trachomatis is the most frequent cause in sexually active men younger than 35.
Gardnerella vaginalis is a common agent in balanoposthitis and female vaginosis, but is not a typical cause of male epididymitis.
Treponema pallidum causes syphilis, which is not a common cause of acute epididymitis.
N. gonorrhoeae is a frequent cause in young, sexually active males, but decreases in frequency as a cause of epididymitis in older men.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 967 (Book Page): In men older than age 35, common urinary tract pathogens, such as E. coli and Pseudomonas, are responsible for most infections.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
coreConcept: Stromal fat as a histological discriminator in parathyroid pathology
statement: In the histopathological evaluation of primary parathyroid hyperplasia, what is the typical status of the stromal adipose tissue within the hyperplastic areas?
options: Stromal fat is characteristically inconspicuous or absent within the hyperplastic nodules.
Adipose tissue remains constant at the normal adult level of approximately thirty percent.
Adipose tissue undergoes metaplastic transformation into Hürthle-like eosinophilic cells.
Fat cells are only present in the 'water-clear' variant of parathyroid hyperplasia.
Adipose tissue is significantly increased, often constituting over fifty percent of the nodular volume.
correctOption: Stromal fat is characteristically inconspicuous or absent within the hyperplastic nodules.
optionExplanations: A hallmark of both parathyroid adenoma and hyperplasia is that the proliferating cells replace the normal stromal fat, making it inconspicuous or entirely absent.
30% fat is the maximum found in a normal adult gland. In states of cellular proliferation (hyperplasia or adenoma), this percentage drops significantly.
Hürthle cells are a thyroid metaplasia. The parathyroid equivalent is the oxyphil cell, but fat does not transform into these cells.
Inconspicuous fat is a generalized feature of all forms of primary hyperplasia, including the chief cell and water-clear cell variants.
Increased fat is not a feature of hyperplasia; rather, the proliferation of chief cells displaces the normal stromal fat.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): In contrast to the normal parathyroid parenchyma, adipose tissue is inconspicuous... As in the case of adenomas, stromal fat is inconspicuous within hyperplastic glands.

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
statement: What is the characteristic gender and age distribution for individuals most frequently diagnosed with granulomatous thyroiditis?
options: Infants during the first year of life
Adolescent males during puberty
Women between 40 and 50 years of age
Men between 20 and 30 years of age
Postmenopausal women over age 70
correctOption: Women between 40 and 50 years of age
optionExplanations: Hypothyroidism in infants is usually congenital (cretinism) and not an inflammatory thyroiditis.
Sporadic goiter peaks at puberty, but granulomatous thyroiditis is rare in this population compared to middle-aged adults.
Granulomatous thyroiditis most commonly presents in middle-aged women, specifically in the 40-50 age bracket.
Men are affected much less frequently than women (ratio 1:4), and the peak age is older than the third decade.
While the incidence of some thyroid disorders increases with age, De Quervain thyroiditis specifically peaks in middle age (40s-50s).
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): The disorder is most common between 40 and 50 years of age and... affects women more often than men (4 : 1).

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
statement: How does preoperative administration of a concentrated iodine solution affect the morphology of the thyroid gland in a patient with Graves disease?
options: It leads to the formation of numerous lymphoid germinal centers
It promotes glandular involution and the accumulation of colloid
It causes the squamous metaplasia of the follicular lining cells
It exaggerates epithelial hypertrophy by stimulating further TSH release
It induces acute suppurative necrosis of the hyperplastic follicles
correctOption: It promotes glandular involution and the accumulation of colloid
optionExplanations: Lymphoid germinal centers are a primary feature of the autoimmune response in Graves disease (and Hashimoto) and are not a result of iodine administration.
Iodine inhibits the release of thyroglobulin and decreases the vascularity and activity of the gland, causing the tall columnar cells to involute and the follicles to fill with colloid.
Squamous metaplasia is not a typical response of the thyroid to iodine; the cells usually transition from a tall columnar (active) state to a flatter, cuboidal (inactive) state.
Stimulation of hypertrophy by increasing TSH is actually the effect of propylthiouracil (PTU), which blocks hormone synthesis and removes the feedback inhibition on the pituitary.
Iodine solution is used to stabilize the gland for surgery; it does not cause suppurative necrosis, which is typically a result of bacterial infection or extreme acute inflammation.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): Administration of iodine causes involution of the epithelium and the accumulation of colloid by blocking thyroglobulin secretion.

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
statement: A patient in the hyperthyroid phase of granulomatous thyroiditis undergoes a radionuclide thyroid scan. Which physiological finding distinguishes this state from Graves disease?
options: Symmetric uptake in the pyramidal lobe
Cold nodules with hypervascularity on Doppler
Diffusely increased radioactive iodine uptake
Diminished radioactive iodine uptake
Focal 'hot' uptake in a single autonomous nodule
correctOption: Diminished radioactive iodine uptake
optionExplanations: Symmetric uptake across the gland, including the pyramidal lobe, is common in physiologic states or Graves, but is not seen when follicular integrity is compromised by inflammation.
Cold nodules are more indicative of thyroid neoplasms; in granulomatous thyroiditis, the whole gland generally shows reduced uptake due to the diffuse inflammatory process.
Diffusely increased uptake is characteristic of Graves disease, where the entire gland is hyperactive due to TSH-receptor stimulation.

In granulomatous thyroiditis, the hyperthyroidism is caused by the release of preformed hormones from damaged follicles rather than increased synthesis. Therefore, the gland's ability to take up new iodine is severely reduced.
A single 'hot' nodule signifies a toxic adenoma, which produces thyroid hormones autonomously, unlike the global follicular leakage seen in thyroiditis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): However, unlike in hyperthyroid states such as Graves disease, radioactive iodine uptake is diminished.

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
statement: Which of the following events most likely leads to the development of a primary abdominal pregnancy?
options: Direct invasion of the myometrium by trophoblastic cells
Implantation of the placenta over the internal cervical os
Failure of the fertilized ovum to enter or its escape from the fimbriated end of the tube
Fertilization and trapping of the ovum within a graafian follicle
Retrograde menstruation of endometrial tissue
correctOption: Failure of the fertilized ovum to enter or its escape from the fimbriated end of the tube
optionExplanations: Direct myometrial invasion by trophoblastic cells is a feature of an invasive mole or choriocarcinoma, or the adherence pattern in placenta accreta.
Implantation over the internal cervical os defines placenta previa, which remains an intrauterine, though abnormally located, placental site.
Abdominal pregnancies result when the zygote either fails to be picked up by the fimbriae or is expelled from the distal tube, subsequently implanting on peritoneal surfaces.
Fertilization within a follicle defines an ovarian pregnancy, not an abdominal one.
Retrograde menstruation is a theory for the pathogenesis of endometriosis, not the cause of an abdominal pregnancy (gestation).
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1027 (Book Page): Abdominal pregnancies occur when the fertilized ovum fails to enter or drops out of the fimbriated end of the tube.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: Which specific histological alteration is found in the anterior pituitary of individuals with high levels of either endogenous or exogenous glucocorticoids?
options: Psammoma body formation
Amyloid deposition within islets
Zellballen architectural pattern
Hürthle cell metaplasia
Crooke hyaline change
correctOption: Crooke hyaline change
optionExplanations: Psammoma bodies are concentric calcifications frequently seen in papillary thyroid carcinoma, but not as a reactive change in the pituitary during Cushing syndrome.
Amyloid deposition is a feature of insulinomas and some medullary thyroid carcinomas, but it is not seen in the pituitary in response to glucocorticoid levels.
Zellballen patterns are characteristic of pheochromocytomas in the adrenal medulla, not the anterior pituitary.
Hürthle cells are metaplastic follicular cells found in the thyroid gland (e.g., Hashimoto thyroiditis), not in the adenohypophysis.
Crooke hyaline change involves the replacement of normal granular cytoplasm in ACTH-secreting cells with pale, homogeneous keratin filaments due to the feedback effects of high cortisol.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1114 (Book Page): The most common alteration, resulting from high levels of endogenous or exogenous glucocorticoids, is termed Crooke hyaline change.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: When comparing the histopathology of a parathyroid adenoma to primary hyperplasia, which feature is classically used to distinguish the two entities?
options: A rim of compressed, non-neoplastic parathyroid tissue at the tumor edge
The presence of amyloid deposits derived from calcitonin
Diffuse water-clear cell change in the adenoma variant
The presence of mitotic figures and necrosis in the adenoma
Extensive stromal fat accumulation within the hyperplastic areas
correctOption: A rim of compressed, non-neoplastic parathyroid tissue at the tumor edge
optionExplanations: Adenomas are typically solitary and well-circumscribed, often displaying a rim of residual normal parathyroid tissue that has been compressed by the expanding neoplastic mass.
Amyloid deposits are a hallmark of medullary thyroid carcinoma or insulinomas, not parathyroid lesions.
Water-clear cell change is a characteristic variant of hyperplasia, not a typical feature used to define an adenoma.
Mitotic figures are rare in parathyroid adenomas, and their presence along with necrosis would raise the suspicion of carcinoma rather than a benign adenoma.
In both adenomas and primary hyperplasia, stromal fat is usually inconspicuous or absent, distinguishing them from the normal adult gland which contains significant adipose tissue.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): A rim of compressed, non-neoplastic parathyroid tissue, generally separated by a fibrous capsule, is often visible at the edge of the adenoma.

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: A patient with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung presents with confusion and a serum calcium of 14 mg/dL. Laboratory results show suppressed levels of parathyroid hormone (PTH). Which mechanism most likely explains this patient's hypercalcemia?
options: Activation of the RANK-ligand pathway by tumor-derived cytokines
Direct osteolysis by metastatic tumor cells
Secretion of parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP)
Ectopic secretion of native parathyroid hormone
Increased renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity leading to Vitamin D toxicity
correctOption: Secretion of parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP)
optionExplanations: Cytokine-induced bone resorption is a mechanism in hematological malignancies (like multiple myeloma), but PTHrP is the classic finding for squamous cell lung carcinomas.
Direct osteolysis by metastases accounts for only about 20% of malignancy-associated hypercalcemia cases; humoral mechanisms are more frequent.

In 80% of cases of hypercalcemia of malignancy, tumors (especially squamous cell carcinomas) secrete PTHrP, which mimics PTH action on bone and kidney but is not detected by standard PTH assays, resulting in low measured PTH.
Ectopic secretion of the actual native PTH molecule by non-parathyroid tumors is an exceedingly rare phenomenon and not the standard mechanism for lung cancer.
Increased 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity is typical of granulomatous diseases like sarcoidosis, where macrophages convert Vitamin D, but not the typical mechanism for squamous cell carcinoma.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1093 (Book Page): The most common mechanism (in ~80% of cases) through which osteolytic tumors induce hypercalcemia is by secretion of PTH-related peptide (PTHrP), which (like PTH) induces osteoclastic bone resorption and hypercalcemia.

category: Define thyroiditis
statement: A 52-year-old female presents with a painless, symmetrically enlarged thyroid and mild symptoms of fatigue and cold intolerance. Histologic evaluation of a biopsy reveals an extensive mononuclear infiltrate with germinal centers and follicles lined by Hürthle cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis
Hashimoto thyroiditis
de Quervain thyroiditis
Riedel thyroiditis
Graves disease
correctOption: Hashimoto thyroiditis
optionExplanations: While subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis has germinal centers, it is distinguished by the absence of Hürthle cell metaplasia and prominent fibrosis.
The combination of painless goiter, hypothyroidism, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates with germinal centers, and eosinophilic Hürthle cell metaplasia is pathognomonic for Hashimoto thyroiditis.
Granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis is characterized by pain, multinucleated giant cells, and granulomas, not Hürthle cells.
Riedel thyroiditis is characterized by dense systemic fibrosis that extends beyond the thyroid capsule into neck structures.
Graves disease shows diffuse hyperplasia with scalloped colloid and tall columnar cells, not Hürthle cell metaplasia or extensive follicular destruction.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1076 (Book Page): Hashimoto thyroiditis is an autoimmune disease that results in destruction of the thyroid gland and gradual and progressive thyroid failure. ... Page 1077 (Book Page): The thyroid follicles are atrophic and are lined in many areas by epithelial cells with abundant eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm, termed Hürthle cells...

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
statement: What is the characteristic macroscopic appearance of a testis in the advanced stages of untreated torsion?
options: Well-circumscribed, fleshy, and homogeneous gray-white
Small, firm, and gray-white
Translucent cyst filled with clear serous fluid
Soft, necrotic, and hemorrhagic tissue
Multiple red papillary excrescences
correctOption: Soft, necrotic, and hemorrhagic tissue
optionExplanations: A fleshy, homogeneous gray-white mass is the typical description of a seminoma.
This describes a chronically atrophic testis, such as in cryptorchidism or old age.
A translucent serous cyst is the definition of a hydrocele.
Advanced torsion results in complete tissue death and extensive bleeding into the parenchyma, making the organ soft and saturated with dark blood.
Papillary excrescences are characteristic of condyloma acuminatum (genital warts).
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 968 (Book Page): In advanced stages, the swollen testis consists entirely of soft, necrotic, hemorrhagic tissue.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Diffuse and Multinodular goiter
statement: In the pathogenesis of sporadic goiter, certain dietary substances known as goitrogens can exacerbate thyroid enlargement. Which specific mechanism is associated with the consumption of cassava root in iodine-deficient populations?
options: Proteolysis of thyroglobulin within the follicular lumen
Thiocyanate-mediated inhibition of iodide transport
Suppression of the alpha-subunit of stimulatory G-proteins
Direct inhibition of the TSH receptor by autoantibodies
Overexpression of the PAX8-PPARG fusion protein
correctOption: Thiocyanate-mediated inhibition of iodide transport
optionExplanations: Increased proteolysis would lead to more hormone release (hyperthyroidism); goitrogens act by blocking synthesis, not increasing release.
Cassava contains compounds that release thiocyanate, which competitively inhibits the iodide pump, preventing the thyroid from gathering the already scarce iodine required for hormone synthesis.
G-protein suppression is not a known mechanism for dietary goitrogens; instead, activating mutations in these proteins cause toxic nodules.
TSH receptor inhibition by antibodies causes hypothyroidism, but this is an autoimmune mechanism (like some forms of thyroiditis), not a nutritional goitrogen effect.
The PAX8-PPARG fusion is a genetic translocation found in follicular carcinomas and some adenomas, not a reactive change caused by dietary intake.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1081 (Book Page): Native populations subsisting on cassava root are particularly at risk. Cassava contains a thiocyanate that inhibits iodide transport within the thyroid, worsening any concurrent iodine deficiency.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
statement: In the pathophysiological development of the most common form of dysfunctional uterine bleeding, which hormonal state is primarily responsible for the endometrial changes?
options: Acute withdrawal of both estrogen and progesterone
Excessive and prolonged estrogen stimulation unopposed by progesterone
Sustained high levels of progesterone leading to atrophy
Overproduction of luteinizing hormone causing stromal hyperthecosis
Selective deficiency of follicle-stimulating hormone
correctOption: Excessive and prolonged estrogen stimulation unopposed by progesterone
optionExplanations: Normal menstruation is caused by withdrawal, but DUB involves persistent hormonal imbalances or irregular breakdown.
Anovulatory cycles lack a corpus luteum, leading to a state where estrogen stimulates the endometrium without the stabilizing and differentiating effects of progesterone.
Progesterone is absent or deficient in the most common form of DUB (anovulation), rather than being sustained and high.
While LH imbalances occur in some conditions like PCOS, the characteristic histopathology of DUB is driven by the unopposed estrogen effect on the lining itself.
FSH deficiency may be a proximal cause of anovulation, but the direct driver of the endometrial histology is the resulting estrogen/progesterone imbalance.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1001 (Book Page): Failure of ovulation results in excessive endometrial stimulation by estrogens that is unopposed by progesterone.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
statement: A 72-year-old bedridden patient with Type 2 Diabetes is brought to the hospital with severe dehydration and altered mental status. Labs reveal a blood glucose of 950 mg/dL, but serum ketones are absent. What physiological factor best explains the absence of ketoacidosis in this patient compared to a patient with Type 1 Diabetes?
options: Low circulating levels of free fatty acids in the systemic circulation
Absolute lack of glucagon secretion from pancreatic alpha cells
Failure of skeletal muscle to release amino acids for gluconeogenesis
Efficient peripheral utilization of glucose despite high blood levels
Presence of residual portal insulin levels sufficient to inhibit hepatic fatty acid oxidation
correctOption: Presence of residual portal insulin levels sufficient to inhibit hepatic fatty acid oxidation
optionExplanations: FFA levels are typically high in T2DM, but insulin's presence in the portal circulation prevents their massive conversion into ketones.
Glucagon levels are actually inappropriately high in T2DM and contribute significantly to the severe hyperglycemia.
Muscle catabolism still occurs; the absence of ketones is specifically an effect of portal insulin on the liver.
Glucose utilization is severely impaired due to insulin resistance, which is why the glucose levels reach such extreme heights.
In T2DM, there is enough insulin to suppress the hepatic ketogenic machinery, preventing DKA, but not enough to prevent massive hyperglycemia.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1104 (Book Page): The lower frequency of ketoacidosis in T2D is believed to be due to higher portal vein insulin levels in these patients, which prevents unrestricted hepatic fatty acid oxidation and keeps the formation of ketone bodies in check.

category: Hashimoto Thyroiditis ii
statement: Which cell type is classically observed in histologic sections of the thyroid as a metaplastic response of the low cuboidal follicular epithelium to chronic injury in Hashimoto thyroiditis?
options: Chief cells
Hürthle cells
Chromaffin cells
Pituicytes
Parafollicular C cells
correctOption: Hürthle cells
optionExplanations: Chief cells are the predominant cell type of the parathyroid glands, responsible for synthesizing and secreting parathyroid hormone (PTH), and are not found in the thyroid follicles.

Hürthle cells (also known as oxyphil cells) are the histologic hallmark of Hashimoto thyroiditis, representing a metaplastic change of follicular epithelial cells characterized by abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm due to mitochondrial accumulation.
Chromaffin cells are the neuroendocrine cells of the adrenal medulla that synthesize catecholamines such as epinephrine and norepinephrine.
Pituicytes are modified glial cells found exclusively in the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) and are unrelated to thyroid pathology.
Parafollicular cells, or C cells, are neuroendocrine cells of the thyroid that secrete calcitonin and do not undergo Hürthle cell metaplasia in autoimmune thyroiditis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1077 (Book Page): The thyroid follicles are atrophic and are lined in many areas by epithelial cells with abundant eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm, termed Hürthle cells, which represent a metaplastic response of the normally low cuboidal follicular epithelium to chronic injury.

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
statement: A patient is found to have a pituitary mass and a mildly elevated serum prolactin level of 45 ng/mL. Which mechanism is most likely responsible if the lesion is classified as a nonfunctional macroadenoma rather than a true lactotroph adenoma?
options: Ectopic secretion of prolactin inhibitory factor
Somatic mutation of the USP8 gene
Constitutive activation of Gs-alpha
Activating mutation of the RET oncogene
Loss of dopamine-mediated inhibition (Stalk effect)
correctOption: Loss of dopamine-mediated inhibition (Stalk effect)
optionExplanations: Hypothalamic dopamine is the prolactin inhibitory factor; mass effects cause its reduction, not an 'ectopic secretion' of it.
USP8 mutations are found in corticotroph adenomas, leading to EGFR stabilization and ACTH production, not hyperprolactinemia.
Gs-alpha mutations are characteristic of somatotroph adenomas and lead to cAMP production, not mild secondary hyperprolactinemia.
RET oncogene mutations are associated with medullary thyroid carcinomas and MEN-2 syndromes, not typical pituitary adenoma pathogenesis.
The 'stalk effect' occurs when a large nonfunctional mass compresses the pituitary stalk, blocking the flow of dopamine (PIF) from the hypothalamus to the lactotrophs.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1069 (Book Page): Any suprasellar mass (e.g., a pituitary adenoma) may disturb the inhibitory influence of the hypothalamus on prolactin secretion, resulting in hyperprolactinemia. Therefore, mild hyperprolactenemia in a person with a pituitary adenoma does not necessarily indicate a prolactin-secreting tumor.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
statement: In the context of primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency, which of the following mechanisms best explains the occurrence of cutaneous hyperpigmentation in affected individuals?
options: Accumulation of lipid-rich vacuolated cells in the zona reticularis
Direct stimulation of melanocytes by excess circulating cortisol
Compensatory hyperplasia of the zona glomerulosa causing dermal darkening
Increased production of pro-opiomelanocortin due to loss of feedback inhibition
Deposition of lipofuscin pigment within the adrenal medulla
correctOption: Increased production of pro-opiomelanocortin due to loss of feedback inhibition
optionExplanations: Lipid-rich cells are typical of the zona fasciculata and some hyperplastic states, but their presence does not lead to cutaneous changes.
Cortisol levels are actually deficient in this condition; moreover, cortisol does not stimulate melanocytes.

The zona glomerulosa is responsible for mineralocorticoids; its hyperplasia is seen in hyperaldosteronism, not Addison disease, and does not affect skin color. In Addison disease, the entire cortex is typically atrophic rather than hyperplastic (unless it is the secondary stage of CAH).

Primary adrenal failure results in a lack of cortisol, which normally inhibits the pituitary. The resulting high ACTH is synthesized as part of a larger precursor molecule, POMC, which also contains MSH sequences, leading to increased melanin production.
Lipofuscin is a 'wear-and-tear' pigment found in aging cells or micronodular hyperplasia, but it does not cause generalized skin darkening.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1122 (Book Page): In individuals with primary adrenal disease, hyperpigmentation of the skin, particularly of sun-exposed areas and at pressure points, such as the neck, elbows, knees, and knuckles, is quite characteristic. This is caused by elevated levels of pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC), which is derived from the anterior pituitary and is a precursor of both ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH).

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
statement: A 55-year-old male with a 20-year history of diabetes presents with significant proteinuria. A renal biopsy is performed, revealing ovoid, laminated, PAS-positive hyaline nodules in the periphery of the glomerulus. What is the specific name and clinical significance of this lesion?
options: Schiller-Duval body; indicative of yolk sac differentiation
Armanni-Ebstein lesion; indicative of acute tubular necrosis
Kimmelstiel-Wilson disease; indicative of advanced diabetic nephropathy
Zellballen; characteristic of a benign neuroendocrine tumor
Crooke hyaline change; indicative of pituitary adenoma
correctOption: Kimmelstiel-Wilson disease; indicative of advanced diabetic nephropathy
optionExplanations: Schiller-Duval bodies are glomerular-like structures seen in yolk sac tumors, distinct from the matrix nodules of diabetes.
Armanni-Ebstein lesions are found in the renal tubules in diabetes (glycogen accumulation) but do not form glomerular nodules.
Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules (nodular glomerulosclerosis) are pathognomonic for diabetic nephropathy and represent a severe form of microvascular damage.
Zellballen are nests of cells seen in pheochromocytomas or paragangliomas, not in the diabetic kidney.
Crooke hyaline change occurs in ACTH-secreting cells of the pituitary in response to high cortisol; it is unrelated to the kidney.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1109 (Book Page): [Nodular Glomerulosclerosis. This is also known as intercapillary glomerulosclerosis or Kimmelstiel-Wilson disease. The glomerular lesions take the form of ovoid or spherical, often laminated, PAS-positive nodules of matrix situated in the periphery of the glomerulus.]

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
statement: A primipara in her third trimester presents with new-onset hypertension and proteinuria. If this patient subsequently develops generalized seizures, what specific clinical designation is applied to her condition?
options: HELLP syndrome
Placenta accreta
Eclampsia
Postpartum psychosis
Gestational hypertension
correctOption: Eclampsia
optionExplanations: HELLP syndrome is a specific complication of preeclampsia involving hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets, but does not inherently define the convulsive stage.
Placenta accreta involves the direct adherence of placental villi to the myometrium due to a lack of decidua, presenting as a failure of placental separation.
Eclampsia is the clinical term used when a patient with preeclampsia develops convulsions or coma that cannot be attributed to other causes.
Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency occurring after delivery, characterized by loss of reality, and is unrelated to the hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
Gestational hypertension is characterized by the development of hypertension during pregnancy without the associated proteinuria that defines preeclampsia.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1029 (Book Page): some of these women become seriously ill, developing convulsions; this particularly severe form of the disorder is termed eclampsia.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
statement: Upon histological examination of a thyroid gland with diffuse hyperplasia, how can the clinician distinguish the papillae of Graves disease from those of a papillary thyroid carcinoma?
options: The follicles in Graves are always filled with dense, dark colloid
Graves papillae show Orphan Annie eye nuclei
Graves papillae are always lined by squamous epithelium
Graves papillae lack central fibrovascular cores
The presence of psammoma bodies in Graves disease
correctOption: Graves papillae lack central fibrovascular cores
optionExplanations: The colloid in Graves is actually pale and shows scalloped margins due to active resorption by the hyperplastic cells.
Orphan Annie eye nuclei are characteristic of papillary thyroid carcinoma, not Graves disease.
The lining in Graves is tall columnar or cuboidal follicular epithelium, not squamous epithelium.
The papillae in Graves are created by crowding of the hyperplastic epithelium and crucially lack the fibrovascular cores seen in malignant papillae.
Psammoma bodies are characteristic of papillary thyroid carcinoma and are not found in the diffuse hyperplasia of Graves.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): This crowding often results in the formation of small papillae that project into the follicle lumen and encroach on the colloid, sometimes filling the follicles (Fig. 24.13B). Such papillae lack fibrovascular cores, in contrast to those of papillary carcinoma.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: Which of the following microscopic features helps distinguish duct ectasia from invasive carcinoma upon histological examination?
options: Infiltration of the dermis with tumor emboli
Periductal chronic inflammatory infiltrate containing plasma cells
Irregular calcifications and high mitotic rates
Presence of ragged nests and solid sheets of cells
Destruction of the basement membrane by atypical cells
correctOption: Periductal chronic inflammatory infiltrate containing plasma cells
optionExplanations: Dermal tumor emboli are the hallmark of inflammatory carcinoma, not duct ectasia.
Duct ectasia typically shows a prominent chronic inflammatory response, specifically including plasma cells and lymphocytes, around dilated ducts containing inspissated material.
High mitotic rates and irregular calcifications point towards malignancy.
Ragged nests and solid sheets are characteristic of Grade 3 invasive carcinoma, not duct ectasia.
Duct ectasia is a reactive, non-neoplastic process; therefore, the basement membrane remains intact unless ruptured by inflammation.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1039 (Book Page): With duct rupture, a marked periductal and interstitial chronic inflammatory reaction ensues, consisting of lymphocytes, macrophages, and variable numbers of plasma cells

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
statement: A 45-year-old male presents with newly diagnosed diabetes and progressive sensorineural hearing loss. His mother and maternal uncle also have both diabetes and deafness. What is the most likely etiological classification for this patient's condition?
options: MODY 3 due to mutations in Hepatocyte nuclear factor 1 alpha (HNF1A).
Secondary diabetes due to toxic effects of ototoxic medication.
Maternally inherited diabetes and deafness (MIDD) due to mitochondrial DNA mutations.
Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus with secondary diabetic neuropathy affecting the ear.
Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (Immune-mediated) with incidental hearing loss.
correctOption: Maternally inherited diabetes and deafness (MIDD) due to mitochondrial DNA mutations.
optionExplanations: HNF1A (MODY 3) is a common form of MODY but is not associated with sensorineural deafness.
The scenario describes a genetic/familial pattern rather than an acquired drug-induced state.
MIDD is a rare but distinct etiological category of monogenic diabetes caused by mitochondrial mutations, inherited maternally and associated with deafness.
While diabetes can cause sensory issues, the strong family history and combination with deafness suggest a specific genetic etiology over standard T2D.
Type 1 diabetes does not typically follow a strict maternal inheritance pattern nor is it classically linked with deafness.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1097 (Book Page): Table 24.6 ... Other Types ... Genetic Defects of ̠-Cell Function ... Maternally inherited diabetes and deafness (MIDD) due to mitochondrial DNA mutations (m.3243A → G).

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Diffuse and Multinodular goiter
statement: A geographic region is identified as having a significantly high prevalence of thyroid enlargement due to soil and water conditions. What is the specific percentage threshold used to classify this condition as an endemic goiter within a population?
options: When more than 20% of the population is affected
When more than 50% of the population is affected
When more than 1% of the population is affected
When more than 10% of the population is affected
When more than 5% of the population is affected
correctOption: When more than 10% of the population is affected
optionExplanations: A 20% threshold exceeds the defined criteria for endemic status and would represent a very severe regional health crisis.
A 50% threshold is not used for the formal classification of endemic goiter; it is an arbitrary high figure representing hyper-endemicity in extreme cases only.
A 1% threshold is too low for epidemiological classification of endemnicity in thyroid disease and may represent sporadic cases.
The standard epidemiological definition for endemic goiter is a prevalence exceeding 10% in a given geographic region, often linked to iodine deficiency.
A 5% threshold is sometimes used for other pathologies, but the clinical standard for goiter as an endemic entity is specifically higher.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1081 (Book Page): The term endemic is used when goiters are present in more than 10% of the population in a given region.

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
statement: In preeclampsia, the failure of fetal extravillous trophoblasts to invade the maternal decidual vessels results in which hemodynamic consequence for the placenta?
options: Maternal spiral arteries remain small-caliber resistance vessels, leading to placental ischemia
Systemic maternal blood pressure falls to facilitate the flow into the fetal circulation
The intervillous space is obliterated by the excessive accumulation of amniotic fluid
Arterial hypovolemia occurs because of the excessive renal reabsorption of free water
The placenta becomes hyperperfused due to the loss of smooth muscle resistance
correctOption: Maternal spiral arteries remain small-caliber resistance vessels, leading to placental ischemia
optionExplanations: Failure of trophoblastic invasion means the spiral arteries retain their smooth muscle and small caliber, functioning as resistance vessels that limit flow and cause ischemia.
In preeclampsia, maternal blood pressure rises (hypertension) as a systemic response to the placental factors, rather than falling.
Amniotic fluid volume is not directly tied to the trophoblastic invasion of decidual vessels, which is a structural vascular process.
Arterial hypovolemia and excessive water reabsorption are features of SIADH, whereas preeclampsia features edema and vascular permeability changes.
Normally, remodeling causes hyperperfusion by lowering resistance. In preeclampsia, the lack of remodeling prevents this, causing malperfusion.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1030 (Book Page): In preeclampsia, this vascular remodeling fails to occur, leaving the placenta ill equipped to meet the increased circulatory demands of late gestation and setting the stage for the development of placental ischemia.

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
statement: Which clinical symptom is the most distinctive characteristic of granulomatous thyroiditis compared to subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis?
options: Severe thyroid pain
Painless goiter
Exophthalmos
Pretibial myxedema
Weight loss despite increased appetite
correctOption: Severe thyroid pain
optionExplanations: The presence of referred pain to the jaw or ears and exquisite tenderness upon palpation is the primary clinical feature distinguishing granulomatous from other subacute thyroiditides.
Painless goiter is characteristic of Hashimoto or subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis; de Quervain is notoriously painful.
Exophthalmos is unique to Graves disease due to retro-orbital glycosaminoglycan accumulation and is absent in de Quervain thyroiditis.
Pretibial myxedema is a feature of Graves disease, not found in inflammatory thyroiditis cases.
While both may show this during the hyperthyroid phase, it is a general sign of thyrotoxicosis and not as specific for de Quervain as the localized pain.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): Granulomatous thyroiditis is the most common cause of thyroid pain.

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
statement: A 35-year-old female presents with rapid-onset headache and skin hyperpigmentation. She had a bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing syndrome two years ago. Imaging shows a 1.5 cm invasive pituitary mass. Laboratory analysis shows high ACTH. Which clinical manifestation of corticotroph adenomas is this characteristic of?
options: Conn Syndrome
Laron Syndrome
Cushing Disease
Nelson Syndrome
Sheehan Syndrome
correctOption: Nelson Syndrome
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Conn syndrome is primary hyperaldosteronism due to an adrenal adenoma, not a pituitary disorder.
Incorrect. Laron syndrome is a genetic GH receptor resistance, not a pituitary adenoma subtype or manifestation.
Incorrect. Cushing Disease refers to the pituitary adenoma causing hypercortisolism when the adrenals are still present.
Correct. Nelson syndrome occurs post-adrenalectomy; the lack of cortisol feedback causes an existing corticotroph microadenoma to grow aggressively.
Incorrect. Sheehan syndrome is postpartum ischemic necrosis of the pituitary resulting in hypopituitarism, not hyperfunctioning ACTH-secreting mass.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1070 (Book Page): Large destructive pituitary adenomas can develop in patients after surgical removal of the adrenal glands for treatment of Cushing syndrome. This condition, known as Nelson syndrome, occurs because of loss of the inhibitory effect of adrenal corticosteroids on a corticotroph microadenoma.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
statement: In the pathological loop of testicular torsion, what is the consequence of the persistent antegrade arterial flow into the testis once the venous outflow is mechanically blocked?
options: Intense vascular engorgement of the testicular tissue
Immediate reduction in testicular volume due to fluid loss
Formation of noncaseating granulomas in the tubules
Proliferation of Leydig cells to compensate for androgen loss
Ischemic liquefactive necrosis without hemorrhage
correctOption: Intense vascular engorgement of the testicular tissue
optionExplanations: Correct. The continued delivery of blood through the patent arteries into a space with no outlet (obstructed veins) causes the organ to become intensely engorged with blood.
Incorrect. The testis becomes swollen and enlarged due to the accumulation of blood, not reduced in volume.
Incorrect. Granulomas are features of idiopathic granulomatous orchitis or tuberculosis, not torsion.
Incorrect. Acute torsion leads to necrosis; there is no time for cellular proliferation like Leydig cell prominence seen in chronic conditions like cryptorchidism.
Incorrect. Torsion specifically causes hemorrhagic infarction, not 'dry' ischemic necrosis, due to the continued arterial inflow.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 968 (Book Page): The thick-walled arteries remain patent, producing intense vascular engorgement followed by hemorrhagic infarction.

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: Which pathophysiological mechanism leads to the clinical features of the Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone (SIADH)?
options: Excessive excretion of sodium in the distal tubule
Destruction of the pituicytes in the neurohypophysis
Inhibition of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system
Impaired thirst mechanisms in the hypothalamus
Resorption of excessive free water in the collecting ducts
correctOption: Resorption of excessive free water in the collecting ducts
optionExplanations: While natriuresis can occur, the primary pathology is water retention, not a primary defect in sodium handling.
Destruction of pituicytes or axons would lead to Diabetes Insipidus (ADH deficiency), the opposite of SIADH.
While volume expansion might suppress renin, it is a secondary effect. The primary driver is the inappropriate presence of ADH acting on V2 receptors.
SIADH is a disorder of ADH excess, usually independent of thirst center pathology, although CNS trauma can affect both.
High levels of ADH force the kidneys to resorb free water back into the circulation, which dilutes the blood and leads to hyponatremia and cerebral edema.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1072 (Book Page): ADH excess causes over-resorption of free water, resulting in hyponatremia.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
statement: Statistical analysis of abnormal uterine bleeding causes indicates that a specific condition is the single most frequent driver of dysfunctional bleeding. What is this condition?
options: Chronic endometritis.
Inadequate luteal phase.
Submucosal leiomyoma.
Endometrial polyps.
Anovulation.
correctOption: Anovulation.
optionExplanations: Chronic endometritis is a structural/organic cause of abnormal bleeding, not functional/dysfunctional bleeding.
Inadequate luteal phase is a cause of ovulatory dysfunctional bleeding but is less common than anovulation.
Leiomyomas are structural abnormalities and are therefore not classified as 'dysfunctional' bleeding.
Polyps are structural causes of AUB, not functional/dysfunctional.
The text explicitly states that anovulation is the leading cause of dysfunctional uterine bleeding.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1001 (Book Page): The most frequent cause of dysfunctional bleeding is anovulation (failure to ovulate).

category: Enumerate clinical manifestations along with hormone levels of anterior pituitary
statement: A 45-year-old male with a known pituitary tumor suddenly develops an excruciating headache, double vision, and profound hypotension. On examination, he has bitemporal hemianopsia and cardiovascular collapse. What is the most likely pathological event?
options: Somatotroph Hyperplasia
Empty Sella Syndrome
Pituitary Apoplexy
Diabetes Insipidus
Thyroid Storm
correctOption: Pituitary Apoplexy
optionExplanations: Somatotroph hyperplasia causes acromegaly, a chronic progressive disease of tissue overgrowth. It is not an acute event and would not cause sudden cardiovascular collapse and severe headache.

Empty sella syndrome is a chronic condition where the pituitary is compressed or absent, often asymptomatic or causing slow-onset hormonal changes. It does not present as an acute catastrophic hemorrhagic event.

Pituitary apoplexy is caused by sudden hemorrhage into an adenoma. The rapid expansion causes acute compression of the optic chiasm (hemianopsia) and cranial nerves (diplopia), while sudden loss of ACTH leads to hypotension/collapse.

Diabetes insipidus results from ADH deficiency and presents with polyuria and polydipsia. While it can occur in pituitary damage, it does not explain the acute headache, visual defects, or hemorrhagic shock.

Thyroid storm involves severe hyperthyroidism with tachycardia and fever. It does not cause the sudden localized neuro-ophthalmic signs (visual field defects/diplopia) or the mechanical mass effect seen in this patient.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1065 (Book Page): [On occasion, acute hemorrhage into an adenoma is associated with clinical evidence of rapid enlargement of the lesion, a situation appropriately termed pituitary apoplexy . Acute pituitary apoplexy is a neuro - surgical emergency because it can cause sudden death]

category: Hashimoto Thyroiditis ii
statement: Which of the following genetic factors is most significantly associated with the breakdown of self-tolerance and susceptibility to both Hashimoto thyroiditis and type 1 diabetes?
options: PTPN22 and CTLA4 polymorphisms
GNAS activating mutations
PAX8-PPARG translocations
RET proto-oncogene fusions
BRAF V600E point mutations
correctOption: PTPN22 and CTLA4 polymorphisms
optionExplanations: Polymorphisms in PTPN22 and CTLA4 regulate T-cell signaling and are shared genetic markers for various autoimmune diseases.
GNAS mutations are found in somatotroph adenomas and McCune-Albright syndrome, affecting G-protein signaling.
PAX8-PPARG translocations are characteristic of follicular thyroid carcinomas, not autoimmune destruction.
RET fusions (RET/PTC) are specifically associated with papillary thyroid carcinoma, not the autoimmune mechanism of Hashimoto.
BRAF mutations are specific for papillary thyroid carcinoma and anaplastic carcinoma, not thyroiditis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1077 (Book Page): Increased susceptibility is associated with polymorphisms in several immune regulation–associated genes, such as cytotoxic T lymphocyte–associated antigen-4 (CTLA4), protein tyrosine phosphatase-22 (PTPN22)... GWAS have found similar associations between CTLA4, PTPN22... and systemic autoimmune diseases such as type 1 diabetes (T1D).

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Diffuse and Multinodular goiter
statement: A 52-year-old woman presents with a massive neck swelling that has been present for 20 years. Examination reveals a multilobulated, asymmetric thyroid gland. Which histologic finding would be most useful in distinguishing this multinodular goiter from a follicular adenoma?
options: The presence of follicles containing varying amounts of gelatinous colloid
Foci of hemorrhage, fibrosis, and calcification within the nodules
The absence of a prominent capsule between the nodules and the normal parenchyma
Varying degrees of follicular cell hyperplasia within the same gland
The presence of 'endocrine atypia' in the nuclei of the follicular cells
correctOption: The absence of a prominent capsule between the nodules and the normal parenchyma
optionExplanations: Both multinodular goiters and follicular adenomas contain follicles with colloid, making this a shared feature rather than a distinguishing one.
Hemorrhage, fibrosis, and calcification are common degenerative changes in both large multinodular goiters and large follicular adenomas.

Follicular adenomas are solitary and characteristically surrounded by a well-developed, intact fibrous capsule. Multinodular goiter consists of multiple nodules that lack this circumscribed, thick capsule from the rest of the gland.
While goiters show varying hyperplasia, adenomas can also show different growth patterns. The lack of a distinct, circumferential capsule remains the most reliable morphologic discriminator.
'Endocrine atypia' refers to pleomorphic nuclei that can be seen in both benign adenomas and hyperplastic nodules; it does not help distinguish between them.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1082 (Book Page): In contrast to follicular neoplasms, a prominent capsule between the hyperplastic nodules and residual compressed thyroid parenchyma is not present (Fig. 24.15B).

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Diffuse and Multinodular goiter
statement: When an autonomous hyperfunctioning nodule develops within a long-standing multinodular goiter, leading to hyperthyroidism without the ocular features of Graves disease, the condition is referred to as:
options: Wermer syndrome
Hashimoto syndrome
Cushing disease
Plummer syndrome
Sipple syndrome
correctOption: Plummer syndrome
optionExplanations: Wermer syndrome is another name for Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN-1), involving the pituitary, pancreas, and parathyroid.
Hashimoto syndrome refers to the autoimmune thyroiditis characterized by lymphocytic destruction and eventual hypothyroidism.
Cushing disease involves excess ACTH production by the pituitary leading to hypercortisolism, completely unrelated to thyroid goiters.
Plummer syndrome (toxic multinodular goiter) occurs when one or more nodules in a pre-existing goiter become autonomous and oversecrete T3/T4, independent of TSH.
Sipple syndrome is MEN-2A, characterized by medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and parathyroid hyperplasia.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1082 (Book Page): Most patients are euthyroid or have subclinical hyperthyroidism... but about 10% of patients over a 10-year period develop an autonomous nodule within a long-standing goiter that produces hyperthyroidism (toxic multinodular goiter), also known as Plummer syndrome.

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: A 68-year-old male heavy smoker presents with recent onset of confusion, nausea, and headache. Vitals are stable, and physical examination shows no signs of peripheral edema or dehydration. Laboratory studies reveal a serum sodium of 122 mEq/L and high urine osmolality. A chest radiograph reveals a 5-cm hilar mass. What is the most likely cause of his electrolyte abnormality?
options: Congestive heart failure leading to hypervolemic hyponatremia
Ectopic ADH secretion by a small-cell lung carcinoma
Nephrogenic DI due to renal resistance to ADH
Severe dehydration from excessive osmotic diuresis
Central DI following hypothalamic tumor metastasis
correctOption: Ectopic ADH secretion by a small-cell lung carcinoma
optionExplanations: Congestive heart failure causes hyponatremia but is usually associated with hypervolemia and peripheral edema, which are absent here.
The patient exhibits the classic triad of SIADH: hyponatremia, absence of edema (euvolemia), and a likely source of ectopic ADH (small-cell lung carcinoma).
Nephrogenic DI would present with hypernatremia and polyuria, not the hyponatremia and confusion seen in this patient.
Dehydration usually causes hypernatremia. Osmotic diuresis is a feature of Diabetes Mellitus or DI, neither of which match this clinical lab profile.
Central DI causes hypernatremia and dilute urine. While metastasis to the hypothalamus is possible, it does not explain the hyponatremia.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1072 (Book Page): The most frequent causes of SIADH are the secretion of ectopic ADH by malignant neoplasms (particularly small-cell carcinoma of the lung)... total body water is increased, blood volume remains normal, and peripheral edema does not develop.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: A 48-year-old male with a history of heavy smoking presents with rapid-onset proximal muscle weakness, hypertension, and hyperpigmentation. Labs show serum ACTH of 450 pg/mL (normal 10-60) and cortisol of 80 mcg/dL. Cortisol levels remain unchanged after both 2 mg and 8 mg of dexamethasone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Iatrogenic Cushing syndrome
Functional adrenocortical carcinoma
Bilateral macronodular adrenal hyperplasia
Ectopic ACTH secretion by a bronchial carcinoid
Pituitary corticotroph microadenoma
correctOption: Ectopic ACTH secretion by a bronchial carcinoid
optionExplanations: Exogenous steroid use results in low ACTH due to negative feedback, contradicting the high lab value provided.
Adrenal carcinomas produce cortisol autonomously, which would suppress pituitary ACTH to very low or undetectable levels.
Macronodular hyperplasia is typically ACTH-independent, meaning ACTH levels would be low or suppressed, not 450 pg/mL.
Ectopic ACTH sources, like carcinoids or small-cell lung cancers, produce high ACTH and are typically resistant to feedback suppression by high-dose dexamethasone.
Pituitary adenomas (Cushing disease) usually suppress with high-dose (8 mg) dexamethasone, unlike this patient.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1116 (Book Page): Ectopic ACTH secretion results in an elevated level of ACTH, but its secretion is completely insensitive to low or high doses of exogenous dexamethasone.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
statement: A patient with metastatic prostate cancer undergoing hormonal therapy is noted to have shrinking testes and worsening fertility. Which pharmacological mechanism is responsible for this atrophy?
options: Induction of aromatase expression in the liver
Blockade of alpha-1-adrenergic receptors
Prolonged administration of antiandrogens
Excessive stimulation of the pituitary thyrotrophs
Inhibition of type 2 5-alpha-reductase
correctOption: Prolonged administration of antiandrogens
optionExplanations: Incorrect. While estrogen changes affect the prostate, the primary cause of testicular atrophy in prostate cancer therapy is antiandrogen administration.
Incorrect. Alpha-1-adrenergic blockers are used to manage BPH symptoms by decreasing smooth muscle tone but do not cause testicular atrophy.
Correct. Antiandrogen therapy is a recognized cause of testicular atrophy and decreased fertility because it blocks the hormonal support required for the maintenance of the seminiferous epithelium.
Incorrect. Thyrotroph stimulation relates to the thyroid gland, not to direct testicular support.

Incorrect. 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors decrease DHT synthesis to shrink the prostate in BPH, but total testicular atrophy is specifically listed in the text as a consequence of antiandrogens used for cancer.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 967 (Book Page): Testicular atrophy may be caused by one of several conditions, including... (7) prolonged administration of antiandrogens (e.g., for treatment of carcinoma of the prostate).

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: What is the primary histological hallmark of Squamous Metaplasia of Lactiferous Ducts (Zuska disease)?
options: Dense lymphocytic infiltrate forming germinal centers in the lobules
Liquefactive fat necrosis surrounded by neutrophils
Dilated ducts filled with lipid-laden macrophages
Atrophic ducts with thickened basement membranes
Keratinizing squamous metaplasia extending deep into the nipple duct
correctOption: Keratinizing squamous metaplasia extending deep into the nipple duct
optionExplanations: Germinal centers are seen in various inflammatory conditions but are not the defining feature of squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts.
Liquefactive fat necrosis is the acute phase of fat necrosis, not a feature of squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts.
This feature is characteristic of duct ectasia, not squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts.
Atrophic ducts with thickened basement membranes are the diagnostic findings of lymphocytic mastopathy.
The fundamental morphological change in Zuska disease is the abnormal extension of keratinizing squamous epithelium into the lactiferous ducts, leading to keratin plugging.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1038 (Book Page): The key feature is keratinizing squamous metaplasia, which extends into the nipple duct well past the usual point of transition from squamous to glandular epithelium

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
coreConcept: Genetic Basis of Autoimmune Thyroid Disease
statement: Which genetic polymorphisms are shared between Hashimoto thyroiditis and Graves disease, reflecting a common breakdown in immune tolerance?
options: GNAS and TSHR gain-of-function mutations
CTLA4, PTPN22, and IL2RA
PAX8 and PPARG fusions
BRAF V600E and TP53 mutations
RET and NTRK1 rearrangements
correctOption: CTLA4, PTPN22, and IL2RA
optionExplanations: GNAS and TSHR mutations are somatic gain-of-function mutations found in toxic adenomas, not the germline polymorphisms associated with autoimmunity.

Polymorphisms in genes that regulate T-cell responses, such as CTLA4 (an inhibitor), PTPN22 (a phosphatase), and IL2RA (part of the IL-2 receptor), are shared risk factors across multiple autoimmune diseases including Graves and Hashimoto.
PAX8-PPARG fusions are chromosomal translocations characteristic of follicular carcinomas.
BRAF and TP53 mutations are markers of thyroid malignancy and progression, not the underlying cause of autoimmune thyroiditis.
RET and NTRK1 rearrangements are somatic driver mutations associated with papillary thyroid carcinoma, not autoimmune disease.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): . . . genetic susceptibility is associated with polymorphisms in immune-function genes like CTLA4, PTPN22, and IL2RA. . . GWAS data has also implicated variants in the TSH receptor (TSHR) gene locus in susceptibility to Graves disease.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
coreConcept: Anatomic predisposition in adolescent testicular torsion
statement: A 14-year-old male presents with the sudden onset of severe unilateral testicular pain without prior trauma. Physical examination reveals an extremely tender, high-riding testis. Based on the clinical presentation and pathological associations for this age group, what is the most likely underlying predisposing factor?
options: Incomplete descent of the testis (cryptorchidism)
A bilateral anatomic defect resulting in increased testicular mobility
Acquired narrowing of the inguinal canal following hernia repair
Fibrous scarring from a prior subclinical episode of epididymitis
A congenital absence of the pampiniform plexus
correctOption: A bilateral anatomic defect resulting in increased testicular mobility
optionExplanations: While cryptorchidism has other risks, the specific 'bell-clapper' abnormality is the classic driver for torsion in adolescents with descended testes.
The bell-clapper abnormality allows the testis to rotate freely within the tunica vaginalis, and this structural defect is typically bilateral.
Inguinal canal narrowing might cause compression, but the primary pathology of adolescent torsion is the rotation of the cord due to mobility, not canal constriction.
Prior inflammation usually leads to adhesions that might actually decrease mobility, whereas torsion requires hypermobility.
Absence of the plexus is not a recognized cause; the cord contains all normal structures but is hypermobile.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 968 (Book Page): In adults, torsion results from a bilateral anatomic defect that leads to increased mobility of the testes (bell-clapper abnormality).

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
statement: What is the characteristic gross appearance of the thyroid parenchyma in an untreated case of Graves disease?
options: Shrunken and fibrotic with sacs of clotted blood
Pale, yellow-tan, and firm with visible nodules
Symmetrically enlarged with a meaty, soft appearance resembling muscle
Asymmetrically enlarged with gelatinous, brown colloid-filled cysts
Normal size with a solitary gray-white, well-circumscribed mass
correctOption: Symmetrically enlarged with a meaty, soft appearance resembling muscle
optionExplanations: Shrunken glands are seen in atrophic thyroiditis; clotted blood sacs are seen in Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.
Pale, firm, and nodular appearance is more typical of Hashimoto thyroiditis.
The diffuse hyperplasia increases vascularity and cellularity, giving the gland a characteristic reddish, meaty texture.
Asymmetric enlargement with brown cysts is the hallmark of multinodular goiter.
A solitary circumscribed mass is the description of an adenoma or localized carcinoma, not diffuse Graves disease.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): The thyroid gland is usually symmetrically enlarged due to diffuse hypertrophy and hyperplasia... On cut section, the parenchyma has a soft, meaty appearance resembling muscle.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
statement: Under the current etiological classification, a mutation in the hepatocyte nuclear factor 1 ̡ (HNF1A) gene resulting in impaired ̡-cell function is specifically designated as:
options: Maturity-onset diabetes of the young, type 1 (MODY1)
Maturity-onset diabetes of the young, type 4 (MODY4)
Maturity-onset diabetes of the young, type 5 (MODY5)
Maturity-onset diabetes of the young, type 3 (MODY3)
Maturity-onset diabetes of the young, type 2 (MODY2)
correctOption: Maturity-onset diabetes of the young, type 3 (MODY3)
optionExplanations: MODY1 is specifically caused by mutations in the hepatocyte nuclear factor 4 ̡ (HNF4A) gene, not HNF1A.
MODY4 is associated with mutations in the pancreatic and duodenal homeobox 1 (PDX1) gene, which is critical for pancreatic development.
MODY5 is caused by mutations in the hepatocyte nuclear factor 1 ̡ (HNF1B) gene, which is often associated with renal cysts and other extra-pancreatic anomalies.
MODY3 is the specific classification for patients with germline mutations in HNF1A. This is a common form of monogenic diabetes that leads to progressive ̡-cell dysfunction.
MODY2 results from mutations in the glucokinase (GCK) gene, which serves as the glucose sensor for the pancreatic ̡-cell.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1097 (Book Page): Hepatocyte nuclear factor 1 ̡ (HNF1A), (MODY3)

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
statement: Which of the following is considered a true 'urologic emergency' because it rapidly leads to testicular infarction if untreated?
options: Acute gonococcal epididymitis
Large symptomatic hydrocele
Grade III Varicocele
Spermatocele of the rete testis
Torsion of the spermatic cord
correctOption: Torsion of the spermatic cord
optionExplanations: Epididymitis is an inflammatory/infectious condition that is serious but usually treated with antibiotics rather than emergency surgery for detorsion.
A hydrocele is a slow accumulation of fluid and is not an emergency.
A varicocele is a chronic dilation of veins and is generally managed electively.
A spermatocele is a benign cystic lesion and is not an emergency.
Torsion is an emergency because complete twisting of the cord leads to irreversible ischemia and necrosis within hours.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 968 (Book Page): Twisting of the spermatic cord typically cuts off the venous drainage of the testis. If untreated, it frequently leads to testicular infarction and thus represents one of the few true urologic emergencies.

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
coreConcept: Clinical presentation and biopsy diagnosis of ruptured ectopic pregnancy
statement: A 26-year-old female presents to the emergency department with acute onset lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. Her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago. Vitals show BP 85/55 mmHg and HR 120 bpm. An endometrial biopsy reveals decidua but no chorionic villi. What is the most likely location of the pregnancy?
options: Cervical os
Lower uterine segment
Fundus of the uterus
Extrauterine fallopian tube
Normal intrauterine position
correctOption: Extrauterine fallopian tube
optionExplanations: Cervical os involvement is extremely rare and usually presents with different clinical markers than acute intraperitoneal shock.
Implantation in the lower uterine segment (placenta previa) is intrauterine; the absence of villi on biopsy rules this out as the primary location of the conceptus tissue.
The uterine fundus is the normal site; the biopsy findings here specifically exclude an intrauterine gestation.
The combination of shock (low BP, high HR), timing (7 weeks), and a biopsy showing only decidua strongly indicates an extrauterine site, most commonly the fallopian tube.
A normal intrauterine pregnancy would show chorionic villi or an implantation site on endometrial biopsy.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1028 (Book Page): The clinical course of ectopic tubal pregnancy is characterized by the onset of moderate to severe abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding 6 to 8 weeks after the last menstrual period... endometrial biopsy (which shows decidua without chorionic villi or implantation site).

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
statement: Which set of findings typically constitutes the classic clinical presentation of Graves disease?
options: Hyperthyroidism, ophthalmopathy, and localized dermopathy
Exophthalmos, tachycardia, and multinodular goiter
Hypothyroidism, lid lag, and diffuse goiter
Thyrotoxicosis, pretibial myxedema, and painful thyroid nodules
Goiter, hypercalcemia, and periorbital edema
correctOption: Hyperthyroidism, ophthalmopathy, and localized dermopathy
optionExplanations: The classic triad consists of thyrotoxicosis due to diffuse hyperplasia, infiltrative ophthalmopathy leading to exophthalmos, and dermopathy (pretibial myxedema).
While tachycardia and exophthalmos occur, Graves is associated with diffuse goiter rather than multinodular goiter.
Hypothyroidism is not a feature of Graves; it is typically associated with Hashimoto thyroiditis.
Thyroid nodules in Graves are usually diffuse, not painful; painful enlargement is seen in granulomatous thyroiditis.
Hypercalcemia is characteristic of hyperparathyroidism, not Graves disease.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): The disease is characterized by a triad of clinical findings: • Hyperthyroidism associated with diffuse enlargement of the gland • Infiltrative ophthalmopathy and resultant exophthalmos • Localized, infiltrative dermopathy, sometimes called pretibial myxedema, which is present in a minority of patients

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Diffuse and Multinodular goiter
statement: The phase of 'colloid involution' in a simple goiter results in a specific gross and microscopic morphology. Which finding is most characteristic of this stage?
options: Small, inconspicuous follicles with scanty or absent colloid
A pale, yellow-tan, and firm gland with Hürthle cell metaplasia
Multiple nodules separated by prominent, thick fibrous capsules
Intense vascular engorgement giving the gland a meaty, beefy red appearance
A brown, glassy, and translucent cut surface with flattened follicular epithelium
correctOption: A brown, glassy, and translucent cut surface with flattened follicular epithelium
optionExplanations: This is the opposite of colloid involution; involution is characterized by an abundance of colloid and enlarged, distended follicles.
This describes Hashimoto thyroiditis, where the gland is firm and pale due to lymphocytic infiltration and fibrosis, and contains Hürthle cells.
While colloid goiters can become multinodular over time, the phase of involution itself refers to the distension of follicles; encapsulated nodules specifically suggest adenomas.
A meaty, beefy red appearance is characteristic of the diffuse hyperplasia in Graves disease, caused by high vascularity and tall cells.

During colloid involution, the previous hyperplasia recedes, and follicles become distended with colloid. Microscopically, the cells flatten to a cuboidal or atrophic state, and grossly the abundant colloid gives the gland a translucent, glassy appearance.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1081 (Book Page): the stimulated follicle epithelium involutes to form an enlarged, colloid-rich gland (colloid goiter). In these cases, the cut surface of the thyroid is usually brown, somewhat glassy, and translucent. Histologically the follicle epithelium is flattened and cuboidal

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: A 35-year-old female presents with symptoms of thyrotoxicosis. Which diagnostic finding would most accurately distinguish Graves disease from subacute thyroiditis?
options: The presence of a wide, staring gaze
Basal metabolic rate (BMR) measurements
Radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU) scintigraphy
Serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels
Total serum thyroxine (T4) levels
correctOption: Radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU) scintigraphy
optionExplanations: Lid lag and a staring gaze are caused by sympathetic overactivity and can occur in any form of thyrotoxicosis, regardless of cause.
The basal metabolic rate is elevated in any state of thyroid hormone excess and does not identify the specific underlying pathology.
Graves disease involves active synthesis (increased uptake), whereas thyroiditis involves the leak of pre-formed hormone from damaged follicles (decreased uptake).
TSH will be suppressed in both conditions during the thyrotoxic phase due to negative feedback from high circulating hormone levels.
Both Graves disease and subacute thyroiditis cause elevated T4 during the thyrotoxic phase, so this cannot differentiate the two.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1075 (Book Page): measurement of radioactive iodine uptake by the thyroid gland can help determine the etiology. For example, there may be diffusely increased uptake in the gland (Graves disease)... or decreased uptake (thyroiditis).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
statement: A 12-year-old female with a history of chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis and abnormal dental enamel presents with progressive fatigue, nausea, and new-onset darkening of her knuckles. Laboratory testing confirms primary adrenal failure. Which genetic defect is most likely present?
options: Mutation in the ABCD1 gene on the X-chromosome
Germline inactivation of the PRKAR1A gene
Mutation in the autoimmune regulator (AIRE) gene
Loss-of-function mutation in the NR0B1 gene
A chromosomal rearrangement of the CYP11B2 promoter
correctOption: Mutation in the autoimmune regulator (AIRE) gene
optionExplanations: ABCD1 mutations cause adrenoleukodystrophy, which typically presents with neurological regression and is distinct from the triad of APS-1.
PRKAR1A mutations are linked to Carney complex, which involves micronodular hyperplasia and skin spots, but not chronic candidiasis.
The combination of candidiasis, ectodermal dystrophy (dental/nail issues), and adrenalitis is pathognomonic for APS-1, caused by AIRE mutations which disrupt central T-cell tolerance.
NR0B1 (DAX1) mutations cause X-linked congenital adrenal hypoplasia, which lacks the autoimmune/ectodermal components described here.
CYP11B2 rearrangements are associated with glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism, not adrenal destruction.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1121 (Book Page): APS-1, also known as autoimmune polyendocrinopathy, candidiasis, and ectodermal dystrophy... is caused by mutations in the autoimmune regulator (AIRE) gene on chromosome 21q22.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
statement: Which of the following autoantibodies is the most specific for the hyperthyroidism observed in Graves disease, typically detected in approximately 90% of patients?
options: Anti-thyroglobulin antibody
Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody
TSH receptor blocking antibody
Thyrotropin-binding inhibitory immunoglobulin
Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI)
correctOption: Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI)
optionExplanations: Anti-thyroglobulin antibodies are found in both Graves disease and Hashimoto thyroiditis and are not the primary driver of hyperthyroidism.
Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies are more characteristic of Hashimoto thyroiditis, although they can be present in Graves disease as well.
Blocking antibodies can be present in some Graves patients but they lead to hypothyroidism rather than the characteristic hyperthyroidism.
These antibodies generally refer to those that inhibit TSH binding and are not the primary stimulatory agents responsible for the Graves triad.
TSI is a specific IgG antibody that binds the TSH receptor, mimicking TSH and stimulating the release of thyroid hormones, making it the hallmark of Graves disease hyperthyroidism.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): The most common antibody subtype, known as thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI), is observed in approximately 90% of patients.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
statement: A patient presents to the clinic with classic symptoms of diabetes, including polyuria and polydipsia. According to the current diagnostic criteria, a random plasma glucose level above which threshold is sufficient to establish the diagnosis in this symptomatic individual?
options: 140 mg/dL
200 mg/dL
126 mg/dL
180 mg/dL
correctOption: 200 mg/dL
optionExplanations: 140 mg/dL is the lower limit of the impaired glucose tolerance range during an oral glucose tolerance test, not diagnostic for overt diabetes.
In the presence of classic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, unexplained weight loss), a single random plasma glucose of 200 mg/dL or greater is diagnostic.
126 mg/dL is the threshold for fasting plasma glucose, not random glucose measurement.
180 mg/dL is often used as a threshold for 'time-in-range' monitoring with continuous sensors, but it is not a primary diagnostic threshold for a random check.
