category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
coreConcept: Functional Reserve of the Adrenal Cortex
statement: Why do patients with metastatic cancer involving the adrenal glands often maintain normal endocrine function for long periods?
options: Clinical symptoms only manifest after 90% of the cortex is destroyed
The contralateral adrenal gland undergoes immediate massive hyperplasia
Metastatic cells typically differentiate into functional steroidogenic tissue
The adrenal medulla can compensate for cortical loss by secreting cortisol
Renin from the kidney stimulates the remaining zona glomerulosa to hypertrophy
correctOption: Clinical symptoms only manifest after 90% of the cortex is destroyed
optionExplanations: The adrenal cortex has a massive functional reserve; chronic insufficiency remains asymptomatic until almost the entire gland is obliterated by the disease process.
Metastases are usually bilateral in the adrenals; while the remaining tissue tries to compensate, symptoms only emerge when the destruction threshold is reached.
Metastatic cancer cells (e.g., from the lung) do not acquire the specialized enzymatic machinery required to produce adrenal steroid hormones.
The adrenal medulla and cortex have distinct embryological origins and functions; the medulla cannot synthesize or secrete corticosteroids.
Renin can stimulate the glomerulosa, but this cannot compensate for the widespread loss of the zona fasciculata and reticularis that occurs in advanced metastatic disease.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1121 (Book Page): Typically, clinical manifestations of adrenocortical insufficiency do not appear until at least 90% of the adrenal cortex has been compromised.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
statement: In the physiological regulation of testicular blood flow during torsion, why does the testis appear 'intensely engorged' before it becomes necrotic?
options: Due to the immediate development of a secondary bacterial orchitis
Due to the release of histamine from mast cells in the tunica vaginalis
Due to the failure of the cremasteric muscle to contract
Due to the reflexive sympathetic surge causing arterial dilation
Due to arterial inflow continuing despite the cessation of venous outflow
correctOption: Due to arterial inflow continuing despite the cessation of venous outflow
optionExplanations: Orchitis is an inflammatory condition; engorgement in torsion is purely vascular/mechanical.
Histamine-mediated responses are typical of hypersensitivity, not mechanical vascular obstruction.
Cremasteric contraction is often absent in torsion (diagnostic sign), but its failure doesn't cause engorgement; the venous blockage does.
Engorgement is mechanical (trapped blood), not a result of active vasodilation.
Correct. This is the physiological basis for the hemorrhagic nature of the infarction.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 968 (Book Page): Twisting of the spermatic cord typically cuts off the venous drainage of the testis... The thick-walled arteries remain patent, producing intense vascular engorgement followed by hemorrhagic infarction.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Diffuse and Multinodular goiter
statement: What classic macroscopic appearance characterizes the 'colloid goiter' phase that follows hyperplastic stimulation?
options: Small, shrunken, and pale gray glands with a firm texture
A beefy, deep red, meaty appearance resembling skeletal muscle
Brown, somewhat glassy, and translucent cut surface
Diffuse greenish-opaque membranes covering the lobes
Presence of multiple small, white, chalky foci of fat necrosis
correctOption: Brown, somewhat glassy, and translucent cut surface
optionExplanations: Small shrunken glands are typical of late-stage Hashimoto thyroiditis or primary atrophy, not the enlarged state of a colloid goiter.
A beefy red, meaty appearance is characteristic of the diffuse hyperplasia in Graves disease due to extreme vascularity.
Correct. The accumulation of abundant colloid in distended follicles gives the involuted goiter a translucent, glassy, brown appearance.
Greenish-opaque membranes are described in the reference text for placental infections (chorioamnionitis), not thyroid pathology.
White chalky foci of fat necrosis are seen in the breast or peripancreatic tissue, not as a standard feature of thyroid goiter.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1081 (Book Page): In these cases, the cut surface of the thyroid is usually brown, somewhat glassy, and translucent.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
statement: The thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) in Grave's disease activate the TSH receptor, which then signals through a specific second-messenger pathway to increase hormone release. Which pathway is utilized?
options: JAK/STAT pathway signaling
Inositol triphosphate (IP3) and Diacylglycerol (DAG)
Tyrosine kinase autophosphorylation
Adenyl cyclase and cAMP
Cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP)
correctOption: Adenyl cyclase and cAMP
optionExplanations: The JAK/STAT pathway is typically associated with cytokine receptors and growth hormone, not the TSH receptor.
While some hormones use the IP3/DAG pathway, the TSH receptor primarily signals through G-protein activation of adenyl cyclase.
Tyrosine kinase signaling is used by growth factor receptors and the insulin receptor, while the TSH receptor is a G-protein coupled receptor.
The TSH receptor is a G-protein coupled receptor that activates adenyl cyclase, which increases intracellular cAMP levels to stimulate hormone synthesis and release.
cGMP is a common second messenger for nitric oxide and atrial natriuretic peptide, not TSH receptor signaling.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): TSI binds to the TSH receptor and mimics its actions, stimulating adenyl cyclase and increasing the release of thyroid hormones.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
coreConcept: Clinical and histological presentation of solitary parathyroid adenoma
statement: A 58-year-old female presents with persistent hypercalcemia and elevated serum parathyroid hormone. Imaging reveals a single 2.5 cm mass in the inferior-left neck region. Surgical excision reveals a soft, tan-brown, well-circumscribed nodule. Microscopic evaluation shows uniform polygonal cells with rare mitoses and inconspicuous stromal fat. Which of the following best describes the most likely diagnosis and its associated feature?
options: Parathyroid carcinoma; diagnosis is based on the presence of endocrine atypia
Primary hyperplasia; usually involves only a single gland and weighs over 10 grams
Parathyroid adenoma; the surrounding non-neoplastic glands are typically normal in size or shrunken
Secondary hyperplasia; always associated with chronic renal failure and hyperphosphatemia
Follicular adenoma; histology reveals well-differentiated follicles filled with colloid
correctOption: Parathyroid adenoma; the surrounding non-neoplastic glands are typically normal in size or shrunken
optionExplanations: Diagnosis of parathyroid carcinoma cannot be based on endocrine atypia (which is common in benign adenomas) but requires evidence of invasion or metastasis.
Primary hyperplasia is usually a multiglandular process, and the combined weight of all hyperplastic glands rarely exceeds 1 gram, making a solitary 10-gram mass unlikely for hyperplasia.

Correct. The patient's solitary mass and histological description (uniform cells, circumscribed) point to parathyroid adenoma. A key clinical feature is that the other parathyroid glands are often shrunken due to negative feedback from high calcium.
Secondary hyperplasia is a reactive process to hypocalcemia (e.g., in renal failure) and typically involves all four glands symmetrically, not a solitary 2.5 cm mass.
Follicular adenoma is a thyroid tumor. Parathyroid tumors are composed of chief or oxyphil cells, not colloid-filled follicles.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): Parathyroid adenomas are almost always solitary... In contrast to primary hyperplasia, the glands outside the adenoma are usually normal in size or shrunken because of feedback inhibition by elevated levels of serum calcium.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
statement: During a screening clinic, which of the following laboratory values for glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) would classify a patient as having 'prediabetes' according to current clinical guidelines?
optionExplanations: An HbA1c below 5.7% (specifically <5.6% in most guidelines) is considered within the normal range.
6.5% is the threshold for a diagnosis of overt diabetes mellitus.
An HbA1c of 7.1% to 8.0% indicates established diabetes, often with suboptimal glycemic control if the patient is already on treatment.
Correct. The range of 5.7% to 6.4% identifies individuals at high risk for developing frank diabetes and cardiovascular complications, categorized as prediabetes.
Values above 8.5% indicate established diabetes with very poor glycemic control, significantly increasing the risk of long-term microvascular complications.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1097 (Book Page): Prediabetes ... 3. A glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) level between 5.7% and 6.4%

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
statement: Which of the following morphological features is considered a diagnostic hallmark of granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis during its later stages?
options: Laminated calcified structures known as psammoma bodies
Extensive interstitial fibrosis extending beyond the thyroid capsule
Multinucleate giant cells enclosing pools of colloid
Ring-like deposition of cytokeratin within follicular cells
Optically clear nuclei with prominent nuclear grooves
correctOption: Multinucleate giant cells enclosing pools of colloid
optionExplanations: Psammoma bodies are characteristic of Papillary Carcinoma and are almost never found in granulomatous thyroiditis.
Fibrosis extending beyond the capsule is the defining feature of Riedel thyroiditis, a rare IgG4-related disease; in de Quervain, fibrosis is usually internal and temporary.
The presence of a granulomatous reaction including multinucleated giant cells responding to released colloid is the definitive histological finding that gives the disease its name.
Crooke change (cytokeratin rings) occurs in pituitary corticotroph cells exposed to high glucocorticoids, not in thyroid follicular cells.
Optically clear nuclei (Orphan Annie eye nuclei) are the classic feature of Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma, not inflammatory thyroiditis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): Multinucleate giant cells enclose pools of colloid, hence the designation granulomatous thyroiditis.

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: The activity of the parathyroid glands is primarily regulated by the level of free (ionized) calcium in the blood. When serum ionized calcium levels rise above the physiological set-point, what is the expected physiological response of the parathyroid glands?
options: Stimulation of renal alpha-1-hydroxylase activity
Increased differentiation of osteoclast progenitor cells
Hyperplasia of the oxyphil cell population
Inhibition of parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion
Activation of the G-protein cAMP signaling pathway
correctOption: Inhibition of parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion
optionExplanations: Renal alpha-1-hydroxylase is stimulated by PTH; high calcium suppresses PTH, leading to decreased active Vitamin D production.
Increased osteoclast differentiation is a result of high PTH; when calcium is high, PTH is inhibited, thus reducing osteoclast activity.
Hyperplasia of oxyphils is not a standard physiological response to high calcium; oxyphils are mitochondria-rich cells of unknown function.
Elevated free calcium serves as a negative feedback signal to the parathyroid glands, suppressing the synthesis and release of PTH.
Activation of the cAMP pathway usually stimulates hormone release; calcium binding to its receptor inhibits this pathway in the parathyroid.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1091 (Book Page): The net result of these activities is to elevate the level of free calcium, which, in turn, inhibits further PTH secretion in a classic feedback loop.

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: A 34-year-old female presents with a 2-month history of palpitations, excessive sweating, and a 4 kg weight loss. On examination, she has a symmetric, non-tender thyroid enlargement, a fine tremor of the hands, and proptosis. Which laboratory finding is most likely in this patient?
options: Low TSH, Elevated free T4, Elevated T3
Normal TSH, Elevated free T4
Low TSH, Normal free T4, Normal T3
Elevated TSH, Elevated free T4
Elevated TSH, Low free T4
correctOption: Low TSH, Elevated free T4, Elevated T3
optionExplanations: The patient has Graves disease (proptosis is pathognomonic). Overt hyperthyroidism shows suppressed TSH and elevated thyroid hormones.
A normal TSH with high T4 is rare and might suggest T4 resistance or assay interference, but does not fit the classic Graves presentation.
This profile describes subclinical hyperthyroidism, which is usually asymptomatic or very mild, unlike the overt symptoms seen here.
Elevated TSH with elevated T4 suggests a TSH-secreting pituitary tumor (secondary hyperthyroidism), but this would not cause proptosis.
This profile describes primary hypothyroidism, which would present with lethargy and weight gain, not weight loss and proptosis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1074 (Book Page): Laboratory findings that support the diagnosis of hyperthyroidism include a low TSH value accompanied by an increase in free T4.

category: Enumerate clinical manifestations along with hormone levels of anterior pituitary
statement: A patient underwent bilateral adrenalectomy to treat refractory Cushing syndrome. Years later, they present with severe skin darkening and a rapidly enlarging pituitary mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Corticotroph Carcinoma
Lactotroph Hyperplasia
Empty Sella Syndrome
Nelson Syndrome
Sheehan Syndrome
correctOption: Nelson Syndrome
optionExplanations: While the tumor in Nelson syndrome is aggressive, it is typically a macroadenoma. Pituitary carcinoma is defined strictly by the presence of distant metastases, not just local growth.
Lactotroph hyperplasia involves prolactin-producing cells. The presentation of hyperpigmentation and post-adrenalectomy growth is specific to corticotrophs.
Empty sella syndrome is characterized by the absence or compression of the pituitary, whereas Nelson syndrome involves a significantly enlarging pituitary mass.

Nelson syndrome occurs when the removal of the adrenals eliminates the negative feedback of cortisol on a preexisting pituitary microadenoma. The tumor then grows aggressively and secretes high levels of ACTH/MSH.
Sheehan syndrome is a condition of hormone deficiency following ischemic necrosis, not a condition of hormone excess and tumor growth.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1070 (Book Page): Nelson syndrome, occurs because of loss of the inhibitory effect of adrenal corticosteroids on a corticotroph microadenoma. Because the adrenals are absent... patients present with mass effects due to the pituitary tumor, and there can be hyperpigmentation.

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: Which of the following autoimmune conditions is recognized as the most frequent cause of endogenous hyperthyroidism in patients residing in iodine-sufficient regions?
options: Hashimoto thyroiditis
Toxic multinodular goiter
Graves disease
Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis
Thyrotroph pituitary adenoma
correctOption: Graves disease
optionExplanations: Hashimoto thyroiditis is primarily a cause of hypothyroidism; although a transient 'hashitoxicosis' may occur early, it is not the most common cause of endogenous hyperthyroidism.
Toxic multinodular goiter is a common cause but is less frequent than Graves disease, typically occurring in older adults with long-standing simple goiters.
Graves disease is an autoimmune disorder where antibodies stimulate the TSH receptor, causing diffuse thyroid hyperfunction; it accounts for approximately 85% of cases of thyrotoxicosis.
Granulomatous thyroiditis causes thyrotoxicosis due to the release of preformed hormone, not endogenous hyperfunction, and is typically self-limited.
Thyrotroph adenomas cause secondary hyperthyroidism due to TSH excess but are extremely rare, accounting for only about 1% of pituitary tumors.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): [Graves disease is the most common cause of endogenous hyperthyroidism.]

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
statement: What microscopic feature of the intrafollicular colloid is most indicative of the hyperactive state of the follicular cells in Graves disease?
options: Homogeneous, deep eosinophilic staining with no peripheral gaps
Presence of numerous cholesterol clefts and giant cells
Dense, laminated calcifications in the center of the colloid
Pale staining with prominent scalloped margins
Complete absence of colloid replaced by neutrophilic abscesses
correctOption: Pale staining with prominent scalloped margins
optionExplanations: Deeply stained, dense colloid is more typical of an inactive gland or simple colloid goiter.
Cholesterol clefts and giant cells are features of granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis, not Graves.
Calcifications (psammoma bodies) are not a feature of hyperplastic Graves follicles.
Pale colloid with peripheral scalloping represents 'resorption lacunae' where hyperactive follicular cells are rapidly engulfing colloid for hormone synthesis.
Neutrophilic abscesses are seen in acute infections or early stages of de Quervain thyroiditis, not the autoimmune hyperplasia of Graves.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1080 (Book Page): The colloid within the follicle lumen is pale, with scalloped margins... These cells actively resorb the colloid in the centers of the follicles, resulting in the scalloped appearance of the edges of the colloid.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
coreConcept: Pathogenesis of infiltrative ophthalmopathy in Graves
statement: A 32-year-old female presents with palpitations, heat intolerance, and bilateral proptosis. Examination reveals an audible bruit over a diffuse goiter and scaly thickening of the pretibial skin. Which specific mechanism is responsible for the ocular protrusion seen in this patient?
options: Accumulation of hydrophilic glycosaminoglycans and T-cell infiltration in the retro-orbital space
Direct antibody-mediated destruction of the optic nerve sheath
Hypertrophy of the superior tarsal muscle due to catecholamine excess
Fatty atrophy of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle
Ischemic necrosis of the orbital adipose tissue
correctOption: Accumulation of hydrophilic glycosaminoglycans and T-cell infiltration in the retro-orbital space
optionExplanations: The ophthalmopathy is an autoimmune process where T-cells and cytokines stimulate fibroblasts to produce glycosaminoglycans, causing edema and volume increase.
The optic nerve can be compressed by the high volume of retro-orbital tissue, but it is not directly destroyed by autoantibodies.
Sympathetic overstimulation of the superior tarsal muscle causes lid lag, but not the infiltrative proptosis.
The extraocular muscles in Graves undergo swelling and inflammation, not fatty atrophy.
There is an increase in tissue volume and adipocyte numbers, not ischemic necrosis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): [The protrusion of the eyeball (exopthalmos) is caused by an increase in the volume of the retro-orbital connective tissues and extraocular muscles, which occurs for several reasons: (1) marked infiltration of connective tissue by mononuclear cells, predominantly T cells;... (3) accumulation of extracellular matrix components, specifically hydrophilic glycosaminoglycans...]

category: Enumerate clinical manifestations along with hormone levels of anterior pituitary
statement: Many of the systemic manifestations of growth hormone hypersecretion are not caused directly by GH but are mediated by a peptide hormone synthesized in the liver. Which hormone completes this physiological loop?
options: Ghrelin
Insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1)
Thyroxine-binding globulin
Glucagon-like peptide-1
Somatostatin
correctOption: Insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1)
optionExplanations: Ghrelin is a stomach-derived hormone that stimulates hunger and GH release, acting upstream of the pituitary somatotrophs.
GH acts on the liver to stimulate the production of IGF-1 (somatomedin C), which is responsible for the soft tissue and skeletal overgrowth seen in acromegaly and gigantism.
Thyroxine-binding globulin is a carrier protein for thyroid hormones and is not involved in the growth hormone signaling loop.
GLP-1 is an incretin hormone involved in glucose homeostasis and insulin secretion, not the mediation of growth hormone effects.
Somatostatin is a hypothalamic factor that inhibits GH release; it does not mediate the peripheral growth effects of GH.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1069 (Book Page): Persistently elevated levels of GH stimulate the hepatic secretion of insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), which causes many of the clinical manifestations.

category: Enumerate clinical manifestations along with hormone levels of anterior pituitary
coreConcept: Classification of pituitary adenomas by size
statement: What clinical and radiologic threshold is utilized to classify a pituitary adenoma as a 'macroadenoma'?
options: Weight exceeding 5 grams
Evidence of suprasellar extension
Presence of hormone hypersecretion
Diameter greater than 1 cm
Erosion of the anterior clinoid process
correctOption: Diameter greater than 1 cm
optionExplanations: Classification is based on radiographic dimension (diameter), not the physical weight of the tumor tissue.
Suprasellar extension is a feature often seen in macroadenomas but is not the defining criterion for the term.
Functionality (hypersecretion) is a separate classification system (functional vs. silent) and does not define micro- vs. macroadenoma status.
The standard anatomical threshold for a pituitary macroadenoma is a diameter larger than 1 cm (10 mm).
Bone erosion of the sella or clinoid process indicates an aggressive or large tumor, but the 1 cm rule remains the primary classification metric.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1066 (Book Page): They are designated, somewhat arbitrarily, microadenomas if they are less than 1 cm in diameter and macroadenomas if they exceed 1 cm in diameter.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: Which genetic mutation is most commonly identified in familial cases of bilateral macronodular adrenal hyperplasia (BMAH)?
options: GNAS
RET proto-oncogene
AIRE
VHL
ARMC5
correctOption: ARMC5
optionExplanations: GNAS mutations are seen in McCune-Albright syndrome and some somatotroph adenomas, but ARMC5 is the primary link for BMAH.
RET mutations are associated with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2 (MEN-2) and medullary thyroid carcinoma.
AIRE mutations cause Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome type 1, which leads to adrenal insufficiency, not hyperplasia.
VHL mutations are associated with von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, including pheochromocytomas, but not macronodular hyperplasia.
ARMC5 is a tumor suppressor gene recently linked to macronodular adrenal hyperplasia, where nodules are >10mm.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1113 (Book Page): Familial forms associated with germline mutations in the armadillo repeat containing 5 (ARMC5) gene... up to 50% of apparently sporadic BMAH cases harbor germline ARMC5 mutations.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
statement: A 16-year-old female presents with severe hyperglycemia, acanthosis nigricans, and polycystic ovaries. Despite very high doses of insulin, her blood glucose remains elevated. Which etiological subtype of diabetes is most likely?
options: Maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY3)
Type 1 diabetes with secondary resistance
Maternally inherited diabetes and deafness (MIDD)
Wolff-Parkinson-White associated diabetes
Type A insulin resistance
correctOption: Type A insulin resistance
optionExplanations: MODY3 involves a defect in the HNF1A transcription factor affecting insulin secretion, not the severe resistance and cutaneous features seen here.
Type 1 diabetes involves insulin deficiency; the presence of acanthosis nigricans and severe resistance suggests a primary receptor/signaling defect.
MIDD is characterized by a defect in insulin secretion (beta-cell function) and hearing loss, not severe receptor resistance.
This is a cardiac conduction syndrome and is not a recognized etiological classification of diabetes mellitus.
Type A resistance is a specific monogenic category where insulin receptor mutations prevent the body from utilizing even high levels of insulin.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1103 (Book Page): Rare insulin receptor mutations ... can cause severe insulin resistance ... (type A insulin resistance). Such patients often show a velvety hyperpigmentation of the skin known as acanthosis nigricans.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
coreConcept: Primary vs Secondary Adrenal Insufficiency Contrast
statement: Which clinical finding is typically preserved in patients with secondary adrenocortical insufficiency but lost in those with primary Addison disease?
options: Androgen production
Normal skin pigmentation
Aldosterone synthesis
Basal cortisol rhythm
Glucocorticoid response to stress
correctOption: Aldosterone synthesis
optionExplanations: Adrenal androgen production in the zona reticularis is stimulated by ACTH. Therefore, secondary insufficiency leads to a deficiency in both cortisol and androgens, similar to primary disease.

Secondary insufficiency is actually characterized by skin pallor due to low levels of ACTH and MSH. While 'normal' pigmentation might be a comparative feature, the prompt asks what physiological synthesis is preserved. Skin pigmentation is a feature, but aldosterone synthesis is a vital physiological process.

In secondary hypoadrenalism (caused by pituitary disease), the adrenal gland remains intact. While ACTH-dependent zones (fasciculata and reticularis) atrophy, the zona glomerulosa is primarily regulated by the renin-angiotensin system and remains functional, preserving aldosterone levels.

The basal cortisol rhythm is disrupted in any form of adrenal insufficiency because the adrenal glands are either destroyed (primary) or lack the necessary trophic stimulation (secondary) to maintain diurnal variations.

Secondary insufficiency results from pituitary or hypothalamic failure. Since the adrenal is not stimulated by ACTH, the glucocorticoid response to stress is severely impaired in both primary and secondary forms.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1122 (Book Page): The manifestations also differ in that secondary hypoadrenalism is characterized by deficient cortisol and androgen output but normal or near-normal aldosterone synthesis.

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: Which disorder is documented as the most frequent cause of hypothyroidism in regions of the world where dietary iodine levels are sufficient?
options: Iatrogenic hypothyroidism following radioiodine ablation
Secondary hypothyroidism due to pituitary necrosis
Dietary iodine deficiency causing endemic goiter
Hashimoto thyroiditis
Inborn errors of thyroid metabolism (dyshormonogenetic goiter)
correctOption: Hashimoto thyroiditis
optionExplanations: Iatrogenic causes are common but are outnumbered by the incidence of spontaneous autoimmune Hashimoto thyroiditis in the general population.
Secondary hypothyroidism is rare and accounts for a small percentage of cases compared to primary thyroid failure.
Iodine deficiency is the #1 cause worldwide, but only in areas where dietary intake is low (endemic areas).
In developed, iodine-sufficient countries, autoimmune destruction (Hashimoto) is the leading cause of primary hypothyroidism.
Dyshormonogenetic goiter is a rare congenital cause, typically presenting in infants or children, and is much less common than autoimmune disease.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1075 (Book Page): Autoimmune hypothyroidism is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas of the world. The vast majority of cases of autoimmune hypothyroidism are due to Hashimoto thyroiditis.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: Which of the following is considered the only reliable criterion for establishing a diagnosis of parathyroid carcinoma rather than parathyroid adenoma?
options: Nuclear pleomorphism in more than 50% of cells
Invasion of surrounding tissues or metastasis
The presence of mitotic figures
A tumor weight exceeding 1.0 gram
The presence of cystic brown tumors in bone
correctOption: Invasion of surrounding tissues or metastasis
optionExplanations: Nuclear pleomorphism is a feature of 'endocrine atypia' often found in benign adenomas.
Parathyroid carcinoma diagnosis is vexing because cytology is unreliable; only biological behavior (invasion/metastasis) is definitive.
Mitotic figures can occasionally be seen in benign lesions and are not definitive for cancer in parathyroid pathology.
Adenomas often exceed 1.0 gram (up to 5g); carcinoma usually exceeds 10g but weight alone is not the definitive criterion.
Brown tumors are a consequence of severe hyperparathyroidism, which can be caused by benign adenomas, hyperplasia, or carcinoma.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1093 (Book Page): [Diagnosis of carcinoma based on cytologic detail is unreliable, and invasion of surrounding tissues and metastasis are the only reliable criteria.]

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: Propylthiouracil is frequently utilized in the management of hyperthyroid states. Beyond inhibiting thyroid hormone synthesis within the gland, what additional metabolic step does it target?
options: It inhibits the proteolytic cleavage of thyroglobulin in the follicle
It blocks the intestinal absorption of dietary iodine
It increases the hepatic synthesis of thyroxine-binding globulin
It competitively inhibits the binding of TSH to its follicular receptor
It inhibits the peripheral deiodination of T4 into T3
correctOption: It inhibits the peripheral deiodination of T4 into T3
optionExplanations: Inhibiting the release of hormone via proteolysis is a characteristic effect of high-dose iodide solutions, not the primary mechanism of thionamides.
Propylthiouracil does not affect iodine absorption from the gut; it works at the level of the thyroid gland and peripheral tissues.
Changes in thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) are usually induced by estrogens or liver disease; PTU does not specifically target hepatic TBG synthesis.
PTU works by inhibiting thyroid peroxidase and peripheral conversion; it has no direct antagonistic effect on the TSH receptor itself.
A unique advantage of PTU over methimazole is its ability to block the conversion of T4 to the more active T3 in peripheral tissues, rapidly lowering active levels.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1073 (Book Page): propylthiouracil also inhibits the peripheral deiodination of circulating T4 into T3, thus ameliorating symptoms of thyroid hormone excess.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: Which of the following clinical conditions is most strongly associated with the morphological finding of densely collagenized stroma and prominent lymphocytic lobulitis in the breast?
options: Type 1 (insulin-dependent) diabetes mellitus
High-risk Human Papillomavirus (HPV) infection
Cystic fibrosis related exocrine deficiency
Lactational Staphylococcus infection
Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome)
correctOption: Type 1 (insulin-dependent) diabetes mellitus
optionExplanations: Lymphocytic mastopathy (sclerosing lymphocytic lobulitis) is characteristically associated with Type 1 diabetes and autoimmune thyroid disease; it presents with atrophic lobules and dense stromal fibrosis.
HPV is associated with anogenital and oropharyngeal cancers, not inflammatory lymphocytic mastopathy of the breast.
Cystic fibrosis can cause secondary pancreatic issues but is not a recognized cause of lymphocytic lobulitis in the breast.
Staphylococcus infection causes acute mastitis with neutrophil infiltrates and abscesses, not lymphocytic lobulitis.
Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension and electrolyte imbalances but has no morphological link to inflammatory breast lesions.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1039 (Book Page): This condition is most common in women with type 1 (insulin-dependent) diabetes or autoimmune thyroid disease and is hypothesized to have an autoimmune basis.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
statement: Which of the following drug classes is etiologically linked to the development of diabetes by interfering with the processing of insulin precursors?
options: Protease inhibitors used in HIV treatment
Nicotinic acid used for dyslipidemia
Beta-adrenergic agonists
Anticonvulsants like Phenytoin
Thiazide diuretics
correctOption: Protease inhibitors used in HIV treatment
optionExplanations: Protease inhibitors, essential in antiretroviral therapy, are known to cause metabolic derangements and can etiologically lead to drug-induced diabetes.
Nicotinic acid increases insulin resistance but is not specifically noted for precursor processing interference.
Beta-agonists are listed as causes of drug-induced diabetes but generally work through metabolic antagonism rather than precursor processing.
Phenytoin inhibits insulin release from the beta cell rather than interfering with its processing.
Thiazides can impair insulin secretion or sensitivity but do not primarily target insulin precursor processing.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1097 (Book Page): Table 24.6 ... Drugs: Glucocorticoids, Thyroid hormone, Interferon-̠, Protease inhibitors, ̢-adrenergic agonists, Thiazides, Nicotinic acid, Phenytoin (Dilantin).

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: Histopathological examination of a parathyroid gland reveals cells with a clear appearance in standard sections. If this is identified as a variant of primary hyperplasia, what is the specific intracellular substance responsible for this appearance?
options: Mucin vacuoles
Amyloid fibrils
Dense secretory granules
Large lipid droplets
Abundant glycogen
correctOption: Abundant glycogen
optionExplanations: Mucin is characteristic of certain gastrointestinal or respiratory tumors, not the parathyroid gland.
Amyloid is an extracellular deposit (seen in medullary thyroid cancer or insulinomas), not an intracellular substance causing clear cell change in parathyroid hyperplasia.
Secretory granules are usually dense and eosinophilic, making the cytoplasm darker or granular, not clear.
While normal parathyroid glands contain stromal fat, 'clear cell' morphology in the epithelium is not primarily due to lipid storage.
The 'clear' appearance of cells in water-clear cell hyperplasia is due to the accumulation of intracytoplasmic glycogen.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): Less commonly, the constituent cells contain abundant glycogen, giving them a clear appearance in histologic sections (“water-clear cell hyperplasia”).

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: Which physiological trigger is most likely to cause an immediate release of preformed antidiuretic hormone from the neurohypophysis?
options: Increase in arterial blood pressure
Excessive renal reabsorption of free water
Distention of the cardiac atria
Decrease in plasma osmotic pressure
Increase in plasma osmotic pressure
correctOption: Increase in plasma osmotic pressure
optionExplanations: Increased blood pressure actually inhibits ADH release via baroreceptor signaling to encourage diuresis and lower volume.
Reabsorption of water is the result of ADH action, not the initial trigger for its release from the posterior pituitary.
Atrial distention indicates hypervolemia, which inhibits ADH secretion to reduce total body water.
Decrease in osmotic pressure (low solute concentration) inhibits ADH release to allow excess water to be excreted.
Increased osmotic pressure signifies dehydration, triggering ADH to conserve water and return osmolality to normal.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1071 (Book Page): An increase in plasma osmotic pressure detected by osmoreceptors also triggers ADH secretion. In contrast, states of hypervolemia and increased atrial distention result in inhibition of ADH secretion.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Diffuse and Multinodular goiter
statement: A 35-year-old woman residing in a mountainous region presents with a painless, symmetric swelling in the anterior neck. Physical examination reveals a diffuse, soft thyroid enlargement without palpable nodules. Laboratory studies show a euthyroid state. What is the most common underlying environmental factor responsible for this presentation globally?
options: Bacterial infection causing suppurative thyroiditis
Excessive intake of selenium in the local water supply
Chronic exposure to ionizing radiation during childhood
Autoimmune destruction of follicular cells by T-lymphocytes
Deficiency of dietary iodine resulting in hormone synthesis failure
correctOption: Deficiency of dietary iodine resulting in hormone synthesis failure
optionExplanations: Infections usually cause acute thyroiditis characterized by pain and fever, whereas simple goiters are typically painless and chronic structures.
Selenium excess is not a primary driver of goitrogenesis; iodine is the critical trace element required for thyroid hormone production.
Ionizing radiation is a major risk factor for thyroid malignancies, particularly papillary carcinoma, rather than diffuse simple goiter.
Autoimmune destruction of the gland is the hallmark of Hashimoto thyroiditis, which typically leads to hypothyroidism rather than simple goiter.

Iodine is essential for thyroid hormone synthesis. Its lack leads to decreased T3/T4 production, triggering a compensatory rise in TSH, which stimulates follicular cell hyperplasia and subsequent thyroid enlargement.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1080 (Book Page): Enlargement of the thyroid, or goiter, is caused by impaired synthesis of thyroid hormone, which is most often the result of dietary iodine deficiency.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: A patient has been taking high-dose prednisone for systemic lupus erythematosus for two years. What is the expected morphology of the adrenal glands?
options: Bilateral hemorrhagic infarction of the medulla
Bilateral reduction in cortical thickness involving the zonae fasciculata and reticularis
Multiple 1-3 mm darkly pigmented micronodules
Diffusely thickened cortex with lipid-rich cells
Macro-nodular replacement of the zona glomerulosa
correctOption: Bilateral reduction in cortical thickness involving the zonae fasciculata and reticularis
optionExplanations: Hemorrhagic infarction of the adrenals refers to Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome, an acute insufficiency.
Exogenous steroids provide negative feedback that shuts down ACTH; the adrenal cortex (specifically the ACTH-dependent zones) shrinks from disuse.
Pigmented micronodules are characteristic of primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease, not steroid use.
This describes diffuse hyperplasia seen in Cushing disease, where ACTH is elevated.
The zona glomerulosa is generally spared in iatrogenic atrophy because it is not primarily regulated by ACTH.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1114 (Book Page): In patients in whom the syndrome results from exogenous glucocorticoids, suppression of endogenous ACTH results in bilateral cortical atrophy, due to a lack of stimulation of the zonae fasciculata and reticularis by ACTH.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: In the initial screening for Cushing syndrome, which laboratory test is preferred for assessing the overall integrated secretion of cortisol over a full day?
options: 24-hour urine free-cortisol concentration
Single plasma ACTH measurement
Serum insulin-like growth factor-1 level
Random plasma glucose level
Morning serum cortisol level
correctOption: 24-hour urine free-cortisol concentration
optionExplanations: The 24-hour urine collection provides an integrated measurement of free (unbound) cortisol production, making it a highly sensitive screening tool.
A single ACTH measurement is used to categorize the type of Cushing (dependent vs independent) but not to screen for the presence of hypercortisolism.
IGF-1 is the screening test of choice for acromegaly (growth hormone excess), not Cushing syndrome.
While hyperglycemia is common in Cushing, it is a non-specific metabolic effect and not a diagnostic test for the syndrome.
A single morning cortisol level is often misleading because it does not reflect the loss of diurnal variation seen in Cushing syndrome.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1116 (Book Page): The laboratory diagnosis of Cushing syndrome is based on the following: (1) the 24-hour urine free-cortisol concentration, which is increased;

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
statement: In the histopathological evaluation of anovulatory cycles, which morphological feature is characteristically absent due to the failure of the corpus luteum to form and secrete progesterone?
options: Eosinophilic epithelial metaplasia
Cystic glandular dilation
Glandular secretory changes
Stromal condensation
Pseudostratified epithelium
correctOption: Glandular secretory changes
optionExplanations: Eosinophilic epithelial metaplasia is a common finding in anovulatory endometrium representing the effect of persistent, unopposed estrogen.
Cystic glandular dilation often occurs in the setting of repeated anovulation due to excessive, unopposed estrogenic stimulation of the endometrial glands.
Progesterone is essential for inducing secretory changes (like subnuclear vacuoles) and predecidualization; in anovulatory cycles, these changes cannot occur because no corpus luteum exists.
Stromal condensation is a feature associated with anovulatory endometrium during breakdown, often visible in biopsy specimens.
Pseudostratified epithelium is a feature of the proliferative phase, which is maintained by estrogen and is typically present in anovulatory cycles.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1002 (Book Page): However, unlike menstrual endometrium, progesterone-dependent morphologic features (e.g., glandular secretory changes and stromal pre-decidualization) are absent because the source of progesterone, the corpus luteum, does not develop without ovulation.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
coreConcept: Morphological differences between T1D and T2D islets
statement: A pathologist examining pancreatic tissue from a patient with a 20-year history of diabetes mellitus observes prominent extracellular pink, amorphous material within the islets. Which of the following best differentiates this finding from the classic histopathology of type 1 diabetes?
options: This material represents Hürthle cell metaplasia of the pancreatic acini.
This material represents neutrophilic microabscesses seen in acute pancreatitis.
This material represents lymphocytic infiltration, characteristic of type 1 diabetes.
This material represents fibrosis resulting from cystic fibrosis–related diabetes.
This material represents amyloid, which is characteristic of type 2 diabetes.
correctOption: This material represents amyloid, which is characteristic of type 2 diabetes.
optionExplanations: Hürthle cell metaplasia is a feature of the thyroid (Hashimoto thyroiditis), not the pancreatic islets in diabetes.
Neutrophilic microabscesses are not typical of either chronic diabetic state; they occur in acute inflammatory or infectious conditions of the pancreas.
Lymphocytic infiltration is the hallmark of type 1 diabetes (stage 3/symptomatic phase) and is referred to as insulitis. It appears as cellular nuclei, not amorphous extracellular pink material.
While fibrosis occurs in many pancreatic pathologies, the specific deposition of amorphous material in the islets that can obliterate them in a diabetic context is distinctively amyloid.

Correct. Amyloid deposition (derived from amylin) is a classic feature of long-standing type 2 diabetes. In contrast, type 1 diabetes is characterized by 'insulitis,' which consists of lymphocytic infiltrates.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1107 (Book Page): Amyloid deposition within islets in T2D begins in and around capillaries and between cells. At advanced stages, the islets may be virtually obliterated.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
statement: In a clinical setting within a high-income nation, which of the following is statistically identified as the most frequent underlying cause of primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency?
options: Metastatic lung carcinoma
Disseminated fungal infection
Autoimmune adrenalitis
Amyloid deposition
Tuberculous adrenalitis
correctOption: Autoimmune adrenalitis
optionExplanations: Metastatic neoplasms are common in the adrenal glands but rarely destroy enough tissue to cause overt insufficiency; they account for only a small fraction of Addison disease compared to autoimmune causes.

Fungal infections like Histoplasma can cause adrenal destruction, but this occurs far less frequently than autoimmune or tuberculous causes globally and is not the primary driver in developed nations.
Autoimmune adrenalitis is the predominant cause in high-income countries, where the immune system destroys steroidogenic cells, often involving autoantibodies to 21-hydroxylase.
Amyloidosis can involve the adrenal glands, but it is a rare cause of functional insufficiency compared to the common autoimmune and infectious processes.
Historically, tuberculosis was the leading cause, accounting for 90% of cases; however, it has been largely surpassed by autoimmune etiologies in modern high-income medical environments.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1121 (Book Page): Autoimmune adrenalitis accounts for 80% to 90% of cases of primary adrenal insufficiency in high-income countries.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
coreConcept: Clinical and Histological Evolution of Fat Necrosis
statement: A 48-year-old woman presents with a firm, irregular gray-white breast mass following accidental trauma. Histological sections reveal central liquefactive necrosis of adipocytes surrounded by neutrophils, while older areas show giant cells and hemosiderin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Mammary duct ectasia
Squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts
Lymphocytic mastopathy
Granulomatous lobular mastitis
Fat necrosis
correctOption: Fat necrosis
optionExplanations: Mammary duct ectasia involves dilated ducts filled with inspissated secretions and periductal chronic inflammation, not primarily adipocyte necrosis.
Squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts involves the subareolar region and keratinizing epithelium rather than necrotic fatty tissue and hemosiderin deposition in the breast parenchyma.
Lymphocytic mastopathy is defined by dense collagenized stroma and lymphocytic lobulitis, typically associated with autoimmune disorders, not trauma-induced necrosis.
Granulomatous lobular mastitis presents with granulomas restricted to the lobules and is specific to parous women; it does not feature primary liquefactive fat necrosis.
Fat necrosis clinically and radiologically mimics carcinoma; histologically it evolves from acute liquefactive necrosis and hemorrhage to chronic inflammation with giant cells and scarring.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1039 (Book Page): Acute lesions may be hemorrhagic and contain central areas of liquefactive fat necrosis with neutrophils and macrophages... giant cells, calcifications, and hemosiderin appear, and eventually the lesion is replaced by scar tissue

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: Regarding the stromal composition of the parathyroid gland, how does the adipose tissue content typically change during the development of an adenoma or hyperplasia?
options: Stromal fat becomes inconspicuous within the lesion
Adipocytes undergo Hürthle cell metaplasia
Adipose tissue replaces the chief cell population
Fat cells form a protective layer around the capsule
Adipose tissue increases significantly to fill empty spaces
correctOption: Stromal fat becomes inconspicuous within the lesion
optionExplanations: Correct. One of the markers of a hypercellular parathyroid state (adenoma or hyperplasia) is the lack of normal stromal fat.
Hürthle cell change occurs in epithelial cells, not adipocytes.
This describes atrophy, the opposite of the hypercellularity seen in adenoma/hyperplasia.
The fat is normally dispersed within the stroma, not concentrated specifically at the capsule edge.
Fat decreases as the cellular population expands in neoplastic or hyperplastic states.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): As in the case of adenomas, stromal fat is inconspicuous within hyperplastic glands.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: An elite board of clinicians is evaluating the epidemiologic data for hypercortisolism. Which of the following is identified as the most frequent underlying cause for the development of Cushing syndrome across all patient populations?
options: Hypersecretion of ACTH by a pituitary microadenoma
Administration of exogenous glucocorticoid medications
Autonomous secretion of cortisol by a functional adrenal cortical adenoma
Primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease
Paraneoplastic production of ACTH by a small-cell lung carcinoma
correctOption: Administration of exogenous glucocorticoid medications
optionExplanations: While pituitary microadenomas (Cushing disease) are the most common cause of endogenous Cushing syndrome, they are not the most common cause overall when exogenous factors are included.
The most frequent cause of clinical Cushing syndrome in medical practice is the pharmacological use of steroids for various inflammatory or autoimmune conditions.
Primary adrenal neoplasms are a cause of ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome but are far less prevalent than the use of medicinal steroids.
Primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease is a rare micronodular hyperplasia often associated with the Carney complex.
Ectopic ACTH production is a significant but relatively rare cause of ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome compared to iatrogenic sources.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1113 (Book Page): The vast majority of cases of Cushing syndrome are the result of the administration of exogenous glucocorticoids (iatrogenic Cushing syndrome).

category: Define thyroiditis
statement: What is considered the most frequent etiology for the development of hypothyroidism in geographic regions where dietary iodine levels are sufficient?
options: Iatrogenic surgical ablation
Graves disease
Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis
Hashimoto thyroiditis
Dietary goitrogen consumption
correctOption: Hashimoto thyroiditis
optionExplanations: Surgical ablation or radioiodine therapy are recognized causes of iatrogenic hypothyroidism. While common post-treatment, they are not the primary disease-based cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-replete populations.

Graves disease is primarily an autoimmune cause of hyperthyroidism, not hypothyroidism. It results from the production of thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins that mimic TSH, leading to thyroid hyperfunction.

Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis is typically a self-limited inflammatory condition characterized by thyroid pain and transient thyroid dysfunction. It rarely results in permanent thyroid failure or chronic hypothyroidism.

Hashimoto thyroiditis is the primary cause of chronic autoimmune thyroid failure in iodine-sufficient areas. It involves the progressive destruction of the thyroid parenchyma by immune cells, eventually leading to overt hypothyroidism.

Goitrogens, such as those found in cassava or certain vegetables, interfere with thyroid hormone synthesis. While they cause goiter, they are a less frequent cause of clinical hypothyroidism compared to Hashimoto in iodine-replete settings.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1076 (Book Page): Hashimoto thyroiditis is an autoimmune disease that results in destruction of the thyroid gland and gradual and progressive thyroid failure. It is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in areas of the world where iodine levels are sufficient.

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
statement: A patient with long-standing Cushing syndrome undergoes bilateral adrenalectomy. Shortly after, the patient develops hyperpigmentation and a large, rapidly expanding pituitary mass. Which classification best fits this syndrome?
options: Waterhouse-Friderichsen Syndrome
Sipple Syndrome
Nelson Syndrome
Addison Disease
Cushing Disease
correctOption: Nelson Syndrome
optionExplanations: Waterhouse-Friderichsen is acute adrenal crisis due to hemorrhage, usually from Neisseria infection.
Sipple syndrome is MEN-2A, which involves medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and parathyroid hyperplasia, not aggressive pituitary ACTH tumors.
Nelson syndrome occurs when the loss of cortisol feedback (post-adrenalectomy) allows a pre-existing corticotroph microadenoma to grow aggressively, leading to mass effects and hyperpigmentation.
Addison disease is primary adrenal insufficiency, typically autoimmune, and does not involve an ACTH-secreting pituitary tumor.
Cushing disease refers to the initial ACTH-secreting pituitary tumor causing hypercortisolism when adrenals are intact.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1070 (Book Page): Large destructive pituitary adenomas can develop in patients after surgical removal of the adrenal glands for treatment of Cushing syndrome. This condition, known as Nelson syndrome, occurs because of loss of the inhibitory effect of adrenal corticosteroids on a corticotroph microadenoma.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
coreConcept: Pathophysiological basis of Crooke hyaline change
statement: What is the primary cellular mechanism underlying the formation of 'Crooke hyaline change' observed in the anterior pituitary of patients suffering from chronic hypercortisolism?
options: Deposition of amyloid derived from calcitonin precursors
Apoptotic loss of somatotrophs due to feedback inhibition
Hypertrophy of chromophobe cells lacking hormone expression
Accumulation of intermediate keratin filaments in the cytoplasm
Accumulation of eosinophilic secretory granules containing ACTH
correctOption: Accumulation of intermediate keratin filaments in the cytoplasm
optionExplanations: Amyloid deposition is characteristic of medullary thyroid carcinoma or insulinomas, not the pituitary response to high cortisol levels.
While high cortisol inhibits ACTH release, it does not typically cause the apoptotic loss of somatotroph cells, which are part of the GH lineage.
Though the cells appear paler (resembling chromophobes), the change is a specific cytoplasmic alteration of existing ACTH-producing cells, not simple hypertrophy of non-functioning cells.

Crooke hyaline change is a reactive morphological adaptation in pituitary corticotrophs. It occurs regardless of the cause of Cushing syndrome (endogenous or exogenous) and is defined by the displacement of normal basophilic granules by a pale, homogeneous accumulation of cytokeratin filaments.
Granular basophilic cytoplasm is the normal state of corticotrophs; Crooke change involves a loss of this granularity in favor of a paler, homogeneous appearance.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1114 (Book Page): This alteration is the result of the accumulation of intermediate keratin filaments in the cytoplasm, a finding that is also seen in “Crooke cell” corticotroph adenoma.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
statement: A pathologist examines a pancreatic section from a patient who had long-standing Type 2 Diabetes. Which of the following morphologic changes is most likely to be observed in the islets of Langerhans?
options: Complete absence of the reticulin network within the islets
Massive hyperplasia of beta cells and absence of alpha cells
Formation of psammoma bodies within the exocrine parenchyma
A dense infiltrate of T lymphocytes (insulitis)
Replacement of islets by amyloid (amylin) deposits
correctOption: Replacement of islets by amyloid (amylin) deposits
optionExplanations: Option D refers to the diagnostic feature of pituitary adenomas, not diabetic islets.
Option C is incorrect because Type 2 DM is eventually characterized by a decline in beta-cell mass rather than massive hyperplasia in the late stages.
Option E refers to papillary thyroid or ovarian carcinomas and is not a feature of diabetic pancreatic pathology.
Option A (insulitis) is the classic finding in Type 1 Diabetes, reflecting the autoimmune T-cell mediated attack.
Option B is correct. In Type 2 DM, islets often show extracellular amyloid deposition, which can eventually obliterate the functional cell mass.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1107 (Book Page): Amyloid deposition within islets in T2D begins in and around capillaries and between cells. At advanced stages, the islets may be virtually obliterated.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: During the evaluation of a lactating patient with a painful, erythematous breast mass, a biopsy reveals localized abscess formation. Which pathogen is the most likely morphological driver of this specific presentation?
options: Staphylococcus aureus
Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Candida albicans
Streptococcus pyogenes
Corynebacterium species
correctOption: Staphylococcus aureus
optionExplanations: Staphylococcus aureus is the classic cause of localized abscesses in acute mastitis during the first month of breastfeeding.
Mycobacteria cause granulomatous inflammation, which is rare and usually associated with immunocompromise or foreign bodies.
Candida is a fungal agent and is not a typical cause of acute bacterial mastitis or acute abscess formation in this context.
Streptococcus typically causes a diffuse, spreading infection known as cellulitis rather than localized abscesses.
Corynebacterium is associated with cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis, a specific rare granulomatous variant.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1038 (Book Page): Staphylococci infection often leads to single or multiple abscesses, whereas streptococci cause spreading infection in the form of cellulitis.

category: Hashimoto Thyroiditis ii
coreConcept: Morphological contrast between Hashimoto and subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis
statement: A clinician is comparing the pathological features of Hashimoto thyroiditis with subacute lymphocytic (painless) thyroiditis. Which morphologic finding is significantly more characteristic of Hashimoto thyroiditis and serves as a distinguishing feature?
options: The presence of germinal centers
A mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate
Extensive Hürthle cell metaplasia
Patchy collapse of thyroid follicles
Mild and transient hyperthyroidism
correctOption: Extensive Hürthle cell metaplasia
optionExplanations: While germinal centers are very prominent in Hashimoto, they can also be seen in lymphocytic thyroiditis, although they are generally better developed in the former.
Mononuclear infiltrates are common to both Hashimoto and subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis, making them poor discriminators.
Hürthle cell metaplasia and prominent interstitial fibrosis are distinguishing features that are significantly more pronounced in Hashimoto compared to subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis.
Follicular collapse is a shared feature of many types of thyroiditis during the active inflammatory stage and does not uniquely identify Hashimoto.
Hyperthyroidism can occur transiently in both (hashitoxicosis vs. initial painless phase) and is a clinical rather than a specific morphologic differentiator.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): [Unlike Hashimoto thyroiditis, however, fibrosis and Hürthle cell metaplasia are not prominent.]

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
statement: A 48-year-old woman experiences heavy, irregular bleeding. Histological examination of an endometrial biopsy shows 'corkscrew' glands with focal stromal breakdown and no evidence of plasma cells or polyps. The glands show no atypia but are mildly dilated. What age-related category of bleeding does this most likely represent?
options: Reproductive age complications of pregnancy.
Prepubertal precocious puberty.
Adolescent coagulation disorder.
Perimenopausal anovulatory cycle.
Postmenopausal endometrial atrophy.
correctOption: Perimenopausal anovulatory cycle.
optionExplanations: While pregnancy is possible, the description focuses on functional features of the endometrium consistent with anovulation.
Precocious puberty occurs in children, not 48-year-old women.
Coagulation disorders typically present in adolescence with the onset of heavy menses.
The perimenopausal period is characterized by failing ovarian function and frequent anovulatory cycles leading to DUB.
Atrophy would show a thin, inactive endometrium, not dilated glands and stromal breakdown.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1001 (Book Page): Table 22.3... Perimenopausal: Dysfunctional uterine bleeding, Anovulatory cycle.

category: Describe salient morphological features of clinically significant subtypes of thyroiditis: i
statement: A 52-year-old female presents with a painless, diffuse enlargement of the thyroid gland. Histological examination reveals an extensive mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate with well-developed germinal centers. The thyroid follicles are atrophic and lined by epithelial cells with abundant, granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. Which morphological feature is most characteristic of this condition?
options: Palisading granulomas with central fibrinoid necrosis
Neutrophilic microabscesses within disrupted follicles
Metaplastic Hürthle cell change of the follicular epithelium
Extensive fibrosis extending into contiguous neck structures
Multinucleated giant cells enclosing colloid pools
correctOption: Metaplastic Hürthle cell change of the follicular epithelium
optionExplanations: Palisading granulomas are typical of rheumatoid nodules or certain skin conditions, not standard thyroiditis subtypes described in the text.
Neutrophilic microabscesses are seen in the early active inflammatory phase of granulomatous thyroiditis, not the chronic autoimmune destruction of Hashimoto.
Hürthle cells, or oxyphil cells, are metaplastic follicular cells with granular eosinophilic cytoplasm due to mitochondrial accumulation; they are a classic finding in Hashimoto thyroiditis.
Fibrosis extending beyond the thyroid capsule into neck structures is the defining feature of Riedel thyroiditis, whereas fibrosis in Hashimoto is confined to the gland.
Multinucleated giant cells are the hallmark of subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis, not Hashimoto thyroiditis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1077 (Book Page): [The thyroid follicles are atrophic and are lined in many areas by epithelial cells with abundant eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm, termed Hürthle cells, which represent a metaplastic response of the normally low cuboidal follicular epithelium to chronic injury.]

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
statement: Which of the following pathogens is most frequently responsible for acute epididymitis in a sexually active 28-year-old male?
options: Gram-negative rods associated with urinary tract abnormalities
Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas species
Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus species
Mycobacterium tuberculosis following lymphatic spread
correctOption: Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
optionExplanations: Gram-negative rods are the primary pathogens in childhood epididymitis, often linked to congenital genitourinary malformations.
E. coli and Pseudomonas are the primary causes in men older than 35 years, usually related to common urinary tract infections.
In the cohort of sexually active men under 35, the majority of epididymitis cases are sexually transmitted, specifically by C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae.
These are common causes of acute mastitis or general pyogenic infections but are not the specific primary agents for epididymitis in this age group.
Tuberculosis involves the epididymis but usually presents as a chronic granulomatous condition rather than the typical acute presentation in this age group.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 967 (Book Page): In sexually active men younger than age 35 years, the sexually transmitted pathogens C. trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae are most frequent.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
coreConcept: Differentiating hyperplastic vs neoplastic thyroid papillae
statement: On histological examination of a thyroidectomy specimen, how are the epithelial papillae seen in Graves disease distinguished from those found in Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma (PTC)?
options: Graves papillae lack fibrovascular cores, unlike the papillae of PTC.
Graves papillae are always associated with psammoma bodies.
Graves papillae are lined by cuboidal cells with intranuclear pseudo-inclusions.
Graves papillae contain dense fibrovascular cores, whereas PTC papillae do not.
Graves papillae show Orphan Annie eye nuclei with ground-glass appearance.
correctOption: Graves papillae lack fibrovascular cores, unlike the papillae of PTC.
optionExplanations: In Graves, the epithelial crowding creates small papillae that project into the follicles. These are distinguished from malignancy by the absence of supportive fibrovascular cores.
Psammoma bodies are highly characteristic of Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma and are almost never seen in the hyperplastic papillae of Graves disease.
Intranuclear pseudo-inclusions are a cytological hallmark of Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma. Graves cells are tall and columnar but lack these specific neoplastic nuclear changes.
This is incorrect; it is the papillae of Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma that characteristically possess fibrovascular stalks.
Ground-glass or 'Orphan Annie' nuclei are a diagnostic nuclear feature of Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma, not Graves disease.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): Such papillae lack fibrovascular cores, in contrast to those of papillary carcinoma.

category: Enumerate clinical manifestations along with hormone levels of anterior pituitary
coreConcept: Pituitary apoplexy as a clinical emergency
statement: A patient with a known pituitary macroadenoma presents with the sudden onset of an excruciating headache, double vision (diplopia) due to pressure on the oculomotor nerves, and signs of cardiovascular collapse. This life-threatening neurosurgical emergency is known as:
options: Empty sella syndrome
Pituitary apoplexy
Rathke cleft cyst expansion
Sheehan syndrome
Nelson syndrome
correctOption: Pituitary apoplexy
optionExplanations: Empty sella syndrome is a condition where the sella is filled with CSF and the pituitary is compressed; it is usually a chronic finding, not an acute hemorrhagic emergency.

Pituitary apoplexy results from sudden hemorrhage into an existing adenoma, causing rapid expansion, pressure on cranial nerves, and acute hypopituitarism, requiring urgent surgical and medical management.
Rathke cleft cysts can expand and cause hypopituitarism, but they do not typically cause the 'sudden, excruciating' hemorrhagic presentation associated with apoplexy.
Sheehan syndrome is postpartum ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary usually following obstetric hemorrhage. It presents with chronic hormone failure rather than acute headache and nerve palsy.
Nelson syndrome is the growth of an ACTH-secreting adenoma following adrenalectomy. While it can cause mass effects, it does not typically present as an acute hemorrhagic crisis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1071 (Book Page): [Pituitary apoplexy: As mentioned earlier, this is caused by a sudden hemorrhage into the pituitary gland, often occurring into a pituitary adenoma. In its most dramatic presentation, apoplexy causes the abrupt onset of excruciating headache, diplopia... can cause sudden death.]

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Diffuse and Multinodular goiter
statement: In the context of the epidemiology of diffuse goiter, which of the following criteria is used to classify a goiter as being endemic in a specific geographic region?
options: Requirement of total thyroidectomy in 1% of the population
Presence of goiter in more than 10% of the population
Evidence of goiter in at least 5% of the total population
Elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone levels in 15% of newborns
Discovery of multinodular changes in 20% of adult females
correctOption: Presence of goiter in more than 10% of the population
optionExplanations: The clinical management or surgical intervention rate (such as thyroidectomy) is not a defining metric for the epidemiological classification of endemic goiter.

According to standardized endocrine pathology, a geographic region is considered endemic for goiter when the prevalence of the condition exceeds 10% of the population, often linked to low iodine levels in soil and water.
A 5% prevalence rate is insufficient to meet the standardized definition of endemicity for goiter, which requires a higher threshold of community involvement.
Elevated TSH in newborns is a sign of congenital hypothyroidism or iodine deficiency but is not the specific threshold used to define an endemic goiter area for the general population.
While multinodular changes are common in endemic areas, the definition of endemicity is based on total goiter prevalence rather than specifically multinodular morphology in a single gender.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1081 (Book Page): The term endemic is used when goiters are present in more than 10% of the population in a given region.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
coreConcept: Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY) Pathogenesis
statement: A 16-year-old patient is diagnosed with a monogenic form of diabetes characterized by a primary defect in ̠-cell function. Genetic testing reveals a germline mutation in the gene encoding a rate-limiting enzyme of glucose metabolism. Which of the following is the most likely genetic defect?
options: PDX1 (MODY4)
HNF1A (MODY3)
HNF4A (MODY1)
NEUROD1 (MODY6)
Glucokinase (GCK/MODY2)
correctOption: Glucokinase (GCK/MODY2)
optionExplanations: PDX1 mutations cause MODY4, which involves a transcription factor essential for pancreatic development.
HNF1A mutations cause MODY3; while common, it is a transcription factor defect, not an enzyme defect like GCK.
HNF4A mutations cause MODY1, which is a transcription factor defect rather than the most common rate-limiting enzyme defect.
NEUROD1 mutations cause MODY6, which is a rare transcription factor-related etiology of monogenic diabetes.
Glucokinase (GCK) mutations cause MODY2 and are the most common form of MODY; GCK acts as the glucose sensor/rate-limiting step in the ̠ cell.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1103 (Book Page): MODY can result from germline loss-of-function mutations in one of six genes (see Table 24.6), of which mutations of glucokinase (GCK) are the most common. Glucokinase is a rate-limiting step in oxidative glucose metabolism, which, in turn, is coupled to insulin secretion within islet ̠ cells.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: A pathologist examining a parathyroid specimen notes a solitary tan-red nodule weighing 2 grams. Which histologic finding would most strongly support a diagnosis of parathyroid adenoma over primary hyperplasia?
options: Focal aggregates of oxyphil cells
Presence of a rich vascular network
A rim of compressed, non-neoplastic parathyroid tissue at the edge
Inconspicuous stromal adipose tissue
Monotonous sheets of chief cells
correctOption: A rim of compressed, non-neoplastic parathyroid tissue at the edge
optionExplanations: Oxyphil cells are normal constituents of the gland and can be seen in various amounts in both hyperplasia and adenomas.
A rich vascular network is common to both adenomas and hyperplastic glands as they are highly active endocrine tissues.
The presence of a peripheral rim of normal, compressed parathyroid parenchyma outside the lesion's capsule is a classic indicator of a solitary adenoma.
Stromal fat is reduced or absent in any hyperactive parathyroid state, whether it is neoplastic (adenoma) or reactive (hyperplasia).
Monotonous sheets of chief cells are found in both conditions, making this feature non-discriminatory for a definitive diagnosis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): [A rim of compressed, non-neoplastic parathyroid tissue, generally separated by a fibrous capsule, is often visible at the edge of the adenoma.]

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Diffuse and Multinodular goiter
coreConcept: Clinical presentation of endemic multinodular goiter
statement: A 48-year-old woman from a remote village in the Andes mountains presents with a slow-growing, massive midline neck swelling that has been present for 15 years. Physical examination reveals an irregularly enlarged, nontender thyroid. Laboratory studies show TSH is 6.5 mU/L (Ref: 0.4-4.0) and free T4 is 0.8 ng/dL (Ref: 0.9-1.7). Radioactive iodine scan shows heterogeneous uptake. What is the most likely morphological diagnosis?
options: Graves disease
Papillary carcinoma
Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis
Hashimoto thyroiditis
Multinodular goiter
correctOption: Multinodular goiter
optionExplanations: Graves disease typically presents with diffuse, symmetric enlargement and hyperthyroid symptoms, not the chronic, irregular nodularity seen in this scenario.
While thyroid carcinoma is possible, the massive size and long duration in an endemic region characterize benign multinodular goiter.
Subacute thyroiditis is a painful, self-limited condition associated with viral prodromes, not a decades-long massive swelling.
While Hashimoto's can cause goiter and hypothyroidism, the massive, irregular nodularity and endemic geographic history strongly favor multinodular goiter over autoimmune destruction.

Long-standing iodine deficiency leads to cycles of hyperplasia and involution, eventually resulting in the extreme, asymmetric enlargement of multinodular goiter. The labs show subclinical to mild hypothyroidism, common in these patients.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1081 (Book Page): Virtually all long-standing simple goiters convert into multinodular goiters. Multinodular goiters produce the most extreme thyroid enlargements and are more frequently mistaken for neoplasms than any other form of thyroid disease.

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
statement: Which of the following is considered the most common clinical cause of pain originating within the thyroid gland?
options: Hashimoto thyroiditis
Subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis
Riedel thyroiditis
Granulomatous thyroiditis
Papillary thyroid carcinoma
correctOption: Granulomatous thyroiditis
optionExplanations: Hashimoto thyroiditis typically presents as a painless, symmetric enlargement of the thyroid gland rather than an acute painful episode.
Subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis is also known as painless thyroiditis, specifically presenting without the tenderness seen in granulomatous forms.
Riedel thyroiditis presents with a hard, fixed mass that mimics malignancy but is typically not associated with acute pain.
Granulomatous thyroiditis (De Quervain thyroiditis) is classically associated with acute onset of neck pain and tenderness, often radiating to the jaw or ears.
Most thyroid neoplasms, including papillary carcinoma, present as asymptomatic nodules; pain is an uncommon feature unless there is hemorrhage into the tumor.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): Granulomatous thyroiditis is the most common cause of thyroid pain.
