correctOption: Neonatal torsion occurs in the absence of a defined anatomic defect, unlike the adult type
optionExplanations: The anatomic defect in adult torsion is often bilateral, but the clinical event of torsion itself is usually unilateral.
The bell-clapper deformity is the anatomic hallmark of adult (adolescent) torsion, not neonatal torsion.
Correct. Neonatal torsion happens in utero or shortly after birth without a predisposing anatomic abnormality, whereas adult torsion is linked to specific increased mobility (bell-clapper).
Both types result in hemorrhagic infarction due to the persistence of arterial flow into a venous-obstructed testis.
Neonatal torsion occurs in utero or perinatally without trauma; adult torsion also often occurs without inciting injury.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 968 (Book Page): Neonatal torsion occurs either in utero or shortly after birth. It lacks any associated anatomic defect to account for its occurrence. 'Adult' torsion is typically seen in adolescence... results from a bilateral anatomic defect that leads to increased mobility of the testes (bell-clapper abnormality).

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
statement: In the pathophysiological development of tubal ectopic pregnancy, how does prior pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) contribute to abnormal implantation sites?
options: By promoting the trapped fertilization of the ovum within the follicle
By inducing cystic swelling of the chorionic villi in the ampulla
By inducing an absolute deficiency of human chorionic gonadotropin
By causing intraluminal scarring known as chronic salpingitis
By preventing the decidualization of the endometrial stroma
correctOption: By causing intraluminal scarring known as chronic salpingitis
optionExplanations: Trapping of the ovum within the follicle at the time of rupture is the specific mechanism for ovarian ectopics, not tubal ectopics caused by PID.
Cystic swelling of chorionic villi is the defining feature of hydatidiform moles, not the mechanism by which PID leads to ectopic pregnancy.
Ectopic pregnancies generally produce detectable hCG, and PID does not cause an absolute deficiency of this hormone.
Chronic salpingitis leads to the fusion of tubal plicae and formation of blind pouches, which physically trap the zygote before it reaches the uterus.
Endometrial decidualization occurs in the uterus during ectopic pregnancy; PID-induced scarring specifically affects the extrauterine transit site.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1027 (Book Page): The most important predisposing condition, present in 35% to 50% of patients, is prior pelvic inflammatory disease resulting in intraluminal fallopian tube scarring (chronic salpingitis).

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: What is the most common underlying pathology found in primary hyperparathyroidism?
options: Parathyroid carcinoma
Solitary parathyroid adenoma
Multiglandular hyperplasia
Ectopic PTH secretion
Secondary renal osteodystrophy
correctOption: Solitary parathyroid adenoma
optionExplanations: Parathyroid carcinoma is rare, accounting for approximately 1% of cases of primary hyperparathyroidism.
Correct. A solitary sporadic adenoma is the cause of the vast majority (85-95%) of primary hyperparathyroidism cases.
Primary hyperplasia accounts for about 5% to 10% of cases, making it much less common than adenoma.
Ectopic PTH secretion is an extremely rare cause; usually, hypercalcemia of malignancy is caused by PTHrP, not PTH.
Secondary renal osteodystrophy is related to secondary hyperparathyroidism (renal failure), not primary hyperparathyroidism.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1091 (Book Page): [Adenoma: 85% to 95%] [The most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism is a solitary sporadic parathyroid adenoma.]

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
coreConcept: Pathophysiology of Hyperpigmentation in Addison Disease
statement: A patient with primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency presents with a distinctive bronzing of the skin. This physiological change is most accurately attributed to which biochemical mechanism?
options: Reduced clearance of bilirubin following hepatic steroid-induced congestion
Direct stimulatory effect of hyperkalemia on dermal melanocytes
Elevated circulating levels of pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) precursors
Primary deposition of hemosiderin due to concurrent hemolytic anemia
Retention of dietary carotenoids due to lack of glucocorticoid-mediated metabolism
correctOption: Elevated circulating levels of pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) precursors
optionExplanations: Jaundice (bilirubin accumulation) causes yellowing rather than the bronze hyperpigmentation seen in primary adrenal failure.
Hyperkalemia is an electrolyte disturbance in Addison disease but has no known direct stimulatory pathway on dermal pigment cells.
In primary failure, lack of cortisol feedback causes the pituitary to overproduce POMC, which is then cleaved into ACTH and MSH, both of which stimulate melanin production.
While iron deposition causes darkening, it is not the mechanism of pigmentation in Addison's disease; it is typical of hemochromatosis.
Carotenemia occurs from excessive intake or hypothyroidism, but not as a consequence of adrenal steroid deficiency.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1122 (Book Page): This is caused by elevated levels of pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC), which is derived from the anterior pituitary and is a precursor of both ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH).

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
statement: In the initial stages of testicular torsion, what is the primary vascular consequence of the twisting of the spermatic cord?
options: Spasmodic contraction of the cremasteric artery
Obstruction of the venous drainage system
Isolated lymphatic insufficiency leading to chylocele
Nerve entrapment resulting in ischemic atrophy
Immediate occlusion of the thick-walled testicular arteries
correctOption: Obstruction of the venous drainage system
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The pathophysiology is mechanical twisting of the cord leading to venous obstruction, not a primary arterial spasm of the cremasteric system.
Correct. The primary event in testicular torsion is the mechanical obstruction of venous drainage due to the lower pressure in the veins compared to the arterial system.
Incorrect. While lymphatic drainage may be affected, the defining urologic emergency is related to venous and subsequent hemorrhagic infarction, not isolated lymphatic issues.
Incorrect. Nerve compression occurs but the clinical emergency is defined by vascular compromise and necrosis, not nerve-mediated atrophy.
Incorrect. The text specifies that thick-walled arteries remain patent initially, even when the spermatic cord is twisted.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 968 (Book Page): Twisting of the spermatic cord typically cuts off the venous drainage of the testis.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Diffuse and Multinodular goiter
coreConcept: Morphological distinction between hyperplastic and involutional phases
statement: During the morphologic evolution of a diffuse nontoxic goiter, the 'colloid involution' phase is histologically characterized by which of the following features?
options: Intercellular deposition of amyloid derived from calcitonin polypeptides.
Tall, crowded columnar cells forming small intra-follicular papillae.
Enlarged follicles lined by a flattened, inactive epithelium.
Hürthle cell metaplasia with abundant eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm.
Extensive infiltration by mononuclear cells with well-developed germinal centers.
correctOption: Enlarged follicles lined by a flattened, inactive epithelium.
optionExplanations: Amyloid deposition is a diagnostic feature of medullary thyroid carcinoma, which originates from C cells, not the follicular cells involved in goitrogenesis.
Tall, crowded columnar cells are typical of the hyperplastic phase of diffuse goiter, reflecting active stimulation by TSH, rather than the involution phase.

The colloid involution phase (colloid goiter) occurs when TSH levels drop or iodine availability increases, leading to a state where follicles are distended with colloid and the active epithelium becomes inactive and flattened.
Hürthle cell metaplasia is characteristic of chronic autoimmune injury seen in Hashimoto thyroiditis and is not a feature of simple goiter.
Mononuclear infiltrates and germinal centers are hallmark features of Hashimoto thyroiditis, not diffuse nontoxic goiter.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1081 (Book Page): Histologically the follicle epithelium is flattened and cuboidal, and colloid is abundant during periods of involution.

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
statement: Histologically, the early active phase of granulomatous thyroiditis is most likely to show which of the following features?
options: Replacement of the entire parenchyma by dense, hyalinized fibrous tissue
Formation of amyloid deposits derived from calcitonin polypeptides
Large, encapsulated nodules composed of uniform polygonal cells
Scattered follicles replaced by neutrophils forming microabscesses
Extensive fibrosis extending beyond the thyroid capsule into the neck
correctOption: Scattered follicles replaced by neutrophils forming microabscesses
optionExplanations: Total parenchymal hyalinization is not characteristic of this self-limited condition; any resulting fibrosis is usually patchy and replaces only the foci of injury.
Amyloid is associated with Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma, a neuroendocrine tumor of C cells.
Encapsulated nodules describe follicular adenomas, which are neoplastic rather than inflammatory.
The disease begins with an acute inflammatory reaction featuring neutrophils and microabscesses before progressing to the characteristic granulomatous stage with giant cells.
Fibrosis extending beyond the capsule is the hallmark of Riedel thyroiditis, which is distinct from the granulomatous variant.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): Early in the active inflammatory phase, scattered follicles may be disrupted and replaced by neutrophils forming microabscesses.

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: A 55-year-old female presents with recurrent renal stones and skeletal pain. Imaging reveals multiple cystic bone lesions and subperiosteal resorption in the phalanges. Laboratory tests show serum Calcium of 12.5 mg/dL and PTH of 450 pg/mL (Normal 10-65). What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Secondary hyperparathyroidism
Vitamin D toxicity
Hypoparathyroidism
Primary hyperparathyroidism with osteitis fibrosa cystica
Sarcoidosis
correctOption: Primary hyperparathyroidism with osteitis fibrosa cystica
optionExplanations: Secondary hyperparathyroidism is characterized by low or normal calcium levels resulting from a primary hypocalcemic stimulus like renal failure.
Vitamin D toxicity causes hypercalcemia but would typically result in suppressed (low) PTH levels due to feedback inhibition.
Hypoparathyroidism presents with hypocalcemia and low PTH, the opposite of this patient's presentation.
Recurrent stones, high calcium, and inappropriately high PTH signify primary hyperparathyroidism. The bone findings describe the classic osteitis fibrosa cystica.
Sarcoidosis produces hypercalcemia via extra-renal conversion of Vitamin D by macrophages, which also suppresses endogenous PTH.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1093 (Book Page): The combination of increased osteoclast activity, peritrabecular fibrosis, and cystic brown tumors is the hallmark of severe hyperparathyroidism and is known as generalized osteitis fibrosa cystica

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
statement: Which specific autoantibody is the primary mediator of the hypermetabolic state in Graves disease and mimics the physiological action of its corresponding trophic hormone?
options: Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody
Anti-thyroglobulin antibody
Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI)
TSH receptor blocking antibody
Anti-microsomal antibody
correctOption: Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI)
optionExplanations: Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies are found in most patients with Hashimoto thyroiditis and are less specific for Graves.
Anti-thyroglobulin antibodies are seen in multiple autoimmune thyroid disorders, including Hashimoto thyroiditis, and do not mimic TSH.
TSI is characteristic of Graves, mimicking TSH by binding to the TSH receptor and activating adenyl cyclase.
Blocking antibodies can be present in Graves but lead to hypothyroidism rather than the classic hyperthyroid state.
Anti-microsomal antibodies are classic markers for Hashimoto thyroiditis rather than the primary stimulatory mechanism of Graves.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): The most common antibody subtype, known as thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI), is observed in approximately 90% of patients. In contrast to antibodies against thyroglobulin and thyroid peroxidase, TSI is almost never observed in other autoimmune diseases of the thyroid. TSI binds to the TSH receptor and mimics its actions, stimulating adenyl cyclase and increasing the release of thyroid hormones.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
statement: According to current clinical guidelines, which laboratory value is considered the minimum threshold for the definitive diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus?
options: A 2-hour plasma glucose of 180 mg/dL during an oral glucose tolerance test
A glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) level of 6.5%
A C-peptide level that is double the normal reference range
A fasting plasma glucose of 110 mg/dL
A random plasma glucose of 160 mg/dL in an asymptomatic patient
correctOption: A glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) level of 6.5%
optionExplanations: The 2-hour plasma glucose must be ≥ 200 mg/dL during an OGTT for a diagnosis of diabetes.
An HbA1c of 6.5% or higher is one of the four standard criteria used to diagnose diabetes.
C-peptide is a measure of beta cell function, not a diagnostic criterion for diabetes itself.
A fasting glucose of 110 mg/dL falls into the 'prediabetes' range (100-125 mg/dL), not frank diabetes.
A random glucose must be ≥ 200 mg/dL and accompanied by classic symptoms to be diagnostic.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1097 (Book Page): Diagnostic criteria for diabetes include... 4. A glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) level ≥ 6.5%

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Diffuse and Multinodular goiter
statement: What morphological feature most reliably distinguishes a dominant hyperplastic nodule of a multinodular goiter from a follicular thyroid adenoma?
options: Marked nuclear pleomorphism and high mitotic activity
The absence of a prominent capsule between the nodule and residual parenchyma
Infiltration of the lesion by Hürthle cells with granular eosinophilic cytoplasm
The presence of numerous psammoma bodies within the stroma
A well-defined, intact fibrous capsule circumferentially surrounding the lesion
correctOption: The absence of a prominent capsule between the nodule and residual parenchyma
optionExplanations: Benign nodules in a goiter typically show little nuclear variation; pleomorphism is more common in anaplastic cancers or 'endocrine atypia' of adenomas.
Correct. Hyperplastic nodules in a goiter lack a true, complete circumferential capsule, although they may compress the surrounding thyroid tissue.
Hürthle cell change can occur in goiters, adenomas, and Hashimoto thyroiditis; it is a metaplastic response to injury and not a specific discriminator for goiter nodules.
Psammoma bodies are characteristic of papillary thyroid carcinoma and are almost never seen in benign multinodular goiters or follicular adenomas.
A well-defined fibrous capsule is the diagnostic hallmark of a follicular adenoma; its presence helps differentiate a true neoplasm from a hyperplastic nodule.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1082 (Book Page): In contrast to follicular neoplasms, a prominent capsule between the hyperplastic nodules and residual compressed thyroid parenchyma is not present.

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: A 32-year-old female with a history of Graves disease presents to the emergency department with high fever (104°F), tachycardia (150 bpm), and acute delirium following a severe pulmonary infection. Which of the following laboratory and physiological profiles is most characteristic of this patient's acute presentation?
options: High TSH, high free T4, and impaired peripheral deiodination
Normal TSH, high free T3, and sympathetic blockade
Low TSH, low free T4, and adrenal cortical suppression
Low TSH, high free T4, and acute elevation in catecholamine effects
High TSH, low free T4, and decreased metabolic rate
correctOption: Low TSH, high free T4, and acute elevation in catecholamine effects
optionExplanations: High TSH with high T4 is typical only of rare pituitary adenomas; thyroid storm in Graves disease involves suppressed TSH.
TSH must be suppressed in Graves-related thyrotoxicosis; a 'normal' TSH in the presence of high thyroid hormones is pathologically inappropriate.
While low TSH is correct, high levels of T4/T3 are necessary to drive the clinical features of a thyroid storm.
Thyroid storm is a medical emergency featuring extreme hyperthyroidism (Low TSH/High T4) and hypermetabolism often triggered by stress-induced catecholamine surges.
This profile describes primary hypothyroidism, which is the physiological opposite of the hypermetabolic thyroid storm.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1074 (Book Page): Thyroid storm refers to the abrupt onset of severe hyperthyroidism. ... Laboratory findings that support the diagnosis of hyperthyroidism include a low TSH value accompanied by an increase in free T4.

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: Which of the following is identified as the most frequent cause of endogenous hyperthyroidism in clinical practice?
options: Struma ovarii
Toxic multinodular goiter
Factitious thyrotoxicosis
TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma
Graves disease
correctOption: Graves disease
optionExplanations: Struma ovarii is a rare ectopic source of thyroid hormone within an ovarian teratoma and does not represent a common endogenous cause.
Toxic multinodular goiter is an important cause but accounts for fewer cases than Graves disease, usually occurring as a late complication of simple goiter.
Factitious thyrotoxicosis results from exogenous ingestion of thyroxine rather than endogenous hyperfunction of the thyroid gland itself.
TSH-secreting pituitary adenomas are extremely rare causes of secondary hyperthyroidism and typically present with high, rather than low, TSH levels.
Graves disease is the leading etiology, characterized by the autoimmune production of thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins that activate the TSH receptor.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): Graves disease is the most common cause of endogenous hyperthyroidism.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
statement: What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism responsible for the infiltrative ophthalmopathy and resultant exophthalmos seen in patients with Graves disease?
options: Direct cytotoxic destruction of extraocular muscles by autoantibodies
Hypertrophy of the lacrimal glands resulting in anterior displacement of the globe
Overstimulation of Müller’s muscle by the sympathetic nervous system
Increased orbital volume due to cytokine-stimulated glycosaminoglycan synthesis
Excessive deposition of thyroid hormones in the orbital fat
correctOption: Increased orbital volume due to cytokine-stimulated glycosaminoglycan synthesis
optionExplanations: While T-cells are involved, the process is proliferative and infiltrative (inflammation and matrix deposition) rather than primary direct cytotoxic destruction of the muscles.
Lacrimal gland involvement is not the primary cause of exophthalmos; rather, it is the expansion of retro-orbital connective tissue and extraocular muscles themselves.
Sympathetic overstimulation causes lid lag and a wide stare, which are part of hyperthyroidism generally, but not the mechanical exophthalmos caused by retro-orbital tissue volume increase.
The exophthalmos is due to T-cell cytokines stimulating fibroblasts to produce hydrophilic glycosaminoglycans (like hyaluronic acid), which increases retro-orbital volume and pressure.
Thyroid hormones are not deposited in the orbit; the pathology is immune-mediated involving T-cell infiltration and secondary tissue remodeling.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): Activated CD4+ helper T cells secrete cytokines that stimulate fibroblast proliferation and synthesis of extracellular matrix proteins (glycosaminoglycans), leading to progressive infiltration of the retro-orbital space and ophthalmopathy. The protrusion of the eyeball (exopthalmos) is caused by an increase in the volume of the retro-orbital connective tissues and extraocular muscles

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: A 58-year-old multiparous woman presents with a firm, palpable periareolar mass and thick, white nipple discharge. Histological examination reveals ectatic ducts filled with inspissated debris. Which cell type is the characteristic finding within these dilated lumens?
options: Myoepithelial cells with clear cytoplasm
Malignant signet ring cells
Plasma cells forming periductal cuffs
Neutrophilic microabscesses
Lipid-laden macrophages
correctOption: Lipid-laden macrophages
optionExplanations: Myoepithelial cells are part of the normal double layer of the duct; they do not fill the lumen in this disorder.
Signet ring cells would indicate invasive lobular carcinoma, which is a critical differential but not a feature of benign inflammatory ectasia.
While plasma cells are part of the periductal inflammatory infiltrate (giving it the name 'plasma cell mastitis'), the luminal content is characterized specifically by macrophages.
Neutrophils are typical of acute mastitis; duct ectasia is a chronic, non-bacterial inflammatory process.
Lipid-laden macrophages (foamy cells) are the hallmark luminal finding in duct ectasia, reflecting the ingestion of fatty secretions within the dilated ducts.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1039 (Book Page): Ectatic dilated ducts are filled with inspissated secretions and numerous lipid-laden macrophages. With duct rupture, a marked periductal and interstitial chronic inflammatory reaction ensues, consisting of lymphocytes, macrophages, and variable numbers of plasma cells.

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
statement: A 32-year-old female undergoes bilateral adrenalectomy for the treatment of refractory Cushing disease. One year later, she presents with severe headaches, bitemporal hemianopsia, and marked hyperpigmentation of the skin. Laboratory tests show extremely high plasma ACTH levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Carney complex
Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome
Schmidt syndrome
Addison disease
Nelson syndrome
correctOption: Nelson syndrome
optionExplanations: Carney complex involves PRKAR1A mutations and spotty skin pigmentation but is a genetic syndrome involving multiple tumors, not a specific post-surgical complication of Cushing disease.
Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome involves acute adrenal failure due to massive hemorrhage, usually secondary to sepsis, not post-surgical pituitary expansion.
Schmidt syndrome is a form of autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome involving thyroiditis and adrenalitis, unrelated to post-adrenalectomy pituitary changes.
While she has symptoms of hypocortisolism-induced ACTH rise (hyperpigmentation), the presence of a mass effect (hemianopsia) after bilateral adrenalectomy specifically defines Nelson syndrome.
Nelson syndrome occurs when the negative feedback of cortisol is removed by adrenalectomy, allowing a pre-existing corticotroph microadenoma to expand rapidly and aggressively.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1070 (Book Page): Large destructive pituitary adenomas can develop in patients after surgical removal of the adrenal glands for treatment of Cushing syndrome. This condition, known as Nelson syndrome, occurs because of loss of the inhibitory effect of adrenal corticosteroids on a corticotroph microadenoma.

category: Enumerate clinical manifestations along with hormone levels of anterior pituitary
statement: During anterior pituitary organogenesis, several specialized cell lineages arise from common precursors. Which of the following transcription factors is essential for the development of somatotrophs, lactotrophs, and thyrotrophs?
options: PIT-1
Tbx19
GATA-2
SF-1
TPIT
correctOption: PIT-1
optionExplanations: PIT-1 is the primary transcription factor required for the terminal differentiation of the somatotroph (GH), lactotroph (PRL), and thyrotroph (TSH) lineages.
Tbx19 is another name for TPIT and is not associated with the somatotroph, lactotroph, or thyrotroph lineages.
GATA-2 is co-expressed with SF-1 in the development and differentiation of gonadotroph cells.
SF-1 (Steroidogenic factor-1) is a regulator involved in the differentiation of the gonadotroph lineage (FSH/LH).
TPIT is the transcription factor specifically required for the differentiation of the corticotroph lineage (ACTH).
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1065 (Book Page): Somatotrophs, mammosomatotrophs, lactotrophs, and thyrotrophs are all derived from a common precursor that expresses the transcription factor PIT-1

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
statement: A 52-year-old male with a BMI of 34 kg/m² presents with polyuria and thirst. Laboratory results confirm hyperglycemia. Pathophysiologically, his condition is classified as being caused by which combination of defects?
options: Autoantibodies against the insulin receptor causing severe resistance
Mitochondrial DNA mutations leading to impaired glucose sensing
Peripheral insulin resistance and inadequate secretory compensation
Primary autoimmune destruction and absolute insulin deficiency
Single-gene mutations affecting the glycolytic enzyme glucokinase
correctOption: Peripheral insulin resistance and inadequate secretory compensation
optionExplanations: This describes Type A insulin resistance, which is classified as a genetic defect in insulin action, not typical Type 2 diabetes associated with obesity.
This describes Maternally Inherited Diabetes and Deafness (MIDD), which is a specific monogenic category of beta-cell function defect.
Type 2 diabetes is etiologically unique because it requires both a failure of tissues to respond to insulin and a failure of beta cells to compensate for that resistance.
This describes Type 1 diabetes, which typically occurs in younger, non-obese individuals and involves absolute deficiency.
This describes MODY2, a monogenic form of diabetes classified under genetic defects of beta-cell function.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1097 (Book Page): Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is caused by a combination of peripheral resistance to insulin action and a secretory response by pancreatic β cells that is inadequate to overcome insulin resistance ('relative insulin deficiency').

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: Histologic examination of a breast mass in a patient with a history of autoimmune thyroiditis reveals atrophic lobules with thickened basement membranes and a prominent infiltrate of small lymphocytes. What is the most appropriate name for this condition?
options: Lymphocytic mastopathy
Granulomatous lobular mastitis
Complex sclerosing lesion
Sclerosing adenosis
Duct ectasia
correctOption: Lymphocytic mastopathy
optionExplanations: Lymphocytic mastopathy, also called sclerosing lymphocytic lobulitis, is a rare autoimmune-associated finding in the breast, classically linked to type 1 diabetes.
Granulomatous mastitis is characterized by granulomas, often associated with parity or infection, not the specific sclerosing lymphocytic pattern described.
Complex sclerosing lesions (radial scars) have a central nidus of entrapped glands and radiating fibrosis, distinct from the autoimmune lymphocytic pattern.
Sclerosing adenosis involves an increase in acini that are compressed by stroma, but not the specific diabetic-associated lymphocytic infiltrate.
Duct ectasia involves dilated ducts with plasma cells and macrophages, whereas this condition involves lobular atrophy and lymphocytes.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1039 (Book Page): Within the stroma are atrophic ducts and lobules with thickened basement membranes that are surrounded by a prominent lymphocytic infiltrate. This condition is most common in women with type 1 (insulin-dependent) diabetes or autoimmune thyroid disease.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
statement: A 49-year-old female presents with increasingly irregular and heavy uterine bleeding over six months. Endometrial biopsy reveals a dense stroma with areas of stromal condensation, eosinophilic epithelial metaplasia, and pseudostratified glands containing numerous mitotic figures. No secretory vacuoles are identified. What is the most likely pathophysiological state?
options: Structural bleeding due to a pedunculated endometrial polyp.
Chronic endometritis characterized by plasma cell infiltration.
Inadequate luteal phase bleeding with delayed secretory maturation.
Acute endometritis following retained products of conception.
Dysfunctional uterine bleeding secondary to repeated anovulatory cycles.
correctOption: Dysfunctional uterine bleeding secondary to repeated anovulatory cycles.
optionExplanations: Polyps are structural masses with altered stroma and thick-walled vessels; they are not primarily defined by these generalized hormonal epithelial changes.
Chronic endometritis requires the identification of plasma cells, which are not mentioned in this scenario focused on hormonal growth patterns.
Inadequate luteal phase would show secretory features, but they would be out of sync with the cycle day; the case specifically notes an absence of secretory vacuoles.
Acute endometritis is characterized by a nonspecific inflammatory response in the stroma, typically following delivery or miscarriage, not the proliferative features described.
The combination of proliferative features (mitoses, pseudostratification) and markers of breakdown (stromal condensation, metaplasia) without secretory changes is pathognomonic for anovulatory DUB.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1001 (Book Page): In this setting, biopsies reveal stromal condensation and eosinophilic epithelial metaplasia, features similar to those seen in menstrual endometrium. However, unlike menstrual endometrium, progesterone-dependent morphologic features... are absent... Most commonly, the endometrium is composed of pseudostratified glands and contains scattered mitotic figures.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
coreConcept: Predominant Cell Type in Parathyroid Adenoma
statement: Which cell type is most common within a typical parathyroid adenoma?
options: Chief cells
Sustentacular cells
Parafollicular cells
Water-clear cells
Oxyphil cells
correctOption: Chief cells
optionExplanations: Chief cells are the primary constituent of both the normal gland and the majority of parathyroid adenomas.
Sustentacular cells are supporting cells found in pheochromocytomas or paragangliomas.
Parafollicular cells (C cells) are located in the thyroid gland and secrete calcitonin.
Water-clear cells are a specific cytoplasmic variant seen more typically in a rare form of primary hyperplasia.
Oxyphil cells can be present in nests or form rare 'oxyphil adenomas,' but they are not the predominant cell in a typical adenoma.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): Microscopically, parathyroid adenomas are mostly composed of uniform, polygonal chief cells with small, centrally placed nuclei.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
statement: When distinguishing between primary and secondary adrenocortical insufficiency, which biochemical profile is most indicative of a secondary (pituitary-based) origin?
options: Massive bilateral adrenal hemorrhage
Elevated serum levels of ACTH and MSH
Marked hyperpigmentation of sun-exposed areas
Normal or near-normal aldosterone synthesis
Hyponatremia with severe hyperkalemia
correctOption: Normal or near-normal aldosterone synthesis
optionExplanations: Adrenal hemorrhage is a cause of primary acute insufficiency (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome), which involves direct destruction of the gland, not a secondary loss of stimulus.
Low, rather than elevated, levels of ACTH are the biochemical signature of secondary insufficiency caused by pituitary or hypothalamic failure.
Hyperpigmentation is a feature restricted to primary Addison disease where high ACTH/POMC levels occur; in secondary disease, ACTH levels are low, preventing darkening of the skin.
In secondary insufficiency, the adrenal glands are intact and the renin-angiotensin system can still stimulate aldosterone production, keeping mineralocorticoid levels relatively stable.
Severe hyponatremia and hyperkalemia are hallmarks of primary insufficiency because the mineralocorticoid (aldosterone) production is compromised when the adrenal cortex itself is destroyed.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1122 (Book Page): secondary hypoadrenalism is characterized by deficient cortisol and androgen output but normal or near-normal aldosterone synthesis.

category: Enumerate clinical manifestations along with hormone levels of anterior pituitary
statement: A 32-year-old woman experiences massive hemorrhage during the delivery of her child, requiring multiple transfusions. Six months later, she reports an inability to breastfeed, persistent amenorrhea, and increased sensitivity to cold. Which pathological process is most consistent with this presentation?
options: Lymphocytic hypophysitis
Rathke cleft cyst expansion
Pituitary apoplexy
Ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary
Primary empty sella syndrome
correctOption: Ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary
optionExplanations: Lymphocytic hypophysitis is an autoimmune inflammatory condition of the pituitary that often occurs late in pregnancy or postpartum but is not specifically associated with hemorrhagic shock.
Rathke cleft cysts are benign cysts that can cause pressure effects, but their pathogenesis is unrelated to obstetric hemorrhage.
Pituitary apoplexy involves sudden hemorrhage into an existing adenoma, presenting with acute headache and visual loss, not a gradual postpartum onset.

During pregnancy, the pituitary undergoes physiologic hyperplasia. This enlarged gland is supplied by a low-pressure venous portal system, making it highly vulnerable to ischemia if systemic blood pressure drops (e.g., postpartum hemorrhage). The clinical triad of failed lactation, amenorrhea, and hypothyroidism reflects panhypopituitarism.
Primary empty sella syndrome is an anatomic variant where the subarachnoid space herniates into the sella; it is typically seen in obese, multiparous women but is not triggered by acute hemorrhage.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1071 (Book Page): Sheehan syndrome, also known as postpartum necrosis, is the most common form of ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary. During pregnancy, the anterior pituitary enlarges... Any further reduction in blood supply caused by obstetric hemorrhage or shock may precipitate infarction.

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: Which of the following describes the dual therapeutic mechanism of propylthiouracil in the management of thyrotoxicosis?
options: Inhibition of iodine uptake and stimulation of thyroid hormone proteolysis
Inhibition of the sodium-iodide symporter and induction of T3 excretion
Blockade of TSH receptors and increased metabolic clearance of T3
Direct destruction of follicular cells and inhibition of adenyl cyclase
Inhibition of iodide oxidation and blocking peripheral deiodination of T4 to T3
correctOption: Inhibition of iodide oxidation and blocking peripheral deiodination of T4 to T3
optionExplanations: Iodide blocks the release of hormone by inhibiting proteolysis; propylthiouracil works on the synthesis and peripheral conversion instead.
Inhibition of the symporter is a mechanism of different agents (like perchlorate); propylthiouracil acts on oxidation and peripheral conversion.
Propylthiouracil does not block the TSH receptor directly; its action is on the biosynthetic enzymes and peripheral conversion.
Radioactive iodine causes follicular destruction, whereas propylthiouracil is a chemical inhibitor of hormone processing.
Propylthiouracil interferes with thyroid peroxidase-mediated oxidation (synthesis) and the peripheral conversion of the less active T4 to the more active T3.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1073 (Book Page): The antithyroid agent propylthiouracil inhibits the oxidation of iodide and thus blocks the production of thyroid hormones; propylthiouracil also inhibits the peripheral deiodination of circulating T4 into T3.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
statement: Which genetic association provides the strongest known link to the susceptibility of developing Type 1 Diabetes in Caucasian populations?
options: Mutations in the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene
HLA-DR3 or HLA-DR4 haplotypes
Polymorphisms in the TCF7L2 gene
Biallelic mutations in the AIRE gene
Activating mutations in the GNAS gene
correctOption: HLA-DR3 or HLA-DR4 haplotypes
optionExplanations: MEN1 mutations are associated with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1, which includes pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, not Type 1 Diabetes.
The MHC Class II region, specifically the DR3 and DR4 alleles, accounts for about 50% of the genetic susceptibility to Type 1 Diabetes.
TCF7L2 is one of the most significant genetic risk factors for Type 2 Diabetes, but it is not linked to the autoimmune Type 1 Diabetes.
While AIRE mutations cause Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome Type 1 (which includes diabetes), the HLA association is much more common in the general T1D population.
GNAS mutations are involved in pituitary somatotroph adenomas and McCune-Albright syndrome, unrelated to islet cell autoimmunity.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1099 (Book Page): Ninety percent to 95% of Caucasians with this disease have either an HLA-DR3 or HLA-DR4 haplotype

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: A 45-year-old male experiences a significant drop in blood pressure following acute blood loss. Which physiological pathway is most likely activated to stimulate the release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) for water conservation?
options: Inhibition of hypothalamic neuronal firing by hypervolemia
Suppression of the portal venous plexus flow to the stalk
Sensing of decreased pressure by baroreceptors in the atria and carotids
Activation of osmoreceptors in the anterior pituitary
Direct stimulation of pituicytes by circulating catecholamines
correctOption: Sensing of decreased pressure by baroreceptors in the atria and carotids
optionExplanations: Hypervolemia would inhibit ADH secretion to promote diuresis; in hypotension, this inhibitory mechanism is absent.
The portal venous plexus primarily carries releasing factors to the anterior pituitary, while ADH is transported via axons directly to the posterior lobe.
Baroreceptors located in the low-pressure atria and high-pressure carotid sinuses detect hypovolemia or hypotension, signaling the hypothalamus to release ADH.
Osmoreceptors are primarily hypothalamic, and ADH release is triggered by an increase in plasma osmotic pressure, not anterior pituitary activation.
Pituicytes are supporting glial cells and do not directly synthesize or release ADH in response to catecholamines.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1065 (Book Page): Decreased blood pressure, sensed by baroreceptors (pressure-sensing receptors) in the cardiac atria and carotids, stimulates ADH release.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Diffuse and Multinodular goiter
coreConcept: Clinical presentation of plunging multinodular goiter
statement: A 58-year-old female presents with an asymmetrically enlarged thyroid gland weighing approximately 1.5 kg. Radiographic imaging shows the mass extending behind the sternum, and the patient reports difficulty swallowing. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Multinodular goiter
Thyroglossal duct cyst
Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis
Papillary microcarcinoma
Diffuse nontoxic goiter
correctOption: Multinodular goiter
optionExplanations: Multinodular goiter (MNG) is associated with the most extreme glandular enlargement, often exceeding 1000g. Its irregular growth pattern frequently leads to compression of the esophagus (dysphagia) and intrathoracic extension.
Thyroglossal duct cysts are typically small (2-3 cm) midline structures, not massive plunging masses.
Granulomatous thyroiditis typically presents with pain and transient hyperthyroidism rather than a massive, chronic obstructive mass.
Papillary microcarcinomas are by definition less than 1 cm in size and would not cause the massive enlargement or compressive symptoms described.
Diffuse nontoxic goiter usually results in modest, symmetric enlargement, rarely reaching the extreme weights associated with multinodular forms.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1082 (Book Page): Multinodular goiters produce the most extreme thyroid enlargements... the goiter grows behind the sternum and clavicles to produce the intrathoracic or plunging goiter.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Diffuse and Multinodular goiter
statement: The most common global underlying cause for the development of both diffuse and multinodular goiter is which of the following?
options: Chronic ingestion of high-selenium foods
Mutations in the RET proto-oncogene
Autoimmune-mediated follicular destruction
Autonomous TSH-independent hormone synthesis
Dietary iodine deficiency
correctOption: Dietary iodine deficiency
optionExplanations: Selenium deficiency, rather than excess, is sometimes associated with thyroid issues, but iodine deficiency remains the nearly universal primary cause of endemic goiter.
RET mutations are specifically linked to medullary thyroid carcinoma and are not involved in the pathogenesis of common compensatory goiters.
Autoimmune destruction is characteristic of Hashimoto thyroiditis, which leads to hypothyroidism, but it is not the primary cause of simple or multinodular goiter.
Autonomous synthesis is the hallmark of toxic adenomas or toxic multinodular goiter (Plummer syndrome), but it is a secondary development, not the primary cause of goiter itself.
In environments where iodine is scarce, the thyroid cannot synthesize adequate thyroid hormone, triggering a compensatory rise in TSH that results in glandular hypertrophy and hyperplasia.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1080 (Book Page): Enlargement of the thyroid, or goiter, is caused by impaired synthesis of thyroid hormone, which is most often the result of dietary iodine deficiency.

category: Hashimoto Thyroiditis ii
coreConcept: Differential morphology of fibrosing thyroid lesions
statement: The histology of Hashimoto thyroiditis can sometimes be confused with other forms of thyroiditis. Which morphological feature best helps distinguish Hashimoto from Reidel thyroiditis?
options: Destruction of thyroid follicles
Infiltration by plasma cells
Presence of Hürthle cell metaplasia
Extent of fibrosis beyond the thyroid capsule
Presence of a lymphoid infiltrate
correctOption: Extent of fibrosis beyond the thyroid capsule
optionExplanations: Both conditions result in the loss of normal thyroid follicles as they are replaced by either lymphoid tissue or dense fibrous tissue.
Both conditions can have plasma cells; Reidel thyroiditis specifically involves IgG4-secreting plasma cells.
Hürthle cells are very common in Hashimoto but usually absent in Reidel thyroiditis, but the capsular extension is the most definitive surgical/gross distinction.
In Hashimoto, fibrosis is confined to the gland. In Reidel thyroiditis (an IgG4-related disease), the intense fibrosis extends into adjacent neck structures, mimicking malignancy.
Both conditions feature inflammatory infiltrates, though the nature of the infiltrate in Hashimoto is classically lymphocytic with germinal centers.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1077 (Book Page): In “classic” Hashimoto thyroiditis, interstitial connective tissue is increased and may be abundant. Unlike Reidel thyroiditis (see later), the fibrosis does not extend beyond the capsule of the gland.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
statement: How can the small papillae seen in Graves-related follicular hyperplasia be morphologically distinguished from those in papillary thyroid carcinoma?
options: Graves papillae are always associated with psammoma bodies
Graves papillae possess dense fibrovascular cores
Graves papillae show Orphan Annie eye nuclei
Graves papillae lack central fibrovascular stalks
Graves papillae demonstrate nuclear pseudo-inclusions
correctOption: Graves papillae lack central fibrovascular stalks
optionExplanations: Psammoma bodies (concentric calcifications) are virtually pathognomonic for papillary carcinoma and are not found in Graves hyperplasia.
Dense fibrovascular cores are characteristic of malignancy (papillary carcinoma); hyperplasia in Graves results from cell crowding without organizing into complex stalks.
Optically clear (Orphan Annie) nuclei are the diagnostic hallmark of papillary carcinoma, not Graves disease.
The papillae in Graves disease are simply intrafollicular projections of crowded, tall epithelial cells and crucially lack a supportive fibrovascular core or stalk.
Nuclear inclusions and grooves are diagnostic features of papillary thyroid cancer, whereas Graves nuclei remain uniform and monomorphic.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1081 (Book Page): [Such papillae lack fibrovascular cores, in contrast to those of papillary carcinoma.]

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: A 68-year-old male with a history of heavy smoking presents with progressive confusion, lethargy, and a recent seizure. Physical examination reveals no peripheral edema or signs of dehydration. Laboratory results show a serum sodium of 118 mEq/L and a urine osmolality that is significantly higher than expected for his serum concentration. Imaging reveals a mass in the right lung apex. Which of the following is the most likely pathological driver of his symptoms?
options: Excessive thirst due to hypothalamic tumor stimulation
Renal tubular resistance to circulating vasopressin
Adrenal cortical insufficiency leading to salt wasting
Destruction of the neurohypophysis by metastatic disease
Ectopic secretion of ADH by a small-cell lung carcinoma
correctOption: Ectopic secretion of ADH by a small-cell lung carcinoma
optionExplanations: Hypothalamic stimulation of thirst (polydipsia) would lead to diluted urine, not the concentrated urine seen in this patient's SIADH profile.
Renal resistance (nephrogenic DI) would cause polyuria and hypernatremia, not the hyponatremia and water retention observed here.
While adrenal insufficiency can cause hyponatremia, it typically involves volume depletion and hyperkalemia, and does not correlate with the lung mass finding.
Destruction of the neurohypophysis would cause Diabetes Insipidus, which presents with hypernatremia and dilute urine, the exact opposite of this case.
The clinical picture of severe hyponatremia, neurologic dysfunction, lack of edema, and a lung mass is classic for SIADH caused by ectopic ADH secretion from a small-cell lung carcinoma.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1072 (Book Page): The most frequent causes of SIADH are the secretion of ectopic ADH by malignant neoplasms (particularly small-cell carcinoma of the lung)... The clinical manifestations of SIADH are dominated by hyponatremia, cerebral edema, and resultant neurologic dysfunction.

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
coreConcept: Clinical Presentation of de Quervain Thyroiditis
statement: Which clinical symptom is considered the most common presenting complaint in patients with granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis?
options: Chronic progressive hoarseness
Cold intolerance and constipation
Exophthalmos and proptosis
Painless rapid weight loss
Anterior neck pain
correctOption: Anterior neck pain
optionExplanations: Hoarseness typically suggests compression of the recurrent laryngeal nerve by advanced malignancy or a large goiter, not typically seen in this self-limiting condition.
Cold intolerance and constipation are symptoms of hypothyroidism; while these can occur in the post-inflammatory phase, pain is the primary presentation.
Exophthalmos is unique to Graves disease and results from autoimmune-mediated orbital tissue expansion; it is absent in granulomatous thyroiditis.
Painless weight loss is characteristic of hyperthyroidism, which can occur in this condition, but the defining and most common feature is localized pain.
Pain is the hallmark clinical feature of de Quervain thyroiditis, often presenting as sudden or gradual soreness in the thyroid region.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): Granulomatous thyroiditis is the most common cause of thyroid pain.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
statement: Activating mutations in the KCNJ11 and ABCC8 genes, which encode components of the ATP-sensitive potassium channel, are the primary cause of which diabetic category?
options: Maturity-onset diabetes of the young, type 3
Type A insulin resistance
Autoimmune Type 1 Diabetes
Cystic fibrosis-related diabetes
Neonatal diabetes
correctOption: Neonatal diabetes
optionExplanations: MODY3 is caused by mutations in Hepatocyte nuclear factor 1 alpha (HNF1A), not potassium channel genes.
Type A insulin resistance involves the insulin receptor, not the secretory apparatus of the beta-cell.
Type 1 diabetes is classified by autoimmune markers (HLA linkage), not activating channel mutations.
Cystic fibrosis-related diabetes is classified as an exocrine pancreatic defect resulting from structural damage.
Neonatal diabetes is distinctively caused by these channel mutations, which prevent the beta-cell from depolarizing and releasing insulin.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1097 (Book Page): Table 24.6: Neonatal diabetes (activating mutations in KCNJ11 and ABCC8, encoding Kir6.2 and SUR1, respectively).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: A patient presents with hypertension and truncal obesity. Lab tests reveal elevated serum cortisol and elevated serum ACTH. A high-dose dexamethasone suppression test results in a significant reduction in urinary steroid excretion. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?
options: Ectopic secretion of CRH by a bronchial carcinoid
Functional adrenocortical carcinoma
Bilateral micronodular adrenal hyperplasia
Small-cell carcinoma of the lung
Pituitary ACTH-secreting microadenoma
correctOption: Pituitary ACTH-secreting microadenoma
optionExplanations: Ectopic CRH is extremely rare and typically presents like ectopic ACTH with failure to suppress.
Primary adrenal tumors are ACTH-independent; serum ACTH would be low, and steroids would not suppress with dexamethasone.
This is an ACTH-independent cause; ACTH would be low, and cortisol production would be autonomous (non-suppressible).
Ectopic ACTH from lung cancer typically does not suppress even with high doses of dexamethasone.
Pituitary-dependent Cushing disease maintains partial feedback sensitivity; thus, high-dose dexamethasone can suppress ACTH and cortisol levels, unlike ectopic or adrenal sources.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1116 (Book Page): In pituitary Cushing syndrome, the most common form, ACTH levels are elevated and are not suppressed by the administration of a low dose of dexamethasone... After higher doses of injected dexamethasone, however, the pituitary responds by reducing ACTH secretion, which is reflected by suppression of urinary steroid secretion.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
statement: A 35-year-old male with a history of recurrent pulmonary infections and chronic malabsorption due to Cystic Fibrosis is found to have a fasting plasma glucose of 140 mg/dL. According to the etiological classification of diabetes, his condition is best categorized as:
options: Genetic defect in ̠-cell function
Endocrinopathy-associated diabetes
Exocrine pancreatic defect (Type 3C)
Type 1 Immune-mediated Diabetes
Genetic defect in insulin action
correctOption: Exocrine pancreatic defect (Type 3C)
optionExplanations: Genetic defects in ̠-cell function refer to MODY or neonatal diabetes, where the defect is intrinsic to the cell's signaling/secretion, not global organ destruction.
Endocrinopathies include conditions like Acromegaly or Cushing's where excess counter-regulatory hormones cause diabetes, which is not the case in Cystic Fibrosis.
Cystic Fibrosis causes structural damage to the pancreas, including the islets, leading to pancreatogenic or Type 3C diabetes.
There is no evidence of an autoimmune attack in this patient; his hyperglycemia is a consequence of the systemic organ damage associated with Cystic Fibrosis.
Defects in insulin action (like Type A resistance) involve the receptors or signaling pathways, not the physical destruction of the gland seen in Cystic Fibrosis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1097 (Book Page): Table 24.6 Classification of Diabetes... Exocrine Pancreatic Defects (“Pancreatogenic” or Type 3C Diabetes): Chronic pancreatitis, Pancreatectomy/trauma, Pancreatic cancer, Cystic fibrosis, Hemochromatosis, Fibrocalculous pancreatopathy.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
statement: In the clinical progression of chronic adrenocortical insufficiency, what is the minimum percentage of functional adrenal cortex that must typically be lost before definitive clinical symptoms appear?
optionExplanations: Addison disease is characterized by a massive loss of functional parenchyma; the body remains remarkably resilient until approximately 9/10ths of the tissue is non-functional.
Total destruction (100%) results in immediate adrenal crisis, but the clinical diagnosis of chronic insufficiency is made well before this absolute state is reached.
At 50% loss, the remaining adrenal tissue is highly capable of maintaining baseline steroid production through hypertrophy and increased biosynthetic efficiency.
A 60% reduction in cortical mass typically remains asymptomatic under normal physiological conditions due to significant functional reserves.
Even at 75% loss, the adrenal glands can usually meet standard metabolic demands, though the reserve to handle extreme stress may be reduced.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1121 (Book Page): Typically, clinical manifestations of adrenocortical insufficiency do not appear until at least 90% of the adrenal cortex has been compromised.

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: What is the direct consequence of the hormone-receptor interaction in the collecting ducts during an episode of SIADH?
options: Inhibition of aquaporin channels leading to polyuria.
Excessive resorption of free water resulting in hyponatremia.
Increased excretion of sodium resulting in hypernatremia.
Stimulation of the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone.
Contraction of vascular smooth muscle causing systemic hypertension.
correctOption: Excessive resorption of free water resulting in hyponatremia.
optionExplanations: Inhibition of water channels occurs in diabetes insipidus; SIADH involves the inappropriate activation of these mechanisms.
In SIADH, the excess ADH causes the kidneys to reabsorb too much water, diluting the blood and leading to hyponatremia and potentially cerebral edema.
SIADH causes hyponatremia (low sodium concentration) due to water retention; it does not cause hypernatremia.
Aldosterone is regulated primarily by the renin-angiotensin system and potassium levels, not by ADH levels from the posterior pituitary.
While ADH (vasopressin) has vasoconstrictive properties at high levels, the dominant clinical feature of SIADH is electrolyte imbalance rather than hypertension.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1072 (Book Page): ADH excess causes over-resorption of free water, resulting in hyponatremia... The clinical manifestations of SIADH are dominated by hyponatremia, cerebral edema, and resultant neurologic dysfunction.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
coreConcept: Pathogenesis of Squamous Metaplasia of Lactiferous Ducts
statement: What is the primary pathological mechanism that leads to the development of an erythematous subareolar mass and subsequent nipple inversion in a patient with Zuska disease?
options: Infiltration of the dermal lymphatics by malignant emboli
Hypertrophy of the smooth muscle of the areola
Keratinizing metaplasia extending deep into the lactiferous ducts
Atrophy of the terminal duct lobular units
Congenital failure of the nipple to evert during puberty
correctOption: Keratinizing metaplasia extending deep into the lactiferous ducts
optionExplanations: Dermal lymphatic infiltration is the hallmark of inflammatory carcinoma (peau d'orange), not the reactive inflammatory scarring seen in squamous metaplasia.
The smooth muscle is not hypertrophic; rather, it is the site where the fistula tract eventually burrows beneath to open at the areolar edge.

Keratin shed from the metaplastic squamous lining becomes trapped, plugging the ductal system and causing dilation and rupture, which elicits an intense inflammatory response and scarring that retracts the nipple.
This condition involves the major nipple ducts rather than the terminal duct lobular units (TDLUs), which are the site of involutional and fibrocystic changes.
Nipple inversion in this condition is acquired due to inflammatory traction, distinguishing it from congenital nipple inversion which corrects with simple traction.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1038 (Book Page): The key feature is keratinizing squamous metaplasia, which extends into the nipple duct well past the usual point of transition from squamous to glandular epithelium.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: A 48-year-old female with a history of MEN-1 presents with hypercalcemia. Technetium-sestamibi scan shows heterogeneous uptake in all four parathyroid glands. Biopsy of one gland reveals multinodular chief cell proliferation with scant stromal fat. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
options: Primary parathyroid adenoma
Chief cell atrophy
Primary parathyroid hyperplasia
Parathyroid oxyphil adenoma
Parathyroid carcinoma
correctOption: Primary parathyroid hyperplasia
optionExplanations: Adenomas are usually solitary and associated with suppression of the other three glands; the sestamibi scan showing all four glands active rules this out.
Atrophy would involve increased stromal fat and shrunken cells, the opposite of what is seen in hypercalcemia.
The combination of MEN-1 history, involvement of all four glands (multiglandular), and multinodular chief cell proliferation with reduced fat characterizes primary hyperplasia.
While oxyphil cells can be part of the process, 'hyperplasia' is the diagnosis describing the multiglandular condition associated with MEN syndromes.
Carcinoma typically presents as a single large mass with specific invasive features, not multiglandular multinodular proliferation.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): [Primary hyperplasia may occur sporadically or as a component of MEN syndrome. ... chief cell hyperplasia, which may involve the glands in a diffuse or multinodular pattern. ... As in the case of adenomas, stromal fat is inconspicuous within hyperplastic glands.]

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
statement: Neonatal testicular torsion differs from adult torsion in that it typically:
options: Is primarily treated with antibiotics rather than surgery
Never results in testicular infarction
Lacks any associated anatomic defect to account for its occurrence
Is always bilateral at the time of presentation
Occurs only in patients with the bell-clapper abnormality
correctOption: Lacks any associated anatomic defect to account for its occurrence
optionExplanations: Torsion is always a mechanical/vascular emergency requiring surgery or manual untwisting, regardless of age; antibiotics are for infections.
Neonatal torsion frequently results in infarction and 'vanishing testis' if it occurs in utero.
Neonatal torsion is often 'extravaginal' and occurs without the specific anatomic pre-dispositions defined in older patients.
While it can be bilateral, it is not 'always' so; the distinguishing factor is the lack of a known anatomic defect.
The bell-clapper abnormality is the predisposing factor for adult (adolescent) torsion, not neonatal torsion.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 968 (Book Page): Neonatal torsion occurs either in utero or shortly after birth. It lacks any associated anatomic defect to account for its occurrence.

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
statement: Which underlying condition is identified as the most important predisposition for the abnormal implantation of a fetus within the fallopian tube?
options: Hypermethylation of the BRCA1 promoter in tubal epithelium
Chronic salpingitis following pelvic inflammatory disease
Congenital absence of the Bartolin gland
Excessive production of Prolactin by a pituitary microadenoma
In utero exposure to Diethylstilbestrol (DES)
correctOption: Chronic salpingitis following pelvic inflammatory disease
optionExplanations: BRCA1 promoter methylation is related to the development of serous carcinomas, not the mechanical mechanisms of ectopic pregnancy.
Chronic salpingitis leads to intraluminal scarring, which physically hinders the passage of the ovum, causing it to implant in the tube rather than the uterus.
Bartholin gland anomalies affect the vulva and do not influence the implantation sites of the fetus in the upper genital tract.
Hyperprolactinemia causes amenorrhea and infertility but does not directly cause the anatomical scarring that leads to ectopic implantation.
DES exposure is associated with vaginal adenosis and clear cell carcinoma, not primarily as the leading cause of ectopic pregnancy.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1027 (Book Page): The most important predisposing condition, present in 35% to 50% of patients, is prior pelvic inflammatory disease resulting in intraluminal fallopian tube scarring (chronic salpingitis).

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Diffuse and Multinodular goiter
statement: On gross examination of a thyroidectomy specimen, the surgeon notes a brown, somewhat glassy, and translucent cut surface. This appearance is highly suggestive of which specific entity?
options: Toxic adenoma with hemorrhage
Papillary microcarcinoma
Colloid goiter
Medullary carcinoma with amyloid
Densely granulated somatotroph adenoma
correctOption: Colloid goiter
optionExplanations: Toxic adenomas are usually solid, yellow-to-brown, and may show hemorrhage, but are not described as glassy/translucent throughout.
Papillary microcarcinoma is typically a small, firm, gray-white infiltrative or circumscribed lesion.
The accumulation of large amounts of gelatinous colloid gives the gland its characteristic glassy, translucent brown appearance.
Medullary carcinoma is firm, pale gray to tan, and often infiltrative, not glassy/translucent.
Somatotroph adenomas are pituitary tumors, not thyroid lesions.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1081 (Book Page): In these cases, the cut surface of the thyroid is usually brown, somewhat glassy, and translucent. ... The term colloid goiter has been applied to this condition.

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: A 58-year-old female presents with recurrent nephrolithiasis, generalized bone pain, and chronic constipation. Laboratory workup reveals a serum calcium of 11.8 mg/dL, a serum phosphate of 2.2 mg/dL, and a significantly elevated serum parathyroid hormone level. Imaging identifies a solitary 2.1 cm nodule inferior to the left thyroid lobe. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Hypercalcemia of malignancy with PTHrP secretion
Secondary hyperparathyroidism due to Vitamin D deficiency
Primary hyperparathyroidism caused by a parathyroid adenoma
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism following renal transplant
Pseudohypoparathyroidism with end-organ resistance
correctOption: Primary hyperparathyroidism caused by a parathyroid adenoma
optionExplanations: Malignancy-associated hypercalcemia would show low or undetectable PTH, as the high calcium would suppress the parathyroid glands.
Secondary hyperparathyroidism is typically associated with hypocalcemia or low-normal calcium, not hypercalcemia.
The combination of hypercalcemia, hypophosphatemia, elevated PTH, stones, and bone pain is the classic presentation of primary hyperparathyroidism.
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism involves autonomous secretion after long-standing renal failure, but the presence of a solitary nodule in a previously healthy patient points to a primary adenoma.
Pseudohypoparathyroidism is characterized by hypocalcemia and resistance to PTH, not hypercalcemia with symptomatic hyperparathyroidism.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1093 (Book Page): Primary hyperparathyroidism is associated with 'painful bones, renal stones, abdominal groans, and psychic moans.' ... abnormalities most directly related to hyperparathyroidism are nephrolithiasis and bone disease.

category: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
coreConcept: Diagnostic Histology of De Quervain Thyroiditis
statement: Which of the following findings is the most common histological hallmark that confirms a diagnosis of subacute granulomatous thyroiditis?
options: Atrophic follicles and replacement by dense fibrous tissue into strap muscles
Extensive stromal amyloid deposits staining with Congo Red
Lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with Hürthle cell metaplasia
Small follicles with 'Orphan Annie eye' nuclei
Granulomas containing multinucleate giant cells around colloid
correctOption: Granulomas containing multinucleate giant cells around colloid
optionExplanations: Dense fibrous tissue extending into neck muscles is the classic definition of Riedel thyroiditis, distinguishing it from the encapsulated fibrosis of granulomatous thyroiditis.
Amyloid deposits are characteristic of Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma, which is derived from C-cells, not follicles.
Hürthle cell metaplasia and lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates are characteristic of Hashimoto thyroiditis.
Nuclei with dispersed chromatin ('Orphan Annie eye') are the diagnostic requirement for Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma.
The hallmark of De Quervain's is the granulomatous reaction. This is composed of activated macrophages and multinucleate giant cells reacting to the escaped colloid from ruptured follicles.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1078 (Book Page): Multinucleate giant cells enclose pools of colloid, hence the designation granulomatous thyroiditis.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
statement: Which of the following physiological sequences correctly describes the progression of events in untreated testicular torsion?
options: Basement membrane thickening -> Loss of spermatogonia -> Hyalinization
Neutrophilic infiltration -> Abscess -> Suppuration -> Fibrosis
Arterial occlusion -> Venous congestion -> Pallor -> Atrophy
Lymphatic obstruction -> Hydrocele -> Compression -> Ischemia
Venous obstruction -> Arterial patency -> Engorgement -> Hemorrhagic infarction
correctOption: Venous obstruction -> Arterial patency -> Engorgement -> Hemorrhagic infarction
optionExplanations: This describes the chronic histologic changes seen in cryptorchidism (Page 968), not acute torsion.
This sequence describes the progression of acute bacterial inflammation/infection, not a vascular twist.
Torsion starts with venous, not arterial, occlusion; arterial patency is what causes the 'hemorrhagic' nature of the infarct.
While lymphatics may be compressed, the clinical emergency is driven by venous/arterial dynamics, not simple fluid accumulation in the tunica (hydrocele).
The obstruction of thin veins with continued arterial inflow leads to massive blood accumulation (engorgement) and eventual tissue death with internal bleeding (hemorrhagic infarction).
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 968 (Book Page): The thick-walled arteries remain patent, producing intense vascular engorgement followed by hemorrhagic infarction.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
coreConcept: Specificity of TSI in Graves disease
statement: Which specific autoantibody subtype is detected in approximately 90% of patients with Graves disease and is considered a primary diagnostic hallmark of the disorder?
options: Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI)
Anti-thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibody
TSH receptor blocking antibody
Anti-thyroglobulin antibody
Anti-microsomal antibody
correctOption: Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI)
optionExplanations: TSI is an IgG autoantibody that binds to the TSH receptor, mimicking the actions of TSH and stimulating the release of thyroid hormones, found in nearly 90% of Graves cases.
Anti-TPO antibodies are characteristic markers for Hashimoto thyroiditis and are not the primary driver of hyperthyroidism in Graves disease.
TSH receptor blocking antibodies are found in a small minority of Graves patients and actually lead to hypothyroidism rather than the classic hyperthyroid state.
Anti-thyroglobulin antibodies are commonly found in Hashimoto thyroiditis and various other thyroid conditions, making them non-specific for Graves disease.
Anti-microsomal antibodies are an older classification largely synonymous with anti-TPO antibodies and are more typical of destructive autoimmune thyroiditis like Hashimoto.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): The most common antibody subtype, known as thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI), is observed in approximately 90% of patients.

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: A 28-year-old female with a known history of Graves disease is brought to the emergency department with a high fever (104°F), marked tachycardia (160 bpm), and atrial fibrillation. The episode was preceded by an acute upper respiratory infection. What is the most likely pathophysiological trigger for this acute clinical deterioration?
options: Sudden decrease in thyroxine-binding globulin
Rapid onset of pituitary thyrotroph hyperplasia
Development of antithyroid peroxidase antibodies
Ischemic necrosis of the thyroid follicles
Acute elevation in catecholamine levels
correctOption: Acute elevation in catecholamine levels
optionExplanations: Changes in binding globulins can alter total hormone levels but are not the primary drivers of life-threatening thyroid storm.
Pituitary hyperplasia is a chronic response to T3/T4 deficiency (hypothyroidism), not an acute trigger for hypermetabolic thyroid storm.
Anti-TPO antibodies are present in many thyroid conditions but do not cause acute systemic hypermetabolic crises.
Ischemic necrosis would likely stop hormone production; thyroid storm is characterized by massive, uncontrolled hormonal effects.
Thyroid storm is an emergency characterized by a surge in catecholamines in a patient with underlying hyperthyroidism, often triggered by stress or infection.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1073 (Book Page): Thyroid storm refers to the abrupt onset of severe hyperthyroidism. ... This condition ... probably results from an acute elevation in catecholamine levels, as might be encountered during infection, surgery, cessation of antithyroid medication, or any form of stress.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
statement: A 45-year-old male presents for a routine check-up. According to the current diagnostic criteria for diabetes mellitus, which of the following fasting plasma glucose levels is the minimum threshold required to establish a diagnosis of diabetes?
options: 100 mg/dL
115 mg/dL
140 mg/dL
126 mg/dL
200 mg/dL
correctOption: 126 mg/dL
optionExplanations: 100 mg/dL is the upper limit of normal fasting glucose; levels between 100 and 125 mg/dL are classified as prediabetes or impaired fasting glucose.
115 mg/dL falls within the range for impaired fasting glucose (prediabetes) and is not sufficient for a diagnosis of frank diabetes.
While 140 mg/dL is high, it is not the minimum threshold; the threshold is set at 126 mg/dL to allow for earlier intervention.
A fasting plasma glucose level of 126 mg/dL or higher, confirmed on repeat testing, is a standard criterion for the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus.
200 mg/dL is the threshold for a random plasma glucose test in a symptomatic patient or a 2-hour glucose tolerance test, but not for fasting glucose.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1096 (Book Page): A fasting plasma glucose ≥ 126 mg/dL

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: A patient with symptoms of thyroid hormone excess undergoes a radioactive iodine uptake scan. The results show a significant decrease in uptake across the entire gland. Which of the following conditions most likely explains this finding?
options: Subacute thyroiditis
Toxic adenoma
TSH-secreting pituitary tumor
Graves disease
Multinodular goiter
correctOption: Subacute thyroiditis
optionExplanations: Thyroiditis involves the release of preformed hormones from damaged follicles rather than increased synthesis, resulting in low radioactive iodine uptake during the thyrotoxic phase.
A toxic adenoma would show increased uptake localized to a solitary functional 'hot' nodule, with suppression of the rest of the gland.
Secondary hyperthyroidism from a pituitary tumor would typically show increased uptake due to the high levels of stimulating TSH.
Graves disease shows diffusely increased radioactive iodine uptake because the entire gland is hyper-functioning due to TSH-receptor stimulation.
Toxic multinodular goiters show an uneven, heterogeneous pattern of uptake with multiple areas of increased activity.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1074 (Book Page): Once the diagnosis of thyrotoxicosis has been confirmed... measurement of radioactive iodine uptake... there may be diffusely increased uptake in the gland (Graves disease)... or decreased uptake (thyroiditis).

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
statement: In Graves disease, the infiltrative ophthalmopathy is primarily driven by which cytokine-mediated cellular event?
options: Infiltration of the retro-orbital space by T cells and glycosaminoglycans
Increased sympathetic tone in the superior tarsal muscle
Malignant transformation of orbital melanocytes
Direct autoimmune destruction of the optic nerve by B cells
Accumulation of fat within the lens of the eye
correctOption: Infiltration of the retro-orbital space by T cells and glycosaminoglycans
optionExplanations: Cytokines from T cells stimulate fibroblasts to produce hydrophilic GAGs, which trap water and expand the orbital tissue volume.
Sympathetic overactivity causes lid lag and a staring gaze, but not the true infiltrative proptosis seen in Graves.
There is no malignant component to the ophthalmopathy of Graves disease.
The ophthalmopathy involves the soft tissues of the orbit, not primary destruction of the nerve itself.
While adipocytes may increase, the primary cause of volume increase is edema and matrix protein deposition.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): Activated CD4+ helper T cells secrete cytokines that stimulate fibroblast proliferation and synthesis of extracellular matrix proteins (glycosaminoglycans), leading to progressive infiltration of the retro-orbital space and ophthalmopathy.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
