Parafollicular C cells are located in the thyroid gland and secrete calcitonin; they are the origin of medullary thyroid carcinoma, not parathyroid lesions.
Chromaffin cells are the catecholamine-secreting cells of the adrenal medulla and are associated with pheochromocytoma.
Syncytiotrophoblasts are multinucleated cells found in choriocarcinoma or the placenta, and are not a feature of parathyroid tissue.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): Microscopically, parathyroid adenomas are mostly composed of uniform, polygonal chief cells with small, centrally placed nuclei.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
statement: When contrasting the acute metabolic complications of diabetes, which mechanism best explains why ketoacidosis is significantly less common in patients with type 2 diabetes compared to those with type 1 diabetes?
options: Increased renal threshold for glucose prevents the development of osmotic diuresis
Higher peripheral insulin resistance prevents fatty acid entry into mitochondria
The presence of higher portal vein insulin levels inhibits hepatic fatty acid oxidation
The absence of epinephrine release during stress in type 2 diabetic patients
Reduced levels of glucagon in type 2 diabetes prevent ketone body synthesis
correctOption: The presence of higher portal vein insulin levels inhibits hepatic fatty acid oxidation
optionExplanations: The renal threshold is not significantly different; T2D patients still experience glycosuria and osmotic diuresis, often leading to hyperosmolar states.
Insulin resistance affects glucose uptake but portal insulin levels specifically regulate the metabolic switch to ketogenesis in the liver.
In T2D, residual insulin secretion maintains portal levels sufficient to block unrestricted fatty acid oxidation in the liver, preventing the massive ketone production seen in T1D.
Stress-induced epinephrine release occurs in all patients and typically worsens hyperglycemia by stimulating glucagon and blocking residual insulin action.
Glucagon is typically elevated or inappropriately high in both types of diabetes, contributing to hyperglycemia; it is the presence of insulin that suppresses ketogenesis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1104 (Book Page): The lower frequency of ketoacidosis in T2D is believed to be due to higher portal vein insulin levels in these patients, which prevents unrestricted hepatic fatty acid oxidation and keeps the formation of ketone bodies in check.

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: A patient is evaluated for chronic polyuria. Following a period of water deprivation, the urine remains dilute. However, the administration of exogenous ADH results in a rapid increase in urine osmolality and a decrease in urine volume. These results confirm which underlying pathology?
options: Central Diabetes Insipidus due to ADH deficiency.
Hypopituitarism resulting from a Rathke cleft cyst.
Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus due to renal unresponsiveness.
Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH (SIADH) from ectopic secretion.
Primary hyperaldosteronism causing osmotic diuresis.
correctOption: Central Diabetes Insipidus due to ADH deficiency.
optionExplanations: If the polyuria corrects with exogenous ADH, it proves the kidney is capable of responding but the body was not producing enough hormone, diagnostic of Central DI.
While a cyst can cause hypopituitarism, the specific response to ADH testing points to the subtype of DI rather than the mechanical cause of pituitary failure.
In nephrogenic DI, the kidneys would not respond to exogenous ADH, and the urine would remain dilute.
SIADH presents with hyponatremia and concentrated urine, not the polyuria and dilute urine described here.
Hyperaldosteronism affects sodium/potassium, not primarily ADH-mediated water resorption.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1072 (Book Page): Diabetes insipidus from ADH deficiency is designated as central to differentiate it from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, which is a result of renal tubular unresponsiveness to circulating ADH.

category: Hashimoto Thyroiditis ii
statement: What is the cellular basis for the appearance of Hürthle cells commonly observed in the atrophic follicles of a gland affected by Hashimoto thyroiditis?
options: Accumulation of lipid-rich vacuoles due to defective beta-oxidation
Hypertrophy of cells in response to excessive TSH stimulation
Metaplastic response of follicular epithelium to chronic autoimmune injury
Infiltration of the follicular lumen by cytotoxic CD8+ T lymphocytes
Clonal neoplastic proliferation of the parafollicular C cells
correctOption: Metaplastic response of follicular epithelium to chronic autoimmune injury
optionExplanations: The granular appearance of Hürthle cells is due to packed mitochondria, not lipid vacuoles. Lipid-rich cells are more characteristic of the adrenal cortex.
While TSH is elevated in Hashimoto, the Hürthle cell phenotype is specifically a response to injury and inflammation rather than simple TSH-induced hypertrophy.
Hürthle cell change is a classic metaplastic adaptation where the follicular cells become enlarged with eosinophilic granular cytoplasm in response to the chronic stress of the autoimmune attack.
Lymphocytes infiltrate the interstitium and form germinal centers, but the Hürthle cells are the altered follicular epithelial cells themselves, not the infiltrating cells.
Hürthle cells are derived from follicular cells, not C cells. C cells are the origin of medullary thyroid carcinoma.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1077 (Book Page): The thyroid follicles are atrophic and are lined in many areas by epithelial cells with abundant eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm, termed Hürthle cells, which represent a metaplastic response of the normally low cuboidal follicular epithelium to chronic injury.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: Endogenous hypercortisolism caused by a primary adrenal cortical neoplasm is biochemically characterized by which of the following laboratory findings?
options: High serum cortisol and high serum aldosterone
Low serum cortisol and low serum ACTH
Low serum cortisol and high serum ACTH
High serum cortisol and high serum ACTH
High serum cortisol and low serum ACTH
correctOption: High serum cortisol and low serum ACTH
optionExplanations: While some carcinomas can secrete both, the definitive diagnostic feature of an adrenal cortisol tumor is the dissociation of cortisol and ACTH.
This occurs in secondary adrenocortical insufficiency (pituitary failure), where the loss of ACTH leads to a loss of cortisol production.
This is the biochemical pattern of Addison disease (primary adrenal insufficiency), not Cushing syndrome.
This pattern is seen in ACTH-dependent causes like Cushing disease (pituitary) or ectopic ACTH secretion.
The autonomous production of cortisol by the adrenal tumor suppresses the pituitary via negative feedback, resulting in low or undetectable ACTH.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1113 (Book Page): The biochemical sine qua non of ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome is elevated serum levels of cortisol with low levels of ACTH.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
statement: Diabetes diagnosed in a previously euglycemic woman during her third trimester of pregnancy is etiologically classified as:
options: Pregestational diabetes mellitus
Neonatal diabetes mellitus
MODY type 4
Type 2 diabetes mellitus
Gestational diabetes mellitus
correctOption: Gestational diabetes mellitus
optionExplanations: Pregestational diabetes refers to women who had established Type 1 or Type 2 diabetes prior to becoming pregnant.
Neonatal diabetes occurs in infants, usually within the first 6 months of life, due to specific genetic mutations like KCNJ11.
MODY type 4 is a monogenic form of diabetes due to PDX1 mutations and is not related to the physiological stresses of pregnancy.
While gestational diabetes shares some pathophysiological mechanisms with Type 2 diabetes, the etiological classification remains distinct for those cases appearing first in pregnancy.
Gestational diabetes is the official etiological classification for any degree of glucose intolerance with onset or first recognition during pregnancy in a previously non-diabetic individual.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1103 (Book Page): previously euglycemic develop impaired glucose tolerance and diabetes for the first time during pregnancy (“gestational” diabetes).

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: A 35-year-old female presents with hypercalcemia, peptic ulcers (gastrinoma), and a pituitary prolactinoma. Histological evaluation of her parathyroid glands is performed. Given the likely genetic syndrome, what is the most expected pathological finding?
options: Bilateral parathyroid carcinomas with lung metastases
A solitary adenoma with a thick fibrous capsule
Multiglandular hyperplasia involving all four parathyroid glands
Metastatic calcification of the parathyroid stroma
Atrophy of chief cells with replacement by oxyphil cells
correctOption: Multiglandular hyperplasia involving all four parathyroid glands
optionExplanations: Parathyroid carcinomas are very rare (~1%) and are not the standard manifestation of MEN-1 syndromes.
Solitary adenomas are typically sporadic (85-95%), whereas familial syndromes like MEN-1 classically involve multiple glands.
The patient presents with the triad of MEN-1 (Pituitary, Pancreas/Duodenum, Parathyroid). In MEN-1, the parathyroid abnormality is typically multiglandular hyperplasia or multiple adenomas.
Metastatic calcification occurs in other organs due to hypercalcemia, but it is not the primary lesional process in the parathyroid glands.
The syndrome involves overactivity (hyperplasia), not atrophy. Chief cells are the proliferating population in this context.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): Primary hyperplasia may occur sporadically or as a component of MEN syndrome. Although classically all four glands are involved, there is frequently asymmetry with apparent sparing of one or two glands.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
statement: A 10-year-old child presents with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis and dental enamel abnormalities. Laboratory testing confirms autoimmune hypoparathyroidism. Which genetic mutation is most likely associated with this patient's condition?
options: Mutation in the AIRE gene
Mutation in the ABCD1 gene
Mutation in the CTLA4 gene
Mutation in the PTPN22 gene
Mutation in the CYP21A2 gene
correctOption: Mutation in the AIRE gene
optionExplanations: APS-1 (Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome type 1) is characterized by the triad of candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and adrenal insufficiency, caused by mutations in the AIRE gene which controls central T-cell tolerance.
ABCD1 mutations cause adrenoleukodystrophy, an X-linked disorder of fatty acid metabolism, not the autoimmune syndrome APS-1.
CTLA4 polymorphisms are linked to general autoimmune susceptibility but do not cause the specific constellation of symptoms seen in APS-1.
PTPN22 is associated with increased risk for many autoimmune diseases including T1D and Hashimoto's, but it is not the primary monogenic cause of APS-1.
CYP21A2 mutations cause congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency), not APS-1.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1121 (Book Page): APS-1... is caused by mutations in the autoimmune regulator (AIRE) gene on chromosome 21q22.

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
statement: What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism by which prior pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) predisposes a patient to an extrauterine tubal pregnancy?
options: Complete obliteration of the fimbriated end
Failure of the corpus luteum to support the zygote
Hormonal imbalance leading to rapid ovum transport
Intraluminal fallopian tube scarring
Increased production of prostaglandins in the tube
correctOption: Intraluminal fallopian tube scarring
optionExplanations: Complete obliteration of the fimbriated end would result in infertility (an inability of the ovum to enter the tube), rather than allowing fertilization and subsequent ectopic implantation.

The corpus luteum usually functions normally in ectopic pregnancies; the issue is the physical location of the blastocyst, not the hormonal support for early pregnancy initially provided by the ovary.
PID typically causes structural damage rather than functional hormonal imbalances that accelerate transport; in fact, it usually slows the transport of the fertilized ovum.

Chronic salpingitis resulting from PID causes intraluminal scarring. These scars create blind pouches or narrowed passages that trap the fertilized ovum before it reaches the uterus, leading to implantation in the tubal wall.
While inflammation involves prostaglandins, the specific risk factor cited for ectopic pregnancy is the physical structural change (scarring) rather than a purely chemical signaling shift.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1027 (Book Page): The most important predisposing condition, present in 35% to 50% of patients, is prior pelvic inflammatory disease resulting in intraluminal fallopian tube scarring (chronic salpingitis).

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: Which of the following represents the most frequent underlying pathology in cases of primary hyperparathyroidism?
options: Parathyroid carcinoma
MEN-1 associated multiglandular disease
Ectopic PTH secretion from lung small cell carcinoma
Bilateral parathyroid hyperplasia
Solitary parathyroid adenoma
correctOption: Solitary parathyroid adenoma
optionExplanations: Parathyroid carcinoma is a rare cause of primary hyperparathyroidism, occurring in approximately 1% of cases.
Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) type 1 is associated with parathyroid disease but is a far less common overall cause than sporadic solitary adenomas.
Small cell carcinoma of the lung typically secretes PTH-related peptide (PTHrP) rather than true PTH, leading to hypercalcemia of malignancy rather than primary hyperparathyroidism.
Bilateral hyperplasia accounts for only about 5% to 10% of cases and is more common in familial syndromes than sporadic primary hyperparathyroidism.
The solitary sporadic adenoma is the most common cause, accounting for roughly 85% to 95% of all cases of primary hyperparathyroidism.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1091 (Book Page): The most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism is a solitary sporadic parathyroid adenoma.

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: A 28-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of weight loss despite an increased appetite, heat intolerance, and prominent bulging of the eyes. On examination, she has a diffusely enlarged, non-tender thyroid and a fine tremor. Which of the following sets of laboratory values is most consistent with her condition?
options: Depressed TSH, Depressed free T4
Depressed TSH, Elevated free T4
Elevated TSH, Depressed free T4
Normal TSH, Elevated T3
Elevated TSH, Elevated free T4
correctOption: Depressed TSH, Elevated free T4
optionExplanations: Low TSH with low T4 indicates secondary (central) hypothyroidism.
The clinical triad (hyperthyroidism, ophthalmopathy, and diffuse goiter) indicates Graves disease. The primary hyperfunction causes high T4/T3, which suppresses TSH via negative feedback.
High TSH with low T4 is the classic pattern for primary hypothyroidism, the clinical opposite of this patient.

A normal TSH would be highly unlikely in Graves disease due to the intact negative feedback loop from elevated thyroid hormones acting on the pituitary thyrotrophs; TSH should be depressed even in subclinical stages or T3 toxicosis (where T4 is normal). Management of Graves disease relies on finding suppressed TSH levels and elevated T4 or T3 levels as stated on page 1082 of the text. Option B is correct as per the diagnostic profile provided for Graves disease on page 1082 and page 1076 of the text.
Elevated TSH with elevated T4 indicates secondary hyperthyroidism (pituitary origin), which would not typically present with the infiltrative ophthalmopathy (bulging eyes) seen in Graves disease.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1080 (Book Page): Laboratory findings in Graves disease include elevated free T4 and T3 levels and depressed TSH levels.

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: In the physiological regulation of Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH), which specific stimulus initiates the most potent release of the hormone to conserve body water?
options: Excessive intake of free water
Increased plasma osmotic pressure
Decreased plasma osmotic pressure
Increased arterial blood pressure
Decreased atrial distention
correctOption: Increased plasma osmotic pressure
optionExplanations: Excessive water intake results in hemodilution and low osmolality, which suppresses ADH secretion.
Hyperosmolality is the primary trigger for osmoreceptors to signal the release of ADH, ensuring water is reabsorbed in the kidneys.
Decreased osmotic pressure (hyposmolality) inhibits ADH release to allow for the excretion of excess water.
Increased blood pressure is sensed by baroreceptors and leads to the inhibition of ADH to reduce total blood volume.
While decreased atrial distention (hypovolemia) does stimulate ADH, the osmotic pressure gradient is a more sensitive regulator in normal homeostasis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1065 (Book Page): An increase in plasma osmotic pressure detected by osmoreceptors also triggers ADH secretion.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Diffuse and Multinodular goiter
statement: During the phase of colloid involution in a diffuse nontoxic goiter, what is the characteristic gross appearance of the thyroid parenchyma?
options: Beefy deep red and meaty
Hemorrhagic with soft, necrotic sacs
Chalky white with granular foci
Brown, glassy, and translucent
Pale gray, firm, and multinodular
correctOption: Brown, glassy, and translucent
optionExplanations: A beefy, deep red appearance is characteristic of the diffuse hyperplasia in Graves disease due to increased vascularity.
This appearance would suggest acute necrosis or massive hemorrhage, not a stable phase of involution.
Chalky white foci are typical of fat necrosis (seen in the breast or pancreas) or heavy calcification, not typical colloid goiter.

When TSH stimulation subsides or iodine becomes available, the hyperplastic follicles fill with abundant colloid and the epithelium flattens. Grossly, the high colloid content gives the gland a brown, glassy, and translucent appearance on cut section.
Pale gray and firm describes the late scarring stages of multinodular goiter, not the involution phase of simple goiter.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1081 (Book Page): In these cases, the cut surface of the thyroid is usually brown, somewhat glassy, and translucent.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: A 55-year-old multiparous woman presents with a firm, palpable periareolar mass and thick, white nipple discharge. Excisional biopsy reveals ectatic ducts filled with granular debris and a prominent periductal chronic inflammatory infiltrate. Which histological feature would most clearly distinguish this from squamous metaplasia of the lactiferous ducts?
options: The absence of keratinizing squamous epithelium within the ducts
Formation of granulomas around cholesterol deposits
Evidence of significant periductal and interstitial fibrosis
Presence of many plasma cells in the inflammatory infiltrate
Accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages in the lumen
correctOption: The absence of keratinizing squamous epithelium within the ducts
optionExplanations: Duct ectasia is characterized by dilation of ducts and chronic inflammation without the keratinizing squamous metaplasia that defines Zuska disease.
Granulomatous reactions can occur in both if there is rupture and spillage of contents into the stroma; however, the contents spilled (keratin vs. secretions/cholesterol) differ.
Fibrosis is a common reactive change to chronic inflammation in several breast disorders and is not specific enough for differentiation.
Both conditions can have plasma cells, though they are often very prominent in duct ectasia. This is not the most definitive structural difference.
Lipid-laden macrophages are characteristic of duct ectasia, but the hallmark difference involves the lining of the ducts themselves.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1039 (Book Page): Unlike squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts, it is not associated with cigarette smoking.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
coreConcept: Morphology and Clinical Mimicry of Fat Necrosis
statement: A 48-year-old woman presents for evaluation of a new, firm, painless mass in her left breast. Physical exam reveals skin retraction over the mass. Vitals: BP 120/80 mmHg, Temp 36.9°C. Labs: Normal CBC. She reports undergoing a lumpectomy for a benign cyst in that quadrant 6 months ago. Mammogram shows an irregular density with clustered calcifications. A biopsy is performed. Which histological constellation would confirm a diagnosis of fat necrosis?
options: Central liquefactive necrosis with neutrophils followed by giant cell and hemosiderin deposition
Hürthle cell metaplasia with prominent germinal centers
Branching fibrovascular cores covered by two cell layers in a dilated duct
Ectatic ducts filled with granular debris and plasma cells
Dense lymphocytic infiltrate surrounding atrophic lobules with thickened basement membranes
correctOption: Central liquefactive necrosis with neutrophils followed by giant cell and hemosiderin deposition
optionExplanations: Fat necrosis progresses from acute hemorrhage and liquefactive fat necrosis to a chronic phase characterized by foam cells, multinucleated giant cells, calcifications, and fibrosis, which can mimic carcinoma clinically and radiologically.
This is characteristic of Hashimoto thyroiditis, which can rarely present as a localized mass in ectopic thyroid tissue but is not a breast disorder.
This describes an intraductal papilloma, which typically presents with serous or bloody nipple discharge rather than a firm, skin-retracting mass.
This describes duct ectasia, which can mimic a mass but usually presents with thick nipple discharge and lacks the history of acute focal trauma/surgery seen in fat necrosis.
This represents lymphocytic mastopathy, typically seen in patients with Type 1 Diabetes or autoimmune thyroid disease.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1039 (Book Page): Subsequently, giant cells, calcifications, and hemosiderin appear, and eventually the lesion is replaced by scar tissue or is encircled and walled off by fibrous tissue.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
statement: A 20-year-old male with a family history of diabetes is diagnosed with a monogenic form of the disease. Genetic sequencing reveals a loss-of-function mutation in the enzyme that acts as the rate-limiting 'glucose sensor' for the pancreatic beta cell. Which specific classification does this common form of MODY belong to?
options: MODY 1 (HNF4A mutation)
MODY 2 (GCK mutation)
Maternally inherited diabetes and deafness (MIDD)
MODY 3 (HNF1A mutation)
MODY 5 (HNF1B mutation)
correctOption: MODY 2 (GCK mutation)
optionExplanations: HNF4A mutations cause MODY 1, which is a genetic defect in beta-cell function but is not the glucose-sensing enzyme.

MODY 2 is caused by mutations in the glucokinase (GCK) gene. Glucokinase serves as the glucose sensor in the beta cell, and its loss-of-function leads to a higher threshold for insulin release and the most common form of MODY.
MIDD is a mitochondrial DNA mutation (m.3243A to G) that affects beta-cell function but is not categorized as a MODY subtype.
HNF1A mutations cause MODY 3, another form of monogenic diabetes involving transcription factor defects rather than glucose sensing.
HNF1B mutations cause MODY 5, which is often associated with renal cysts and other extra-pancreatic features.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1103 (Book Page): The largest subgroup of patients in this category was designated as having 'maturity-onset diabetes of the young' (MODY)... mutations of glucokinase (GCK) are the most common. Glucokinase is a rate-limiting step in oxidative glucose metabolism, which, in turn, is coupled to insulin secretion.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
statement: Which of the following autoantibodies is most specifically associated with the activation of thyroid follicular cells and the development of hyperthyroidism in Graves disease?
options: Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin
TSH receptor blocking antibody
Antimicrosomal antibody
Antithyroglobulin antibody
Antithyroid peroxidase antibody
correctOption: Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin
optionExplanations: Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) is a specific IgG that binds to and activates the TSH receptor, mimicking the effect of TSH and causing thyroid hyperfunction and hyperplasia.

TSH receptor blocking antibodies can be found in some Graves patients, but they lead to hypothyroidism or the euthyroid state rather than the hyperthyroidism that defines the classic disease manifestation.
Antimicrosomal antibodies are non-specific markers of thyroid autoimmunity often seen in Hashimoto thyroiditis rather than the stimulatory state of Graves.
Antithyroglobulin antibodies are found in Hashimoto thyroiditis and other autoimmune thyroid conditions but are not the primary drivers of the hyperthyroid state in Graves disease.
Antithyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies are prevalent in most autoimmune thyroid diseases, including Hashimoto and Graves, but they do not stimulate the receptor to cause hyperthyroidism.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): The most common antibody subtype, known as thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI), is observed in approximately 90% of patients. In contrast to antibodies against thyroglobulin and thyroid peroxidase, TSI is almost never observed in other autoimmune diseases of the thyroid. TSI binds to the TSH receptor and mimics its actions, stimulating adenyl cyclase and increasing the release of thyroid hormones.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
statement: Which specific anatomic abnormality is classically associated with the development of adult (adolescent) testicular torsion?
options: Absence of the tunica vaginalis
Presence of a persistent processus vaginalis
Congenital absence of the gubernaculum
Bell-clapper abnormality
Abnormally short spermatic cord
correctOption: Bell-clapper abnormality
optionExplanations: The tunica vaginalis is present in torsion; it is the high attachment of the tunica that allows the testis to rotate freely.
A persistent processus vaginalis is the primary defect associated with indirect inguinal hernias and hydroceles, not the primary driver of torsion.
The gubernaculum's role is in testicular descent; torsion is related to the mobility of the testis within the scrotum once descended.

The bell-clapper abnormality is a congenital defect where the tunica vaginalis abnormally envelopes the testis, epididymis, and cord, allowing the testis to hang like a clapper in a bell and rotate around its vascular pedicle.
A short spermatic cord would theoretically decrease mobility; torsion requires increased mobility (excessive cord length or high tunica attachment) to allow twisting.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 968 (Book Page): In adults, torsion results from a bilateral anatomic defect that leads to increased mobility of the testes (bell-clapper abnormality).

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
statement: A 28-year-old woman presents with weight gain, abdominal striae, and hirsutism. Tests show elevated serum cortisol that is suppressed by high-dose but not low-dose dexamethasone. A pituitary microadenoma is identified. Which transcription factor is definitively expressed by the neoplastic cells of this tumor?
options: TPIT
PIT-1
GATA-2
Estrogen receptor beta
SF-1
correctOption: TPIT
optionExplanations: TPIT is the specific transcription factor for the corticotroph lineage. The clinical presentation is Cushing disease, caused by an ACTH-secreting corticotroph adenoma.
PIT-1 identifies somatotroph, thyrotroph, and lactotroph lineages. It is not expressed in the corticotroph (ACTH-secreting) lineage.
GATA-2 is a marker for the gonadotroph and thyrotroph lineages but is absent in corticotroph cells.
ER alpha is the hormone receptor associated with lactotroph and gonadotroph cells; there is no role for ER beta in defining these lineages in the pituitary gland.
SF-1 is specific to the gonadotroph lineage and is used to distinguish gonadotroph adenomas from other types.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1064 (Book Page): corticotrophs are derived from progenitor cells expressing the transcription factor TPIT

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
statement: A 45-year-old male undergoes a routine health screening. His laboratory results indicate a glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) level that is used as a criterion for the definitive diagnosis of diabetes mellitus. According to standard professional guidelines, what is the minimum HbA1c percentage required for this diagnosis?
optionExplanations: Option A (5.7%) is the lower limit for the diagnosis of prediabetes, indicating a state of dysglycemia that increases the risk of progression to overt disease but does not meet the threshold for clinical diabetes.
Option C is correct. A confirmed HbA1c level of 6.5% or higher is an established diagnostic criterion for diabetes, reflecting average glycemic control over the preceding 120 days.
Option E (7.5%) is well above the diagnostic threshold and represents poor glycemic control in a diagnosed patient.
Option D (7.0%) is the therapeutic goal for most patients already diagnosed with diabetes to minimize long-term complications, but it is higher than the minimum diagnostic threshold.
Option B (6.0%) falls within the range of prediabetes (5.7% to 6.4%) and is not diagnostic of frank diabetes mellitus.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1097 (Book Page): A glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) level ≥ 6.5% (glycated hemoglobin is further discussed later in the chapter)

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: Which of the following is identified as the most frequent underlying etiology for the development of endogenous hyperthyroidism in clinical practice?
options: TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma
Factitious thyrotoxicosis
Toxic thyroid adenoma
Graves disease
Hyperfunctioning multinodular goiter
correctOption: Graves disease
optionExplanations: Option B is incorrect because TSH-secreting pituitary adenomas are extremely rare causes of secondary hyperthyroidism.
Option E is incorrect because factitious thyrotoxicosis involves exogenous intake and is not considered an 'endogenous' cause of hyperthyroidism.
Option D is incorrect because a hyperfunctioning toxic adenoma is a localized cause of hyperthyroidism and is less prevalent than the diffuse involvement seen in Graves disease.
Option C is correct because Graves disease accounts for approximately 85% of cases of endogenous hyperthyroidism.
Option A is incorrect because hyperfunctioning multinodular goiter, while common, is less frequent than Graves disease as a cause of endogenous hyperthyroidism.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): Graves disease is the most common cause of endogenous hyperthyroidism.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
statement: The development of infiltrative ophthalmopathy in Graves disease is fundamentally driven by which of the following cellular and molecular events in the retro-orbital space?
options: Ischemic necrosis of the orbital fat due to hypercoagulability
Direct destruction of extraocular muscles by cytotoxic CD8+ T cells
Overactivity of the superior tarsal muscle by sympathetic stimulation
Compression of the optic nerve by a primary pituitary macroadenoma
Cytokine-mediated stimulation of fibroblasts and glycosaminoglycan synthesis
correctOption: Cytokine-mediated stimulation of fibroblasts and glycosaminoglycan synthesis
optionExplanations: Ischemic necrosis and hypercoagulability are not recognized pathogenic factors for the infiltrative changes seen in the extraocular muscles and retro-orbital fat of Graves disease patients.
While CD8+ T cells are implicated in the destruction of follicles in Hashimoto thyroiditis, Graves ophthalmopathy involves infiltration and edema rather than direct myocyte destruction.

Sympathetic overstimulation of the superior tarsal muscle causes the characteristic lid lag and staring gaze seen in generalized thyrotoxicosis, but it does not cause the structural retro-orbital changes of exophthalmos.
Pituitary macroadenomas cause bitemporal hemianopsia through compression of the optic chiasm, but they do not cause the infiltrative changes or proptosis characteristic of Graves disease.

The exophthalmos is caused by activated T cells secreting cytokines that trigger retro-orbital fibroblasts to produce hydrophilic glycosaminoglycans like hyaluronic acid, leading to osmotic swelling and volume increase.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): Activated CD4+ helper T cells secrete cytokines that stimulate fibroblast proliferation and synthesis of extracellular matrix proteins (glycosaminoglycans), leading to progressive infiltration of the retro-orbital space and ophthalmopathy.

category: Enumerate clinical manifestations along with hormone levels of anterior pituitary
statement: A 29-year-old female experiences severe postpartum hemorrhage followed by circulatory collapse during her second delivery. Three months later, she reports an inability to breastfeed, cold intolerance, and profound lethargy. Laboratory analysis reveals low free T4, low cortisol, and low prolactin. Which pathologic process best explains this clinical constellation?
options: Hemorrhagic infarction of a pituitary adenoma
Ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary
Compression of the pituitary stalk by a craniopharyngioma
Autoimmune destruction of pituitary thyrotrophs
Primary empty sella syndrome
correctOption: Ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary
optionExplanations: Hemorrhagic infarction of an existing adenoma is pituitary apoplexy, which usually presents with sudden severe headache and acute neurologic collapse rather than insidious postpartum failure.

The anterior pituitary doubles in size during pregnancy without a corresponding increase in blood supply. Postpartum hemorrhage causes shock and relative hypoxia, leading to infarction of the adenohypophysis, resulting in failure of lactation (prolactin deficiency) and other trophic failures.
Craniopharyngiomas are suprasellar tumors that can cause hypopituitarism, but they are not characteristically precipitated by obstetric hemorrhage.
While lymphocytic hypophysitis is autoimmune, this specific clinical history of obstetric hemorrhage and multiple hormone deficiencies (panhypopituitarism) strongly indicates Sheehan syndrome.
Primary empty sella involves herniation of the arachnoid and is typically an incidental finding in obese women; it does not follow the acute ischemic event described.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1071 (Book Page): Ischemic necrosis of the pituitary (Sheehan syndrome), also known as postpartum necrosis, is the most common form of ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary... any further reduction in blood supply caused by obstetric hemorrhage or shock may precipitate infarction of the anterior lobe.

category: Enumerate clinical manifestations along with hormone levels of anterior pituitary
coreConcept: IGF-1 Mediation of Growth Hormone Effects
statement: A 45-year-old male presents with abnormal growth of the jaw (prognathism), sausage-like thickening of the fingers, and new-onset arthritis. Laboratory testing shows an inability to suppress Growth Hormone (GH) after an oral glucose load. Which biochemical mediator directly causes most of these tissue changes?
options: Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)
Dopamine
Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH)
Somatostatin
Insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1)
correctOption: Insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1)
optionExplanations: POMC is the precursor for ACTH and MSH and is unrelated to the somatotroph axis.
Dopamine is the primary inhibitor of prolactin and is not the mediator for acromegaly.
TRH stimulates the release of TSH and is not involved in the pathogenesis of acromegaly.
Somatostatin is a hypothalamic factor that inhibits GH release; it does not mediate the anabolic effects of GH excess.
GH stimulates the liver to produce IGF-1, which is the effector molecule responsible for the bone and soft tissue overgrowth seen in acromegaly.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1069 (Book Page): Persistently elevated levels of GH stimulate the hepatic secretion of insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), which causes many of the clinical manifestations.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: Which metabolic condition is most strongly associated with the morphological finding of sclerosing lymphocytic lobulitis?
options: Type 1 (insulin-dependent) diabetes mellitus
End-stage renal disease (ESRD)
Primary hyperparathyroidism
Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS)
Metabolic syndrome with morbid obesity
correctOption: Type 1 (insulin-dependent) diabetes mellitus
optionExplanations: Lymphocytic mastopathy is highly characteristic of Type 1 diabetics and those with autoimmune thyroiditis, suggesting a shared immune-mediated pathogenesis.
ESRD has no specific association with these localized breast lymphocytic infiltrates.
Primary hyperparathyroidism causes metastatic calcification but does not typically induce lymphocytic lobulitis.
PCOS is associated with endometrial abnormalities but has no specific link to sclerosing lymphocytic lobulitis.
Obesity is a risk factor for breast cancer and T2D, but lymphocytic mastopathy specifically targets autoimmune phenotypes.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1039 (Book Page): This condition is most common in women with type 1 (insulin-dependent) diabetes or autoimmune thyroid disease and is hypothesized to have an autoimmune basis. Its only clinical significance is that it must be distinguished from breast cancer.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
statement: A 17-year-old female presents with severe insulin resistance and a skin condition characterized by velvety hyperpigmented patches in her axilla. Molecular testing reveals a mutation in the insulin receptor that impairs its tyrosine kinase activity. This condition is categorized as:
options: Genetic defects of beta-cell function
Lipoatrophic diabetes
Maturity-onset diabetes of the young
Genetic defects in insulin action
Endocrinopathy
correctOption: Genetic defects in insulin action
optionExplanations: Genetic defects of beta-cell function, such as MODY, involve issues with insulin production or secretion, not the peripheral response to the hormone.
Lipoatrophic diabetes is another defect in action, but it is characterized by the loss of adipose tissue, whereas this case specifically describes a receptor mutation and acanthosis nigricans.
MODY is a genetic defect in beta-cell function, not an action defect; these patients typically do not have the severe insulin resistance or acanthosis nigricans seen here.

Type A insulin resistance, caused by insulin receptor mutations, is specifically classified under 'Genetic Defects in Insulin Action'. It is characterized by severe resistance and acanthosis nigricans.
Endocrinopathies involve excessive secretion of hormones (like cortisol in Cushing's) that interfere with insulin, rather than a primary genetic defect in the receptor itself.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1103 (Book Page): Rare insulin receptor mutations that affect receptor synthesis, insulin binding, or RTK activity can cause severe insulin resistance, accompanied by hyperinsulinemia and diabetes (type A insulin resistance).

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Diffuse and Multinodular goiter
statement: An 80-year-old patient with a decades-long history of a large neck mass develops sudden symptoms of palpitations, weight loss, and tremors. Lab work reveals high T3 and low TSH. Imaging shows a 'hot' spot in one of the many nodules. What name is given to this specific clinical phenomenon?
options: Sheehan syndrome
Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome
De Quervain syndrome
Nelson syndrome
Plummer syndrome
correctOption: Plummer syndrome
optionExplanations: Sheehan syndrome is postpartum pituitary necrosis.
Waterhouse-Friderichsen is adrenal hemorrhage associated with meningococcemia.
De Quervain refers to granulomatous thyroiditis, which is typically painful and transient.
Nelson syndrome involves a pituitary tumor following adrenalectomy.
Plummer syndrome is the development of hyperthyroidism in a patient with a preexisting long-standing multinodular goiter.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1082 (Book Page): about 10% of patients over a 10-year period develop an autonomous nodule within a long-standing goiter that produces hyperthyroidism (toxic multinodular goiter), also known as Plummer syndrome.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
coreConcept: Definition and Scope of Dysfunctional Uterine Bleeding
statement: Which clinical scenario precisely characterizes the term dysfunctional uterine bleeding?
options: Excessive micturition during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle.
Uterine hemorrhage that occurs in the absence of an identifiable structural lesion.
Postmenopausal bleeding directly attributed to advanced endometrial carcinoma.
Irregular bleeding secondary to a submucosal leiomyoma obstructing the canal.
Spotting caused by a benign exophytic growth within the endocervical canal.
correctOption: Uterine hemorrhage that occurs in the absence of an identifiable structural lesion.
optionExplanations: This describes a urinary symptom, whereas dysfunctional uterine bleeding refers specifically to abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB).
Dysfunctional uterine bleeding (DUB) is specifically defined as bleeding caused by hormonal disturbances rather than anatomic or structural lesions like polyps or fibroids.
Carcinoma is a malignant structural lesion; DUB is by definition a functional disorder without such underlying pathology.
Bleeding caused by a leiomyoma is classified as abnormal uterine bleeding due to a structural abnormality, which excludes it from the definition of DUB.
Endocervical polyps are structural lesions; bleeding resulting from them is not classified as dysfunctional.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1000 (Book Page): This is a clinical term for uterine bleeding that lacks an underlying structural abnormality.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
statement: What is the primary histological distinction between the chief cells and oxyphil cells found in parathyroid lesions?
options: Chief cells contain abundant mitochondria, while oxyphil cells contain PTH granules
Chief cells have vacuolated cytoplasm due to lipid, while oxyphil cells contain lipofuscin
Chief cells synthesize and secrete PTH, whereas oxyphil cells are tightly packed with mitochondria and have sparse secretory granules
Chief cells are only found in carcinomas, while oxyphil cells are restricted to adenomas
Chief cells are larger and acidophilic, whereas oxyphil cells are small and polygonal
correctOption: Chief cells synthesize and secrete PTH, whereas oxyphil cells are tightly packed with mitochondria and have sparse secretory granules
optionExplanations: This is a reversal of the actual cell characteristics. Oxyphil cells are the ones rich in mitochondria.
While chief cells can contain glycogen and sparse lipid, the specific description of mitochondrial packing is the defining trait for oxyphil cells.

Correct. Chief cells are the functional endocrine units producing PTH. Oxyphil cells are mitochondrial-rich cells of uncertain function that appear as acidophilic clusters in both normal glands and neoplasms.
Both cell types are present in normal glands, adenomas, and hyperplasia. There is no such restriction to malignancy.
Oxyphil cells are larger and acidophilic (due to mitochondria), while chief cells are smaller and polygonal.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1091 (Book Page): Chief cells have secretory granules containing parathyroid hormone (PTH)... Oxyphil cells... are slightly larger than the chief cells, have acidophilic cytoplasm, and are tightly packed with mitochondria. Glycogen granules are also present in these cells, but secretory granules are sparse or absent.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
statement: A patient with Type 2 Diabetes is prescribed a medication that functions by inhibiting the enzyme dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4). What is the physiological basis for the therapeutic effect of this drug class?
options: Blocking the reabsorption of glucose in the proximal renal tubules
Binding to the sulfonylurea receptor to close K+ channels in beta cells
Decreasing the rate of hepatic gluconeogenesis via AMPK activation
Sensitizing the muscle cells to the actions of circulating insulin
Prolonging the activity of incretin hormones like GLP-1
correctOption: Prolonging the activity of incretin hormones like GLP-1
optionExplanations: Blocking renal glucose reabsorption is the mechanism of SGLT2 inhibitors, which lower blood glucose by promoting glycosuria, distinct from the incretin-based mechanism.
Binding to the sulfonylurea receptor to close K+ channels and trigger insulin release is the mechanism of sulfonylureas and meglitinides.
AMPK activation is the primary mechanism of action for biguanides like metformin, not DPP-4 inhibitors.
Increasing insulin sensitivity in peripheral tissues like muscle and fat is the mechanism of thiazolidinediones, which act via PPAR-gamma, not DPP-4.

DPP-4 inhibitors prevent the breakdown of GLP-1 and GIP. These incretins normally stimulate insulin secretion, inhibit glucagon release, and promote satiety, all of which are beneficial in Type 2 Diabetes.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1099 (Book Page): DPP-4 inhibitors, which enhance levels of endogenous incretins by delaying their degradation.

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
coreConcept: Ectopic ADH Secretion in Lung Malignancy
statement: A 68-year-old male with a 50-pack-year smoking history presents with weight loss and a persistent cough. Imaging reveals a large central hilar mass. Laboratory investigations show a serum sodium of 118 mEq/L (Normal: 135-145) and a serum osmolality of 250 mOsm/kg. He is clinically euvolemic with no peripheral edema. What is the most likely diagnosis for his electrolyte abnormality?
options: Central Diabetes Insipidus
Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH (SIADH)
Hyperaldosteronism
Addisonian Crisis
Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus
correctOption: Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH (SIADH)
optionExplanations: Diabetes insipidus would cause hypernatremia (high sodium) due to excessive free water loss, the opposite of this patient's presentation.
This patient has classic SIADH findings: hyponatremia and low osmolality in the setting of a lung malignancy (likely small-cell carcinoma) and a lack of clinical edema despite water retention.
Hyperaldosteronism is characterized by sodium retention, hypertension, and hypokalemia, not hyponatremia.
While Addison's can cause low sodium, it is typically accompanied by hyperkalemia and signs of hypovolemia/hypotension.
Nephrogenic DI results in dilute polyuria and high serum sodium/osmolality, which contradicts this case.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1072 (Book Page): The most frequent causes of SIADH are the secretion of ectopic ADH by malignant neoplasms (particularly small-cell carcinoma of the lung)... total body water is increased, blood volume remains normal, and peripheral edema does not develop.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: A patient with long-standing Cushing syndrome undergoes total bilateral adrenalectomy. Following the procedure, the patient develops hyperpigmentation and symptoms of a rapidly expanding intracranial mass. Which condition explains this clinical transition?
options: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome
Addison disease
Nelson syndrome
Li-Fraumeni syndrome
Conn syndrome
correctOption: Nelson syndrome
optionExplanations: Waterhouse-Friderichsen is an acute adrenal crisis due to hemorrhage, typically following a meningococcal infection.
Addison disease is primary chronic adrenal insufficiency; while it features pigmentation, it does not involve an expanding pituitary mass.
Nelson syndrome occurs when the 'brake' of cortisol is removed from a preexisting pituitary adenoma, allowing it to grow aggressively and secrete POMC-derived peptides.
Li-Fraumeni syndrome is a genetic predisposition to various cancers due to TP53 mutations, not a post-surgical endocrine complication.
Conn syndrome refers to primary hyperaldosteronism, usually caused by an aldosterone-secreting adenoma.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1114 (Book Page): Large destructive pituitary adenomas can develop in patients after surgical removal of the adrenal glands... This condition, known as Nelson syndrome, occurs because of loss of the inhibitory effect of adrenal corticosteroids on a corticotroph microadenoma.

category: Hashimoto Thyroiditis ii
statement: A pathologist examining a thyroidectomy specimen from a patient with classic Hashimoto thyroiditis notes extensive interstitial fibrosis and a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate. How is this fibrosis distinguished from that seen in Riedel thyroiditis?
options: It demonstrates a storiform pattern
It is associated with granulomatous necrosis
It involves the adjacent carotid sheath
It is restricted within the thyroid capsule
It contains numerous psammoma bodies
correctOption: It is restricted within the thyroid capsule
optionExplanations: A storiform pattern is common in IgG4-related diseases, and while Riedel may be related, Hashimoto fibrosis is generally non-specific in architecture.
Granulomatous necrosis with giant cells is the hallmark of de Quervain (subacute) thyroiditis, not Hashimoto.
Extension of fibrosis into adjacent structures like the carotid sheath is the defining invasive feature of Riedel thyroiditis.
The fibrosis in Hashimoto thyroiditis may be significant but remains confined within the thyroid gland's capsule, distinguishing it from Riedel's.
Psammoma bodies are characteristic of papillary thyroid carcinoma, not the fibrosis of Hashimoto thyroiditis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1077 (Book Page): In “classic” Hashimoto thyroiditis, interstitial connective tissue is increased and may be abundant. Unlike Reidel thyroiditis (see later), the fibrosis does not extend beyond the capsule of the gland.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
statement: Which of the following describes the fundamental pathogenic mechanism used to classify the majority of cases of Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus?
options: Progressive autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta-cells
Overexpression of growth hormone leading to secondary insulin resistance
Peripheral resistance to insulin in skeletal muscle and liver
Germline loss-of-function mutations in the glucokinase gene
Accumulation of amyloid in the pancreatic islets leading to failure
correctOption: Progressive autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta-cells
optionExplanations: Type 1 diabetes is etiologically classified by the immune-mediated destruction of insulin-producing cells, resulting in absolute deficiency.
Secondary diabetes due to growth hormone excess (acromegaly) is classified under endocrinopathies, separate from the Type 1 category.
Peripheral insulin resistance is the defining feature of Type 2 diabetes classification, not Type 1.
Glucokinase mutations characterize Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY), a monogenic form, not typical Type 1.
Amyloid deposition is a hallmark of Type 2 diabetes rather than the primary autoimmune classification for Type 1.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1097 (Book Page): Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is an autoimmune disease characterized by pancreatic beta-cell destruction and an absolute deficiency of insulin. It accounts for approximately 5% to 10% of diabetes.

category: Describe the histopathological features of parathyroid hyperplasia and adenoma
coreConcept: Histologic features and atypia in parathyroid adenoma
statement: A 56-year-old female presents for a routine wellness check. Laboratory evaluation reveals a serum calcium of 11.2 mg/dL (normal 8.5–10.2) and an appropriately elevated parathyroid hormone level. Imaging identifies a single 1.2-cm mass posterior to the right thyroid lobe. Surgical excision is performed. The pathologist identifies a 450-mg encapsulated, tan-colored mass. Histology shows uniform chief cells with rare, bizarre nuclei. The remaining three glands are of normal size. What is the most appropriate classification for this lesion?
options: Secondary parathyroid hyperplasia due to chronic renal compensation
Primary pigmented nodular hyperplasia associated with Carney complex
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism following autonomous nodular transformation
Chief cell parathyroid adenoma with benign endocrine atypia
Parathyroid carcinoma based on the presence of endocrine atypia
correctOption: Chief cell parathyroid adenoma with benign endocrine atypia
optionExplanations: Secondary hyperplasia would involve enlargement of all four glands in response to low calcium, which is not the case here given the high calcium and single enlarged gland.
Primary pigmented nodular hyperplasia refers to the adrenal cortex in Cushing syndrome, not the parathyroid glands.
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism occurs in the setting of long-standing renal failure where hyperplastic glands become autonomous, which does not fit this patient's presentation.
The combination of a solitary enlarged gland, normal size of other glands, encapsulated chief cells, and benign nuclear pleomorphism (atypia) is diagnostic of an adenoma.
Nuclear pleomorphism or 'endocrine atypia' is common in benign endocrine tumors and does not satisfy the criteria for carcinoma, which requires invasion or metastasis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): It is not uncommon to find bizarre and pleomorphic nuclei even within adenomas (so-called endocrine atypia); this is not a criterion for malignancy.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
statement: Autoimmune polyendocrinopathy syndrome type 1 (APS-1) involves chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis and organ-specific autoimmunity. Which gene mutation is responsible for this syndrome?
options: AIRE
MEN1
PRKAR1A
RET proto-oncogene
GNAS1
correctOption: AIRE
optionExplanations: The AIRE gene is critical for central T-cell tolerance; its mutation leads to the failure of deleting self-reactive T cells, causing the multi-organ autoimmunity found in APS-1.
MEN1 is the tumor suppressor gene involved in Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1, causing tumors in the pituitary, parathyroid, and pancreas.
PRKAR1A mutations are linked to the Carney complex and certain pigmented nodular adrenal diseases, but not to the syndrome characterized by candidiasis and adrenalitis.
RET mutations are associated with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2 and medullary thyroid carcinoma, not the autoimmune destruction of the adrenals seen in APS-1.
GNAS1 mutations are linked to McCune-Albright syndrome and certain pituitary adenomas through the cAMP signaling pathway, not systemic autoimmunity.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1121 (Book Page): APS-1... is caused by mutations in the autoimmune regulator (AIRE) gene on chromosome 21q22.

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
statement: Which pathological process is most significantly implicated in the structural predisposition for placental implantation within the fallopian tube?
options: Hypertrophy of the myometrial smooth muscle
Endometrial hyperplasia due to unopposed estrogen
Chronic salpingitis resulting in intraluminal scarring
Dystrophic calcification within the tubal plicae
Acute suppurative salpingitis with neutrophil infiltration
correctOption: Chronic salpingitis resulting in intraluminal scarring
optionExplanations: Myometrial hypertrophy occurs during normal pregnancy but does not cause the anatomical obstruction associated with ectopic tubal implantations.
Endometrial hyperplasia is a uterine pathology related to hormone levels and is not the structural mechanism causing abnormal implantation in the fallopian tube.
Intraluminal scarring from prior pelvic inflammatory disease (chronic salpingitis) is the leading risk factor, present in up to 50% of cases, as it prevents the passage of the zygote.
Calcification may occur in various chronic lesions, but the formation of gland-like spaces and blind pouches from plicae fusion is the specific mechanism for trapping the ovum.
Acute inflammation is the initial stage of infection, but the chronic phase characterized by repair and scarring is what physically blocks the embryo's passage to the uterus.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1027 (Book Page): The most important predisposing condition, present in 35% to 50% of patients, is prior pelvic inflammatory disease resulting in intraluminal fallopian tube scarring (chronic salpingitis).

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: A comparison between primary hyperparathyroidism and hypercalcemia associated with non-parathyroid malignancy typically reveals which biochemical contrast?
options: PTH levels are elevated in malignancy and suppressed in primary hyperparathyroidism.
PTH levels are suppressed in malignancy and inappropriately elevated in primary hyperparathyroidism.
Ionized calcium levels are only elevated in primary hyperparathyroidism.
Secondary hyperparathyroidism is always associated with suppressed PTH levels.
Serum phosphate is always elevated in primary hyperparathyroidism.
correctOption: PTH levels are suppressed in malignancy and inappropriately elevated in primary hyperparathyroidism.
optionExplanations: In malignancy-associated hypercalcemia (unless it is ectopic PTH production), the high calcium feeds back to suppress the normal parathyroid glands, leading to low PTH.
This is the classic diagnostic hallmark; in primary disease, the glands produce PTH autonomously despite high calcium, whereas in most malignancies, high calcium appropriately suppresses PTH.
Elevated ionized calcium is a shared feature of both primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy-associated hypercalcemia.
Secondary hyperparathyroidism is characterized by a compensatory increase in PTH in response to low calcium, so levels are high, not suppressed.
Serum phosphate is typically low (hypophosphatemia) in primary hyperparathyroidism because PTH increases urinary phosphate clearance.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1094 (Book Page): In individuals with primary hyperparathyroidism, serum PTH levels are inappropriately elevated for the level of serum calcium, whereas PTH levels are low to undetectable in hypercalcemia caused by nonparathyroid diseases.

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: A patient is found to have low serum free T4 and low serum TSH. A follow-up test shows a lack of TSH response following the administration of thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH). This clinical picture most strongly suggests failure at the level of the:
options: Thyroid gland
Hypothalamus
Anterior pituitary
Iodine transporters
Peripheral tissues
correctOption: Anterior pituitary
optionExplanations: Primary failure at the thyroid gland would result in elevated TSH due to the loss of negative feedback from T4.
In hypothalamic (tertiary) hypothyroidism, the pituitary is functional; therefore, administering exogenous TRH would typically cause a rise in TSH levels.
Low TSH and low T4 point to central hypothyroidism. A lack of response to TRH localizes the defect to the pituitary, which cannot respond to the releasing hormone.
Failure of iodine transporters would cause primary hypothyroidism with elevated TSH as the pituitary tries to stimulate hormone production.
Peripheral resistance to thyroid hormone would typically show high levels of T4 and high TSH as the body attempts to overcome the resistance.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1076 (Book Page): The TSH level is not increased in persons with hypothyroidism due to primary hypothalamic or pituitary disease.

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Diffuse and Multinodular goiter
statement: On gross examination, a thyroid gland involved in the colloid involution phase of a diffuse nontoxic goiter typically displays which characteristic appearance?
options: Brown, somewhat glassy, and translucent cut surface
Sacs of clotted blood replacing the entire gland
Firm, pale-gray, and meaty parenchyma
Small, shrunken, and fibrotic lobes
Soft, yellow-white, and multinodular surface
correctOption: Brown, somewhat glassy, and translucent cut surface
optionExplanations: The accumulation of massive amounts of thyroglobulin-rich colloid within the distended follicles gives the gland a characteristic brownish, translucent, and gelatinous appearance.
Extensive hemorrhage is a feature of Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome in the adrenal glands, not standard thyroid goitrogenesis.
A meaty, soft, red appearance is more characteristic of the hyperplastic phase of Graves disease.
A shrunken, fibrotic appearance is characteristic of the end-stages of Hashimoto thyroiditis or radioactive iodine ablation.
Multinodularity and variegated color (yellow/white) develop in later stages (multinodular goiter) rather than the simple diffuse colloid phase.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1081 (Book Page): In these cases, the cut surface of the thyroid is usually brown, somewhat glassy, and translucent.

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: Which physiological change serves as a primary trigger for the secretion of antidiuretic hormone (ADH)?
options: Decrease in plasma sodium levels
Expansion of the left atrial volume
Ingestion of a high-volume water load
Increase in arterial blood pressure
Increase in plasma osmotic pressure
correctOption: Increase in plasma osmotic pressure
optionExplanations: A decrease in sodium (hyponatremia) would normally inhibit ADH secretion to allow the body to excrete more water and bring the sodium concentration back up.
Atrial distention (increased volume) inhibits ADH release to promote diuresis. ADH is stimulated by decreased atrial filling (hypovolemia).
Ingesting a large water load decreases plasma osmolality, which inhibits ADH secretion to allow the kidneys to excrete the excess fluid.
An increase in blood pressure is sensed by baroreceptors, which then inhibit ADH secretion to reduce blood volume. ADH is stimulated by a decrease in blood pressure.
Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus sense increases in plasma osmolality. When the blood becomes too concentrated, they trigger the release of ADH to retain water and restore balance.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1065 (Book Page): An increase in plasma osmotic pressure detected by osmoreceptors also triggers ADH secretion.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: On gross examination of a resected breast mass, the surgeon notes a firm, irregular lesion that mimics a carcinoma. Microscopic analysis reveals ectatic ducts filled with inspissated debris and numerous lipid-laden macrophages. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Sclerosing adenosis
Intraductal papilloma
Fibroadenoma with complex features
Duct ectasia
Medullary carcinoma
correctOption: Duct ectasia
optionExplanations: Sclerosing adenosis involves an increase in acini per lobule with stromal fibrosis, but it lacks the characteristic ectatic ducts and lipid-laden macrophages.
Intraductal papillomas consist of branching fibrovascular cores within a duct, not the accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages and inspissated debris.
Fibroadenomas are circumscribed stromal-epithelial tumors; even with complex features like calcifications, they do not show the inflammatory/ectatic features described.
The combination of dilated (ectatic) ducts, thick secretions containing lipid-laden macrophages, and periductal fibrosis is diagnostic of duct ectasia.
Medullary carcinoma is an invasive cancer characterized by sheets of large pleomorphic cells and a lymphocytic infiltrate, not ectatic ducts and foam cells.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1039 (Book Page): Duct ectasia... Ectatic dilated ducts are filled with inspissated secretions and numerous lipid-laden macrophages. ... Subsequent fibrosis produces an irregular mass with skin and nipple retraction.

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
statement: A 40-year-old woman with a history of bilateral adrenalectomy for refractory Cushing syndrome now presents with severe hyperpigmentation, intense headaches, and a visual field defect. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a large, locally invasive sella mass. Which of the following best describes this clinical condition?
options: Pituitary apoplexy
Sheehan syndrome
Nelson syndrome
Hypothalamic craniopharyngioma
Primary empty sella syndrome
correctOption: Nelson syndrome
optionExplanations: While she has headaches, Nelson syndrome specifically follows adrenalectomy and is characterized by the progression of a corticotroph adenoma due to loss of negative feedback.
Sheehan syndrome is postpartum ischemic necrosis of the pituitary, presenting with hypofunction, not a hyperfunctioning invasive mass.
Nelson syndrome occurs when a pre-existing ACTH-secreting microadenoma grows rapidly after adrenalectomy removes the cortisol-mediated inhibition.
Craniopharyngiomas are suprasellar tumors from Rathke pouch remnants; they do not cause hyperpigmentation via ACTH/POMC hypersecretion.
Empty sella syndrome is characterized by the absence of visible pituitary tissue in the sella, not the presence of a large destructive mass.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1070 (Book Page): Large destructive pituitary adenomas can develop in patients after surgical removal of the adrenal glands for treatment of Cushing syndrome. This condition, known as Nelson syndrome...

category: Describe the pathogenesis & salient morphological features of Grave’s Disease
statement: Which specific autoantibody is the primary driver of the hypermetabolic state and diffuse glandular enlargement seen in Graves' disease?
options: Thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor-blocking antibody
Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI)
Anti-thyroglobulin antibody
Anti-microsomal antibody
Anti-thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibody
correctOption: Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI)
optionExplanations: TSH receptor-blocking antibodies can be found in some patients with Graves but they cause hypothyroidism, not the characteristic hyperthyroidism.
Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) acts as an agonist by binding to the TSH receptor, mimicking TSH and causing autonomous thyroid hormone production.
Anti-thyroglobulin antibodies are seen in multiple thyroid disorders, including Hashimoto thyroiditis, but are not the causative agent for hyperfunction in Graves.
Anti-microsomal antibodies are an older term for TPO antibodies and are generally associated with glandular destruction rather than hyperstimulation.
Anti-TPO antibodies are more characteristic of Hashimoto thyroiditis and represent destructive autoimmunity rather than stimulatory activity.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1079 (Book Page): The most common antibody subtype, known as thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI), is observed in approximately 90% of patients.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: In the pathogenesis of squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts, what event directly triggers the intense chronic granulomatous inflammatory response?
options: Autoimmune destruction of the basement membrane
Accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages in the lumen
Spillage of keratin debris into the periductal stroma
Dilation of the terminal duct lobular unit
Liquefactive necrosis of intralobular adipose tissue
correctOption: Spillage of keratin debris into the periductal stroma
optionExplanations: Squamous metaplasia is associated with smoking and environmental factors rather than a primary autoimmune destruction of the basement membrane.
Lipid-laden macrophages are the hallmark of duct ectasia, representing a response to stagnant secretions rather than a granulomatous response to keratin.
The inflammatory reaction is a foreign body-type response to keratin that has leaked out of a ruptured duct previously plugged by metaplastic cells.
Terminal duct lobular unit dilation is characteristic of nonproliferative fibrocystic changes and cyst formation, not squamous metaplasia.
Liquefactive necrosis is the defining feature of the acute phase of fat necrosis, not squamous metaplasia of the ducts.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1038 (Book Page): An intense chronic granulomatous inflammatory response develops once keratin spills into the surrounding periductal tissue.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
coreConcept: Rationale for prophylactic surgery in torsion
statement: In a patient presenting with adult testicular torsion, why is a surgical procedure routinely performed on the contralateral, unaffected testis?
options: To perform a diagnostic biopsy of the spermatic cord
To evaluate for potential metastatic spread of necrotic cells
To reduce the volume of the scrotum to prevent future traction
Because the predisposing anatomic defect is typically bilateral
To remove occult microadenomas that may trigger twisting
correctOption: Because the predisposing anatomic defect is typically bilateral
optionExplanations: The procedure is therapeutic and prophylactic (anchoring), not primarily for tissue biopsy.
There is no metastatic spread of necrotic cells; necrosis is a localized ischemic/hemorrhagic process.
The size of the scrotum is not the mechanical driver; the mobility of the testis within the tunica is the issue.
The bell-clapper defect is a bilateral anatomic developmental variation; therefore, if one side twists, the other side is at high risk for the same event and must be anchored (orchiopexy).
Torsion is not caused by microadenomas or any neoplastic hormone production.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 968 (Book Page): Contralateral orchiopexy is performed to prevent recurrence in the unaffected testis.

category: Enumerate clinical manifestations along with hormone levels of anterior pituitary
statement: A 28-year-old female experiences severe postpartum hemorrhage during the delivery of her child. Weeks later, she is unable to breastfeed, has ceased menstruating, and complains of extreme cold intolerance and fatigue. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Conn Syndrome
Craniopharyngioma
Sheehan Syndrome
Addison Disease
Graves Disease
correctOption: Sheehan Syndrome
optionExplanations: Conn Syndrome is primary hyperaldosteronism, presenting with hypertension and hypokalemia. It does not cause failure of lactation or the symptoms of global pituitary failure seen here.
Craniopharyngiomas can cause hypopituitarism but are tumors of childhood or older adults, not typically associated with an acute trigger like a delivery-related hemorrhage.

Sheehan syndrome involves anterior pituitary infarction after postpartum hemorrhage. The loss of PRL causes lactation failure, loss of FSH/LH causes amenorrhea, and loss of TSH causes cold intolerance/fatigue.
Addison disease is primary adrenal insufficiency. While it causes fatigue and hypotension, it does not explain the failure of lactation (prolactin deficiency) or amenorrhea (gonadotropin deficiency).

Graves disease is a hyperthyroid state (heat intolerance, weight loss). This patient presents with symptoms of hypothyroidism (cold intolerance) and multiple other anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1071 (Book Page): [Ischemic necrosis of the pituitary (Sheehan syndrome) , also known as postpartum necrosis, is the most common form of ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary. . . Any further reduction in blood supply caused by obstetric hemorrhage or shock may precipitate infarction of the anterior lobe.]

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
statement: An asymptomatic 50-year-old male undergoes a routine health screening. Which of the following glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels is the minimum threshold required to establish a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus in this patient?
optionExplanations: A level of 6.4% is the upper limit of the prediabetic range; the patient is at high risk for progression but is not yet diagnostic for DM.
While 7.0% is the recommended treatment target for many diabetic patients, the diagnostic threshold is lower at 6.5%.
According to established diagnostic criteria, an HbA1c of 6.5% or higher, confirmed on a separate day, is diagnostic for diabetes mellitus.
A level of 6.0% falls within the range of prediabetes (5.7% to 6.4%) and does not meet the criteria for diabetes.
A level of 5.7% is the lower limit for the diagnosis of prediabetes, not overt diabetes mellitus.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1097 (Book Page): A glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) level ≥ 6.5% (glycated hemoglobin is further discussed later in the chapter)

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
statement: A 22-year-old non-obese patient is diagnosed with Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY). What is the primary molecular defect associated with the most common subtype of this condition?
options: Mutations in the glucokinase (GCK) gene affecting the glucose sensor
Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic β-islet cells
Peripheral resistance to insulin due to insulin receptor mutations
Ectopic hormone production from a pituitary somatotroph adenoma
Mitochondrial DNA mutation (m.3243A→G)
correctOption: Mutations in the glucokinase (GCK) gene affecting the glucose sensor
optionExplanations: MODY2 is caused by mutations in the GCK gene, which serves as a 'glucose sensor'; this is the most common form of monogenic diabetes resulting from a primary defect in beta-cell function.
This describes the pathogenesis of Type 1 DM, which involves T-cell mediated autoimmunity, unlike the monogenic defects of MODY.
This describes Type A insulin resistance, which is classified under genetic defects in insulin action rather than primary defects in beta-cell function like MODY.
This describes an endocrinopathy that can cause secondary diabetes (secondary to acromegaly), not a primary genetic MODY defect.
This describes Maternally Inherited Diabetes and Deafness (MIDD), a distinct monogenic mitochondrial form of diabetes.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1103 (Book Page): MODY can result from germline loss-of-function mutations in one of six genes (see Table 24.6), of which mutations of glucokinase (GCK) are the most common. Glucokinase is a rate-limiting step in oxidative glucose metabolism, which, in turn, is coupled to insulin secretion.

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: Which radioactive iodine uptake pattern would most effectively help differentiate Graves disease from the hyperthyroid phase of thyroiditis?
options: Localized uptake in a solitary 'hot' nodule
Diffusely increased uptake throughout the entire gland
Elevated uptake limited to the thyroid isthmus
Significantly diminished or low iodine uptake
Irregularly distributed patchy uptake in multiple nodules
correctOption: Diffusely increased uptake throughout the entire gland
optionExplanations: This pattern characterizes a toxic adenoma, where a single autonomous nodule suppresses the rest of the gland.

In Graves disease, thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins continuously stimulate the entire gland, leading to diffuse iodine consumption. Thyroiditis, conversely, shows low uptake as the gland is damaged and not synthesizing new hormone.
