citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1069 (Book Page): sparsely granulated variants are composed of chromophobe cells with patchy, weak staining for GH and a characteristic paranuclear glossy inclusion known as a fibrous body

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: A 55-year-old female presents with chronic bone pain and nephrolithiasis. Laboratory tests reveal a serum calcium of 11.8 mg/dL (Normal: 8.5-10.5) and a serum phosphate of 2.1 mg/dL (Normal: 2.5-4.5). Which diagnostic combination is most consistent with this presentation?
options: Hypoparathyroidism with low PTH and high phosphate
Pseudohypoparathyroidism with high PTH and high phosphate
Primary hyperparathyroidism with high PTH and low phosphate
Secondary hyperparathyroidism with high PTH and high phosphate
Vitamin D toxicity with low PTH and low phosphate
correctOption: Primary hyperparathyroidism with high PTH and low phosphate
optionExplanations: Hypoparathyroidism results in low serum calcium and high serum phosphate, which is the opposite of this patient's profile.
Pseudohypoparathyroidism is characterized by target organ resistance, leading to hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia despite elevated PTH.
Primary hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcemia (due to bone resorption and renal absorption) and hypophosphatemia (due to PTH-induced inhibition of renal phosphate reabsorption).
Secondary hyperparathyroidism typically presents with low or normal serum calcium and high phosphate due to renal retention.
Vitamin D toxicity causes high calcium but would typically show suppressed (low) PTH levels and normal or high phosphate.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1094 (Book Page): [Other laboratory alterations referable to PTH excess include hypophosphatemia and increased urinary excretion of both calcium and phosphate.]

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
coreConcept: Differentiating Duct Ectasia from Zuska Disease
statement: When distinguishing between duct ectasia and squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts, which of the following diagnostic factors is most characteristic of duct ectasia?
options: Occurrence primarily in the fifth or sixth decade of life in multiparous women
Development during the first month of breastfeeding
Strong clinical association with cigarette smoking (>90% of cases)
Histological presence of keratin plugs in the major nipple ducts
Formation of a fistula tract opening at the edge of the areola
correctOption: Occurrence primarily in the fifth or sixth decade of life in multiparous women
optionExplanations: Duct ectasia typically affects older, multiparous women and presents as a palpable periareolar mass, distinguishing it from the younger, smoker-prevalent metaplasia.
Acute mastitis, not duct ectasia, is the primary inflammatory condition occurring during the early breastfeeding period.
Smoking is nearly universally associated with squamous metaplasia (Zuska disease), whereas duct ectasia has no such correlation.
Keratin plugs are the hallmark of squamous metaplasia; duct ectasia involves the accumulation of inspissated secretions and lipid-laden macrophages without keratin metaplasia.
Fistula formation is a common recurrent complication of squamous metaplasia due to chronic abscess rupture, not duct ectasia.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1039 (Book Page): This disorder tends to occur in the fifth or sixth decade of life, usually in multiparous women. Unlike squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts, it is not associated with cigarette smoking.

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: A 30-year-old male presents to the emergency department following a severe head injury. Over the next 24 hours, he develops massive polyuria and extreme thirst. Labs reveal a serum sodium of 158 mEq/L and a urine specific gravity of 1.002. What is the most likely pathophysiological mechanism for his condition?
options: Excessive renal sensitivity to circulating Vasopressin
Ectopic secretion of ADH from a traumatic lung contusion
Primary hyperaldosteronism due to adrenal hemorrhage
Compression of the anterior pituitary by a microadenoma
Trauma-induced deficiency of Antidiuretic Hormone
correctOption: Trauma-induced deficiency of Antidiuretic Hormone
optionExplanations: Excessive sensitivity to ADH would lead to water retention and hyponatremia, not the dilute polyuria seen in this case.
Ectopic ADH secretion (SIADH) would cause hyponatremia and concentrated urine, the opposite of the findings presented here.
Hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension and hypokalemia; it does not present with massive polyuria and very low urine specific gravity.
While microadenomas can cause hormone excess, they rarely cause acute DI unless they lead to apoplexy or significant hypothalamic damage.
Head trauma often damages the hypothalamus or pituitary stalk, leading to central Diabetes Insipidus characterized by ADH deficiency, hypernatremia, and dilute urine.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1071 (Book Page): ADH deficiency causes diabetes insipidus... Diabetes insipidus can occur in a variety of conditions, including head trauma, tumors, inflammatory disorders...

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: What is the single most sensitive screening test for the clinical diagnosis of primary hypothyroidism?
options: Serum total T3 levels
Serum thyroglobulin concentration
Serum TSH concentration
Serum free T4 levels
TRH stimulation test
correctOption: Serum TSH concentration
optionExplanations: Total T3 is often the last value to drop in hypothyroidism and is not a sensitive indicator of early or mild disease.
Thyroglobulin is a protein used to monitor thyroid cancer recurrence; it is not used to screen for functional status like hypothyroidism.
In primary hypothyroidism, the pituitary increases TSH production to compensate for low thyroid output; even subtle drops in T4 trigger significant TSH rises.
While low free T4 confirms hypothyroidism, TSH elevations occur much earlier due to the loss of negative feedback, making TSH a better screening tool.
The TRH stimulation test is primarily used to differentiate between secondary (pituitary) and tertiary (hypothalamic) thyroid disorders, not for routine screening.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1076 (Book Page): Measurement of the serum TSH level is the most sensitive screening test for this disorder.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: A patient with hypercortisolism is found to have increased ACTH levels that do not decrease when administered low-dose dexamethasone, but show significant suppression with high-dose dexamethasone. What is the most likely underlying pathology?
options: A pituitary corticotroph microadenoma
An adrenal cortical carcinoma
A cortisol-secreting adrenal adenoma
Iatrogenic administration of prednisone
A small-cell carcinoma of the lung
correctOption: A pituitary corticotroph microadenoma
optionExplanations: Cushing disease (pituitary source) is unique among the endogenous causes because the neoplastic corticotrophs retain some sensitivity to high levels of glucocorticoids.
Adrenal carcinomas are ACTH-independent; therefore, ACTH levels would be low, and cortisol production would not be suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone.
Primary adrenal adenomas result in suppressed ACTH levels due to negative feedback, and their cortisol output is autonomous, failing to suppress with dexamethasone.
Iatrogenic Cushing syndrome results in low levels of endogenous ACTH because the exogenous steroid suppresses the entire hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis.
Ectopic ACTH production by malignancies like small-cell lung cancer is typically insensitive to both low and high doses of dexamethasone.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1116 (Book Page): In pituitary Cushing syndrome... After higher doses of injected dexamethasone, however, the pituitary responds by reducing ACTH secretion, which is reflected by suppression of urinary steroid secretion.

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
coreConcept: G-protein signaling defects in pituitary tumors
statement: In the metabolic classification of somatotroph adenomas, activating mutations in Gs-alpha interfere with which specific enzymatic function?
options: Adenyl cyclase inhibition
Ubiquitin-specific protease activity
Tyrosine kinase phosphorylation
GTPase activity
Phosphodiesterase degradation
correctOption: GTPase activity
optionExplanations: The mutation leads to constitutive activation of adenyl cyclase, not its inhibition.
USP8 is a deubiquitinase mutated in corticotroph adenomas, not somatotroph adenomas.
The G-protein pathway involves second messengers (cAMP), not direct receptor tyrosine kinase phosphorylation.
Normal Gs-alpha has intrinsic GTPase activity to turn itself off. Mutation abrogates this, keeping the protein in its active GTP-bound state.
Phosphodiesterase breaks down cAMP; the GNAS mutation acts upstream by overproducing cAMP via adenyl cyclase.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1066 (Book Page): Approximately 40% of somatotroph cell adenomas bear somatic GNAS mutations that abrogate the GTPase activity of Gs-alpha, leading to constitutive activation of Gs-alpha.

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: A 28-year-old male is admitted after a severe head injury involving a skull base fracture. Within 24 hours, his urine output increases to 600 mL/hour. Lab results show a serum sodium of 152 mEq/L and a urine specific gravity of 1.002. What is the most likely underlying syndrome?
options: Primary empty sella syndrome
Pituitary apoplexy with hyperprolactinemia
Central diabetes insipidus
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Syndrome of inappropriate ADH (SIADH)
correctOption: Central diabetes insipidus
optionExplanations: Primary empty sella syndrome typically presents with visual field defects and is often asymptomatic or associated with mild endocrine anomalies, not acute polyuric crises.
Pituitary apoplexy is characterized by sudden excruciating headache and visual changes, often following hemorrhage into an existing adenoma.
The combination of severe head trauma, massive polyuria, hypernatremia, and very low urine specific gravity is pathognomonic for central DI due to traumatic ADH deficiency.
While the labs fit, nephrogenic DI is less likely in the setting of acute head trauma, which typically causes central (neurogenic) failure.
SIADH results in low serum sodium (hyponatremia) and concentrated urine, the opposite of the findings in this patient.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1071 (Book Page): ADH deficiency causes diabetes insipidus, a condition characterized by excessive urination (polyuria) due to an inability of the kidney to resorb water properly from the urine. ... can occur in a variety of conditions, including head trauma

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: Granulomatous lobular mastitis is a specific inflammatory disorder of the breast that is distinguished from other granulomatous processes by which of the following features?
options: The disorder manifests as a painless thickening of the nipple skin.
The disease occurs exclusively in parous women.
The granulomas are typically associated with caseous necrosis.
The condition is strongly linked to heavy cigarette smoking.
The lesions are caused by the presence of a ruptured blue-dome cyst.
correctOption: The disease occurs exclusively in parous women.
optionExplanations: A painless thickening of the nipple skin suggests Paget disease or duct ectasia; granulomatous mastitis typically presents as a tender or firm mass.
Granulomatous lobular mastitis is unique in its demographic restriction; it is only observed in women who have been pregnant and/or lactated.
Caseous necrosis is characteristic of tuberculous mastitis, not the idiopathic granulomatous lobular mastitis, which often shows neutrophilic microabscesses.
Smoking is linked to Zuska disease (squamous metaplasia), whereas granulomatous lobular mastitis is related to the parous state.
Blue-dome cysts are a feature of nonproliferative fibrocystic changes and are not the cause of granulomatous lobular mastitis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1039 (Book Page): Granulomatous lobular mastitis is an uncommon disease that occurs only in parous women. The granulomas are closely associated with lobules and may contain lipid vacuoles surrounded by neutrophils.

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: When differentiating causes of hypercalcemia, which laboratory finding most strongly suggests hypercalcemia of malignancy rather than primary hyperparathyroidism?
options: Elevated serum phosphate levels
Low to undetectable serum parathyroid hormone (PTH)
Hypocalciuria with high PTH
Reduced urinary calcium excretion
Elevated serum parathyroid hormone (PTH)
correctOption: Low to undetectable serum parathyroid hormone (PTH)
optionExplanations: Phosphate is often low in primary hyperparathyroidism; elevated phosphate is more characteristic of secondary hyperparathyroidism in renal failure.
In malignancy, hypercalcemia is usually driven by PTHrP or bone resorption, which suppresses the normal parathyroid glands' endogenous PTH production.
Hypocalciuria with high PTH is specific to familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia, not malignancy.
Malignancy-associated hypercalcemia often involves high urinary calcium as the kidneys attempt to clear the excess load.
Elevated PTH is characteristic of primary hyperparathyroidism, where the gland is autonomously overproducing the hormone despite high calcium.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1094 (Book Page): PTH levels are low to undetectable in hypercalcemia caused by nonparathyroid diseases

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: A patient presents with lethargy, cold intolerance, and generalized fatigue. Laboratory evaluation confirms low serum free T4. Which biochemical finding would most reliably distinguish primary from secondary (central) hypothyroidism?
options: Elevated serum cholesterol and LDL
Serum TSH concentration levels
The presence of antithyroglobulin antibodies
Serum levels of transthyretin
Reduced basal metabolic rate
correctOption: Serum TSH concentration levels
optionExplanations: Dyslipidemia is a systemic metabolic consequence of low thyroid hormone and occurs in both primary and secondary hypothyroidism due to altered lipid clearance.
In primary disease, TSH rises due to lack of negative feedback; in secondary (central) disease, TSH is low or inappropriately normal because the defect is at the pituitary/hypothalamus.
Antithyroglobulin antibodies are specific for autoimmune etiologies like Hashimoto thyroiditis but do not differentiate between primary and central failure of the axis.
Transthyretin is a binding protein for T4 and its levels do not serve as a diagnostic indicator to distinguish primary from secondary hypothyroidism.
Reduced basal metabolic rate is a common systemic consequence of any hypothyroid state and does not localize the defect to the gland or the pituitary.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1076 (Book Page): The TSH level is increased in primary hypothyroidism as a result of a loss of feedback inhibition... The TSH level is not increased in persons with hypothyroidism due to primary hypothalamic or pituitary disease.

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
statement: Which of the following lineage-specific transcription factors is the primary marker for the classification of corticotroph adenomas?
options: PIT-1
SF-1
ER alpha
TPIT
GATA-2
correctOption: TPIT
optionExplanations: PIT-1 marks the somatotroph, lactotroph, and thyrotroph lineages.
SF-1 is the primary marker for the gonadotroph lineage.
ER alpha is co-expressed in lactotroph and gonadotroph lineages but not corticotrophs.
TPIT is the specific marker for corticotroph cells and their corresponding adenomas.
GATA-2 is a transcription factor associated with gonadotroph and thyrotroph development.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1064 (Book Page): corticotrophs are derived from progenitor cells expressing the transcription factor TPIT

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: What is the typical laboratory finding regarding urine concentration in a patient suffering from central diabetes insipidus?
options: Specific gravity greater than 1.030
Specific gravity lower than normal
Excretion of highly concentrated urine
Presence of gross hematuria
High urinary sodium concentration
correctOption: Specific gravity lower than normal
optionExplanations: A specific gravity >1.030 indicates highly concentrated urine, the opposite of what is seen in DI.
Because the kidney cannot resorb water, the urine remains very dilute, resulting in a specific gravity that is lower than normal (often <1.005).
DI is defined by the inability to concentrate urine; the urine is dilute and copious.
Hematuria is a sign of renal or urinary tract injury and is not a feature of DI.
While total sodium excretion may be high due to volume, the concentration is low because of the massive water volume.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1072 (Book Page): The clinical manifestations of these two disorders are similar and include the excretion of large volumes of dilute urine with a lower than normal specific gravity.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: When performing biochemical localization for endogenous Cushing syndrome, which laboratory result is most characteristically used to differentiate a pituitary corticotroph adenoma from ectopic ACTH secretion?
options: Suppression of ACTH after a standard dose of metyrapone
A low baseline serum ACTH concentration
Failure to suppress cortisol with low-dose dexamethasone
An elevated 24-hour urine free-cortisol level
A reduction in urinary steroid excretion after high-dose dexamethasone
correctOption: A reduction in urinary steroid excretion after high-dose dexamethasone
optionExplanations: Metyrapone is used in some specialized centers but the definitive classic contrast in standard texts is the high-dose dexamethasone test, which highlights the partial feedback sensitivity of the pituitary.
Low baseline ACTH would indicate an ACTH-independent cause (adrenal tumor). Both pituitary adenomas and ectopic sources typically exhibit elevated or inappropriately normal ACTH levels.
Failure to suppress with low-dose dexamethasone is a screening test to confirm Cushing syndrome of any etiology; it does not help in differentiating the specific source.
Elevated 24-hour urine free cortisol confirms the presence of hypercortisolism but is elevated in all forms of Cushing syndrome, making it useless for differential localization.

Pituitary adenomas (Cushing disease) retain some sensitivity to glucocorticoid feedback; therefore, while they ignore low doses, a high dose of dexamethasone typically suppresses ACTH and cortisol. Ectopic sources are usually completely autonomous and insensitive.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1116 (Book Page): [After higher doses of injected dexamethasone, however, the pituitary responds by reducing ACTH secretion, which is reflected by suppression of urinary steroid secretion. Ectopic ACTH secretion results in an elevated level of ACTH, but its secretion is completely insensitive to low or high doses of exogenous dexamethasone.]

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
coreConcept: Differential diagnosis of inflammatory breast masses
statement: When contrasting Duct Ectasia with Squamous Metaplasia of Lactiferous Ducts, which clinical and morphological feature is uniquely characteristic of Duct Ectasia?
options: Marked acute inflammation with liquefactive necrosis of fat
The presence of a fistula tract opening at the edge of the areola
Predominant occurrence in the first month of breastfeeding
Presentation in multiparous women during the fifth or sixth decade
Strong association with a history of heavy cigarette smoking
correctOption: Presentation in multiparous women during the fifth or sixth decade
optionExplanations: Acute inflammation and fat necrosis are features of physical trauma (Fat Necrosis) or Acute Mastitis, whereas Duct Ectasia is defined by chronic periductal inflammation and fibrosis.
Fistula tracts are a common complication of recurrent subareolar abscesses (Zuska disease) due to chronic inflammation and keratin-induced drainage pathways, but are not typical of Duct Ectasia.
The first month of breastfeeding is the peak period for Acute Mastitis, while Duct Ectasia typically affects older, non-lactating women.
Duct Ectasia characteristically presents in an older demographic (50s-60s) and is associated with multiparity, whereas Zuska disease can affect younger women and men and is smoker-dominant.
Smoking is the hallmark risk factor for Squamous Metaplasia of Lactiferous Ducts (Zuska disease), whereas Duct Ectasia is explicitly not associated with it.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1039 (Book Page): This disorder tends to occur in the fifth or sixth decade of life, usually in multiparous women. Unlike squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts, it is not associated with cigarette smoking.

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: In a patient with suspected primary hypothyroidism, which laboratory evaluation serves as the most sensitive screening indicator?
options: Serum total T3 levels
Thyroglobulin autoantibody titers
Serum total T4 levels
Radioactive iodine uptake scan
Serum TSH levels
correctOption: Serum TSH levels
optionExplanations: Total T3 levels are often misleading due to changes in binding proteins and are generally the last hormone levels to drop in primary hypothyroidism.
While autoantibodies (Anti-TPO, Anti-Tg) help diagnose the cause of hypothyroidism (e.g., Hashimoto's), they do not measure the functional status of the gland.
Total T4 levels are affected by the concentration of binding proteins (like TBG). While low free T4 is used for confirmation, it is less sensitive than TSH for initial screening.
Iodine uptake scans are primarily used to determine the etiology of hyperthyroidism (e.g., hot vs. cold nodules) and are not used for screening hypothyroidism.
Serum TSH is the most sensitive screen because the pituitary gland responds log-linearly to even minute drops in circulating free T4, raising TSH levels well before T4 falls below the normal range.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1076 (Book Page): Measurement of the serum TSH level is the most sensitive screening test for this disorder.

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
statement: A 38-year-old female presents with a pituitary mass. Immunohistochemical staining reveals the expression of the transcription factor PIT-1. Which of the following adenoma types is excluded by this finding?
options: Lactotroph adenoma
Somatotroph adenoma
Mammosomatotroph adenoma
Thyrotroph adenoma
Corticotroph adenoma
correctOption: Corticotroph adenoma
optionExplanations: Lactotrophs are part of the PIT-1 lineage (along with ER alpha expression).
Somatotrophs belong to the PIT-1 lineage and would express this factor.
Mammosomatotrophs secrete both GH and Prolactin and originate from the PIT-1 lineage.
Thyrotrophs differentiate from the common PIT-1 precursor line.
Corticotrophs belong to a distinct lineage defined by the transcription factor TPIT, not PIT-1.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1064 (Book Page): For example, somatotrophs, mammosomatotrophs, lactotrophs, and thyrotrophs are all derived from a common precursor that expresses the transcription factor PIT-1... In contrast, corticotrophs are derived from progenitor cells expressing the transcription factor TPIT

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: A laboratory comparison is performed to distinguish between primary hyperparathyroidism and hypercalcemia caused by nonparathyroid diseases. Which finding uniquely points toward a parathyroid-origin?
options: Elevated serum calcium levels
Inappropriately elevated parathyroid hormone levels
Increased urinary calcium excretion
Reduced levels of PTH-related protein
Suppressed serum phosphate levels
correctOption: Inappropriately elevated parathyroid hormone levels
optionExplanations: Hypercalcemia is a non-specific finding that can be present in both primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy.
High PTH in the setting of high calcium confirms autonomous parathyroid activity, whereas high calcium from other causes would naturally suppress PTH.
Hypercalciuria is seen in many hypercalcemic states as the kidney attempts to clear the excess filtered load, making it non-specific.
Low PTHrP levels simply rule out one specific cause of malignancy-related hypercalcemia but do not confirm a parathyroid origin.
While low phosphate is common in hyperparathyroidism, it can also occur in other states and is not as definitive as a PTH assay.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1093 (Book Page): In individuals with primary hyperparathyroidism, serum PTH levels are inappropriately elevated for the level of serum calcium, whereas PTH levels are low to undetectable in hypercalcemia caused by nonparathyroid diseases.

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: A 10-year-old child presents with extreme thirst and the excretion of 10 liters of very dilute urine daily. A deficiency in which hormone is the most likely underlying cause of this condition?
options: Oxytocin
Adrenocorticotropic hormone
Antidiuretic hormone
Thyroid-stimulating hormone
Growth hormone
correctOption: Antidiuretic hormone
optionExplanations: Oxytocin is primarily involved in uterine contractions during labor and milk ejection during lactation; it does not regulate renal water resorption.

Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) regulates the adrenal cortex; while its deficiency can cause secondary adrenal insufficiency, it does not directly cause the massive polyuria characteristic of diabetes insipidus.
Antidiuretic hormone (ADH), also known as vasopressin, is essential for water conservation in the kidney. Its deficiency lead to the inability to concentrate urine, resulting in diabetes insipidus.
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) deficiency leads to secondary hypothyroidism; it is not the primary mediator of renal water resorption.
Growth hormone deficiency in children results in pituitary dwarfism/growth failure, not polyuria or polydipsia.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1071 (Book Page): ADH deficiency causes diabetes insipidus, a condition characterized by excessive urination (polyuria) due to an inability of the kidney to resorb water properly from the urine.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: Which morphological characteristic is uniquely associated with granulomatous lobular mastitis compared to other granulomatous diseases of the breast?
options: The presence of caseous necrosis and acid-fast bacilli.
Densely collagenized stroma involving the interlobular spaces.
Occurs only in parous women with granulomas restricted to the lobules.
Formation of keratin plugs within the lactiferous sinuses.
Diffuse infiltration of the dermis by tumor emboli within lymphatics.
correctOption: Occurs only in parous women with granulomas restricted to the lobules.
optionExplanations: Caseous necrosis and bacilli are markers of tuberculosis, a specific infection that can involve the breast but is distinct from idiopathic granulomatous lobular mastitis.
Collagenized stroma is the feature of lymphocytic mastopathy, which mimics cancer but lacks lobular-restricted granulomas.
Granulomatous lobular mastitis is specifically identified by its restriction to the breast lobules and its occurrence exclusively in women who have been pregnant.
Keratin plugs are the initiating lesion in Zuska disease, not granulomatous lobular mastitis.
Dermal lymphatic emboli are the hallmark of inflammatory breast cancer, a malignancy that mimics inflammation morphologically.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1039 (Book Page): Granulomatous lobular mastitis is an uncommon disease that occurs only in parous women. The granulomas are closely associated with lobules...

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
coreConcept: Pathophysiology of goiter in iodine deficiency
statement: A patient living in a mountainous region with low dietary iodine develops a massive goiter but remains clinically euthyroid. What is the most likely mechanism sustaining her thyroid hormone levels?
options: Inhibition of the peripheral deiodination of T3
Compensatory hypertrophy and hyperplasia driven by increased TSH
Ectopic hormone production from a struma ovarii
Conversion of TSH to a thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin
Autonomous production of T4 by mutated follicular cells
correctOption: Compensatory hypertrophy and hyperplasia driven by increased TSH
optionExplanations: Inhibiting peripheral deiodination would decrease active T3 levels, worsening hypothyroidism rather than maintaining a euthyroid state.
In iodine deficiency, the initial drop in T4 stimulates the pituitary to release more TSH, which forces the thyroid to enlarge (goiter) to increase functional mass, often maintaining euthyroidism.
Struma ovarii is a rare cause of thyrotoxicosis from an ovarian teratoma, unrelated to endemic iodine-deficiency goiter.
TSH is not converted to immunoglobulin; thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins are autoantibodies produced by B cells in Graves disease.
Autonomous production is seen in toxic adenomas or toxic multinodular goiter, not in typical endemic diffuse goiter.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1080 (Book Page): Reduced thyroid hormone production leads to a compensatory rise in the serum TSH level, which, in turn, causes hypertrophy and hyperplasia of thyroid follicular cells and, ultimately, enlargement of the thyroid gland. This increase in functional mass of the gland usually overcomes the hormone deficiency, ensuring a euthyroid metabolic state in most individuals.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: In the differential diagnosis of hypercortisolism, a pituitary-dependent corticotroph adenoma typically exhibits which specific response during a high-dose dexamethasone suppression test?
options: Malignant transformation into an anaplastic carcinoma
Immediate cardiovascular collapse and shock
Reduction in ACTH secretion and suppressed urinary steroid excretion
Complete insensitivity with no change in cortisol excretion
Paradoxical increase in cortisol and ACTH levels
correctOption: Reduction in ACTH secretion and suppressed urinary steroid excretion
optionExplanations: Dexamethasone does not induce malignant transformation of pituitary cells.
This describes an adrenal crisis, which is associated with acute insufficiency, not the dexamethasone test.
Pituitary adenomas, while abnormal, often retain the ability to respond to high-dose glucocorticoid feedback, allowing for the suppression of ACTH.
Complete insensitivity is the hallmark of ectopic ACTH secretion or adrenal tumors, not pituitary adenomas.
A paradoxical increase is sometimes seen in primary pigmented nodular adrenal disease, but not in typical pituitary Cushing disease.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1116 (Book Page): [After higher doses of injected dexamethasone, however, the pituitary responds by reducing ACTH secretion, which is reflected by suppression of urinary steroid secretion.]

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
statement: A 55-year-old male presents with severe headaches and bitemporal hemianopsia. MRI reveals a 2.5 cm mass in the sella turcica. Endocrine workup shows slightly decreased LH and FSH levels, but no clinical evidence of hormone hypersecretion. Immunohistochemistry of the tumor cells is positive for steroidogenic factor-1 (SF-1) and GATA-2. What is the classification of this adenoma?
options: Lactotroph adenoma
Somatotroph adenoma
Corticotroph adenoma
Thyrotroph adenoma
Gonadotroph adenoma
correctOption: Gonadotroph adenoma
optionExplanations: Lactotroph adenomas express PIT-1 and ER-alpha, and typically cause hyperprolactinemia.
Somatotroph adenomas express PIT-1 and usually cause acromegaly or gigantism.
Corticotroph adenomas express TPIT and are usually functioning (Cushing's) or silent, but not SF-1 positive.
Thyrotroph adenomas express PIT-1 and are rare causes of hyperthyroidism.
Correct. Gonadotroph adenomas are characterized by SF-1 and GATA-2 expression and are frequently nonfunctioning (silent), presenting with mass effects.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1070 (Book Page): Gonadotroph (LH-producing and FSH-producing) adenomas... Gonadotroph adenomas also usually express steroidogenic factor-1 (SF-1), GATA-2, and ER alpha, transcription factors associated with normal gonadotroph differentiation.

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: Which of the following is the primary clinical manifestation of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) deficiency?
options: Reduced serum osmolality and hyponatremia
Excessive urination (polyuria) with dilute urine
Peripheral edema and increased blood pressure
Concentrated urine with high specific gravity
Hypouricemia and hypervolemia
correctOption: Excessive urination (polyuria) with dilute urine
optionExplanations: This describes SIADH (excess ADH), not ADH deficiency. Deficiency leads to hypernatremia and increased serum osmolality due to water loss.
The deficiency of ADH prevents the renal collecting ducts from resorbing water, leading to the excretion of large volumes of dilute urine, which is the hallmark of diabetes insipidus.
Peripheral edema is specifically noted in the text as not developing in ADH-related syndromes like SIADH, and ADH deficiency causes volume depletion, not hypervolemia.
Concentrated urine occurs when ADH is present and active. In its absence, the kidney cannot concentrate urine, resulting in a very low specific gravity.
Hypouricemia is not a feature of ADH deficiency; rather, the loss of free water leads to hemoconcentration of solutes.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1071 (Book Page): ADH deficiency causes diabetes insipidus, a condition characterized by excessive urination (polyuria) due to an inability of the kidney to resorb water properly from the urine.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: Which morphological feature is uniquely characteristic of 'cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis' as described in the reference?
options: Cribriform spaces with rounded 'cookie cutter' margins
Dermal lymphovascular space plugging with tumor emboli
Dense collagenous stroma with a complete absence of lobules
Intraductal branching fibrovascular cores with two cell layers
Granulomas containing lipid vacuoles surrounded by neutrophils
correctOption: Granulomas containing lipid vacuoles surrounded by neutrophils
optionExplanations: Cribriform spaces are characteristic of cribriform ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS).
Lymphovascular plugging is the morphological hallmark of inflammatory carcinoma, a mimic of inflammatory disorders, not granulomatous mastitis.
A complete absence of lobules is a feature of the normal male breast or gynecomastia, not the granulomatous response seen here.
Branching fibrovascular cores define a papilloma, a proliferative epithelial lesion, not an inflammatory disorder.
The specific combination of granulomatous inflammation and neutrophils surrounding lipid-filled spaces is diagnostic for this group of disorders, often linked to Corynebacterium.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1039 (Book Page): Granulomatous lobular mastitis is an uncommon disease that occurs only in parous women. The granulomas are closely associated with lobules and may contain lipid vacuoles surrounded by neutrophils. A similar histologic pattern is seen in cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis, which is often caused by lipophilic Corynebacteria.

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: A pericentromeric inversion on chromosome 11, which relocates the CCDN1 gene adjacent to the PTH gene promoter, is a recognized mechanism in which of the following?
options: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome
Sporadic parathyroid adenomas
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia
Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1
Secondary hyperparathyroidism in renal failure
correctOption: Sporadic parathyroid adenomas
optionExplanations: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome involves acute adrenal insufficiency due to hemorrhagic necrosis, usually following meningococcemia.
The inversion relocates the Cyclin D1 gene near the PTH promoter, causing protein overexpression and driving cell proliferation in 10-20% of sporadic adenomas.
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the calcium-sensing receptor (CASR) gene.
Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 is caused by mutations in the AIRE gene and is characterized by hypoparathyroidism.
Secondary hyperparathyroidism is a reactive process driven by hypocalcemia, not typically characterized by the CCDN1 inversion.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1092 (Book Page): [Between 10% and 20% of sporadic parathyroid adenomas have this clonal rearrangement.]

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
coreConcept: Negative Feedback in the HPT Axis
statement: Which physiological mechanism maintains the metabolic equilibrium of thyroid hormones by suppressing the release of TSH when T3 and T4 levels are elevated?
options: Degradation of thyrotropin-releasing hormone in the portal venous plexus
Feedback inhibition of the anterior pituitary and hypothalamus
Competitive binding of C-peptide to TSH receptors
Positive feedback stimulation of the hypothalamus
Downregulation of thyroid hormone receptors in peripheral tissues
correctOption: Feedback inhibition of the anterior pituitary and hypothalamus
optionExplanations: While TRH has a short half-life, the regulation of the axis is driven by active hormone feedback on secreting cells, not by passive portal degradation.
This is the classic negative feedback loop. Thyroid hormones act on both the hypothalamus (reducing TRH) and the anterior pituitary (reducing TSH) to maintain homeostasis.
C-peptide is a byproduct of insulin synthesis in the pancreas and has no role in the thyroid-stimulating hormone signaling pathway.
Elevated T3/T4 levels inhibit, rather than stimulate, the hypothalamus to prevent excessive metabolic activity.
Downregulation of receptors might occur in some states, but the primary regulator of circulating levels is the feedback to the central control organs (pituitary/hypothalamus).
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1065 (Book Page): [The endocrine hormone inhibits production of the trophic factors, a process known as feedback inhibition, thus maintaining physiologic levels of the hormone.]

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
statement: A patient with long-standing Cushing syndrome undergoes bilateral adrenalectomy. Shortly after, they develop skin hyperpigmentation and a large, aggressive pituitary mass. Which lineage-specific transcription factor would likely be expressed in this tumor?
options: GATA-2
TPIT
ERα
SF-1
PIT-1
correctOption: TPIT
optionExplanations: GATA-2 is expressed in gonadotrophs alongside SF-1; it is not a marker for the ACTH-secreting tumors found in Nelson syndrome.
Nelson syndrome involves the rapid expansion of a pre-existing corticotroph adenoma after the removal of adrenal feedback. Corticotrophs are defined by the expression of TPIT.
ERα (Estrogen receptor alpha) is expressed in lactotrophs and gonadotrophs but is absent in the corticotroph tumors causing Cushing disease and Nelson syndrome.
SF-1 (Steroidogenic factor-1) is the transcription factor for gonadotroph adenomas, which are usually non-functional and do not cause hypercortisolism.
PIT-1 is the transcription factor for the somatotroph, lactotroph, and thyrotroph lineages; it would not be found in an ACTH-secreting Nelson syndrome tumor.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1070 (Book Page): Nelson syndrome... occurs because of loss of the inhibitory effect of adrenal corticosteroids on a corticotroph microadenoma... patients present with mass effects due to the pituitary tumor, and there can be hyperpigmentation... Page 1065 (Book Page): Corticotrophs are derived from progenitor cells expressing the transcription factor TPIT

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: Which genetic finding is associated specifically with the development of X-linked nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?
options: Mutations of arginine vasopressin receptor type 2 (AVPR2)
Activating mutations in the GNAS gene
Inactivating mutations of the AIRE gene
Germline mutations in the DICER1 gene
Autosomal dominant mutations of the AVP gene
correctOption: Mutations of arginine vasopressin receptor type 2 (AVPR2)
optionExplanations: The AVPR2 gene is located on the X chromosome and encodes the V2 receptor in the kidney; its mutation renders the kidney unable to respond to ADH.
GNAS mutations are associated with pituitary somatotroph adenomas (acromegaly) or McCune-Albright syndrome.
AIRE gene mutations cause autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1, which involves hypoparathyroidism and adrenal insufficiency.
DICER1 mutations are linked to pituitary blastomas in children, not diabetes insipidus.
Autosomal dominant AVP gene mutations cause central diabetes insipidus, not nephrogenic.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1071 (Book Page)-1074: Rarely, diabetes insipidus has a genetic basis... or mutations of arginine vasopressin receptor type 2 (AVPR2), an X-linked condition that usually presents in young boys.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: When hypercortisolism is suspected, which laboratory finding would most reliably distinguish a primary adrenocortical neoplasm from Cushing disease?
options: Assessment of the diurnal pattern of cortisol secretion
Measurement of 24-hour urine free-cortisol levels
Serum ACTH level measurement
Identification of cortisol-secreting cells in an FNA biopsy
Initial response to a low-dose dexamethasone test
correctOption: Serum ACTH level measurement
optionExplanations: The diurnal rhythm is lost in all forms of Cushing syndrome, making it unhelpful for distinguishing the primary cause.
Urine free cortisol will be elevated in both primary adrenal and pituitary sources; it is used for diagnosis of the syndrome but not for localization.
Serum ACTH is low in primary adrenal neoplasms because the autonomous cortisol suppresses the pituitary. In Cushing disease (pituitary), ACTH is high or inappropriately normal.
Biopsy of the adrenal does not tell you if the tumor is the primary source or reacting to pituitary ACTH; biochemical markers like ACTH are the standard for localization.
A low-dose dexamethasone test fails to suppress cortisol in both pituitary and adrenal sources; it is a screening test for the presence of the syndrome only.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1113 (Book Page): The biochemical sine qua non of ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome is elevated serum levels of cortisol with low levels of ACTH.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: A 55-year-old multiparous woman presents with a palpable periareolar mass and thick, white nipple discharge. Histological examination reveals ectatic ducts containing numerous lipid-laden macrophages. Which inflammatory cell type is characteristically prominent in the surrounding chronic infiltrate?
options: Plasma cells
Eosinophils
Atypical rhabdomyoblasts
Myofibroblasts in a radial arrangement
Neutrophils in microabscesses
correctOption: Plasma cells
optionExplanations: Duct ectasia is characterized by a periductal chronic inflammatory infiltrate specifically rich in plasma cells, lymphocytes, and macrophages; the presence of plasma cells is so characteristic that the condition was historically linked to 'plasma cell mastitis.'
Eosinophils are not a defining feature of the chronic periductal infiltrate in duct ectasia.
Atypical rhabdomyoblasts are neoplastic cells found in sarcoma botryoides, not inflammatory breast disorders.
Myofibroblasts in a radial arrangement describe a radial scar (complex sclerosing lesion), not the inflammatory pattern of duct ectasia.
Neutrophils forming microabscesses are characteristic of acute bacterial mastitis or the early phase of granulomatous thyroiditis/mastitis, whereas duct ectasia is a chronic process.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1039 (Book Page): The resulting chronic inflammation and fibrosis contribute to palpable nodularity of the breast. ...a marked periductal and interstitial chronic inflammatory reaction ensues, consisting of lymphocytes, macrophages, and variable numbers of plasma cells.

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: Which laboratory measurement is clinically established as the most sensitive screening modality for detecting primary hypothyroidism?
options: Free triiodothyronine (T3)
Reverse T3
Antithyroglobulin antibodies
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)
Total thyroxine (T4)
correctOption: Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)
optionExplanations: T3 levels are often preserved until late in the course of hypothyroidism and are not sensitive for early detection.
Reverse T3 is generally used in the evaluation of euthyroid sick syndrome, not as a primary screen for hypothyroidism.
Antibody tests confirm an autoimmune etiology but do not measure the functional status of the gland.
In primary hypothyroidism, TSH increases significantly even before T4 drops below the normal range, making it the most sensitive marker.
Total T4 is affected by changes in binding proteins and is less sensitive than TSH.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1076 (Book Page): Measurement of the serum TSH level is the most sensitive screening test for this disorder.

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
coreConcept: Transcription Factor Profiling in Pituitary Adenomas
statement: Which pituitary adenoma subtype is classified by the immunohistochemical expression of SF-1 and GATA-2 transcription factors?
options: Gonadotroph adenoma
Lactotroph adenoma
Somatotroph adenoma
Thyrotroph adenoma
Corticotroph adenoma
correctOption: Gonadotroph adenoma
optionExplanations: Gonadotroph adenomas are distinguished from other 'silent' tumors by their expression of SF-1 and GATA-2, confirming their lineage even if they do not secrete high levels of hormones.
Lactotroph adenomas express PIT-1 and the alpha subunit of the estrogen receptor (ERα).
Somatotroph adenomas are defined by the expression of the PIT-1 transcription factor.
Thyrotroph adenomas belong to the PIT-1 lineage group.
Corticotroph adenomas are classified by the expression of the TPIT transcription factor.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1066 (Book Page): gonadotrophs are derived from precursor cells expressing steroidogenic factor-1 (SF-1) and GATA-2. The expression of these lineage-specific transcription factors is retained in pituitary adenomas and is used to classify these tumors.

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: In the differential diagnosis of hypercalcemia, how do PTH levels typically help distinguish between primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy-associated hypercalcemia?
options: PTH is elevated in both conditions due to bone resorption.
PTH is normal in hyperparathyroidism but low in malignancy.
PTH is inappropriately elevated in hyperparathyroidism and suppressed in malignancy.
PTHrP is the only hormone that increases in both conditions.
PTH is high in malignancy but suppressed in hyperparathyroidism.
correctOption: PTH is inappropriately elevated in hyperparathyroidism and suppressed in malignancy.
optionExplanations: Malignancy-associated hypercalcemia usually causes high calcium which feeds back to inhibit the parathyroid, lowering PTH.
A 'normal' PTH level in the setting of hypercalcemia is still considered inappropriately elevated and indicative of hyperparathyroidism.
Primary hyperparathyroidism involves autonomous PTH production despite high calcium; conversely, malignancy-induced high calcium suppresses the normal parathyroid glands.
PTHrP is characteristic of malignancy and is not typically produced in primary hyperparathyroidism.
This statement is the inverse of the actual physiological findings where PTH is elevated in primary parathyroid disorders.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1093 (Book Page): [In individuals with primary hyperparathyroidism, serum PTH levels are inappropriately elevated for the level of serum calcium, whereas PTH levels are low to undetectable in hypercalcemia caused by nonparathyroid diseases]

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: How does the volume status and edema profile typically present in a patient suffering from chronic SIADH?
options: Normal total body water with severe anasarca
Increased blood volume leading to congestive heart failure
Decreased total body water with pitting peripheral edema
Severely reduced blood volume with resulting hypotension
Increased total body water, normal blood volume, and absent peripheral edema
correctOption: Increased total body water, normal blood volume, and absent peripheral edema
optionExplanations: Total body water is increased in SIADH, and anasarca (severe generalized edema) does not occur in this syndrome.
While water is retained, the text explicitly states that blood volume remains normal and congestive heart failure is not the typical presentation.
Total body water is increased in SIADH, not decreased, and peripheral edema is characteristically absent.
Hypotension and reduced blood volume are features of Diabetes Insipidus or adrenal crisis, not SIADH.
SIADH is often described as 'euvolemic hyponatremia' conceptually because while water is retained, compensatory mechanisms maintain near-normal blood volume and prevent peripheral edema.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1072 (Book Page): Although total body water is increased, blood volume remains normal, and peripheral edema does not develop.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
coreConcept: Environmental Risk Factors for Zuska Disease
statement: Regarding the clinical and environmental associations of breast inflammatory disorders, which patient profile is most strongly linked to the development of recurrent subareolar abscesses?
options: Women with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
Lactating women in the first month postpartum
Current cigarette smokers
Individuals with a history of chest wall radiation
Postmenopausal women with hypertension
correctOption: Current cigarette smokers
optionExplanations: While Type 1 Diabetes is linked to lymphocytic mastopathy, Type 2 Diabetes is not a primary driver of recurrent subareolar abscesses.
Lactating women are at risk for acute bacterial mastitis, not the squamous metaplasia-induced recurrent subareolar abscesses.
Cigarette smoking is nearly universally present in these patients; toxins may alter ductal epithelial differentiation, leading to keratinization.
Radiation exposure increases the risk of angiosarcoma or specific stromal changes, but not typically squamous metaplasia of the ducts.
Hypertension is not a recognized risk factor for the squamous metaplasia that leads to subareolar abscesses.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1038 (Book Page): In many affected women the nipple inverts due to traction produced by inflammation and scarring. More than 90% of afflicted individuals are smokers.

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: Which of the following biochemical profiles is most typical for a patient presenting with primary hyperthyroidism caused by Graves disease?
options: Decreased serum TSH and decreased free T4
Elevated serum TSH and elevated free T4
Decreased serum TSH and elevated free T4
Normal serum TSH and normal free T4
Elevated serum TSH and decreased free T4
correctOption: Decreased serum TSH and elevated free T4
optionExplanations: Low TSH with low T4 is characteristic of secondary (central) hypothyroidism, usually due to pituitary or hypothalamic failure.
Elevated TSH with elevated T4 suggests secondary hyperthyroidism, such as a TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma, which is rare.
Primary hyperthyroidism results in high levels of circulating thyroid hormones which exert negative feedback on the anterior pituitary, leading to suppressed (low) TSH levels.
Normal values of both TSH and free T4 generally indicate a euthyroid state, though subclinical disorders can sometimes show normal hormone levels with abnormal TSH.
High TSH with low T4 is the classic pattern for primary hypothyroidism, where the pituitary attempts to compensate for a failing gland.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1075 (Book Page): Laboratory findings that support the diagnosis of hyperthyroidism include a low TSH value accompanied by an increase in free T4.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: A patient is suspected of having a primary adrenal source of hypercortisolism. Which combination of biochemical parameters would be considered the diagnostic sine qua non for ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome?
options: Elevated serum ACTH and elevated serum aldosterone
Elevated serum ACTH and elevated serum cortisol
Elevated serum ACTH and low serum cortisol
Suppressed cortisol following low-dose dexamethasone
Low serum ACTH and elevated serum cortisol
correctOption: Low serum ACTH and elevated serum cortisol
optionExplanations: Elevated aldosterone and ACTH would point toward a more complex mixed syndrome or mineralocorticoid excess, not pure ACTH-independent Cushing.
This pattern defines ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome, where the pituitary or an ectopic source is driving the adrenal cortex.
This pattern describes primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), where high ACTH is a compensatory response to low cortisol.
Suppression of cortisol by low-dose dexamethasone identifies a normal physiological response, excluding Cushing syndrome.
In primary adrenal Cushing (adenoma or carcinoma), the autonomous production of cortisol provides negative feedback to the pituitary, suppressing ACTH levels.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1114 (Book Page): The biochemical sine qua non of ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome is elevated serum levels of cortisol with low levels of ACTH.

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
statement: In the classification of pituitary neoplasms, what is the specific size threshold used to designate an adenoma as a macroadenoma?
options: Greater than 0.5 cm in diameter
Greater than 1.0 cm in diameter
Greater than 2.0 cm in diameter
Greater than 1.5 cm in diameter
Greater than 2.5 cm in diameter
correctOption: Greater than 1.0 cm in diameter
optionExplanations: Neoplasms smaller than 1 cm are classified as microadenomas; 0.5 cm is well within the microadenoma range.
According to standard clinical pathology classification, 1 cm is the arbitrary cutoff separating microadenomas from macroadenomas.
While a 2.0 cm tumor is a macroadenoma, this is not the threshold for the classification category.
While a 1.5 cm tumor is indeed a macroadenoma, the threshold definition begins at 1.0 cm.
Tumors exceeding 2.5 cm are often giant adenomas, but the classification as a macroadenoma begins at 1 cm.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1066 (Book Page): They are designated, somewhat arbitrarily, microadenomas if they are less than 1 cm in diameter and macroadenomas if they exceed 1 cm in diameter.

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: A patient is diagnosed with the Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone (SIADH). In addition to central nervous system trauma and drugs, which of the following neoplasms is most characteristically associated with the ectopic production of ADH?
options: Somatotroph adenoma of the anterior pituitary
Pheochromocytoma of the adrenal medulla
Follicular adenoma of the thyroid gland
Small-cell carcinoma of the lung
Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid gland
correctOption: Small-cell carcinoma of the lung
optionExplanations: Somatotroph adenomas produce excess growth hormone (GH), leading to acromegaly or gigantism; they do not secrete ADH and are located in the anterior, not posterior, pituitary.
Pheochromocytomas secrete catecholamines (epinephrine/norepinephrine), causing hypertension; while they are neuroendocrine, they are not a standard source of ectopic ADH.
Follicular adenomas are benign thyroid tumors that may produce thyroid hormones (T3/T4) but are not associated with the ectopic production of ADH.
Correct. Small-cell carcinoma of the lung is a neuroendocrine tumor that is the most common malignant cause of paraneoplastic SIADH via the autonomous secretion of ADH.
Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from C-cells and secretes calcitonin; while it can produce other peptides like ACTH, it is not the classic tumor associated with SIADH.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1072 (Book Page): The most frequent causes of SIADH are the secretion of ectopic ADH by malignant neoplasms (particularly small-cell carcinoma of the lung)...

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: What is the characteristic gross appearance of fat necrosis in the breast during its more advanced fibrotic stages?
options: Multiple blue-dome translucent cysts filled with brown fluid
Ill-defined firm nodules with central chalky-white foci
Large, fleshy, leaf-like protrusions into a cystic space
Diffusely erythematous, meaty tissue resembling muscle
Soft, rubbery, well-circumscribed grayish-white nodules
correctOption: Ill-defined firm nodules with central chalky-white foci
optionExplanations: Blue-dome cysts are the gross feature of nonproliferative fibrocystic change, specifically apocrine cysts.
The chalky-white foci in an ill-defined nodule represent areas of saponification and calcification within the necrotic fat, a diagnostic gross feature.
Leaf-like protrusions describe the gross morphology of a phyllodes tumor.
A meaty deep red appearance resembling muscle is the gross description of Graves disease in the thyroid, not an inflammatory disorder of the breast.
Rubbery white circumscribed nodules describe the gross appearance of a fibroadenoma.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1039 (Book Page): Ill-defined, firm, gray-white nodules containing small chalky-white foci are seen grossly [in fat necrosis].

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: A 55-year-old female is found to have a serum calcium level of 12.5 mg/dL. Which laboratory finding would most reliably distinguish primary hyperparathyroidism from hypercalcemia associated with malignancy?
options: Inappropriately elevated intact parathyroid hormone level
High serum levels of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
Significant increase in urinary calcium excretion
Elevated levels of parathyroid hormone-related peptide
Reduced levels of serum phosphorus
correctOption: Inappropriately elevated intact parathyroid hormone level
optionExplanations: In primary hyperparathyroidism, the parathyroid glands function autonomously, resulting in high PTH despite high calcium; in malignancy, PTH is suppressed by the hypercalcemia.
While PTH increases the conversion of vitamin D to its active form, this can also occur in granulomatous diseases, making it less specific than the PTH/Calcium ratio.
Hypercalciuria is a common finding in most causes of significant hypercalcemia as the renal filtered load exceeds the reabsorptive capacity.
PTHrP is the common mediator of hypercalcemia in malignancy (especially squamous cell cancers) but its presence does not confirm the absence of parathyroid disease.
Hypophosphatemia can occur in both conditions (due to PTH or PTHrP effects on renal phosphate excretion) and is therefore not a definitive distinguishing factor.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1093 (Book Page): In individuals with primary hyperparathyroidism, serum PTH levels are inappropriately elevated for the level of serum calcium, whereas PTH levels are low to undetectable in hypercalcemia caused by nonparathyroid diseases

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
coreConcept: Negative feedback inhibition in thyroid regulation.
statement: In the physiological regulation of thyroid function, how do elevated levels of circulating free T3 and T4 influence the hypothalamus-pituitary-thyroid axis?
options: Increase the sensitivity of thyrotrophs to TRH
Activate G-proteins on the thyroid cell membrane
Stimulate the release of TRH from the hypothalamus
Suppress the secretion of both TRH and TSH
Induce hyperplasia of the thyroid follicular cells
correctOption: Suppress the secretion of both TRH and TSH
optionExplanations: High levels of thyroid hormone decrease the sensitivity and response of pituitary thyrotrophs to TRH.
TSH binding to its receptor activates G-proteins; high T3/T4 would lead to lower TSH levels and thus less G-protein activation.
Elevated T3/T4 inhibit, rather than stimulate, the release of TRH from the hypothalamus.
The axis works via negative feedback; high levels of the end hormones (T3/T4) suppress the trophic hormones (TRH/TSH) to maintain homeostasis.
TSH stimulates hyperplasia; since high T3/T4 suppress TSH, they would lead to decreased stimulation (atrophy) of the gland.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1073 (Book Page): Elevated T3 and T4 levels, in turn, feed back to suppress the secretion of both TRH and TSH.

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
coreConcept: Cell lineage transcription factors in pituitary tumors
statement: A patient is diagnosed with a 'plurihormonal adenoma' that secretes growth hormone, prolactin, and thyroid-stimulating hormone. Which transcription factor is typically expressed by these tumors, indicating their common cell-lineage origin?
options: PIT-1
SF-1
TPIT
GATA-2
ER-alpha
correctOption: PIT-1
optionExplanations: PIT-1 is the master regulator for the lineage that gives rise to somatotrophs, lactotrophs, and thyrotrophs.
SF-1 (Steroidogenic Factor-1) is the lineage marker for gonadotrophs (FSH/LH).
TPIT is the lineage marker for corticotrophs, which produce ACTH, not GH or TSH.
GATA-2 is a transcription factor associated with gonadotroph and thyrotroph development but does not define the plurihormonal group alone.
ER-alpha is expressed by lactotrophs and gonadotrophs but is not the primary marker for the combined GH/TSH lineage.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1070 (Book Page): [Most [plurihormonal adenomas] are derived from cells of PIT-1–expressing lineage... somatotrophs, mammosomatotrophs, lactotrophs, and thyrotrophs are all derived from a common precursor that expresses the transcription factor PIT-1.]

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: Which of the following describes the characteristic urine findings in a patient suffering from untreated diabetes insipidus?
options: Highly alkaline pH with frequent casts
Presence of high levels of ketone bodies
Low volume and extremely high concentration
High concentration of glucose and proteins
High volume with a very low specific gravity
correctOption: High volume with a very low specific gravity
optionExplanations: Urine pH and casts are markers of infection or intrinsic renal disease, but they are not standard features of diabetes insipidus.
Ketone bodies are found in diabetic ketoacidosis (associated with diabetes mellitus), but not in the electrolyte-driven polyuria of diabetes insipidus.
This describes the urine findings in states of dehydration or SIADH, not the large-volume dilute urine of diabetes insipidus.
Glucosuria is characteristic of diabetes mellitus. Proteins in urine indicate renal glomerular damage, not posterior pituitary dysfunction.
Diabetes insipidus is defined by the inability to concentrate urine, leading to massive volumes of dilute urine (polyuria) with a low specific gravity (typically <1.005).
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1072 (Book Page): The clinical manifestations of these two disorders [Central and Nephrogenic DI] are similar and include the excretion of large volumes of dilute urine with a lower than normal specific gravity.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: In a patient with a functional cortisol-secreting adrenocortical adenoma, what is the expected state of the non-neoplastic portion of the adrenal cortex?
options: Diffuse hyperplasia of the zona glomerulosa
Normal thickness because cortisol does not affect ACTH
Atrophy due to suppression of ACTH
Expansion of the zona reticularis
Pigmented micronodular transformation
correctOption: Atrophy due to suppression of ACTH
optionExplanations: The zona glomerulosa is largely ACTH-independent and would not undergo diffuse hyperplasia in this context.
Cortisol exerts powerful negative feedback on both the hypothalamus (CRH) and the pituitary (ACTH).
Autonomous cortisol secretion by the tumor inhibits pituitary ACTH release, leading to atrophy of the remaining cortex.
High cortisol levels suppress the entire hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, causing reticularis shrinkage.
Pigmentation is a feature of high ACTH levels or specific genetic syndromes, not simple feedback atrophy.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1116 (Book Page): When Cushing syndrome is caused by an adrenal tumor, the ACTH level is quite low because of feedback inhibition of the pituitary.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
statement: Which microscopic finding is characteristic of the 'late' stages of fat necrosis of the breast?
options: Clustered psammoma bodies within the cores of papillae
Atrophic ducts and lobules with small, monomorphic nuclei
Giant cells, calcifications, and hemosiderin within scar tissue
Keratin plugs within a fistula tract
Epithelial hyperplasia with irregular slit-like fenestrations
correctOption: Giant cells, calcifications, and hemosiderin within scar tissue
optionExplanations: Psammoma bodies are characteristic of papillary carcinoma.
Atrophic ducts with monomorphic nuclei is more descriptive of lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS).

As fat necrosis evolves from the acute stage, the body attempts to repair the area, leading to the formation of granulomatous tissue with giant cells, hemosiderin from hemorrhage, and eventual fibrosis (scar).
Keratin plugs are the feature of Zuska disease.
This describes typical epithelial hyperplasia, not fat necrosis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1039 (Book Page): Subsequently, giant cells, calcifications, and hemosiderin appear, and eventually the lesion is replaced by scar tissue or is encircled and walled off by fibrous tissue.

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: A patient presents with clinical signs of thyrotoxicosis. Laboratory results reveal a suppressed TSH and a normal free T4. Which specific condition should be suspected based on these findings?
options: Iatrogenic hypothyroidism
Secondary hyperthyroidism
Hashimoto thyroiditis (early phase)
T3 toxicosis
Apathetic hyperthyroidism
correctOption: T3 toxicosis
optionExplanations: Iatrogenic hypothyroidism would show low T4 and high TSH.
Secondary hyperthyroidism would show an elevated or inappropriately normal TSH, not a suppressed one.
Hashitoxicosis (early Hashimoto) usually shows elevated T4 along with T3 due to follicle rupture.
T3 toxicosis presents with hyperthyroid symptoms and low TSH, but the excess hormone is specifically triiodothyronine while T4 remains normal or low.
Apathetic hyperthyroidism occurs in the elderly and may have subtle symptoms, but still typically shows elevated T4 unless specifically T3-mediated.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1075 (Book Page): In occasional patients, hyperthyroidism results predominantly from increased circulating levels of T3 (“T3 toxicosis”). In these cases, free T4 levels may be decreased, and direct measurement of serum T3 is useful.

category: Classification of pituitary adenomas
statement: A pituitary neoplasm is analyzed by immunohistochemistry and fails to show expression of PIT-1, TPIT, SF-1, or any known pituitary hormones. This tumor is classified as a:
options: Thyrotroph adenoma
Null cell adenoma
Mammosomatotroph adenoma
Plurihormonal adenoma
Silent gonadotroph adenoma
correctOption: Null cell adenoma
optionExplanations: Thyrotroph adenomas express TSH and the transcription factor PIT-1.
Null cell adenomas are defined by their complete lack of immunohistochemical evidence for any specific hormone production or lineage-determining transcription factors.
Mammosomatotroph adenomas express both GH and PRL, and are PIT-1 positive.
Plurihormonal adenomas express multiple hormones (usually from the PIT-1 lineage).
Silent gonadotroph adenomas still express SF-1 and/or FSH/LH despite being clinically nonfunctional.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1070 (Book Page): Null cell adenomas do not express any markers of hormonal or lineage differentiation. Not surprisingly, null cell adenomas typically present with symptoms stemming from mass effects.

category: Enumerate causes of hypercalcemia, hyper and hypoparathyroidism
statement: In the setting of pseudohypoparathyroidism, which of the following biochemical profiles is expected?
options: High Calcium, Low PTH, High Phosphate
Low Calcium, High PTH, Low Phosphate
High Calcium, High PTH, Low Phosphate
Low Calcium, High PTH, High Phosphate
Low Calcium, Low PTH, High Phosphate
correctOption: Low Calcium, High PTH, High Phosphate
optionExplanations: High Calcium with low PTH occurs in malignancy or Vitamin D toxicity.
Low Calcium with high PTH and low phosphate is the classic profile for Vitamin D deficiency.
High Calcium and high PTH with low phosphate describes primary hyperparathyroidism.
Pseudohypoparathyroidism involves end-organ resistance to PTH; the body senses the lack of PTH action, causing a secondary rise in PTH despite hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia.
Low Calcium and low PTH with high phosphate describes classic primary hypoparathyroidism, where the hormone is not produced.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1095 (Book Page): It presents as hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and elevated circulating PTH.

category: Enumerate and describe posterior pituitary syndromes (inappropriate ADH (Anti Diuretic Hormone) secretion, diabetes insipidus)
statement: Which of the following clinical scenarios is specifically noted as a cause for the Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH (SIADH) besides malignant neoplasms?
options: Inadvertent removal of the parathyroid glands
Prolonged difficult delivery resulting in Sheehan Syndrome
Congenital deficiency of the transcription factor PIT1
Drugs that increase ADH secretion and central nervous system trauma
Surgical complication of total thyroidectomy
correctOption: Drugs that increase ADH secretion and central nervous system trauma
optionExplanations: Removal of parathyroid glands leads to hypocalcemia and tetany, not SIADH.
Sheehan syndrome results in ischemic necrosis and hypopituitarism (ADH deficiency), not SIADH (ADH excess).
PIT1 mutations lead to combined pituitary hormone deficiency (hypopituitarism), not excess ADH.
Beyond ectopic production, SIADH is frequently induced by medications or CNS insults (trauma/infections) that disrupt the regulation of ADH release.
Thyroidectomy complications usually involve recurrent laryngeal nerve damage or hypocalcemia, not SIADH.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1072 (Book Page): The most frequent causes of SIADH are the secretion of ectopic ADH by malignant neoplasms... drugs that increase ADH secretion, and a variety of central nervous system disorders, including infections and trauma.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
coreConcept: Histological hallmarks of Granulomatous Lobular Mastitis
statement: A biopsy reveals granulomatous inflammation restricted to the breast lobules, featuring granulomas with central lipid vacuoles surrounded by numerous neutrophils. This histological pattern is pathognomonic for which condition?
options: Tuberculous Mastitis
Lymphocytic Mastopathy
Granulomatous Lobular Mastitis
Sarcoidosis of the Breast
Duct Ectasia
correctOption: Granulomatous Lobular Mastitis
optionExplanations: Tuberculous mastitis typically presents with caseating granulomas and is not restricted to the lobular units, nor does it typically feature lipid-vacuole-associated neutrophilic centers.
Lymphocytic mastopathy is characterized by atrophic lobules and prominent lymphocytic infiltrates, but lacks granuloma formation.
The restriction of granulomas to the lobules and the unique 'suppurative granulomatous' appearance (neutrophils and lipid vacuoles) define this parous-only condition.
Sarcoidosis presents with non-caseating, 'naked' granulomas and typically lacks the neutrophilic micro-abscesses and lipid vacuoles seen in lobular mastitis.
Duct Ectasia shows periductal chronic inflammation and macrophages but does not show lobule-centric granulomas with neutrophils and lipid vacuoles.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1039 (Book Page): Granulomatous lobular mastitis is an uncommon disease that occurs only in parous women. The granulomas are closely associated with lobules and may contain lipid vacuoles surrounded by neutrophils.

category: Enumerate causes of hypo and hyperthyroidism along with levels of thyroid hormones
statement: Which laboratory measurement is considered the most sensitive screening test for the detection of both subclinical and overt primary hypothyroidism?
options: Free T3 index
Reverse T3 level
Thyroglobulin concentration
Total T4 level
Serum TSH level
correctOption: Serum TSH level
optionExplanations: Free T3 is less reliable for screening hypothyroidism because T3 levels often remain normal until the disease is very advanced.
Reverse T3 is a metabolically inactive isomer and is not used as a primary screening tool for thyroid function in clinical practice.
Thyroglobulin is used primarily as a tumor marker for following thyroid cancer recurrence, not as a screening tool for hypothyroidism.
Total T4 is affected by changes in binding proteins and is less sensitive than TSH for detecting early stage (subclinical) disease.
TSH is the most sensitive test because the pituitary amplifies even minor drops in T4 levels through the feedback loop, leading to early TSH elevation.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 1076 (Book Page): Measurement of the serum TSH level is the most sensitive screening test for this disorder [hypothyroidism].

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
statement: A physician is attempting to differentiate the cause of endogenous Cushing syndrome. Which biochemical result is specifically characteristic of a pituitary source (Cushing disease) as opposed to an ectopic ACTH source?
options: Reduction of urinary steroid secretion after high-dose dexamethasone
Failure of cortisol suppression with high-dose dexamethasone
Low serum ACTH with failure of cortisol suppression
Suppression of ACTH levels following low-dose dexamethasone
Significantly elevated serum ACTH with low cortisol output
correctOption: Reduction of urinary steroid secretion after high-dose dexamethasone
optionExplanations: The pituitary corticotroph adenoma retains partial sensitivity to feedback inhibition, meaning it will respond to a massive dose of dexamethasone by reducing ACTH and cortisol output.
Failure to suppress with high-dose dexamethasone is characteristic of ectopic ACTH production or an autonomous adrenal tumor, not a pituitary source.
Low serum ACTH with failed suppression is diagnostic of an ACTH-independent cause, such as a primary adrenal adenoma or carcinoma.
Low-dose dexamethasone typically fails to suppress ACTH in both pituitary and ectopic forms of Cushing syndrome; suppression requires a high dose in the pituitary variant.
ACTH-dependent Cushing's (pituitary or ectopic) always features high cortisol alongside the ACTH. Low cortisol output would imply adrenal insufficiency.
